explanation.summary: Paediatric trauma resuscitation cut-offs differ from paediatric sepsis: trauma limits crystalloid (10 mL/kg) and transitions early to blood components to avoid dilutional coagulopathy and clot disruption (damage-control resuscitation); sepsis allows higher crystalloid (20 mL/kg per bolus, up to 40-60 mL/kg). This is the key cut-off difference. Activate paediatric massive transfusion protocol early when haemorrhagic shock is suspected. Tranexamic acid 15 mg/kg IV (max 1 g) within 3 hours of injury is the AU paediatric trauma standard. Permissive hypotension targets SBP 5th centile for age while damage control is achieved.
key_points: Paeds trauma bolus: 10 mL/kg crystalloid then early blood
Paeds sepsis bolus: 20 mL/kg crystalloid x2-3
Paediatric MTP: PRBC + FFP + platelets in 1:1:1 ratio
TXA 15 mg/kg IV (max 1 g) within 3 hours of injury
Permissive hypotension: target SBP 5th centile for age until damage control
explanation.pearls: Tachycardia is the earliest paediatric shock sign; hypotension is late and often preterminal. Capillary refill >2 seconds + tachycardia is enough to start resuscitation; do not wait for hypotension.

sources.label: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol

options.rationale: Paediatric TRAUMA bolus is smaller than the sepsis bolus to limit dilutional coagulopathy and re-bleeding from clot disruption. The Royal Children's / NSW trauma protocol gives 10 mL/kg crystalloid then early blood, not 20 mL/kg crystalloid loading. Sepsis bolus (20 mL/kg) is the wrong physiology for active haemorrhage. Source: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol; PHANTOM.
source_refs: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol

options.rationale: AU paediatric trauma protocol (NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage; PHANTOM) recommends limited crystalloid (10 mL/kg) then early conversion to packed red cells (10 mL/kg) and FFP (10 mL/kg) in a 1:1 ratio after the first crystalloid bolus, plus activation of paediatric massive transfusion. Goal is permissive hypotension during damage-control resuscitation and avoidance of dilutional coagulopathy. Haemorrhage after trauma calls for limited crystalloid and early blood, unlike septic shock, where crystalloid boluses of 20 mL/kg are the first step. Source: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol; ANZSBT.
source_refs: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol

options.rationale: Adult ATLS recommendations no longer support 40 mL/kg aggressive crystalloid in trauma even in adults (dilutional coagulopathy + clot disruption + ARDS risk); paediatric protocols are even more restrictive. Source: ATLS-AU; NSW Pathway.
Crystalloid is first-line in AU paediatric trauma resuscitation (FEAST trial impact and AU practice). Colloid as primary trauma resus is not supported. Source: NSW Pathway.
source_refs: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol

options.rationale: Withholding all fluid in compensated shock is unsafe; the goal is balanced damage-control resuscitation with limited crystalloid then early blood, not no fluid. Source: NSW Pathway.
source_refs: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol

explanation.summary: Williams syndrome is a contiguous-gene deletion at 7q11.23. The distinguishing constellation is: elfin facies + supravalvular AS (or peripheral pulmonary stenosis) + idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia + characteristic friendly cocktail-party personality + mild ID. Elastin (ELN) deletion explains the vascular phenotype (arterial wall fragility and stenoses). Surveillance includes annual cardiology, calcium monitoring (restrict vitamin D in infancy), school-age neurocognitive assessment, and hearing/vision. Compared with other syndromes that share one or two features, the combination is recognisable from this set.
key_points: Williams = 7q11.23 deletion (includes ELN)
Cardinal cardiac lesion: supravalvular AS - ESM at right upper sternal edge to carotids
Idiopathic hypercalcaemia infancy: restrict vitamin D, avoid IV calcium
Characteristic friendly outgoing personality + mild ID
Diagnosis confirmed by FISH for ELN or microarray
explanation.pearls: Supravalvular AS murmurs are louder over the RIGHT upper sternal edge with carotid transmission (lesion above the valve), unlike valvular AS which is loudest at the LEFT upper sternal edge. This bedside cue points to Williams in an infant with dysmorphism.

options.rationale: Down syndrome facies are upslanting palpebral fissures, brachycephaly, single palmar crease, hypotonia - and the typical cardiac lesion is AVSD or VSD, not supravalvular AS. The described upturned nose and personality phenotype do not fit. Source: RCH CPG.

22q11.2 deletion has different facial features (long face, almond-shaped eyes, tubular nose, short philtrum) and typical conotruncal cardiac defects (tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, interrupted aortic arch), not supravalvular AS. Hypocalcaemia not hypercalcaemia. Source: RCH CPG.

Pattern recognition: elfin facies (prominent forehead, periorbital fullness, upturned nose, full cheeks, wide mouth, small chin), supravalvular aortic stenosis (right upper sternal edge ESM transmitted to carotids - NOT left as in valvular AS), idiopathic hypercalcaemia in infancy, mild intellectual disability with characteristically friendly disinhibited personality, mild generalised hypotonia. Williams syndrome from deletion of ~26 genes at 7q11.23 including ELN (elastin) which causes the vascular phenotype. FISH or microarray confirms. Cardiology surveillance for SVAS progression and PPS. Avoid IV calcium. Source: RCH CPG: Williams Syndrome; Australian Genetic Heart Disease Registry.

Noonan has distinct features (hypertelorism, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, webbed neck, broad chest with widely spaced nipples) and typically pulmonary VALVE stenosis, not supravalvular AS. Source: RCH CPG.
Marfan presents with tall stature, arachnodactyly, joint hypermobility, ectopia lentis - rarely in infancy with this presentation. Source: RCH CPG.

explanation.summary: Pure muscarinic antagonism produces a syndrome that copies sympathomimetic toxicity in vital signs and pupils but separates on exocrine and smooth muscle function. Sweat glands are anatomically sympathetic but pharmacologically cholinergic (muscarinic) so antimuscarinic toxicity produces anhidrosis with reflex flushing rather than diaphoresis. Gut and bladder are tonically parasympathetic so blockade produces ileus and retention rather than hyperactive bowel sounds. These four features separate the two at the bedside.
key_points: Anticholinergic = hot, dry, flushed, blind, mad, full bladder, gut stops
Sympathomimetic = hot, WET, agitated, normal bowel sounds
Sweat innervation is sympathetic anatomy but muscarinic pharmacology
QRS widening suggests sodium-channel blockade overlap (TCA, diphenhydramine)
Call NSW PIC 13 11 26 for paediatric ingestion advice
explanation.pearls: Common culprits in children: diphenhydramine, atropine eye drops, hyoscine patches, Datura/Brugmansia ingestion in older kids. Physostigmine (centrally acting AChE inhibitor) is reserved for severe agitated delirium; not first line in Australia.

options.rationale: Muscarinic antagonism blocks parasympathetic outflow to exocrine glands (anhidrosis with cutaneous vasodilation for heat loss producing flushing), gut smooth muscle (ileus), and detrusor (retention). Sympathomimetic toxidromes produce diaphoresis and active bowel sounds because cholinergic sweat innervation and gut activity are preserved.
Tachycardia and mydriasis occur in both toxidromes; hypertension is more sympathomimetic but does not separate the two in early anticholinergic toxicity. (Source: eTG).
Both toxidromes can produce hyperthermia and agitation; this is non-discriminating. (Source: Murray's Toxicology Handbook).
This is the cholinergic (muscarinic agonist) toxidrome, the opposite of what is described. (Source: eTG).
Describes opioid or sedative-hypnotic toxidrome, not a muscarinic mechanism. (Source: NSW PIC).

explanation.summary: The error is a unit conversion: the family used a 250 mg/5 mL strength instead of 120 mg/5 mL, giving each 6 mL dose 300 mg of paracetamol rather than the intended 144 mg. Five doses over 16 hours = 1500 mg = 159.6 mg/kg in a 9.4 kg child. Australian staggered-ingestion threshold is 150 mg/kg/24h - this child is above. The Rumack-Matthew nomogram applies only to single acute ingestions; for staggered ingestion, decision is based on cumulative dose, ALT, and paracetamol level interpreted in clinical context.
key_points: Staggered paracetamol ingestion: nomogram does NOT apply
AU threshold for treatment in children: >150 mg/kg/24h or >100 mg/kg/day for >2 days
Paracetamol suspension strengths in AU: 120 mg/5 mL (infant) and 250 mg/5 mL (older child) - common dispensing error
Empirical NAC then de-escalate based on bloods is the safe pathway
Australian Prescott 21-hour regimen: 150 mg/kg over 1 h, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h
explanation.pearls: Always confirm the strength of liquid paediatric paracetamol with the parent and look at the bottle. Two-strength availability in Australia is a recurring source of accidental supratherapeutic ingestion.

options.rationale: The calculation: 5 doses x 6 mL x 250 mg/5 mL = 5 x 300 mg = 1500 mg total over 16 hours = 1500 / 9.4 = 159.6 mg/kg. The Australian Poisons Information Centre threshold for repeated supratherapeutic ingestion in children is >150 mg/kg in any 24-hour period (or >100 mg/kg/day for >2 days). This child is above threshold; discharge is wrong. Source: Murray's Toxicology Handbook; NSW PIC.

Cumulative dose is 159.6 mg/kg in <24 hours (5 x 6 mL x 50 mg/mL = 1500 mg; 1500/9.4 = 159.6 mg/kg). This exceeds the 150 mg/kg/24h repeated supratherapeutic threshold. The nomogram does not apply to staggered ingestion; treatment decision is based on dose plus ALT/paracetamol level. NAC is started empirically while bloods are awaited. The 21-hour Prescott regimen (150-50-100 mg/kg) is current Australian standard. Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre; Murray's Toxicology Handbook; eTG Toxicology.
The nomogram is invalid in staggered or repeated supratherapeutic ingestion - it was derived for single acute ingestions only. Source: NSW PIC.
Charcoal is useful only within 1-2 hours of an acute single ingestion, not for staggered ingestion of a now-mostly-absorbed dose. Source: eTG Toxicology.

Delaying NAC past 8 hours from ingestion significantly increases hepatotoxicity risk. Empirical NAC should start now and be discontinued only if labs clearly fall below treatment threshold. Source: NSW PIC.

explanation.summary: Recent mRNA vaccination (24-72 h after second/booster dose, predominantly adolescent and young adult males) is the dominant cause of acute myopericarditis in this demographic since 2021. Managing it as ACS and dismissing the raised troponin are both errors. Standard Australian pathway is admit + telemetry + echo + repeat troponin + cardiology consult; cardiac MRI in 4-12 weeks confirms diagnosis. ATAGI maintains COVID-19 vaccine recommendations because benefit exceeds risk even when myocarditis is counted.
key_points: Post-mRNA-vaccine myocarditis: 1-5 days post 2nd/booster, peaks day 2-3
Male adolescents and young adults at highest relative risk
Always exclude reduced LVEF before outpatient management
Cardiac MRI at 4-12 weeks confirms scar/oedema pattern
ATAGI recommends a temporary 6-12 month pause on further mRNA doses in confirmed cases
explanation.pearls: Differentiating cause-and-effect from confound is a recurring exam skill: post-transfusion bilirubin rise, post-vaccine serology positives, post-surgery troponin rise, post-statin CK rise. Always state the alternative diagnoses you excluded.

options.rationale: While post-mRNA-vaccine myocarditis is the leading differential, any troponin rise warrants echocardiography and cardiology review before discharge to exclude reduced LVEF or wall-motion abnormality. Source: NSW Health post-vaccine myocarditis guidance.

Post-mRNA vaccine myocarditis is the most likely cause (young male, 1-5 days post second/booster dose, chest pain with troponin rise, normal pre-vaccine cardiac state). Confound elimination: ECG and FH excluded primary cardiomyopathy and ischaemic causes. Standard pathway is admission with telemetry, echo, repeat troponin, paediatric cardiology review. Course is usually self-limiting with NSAIDs or low-dose colchicine but ATAGI/NSW Health pathway is mandatory. Source: NSW Health Post-Vaccine Myocarditis Pathway; ATAGI Clinical Recommendations.
ACS in a 16-year-old with no risk factors and a normal ECG is highly unlikely; aspirin loading is inappropriate. Source: eTG Cardiovascular.

CTCA is not first-line in adolescent myocarditis workup; echocardiography is. Cardiac MRI is the gold standard for post-vaccine myocarditis confirmation but is not the immediate next step in ED. Source: NSW Health Pathway.

Outpatient deferral fails to exclude active myocarditis in the acute window when echocardiographic findings (segmental wall-motion abnormality, mild LVEF reduction) determine inpatient versus outpatient management. Source: NSW Health Pathway.

explanation.summary: STEC-HUS (formerly D+HUS) is the dominant paediatric cause of acute kidney injury in Australia in children under 5. Triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, AKI - usually 5-10 days after a prodrome of bloody diarrhoea. Mechanism: Shiga toxin from E. coli O157 (and other STEC strains) binds Gb3 glycosphingolipid on glomerular endothelium → endothelial swelling → microthrombi → mechanical RBC shear and platelet consumption. Antibiotics are contraindicated because Shiga toxin release is upregulated by bacterial stress response (multiple RCT-level signals of harm). Supportive care, blood transfusion when needed, dialysis if oligoanuric or hyperkalaemic. Notifiable to NSW Health public health unit.
key_points: Triad: MAHA + thrombocytopaenia + AKI after bloody diarrhoea prodrome
STEC sources: unpasteurised dairy, ground beef, petting farms, contaminated water
Antibiotics CONTRAINDICATED in suspected STEC-HUS
NSAIDs, antimotility agents, platelet transfusion all contraindicated
Notifiable disease - inform NSW Health public health unit
explanation.pearls: Atypical HUS (complement-mediated) presents without diarrhoea prodrome and is treated with eculizumab; STEC-HUS is supportive only. Always ask about farm visits, raw milk, and recent ground-beef consumption in paediatric AKI workup.

options.rationale: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia, not the microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + AKI triad described. Schistocytes on film exclude ITP. Source: RCH CPG.

Pattern: bloody diarrhoea + microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, low haptoglobin, raised LDH, raised unconjugated bilirubin, Coombs negative) + thrombocytopaenia + AKI = classic STEC-HUS. Non-obvious cue is unpasteurised milk + calf contact at a farm-stay (STEC O157 reservoirs include cattle and unpasteurised dairy in Australia; multiple outbreaks). CONTRAINDICATED: empirical antibiotics (associated with increased Shiga toxin release and worsened HUS in some studies), antimotility agents, NSAIDs, platelet transfusion (paradoxical worsening). Management is supportive (careful IV fluids, monitoring for dialysis indication, blood transfusion if Hb critically low, plasma exchange in atypical HUS only). Eculizumab for atypical HUS, not STEC-HUS. Source: RCH CPG: HUS; eTG Paediatrics; CDNA STEC SoNG.
Coagulation profile is normal (INR/aPTT normal), excluding DIC. WCC is mildly elevated but no blast cells. Source: RCH CPG.

Post-infectious GN typically presents with hypertension, oedema, haematuria, mild proteinuria - not the microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia pattern. ACE inhibitor in AKI worsens renal function. Source: RCH CPG.
Coombs is NEGATIVE - rules out warm or cold AIHA. Pattern is microangiopathic (schistocytes, MAHA), not autoimmune. Source: RCH CPG.

explanation.summary: The current Australian paediatric sepsis pathway sets these cut-offs: bolus volume 10-20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid over 5-10 minutes with reassessment after each, antibiotic within 60 minutes, approximately 40 mL/kg of fluid before considering inotropes. For suspected meningococcaemia (non-blanching petechial rash, fever, unimmunised, shock features), the Australian Medicines Handbook ceftriaxone dose is 100 mg/kg (maximum 4 g) to ensure meningeal penetration; the 50 mg/kg dose is for non-meningitic sepsis. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock until cardiovascular stability is restored. Public health notification within 24 hours for meningococcal disease.
key_points: Bolus 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid over 5-10 minutes, reassess after each
Approximately 40 mL/kg before escalating to inotropes
Antibiotic within 60 minutes of sepsis recognition
Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) for suspected meningococcaemia or meningitis per AMH
Lactate above 4 plus tachycardia plus mottled extremities meets severe sepsis criteria
explanation.pearls: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock until cardiovascular stability is restored. Empirical antibiotics first; lumbar puncture later. Notify the public health unit for confirmed or suspected meningococcal disease.

options.rationale: Antibiotics must be given within the first hour of sepsis recognition and lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock until cardiovascular stability is restored. (Source: NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)

The current Australian paediatric sepsis approach uses 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid boluses with reassessment after each, given concerns from FEAST and subsequent NSW Health updates. Suspected meningococcaemia requires the meningitis-dose of ceftriaxone, which the Australian Medicines Handbook lists as 100 mg/kg (maximum 4 g) per dose. Inotropes (peripheral adrenaline 0.05-0.3 mcg/kg/min) are added after approximately 40 mL/kg of fluid without response. (Source: NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway; AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

Isotonic crystalloid (not colloid) is first-line in paediatric sepsis, given as 10-20 mL/kg boluses with reassessment after each. Vancomycin plus meropenem is not first-line for community-acquired sepsis without specific resistance risk. (Source: NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)

Fluid resuscitation precedes inotropes in compensated paediatric septic shock; inotropes are added after approximately 40 mL/kg of fluid without response. (Source: NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)

Bolus over 60 minutes is too slow for resuscitation (target 5-10 minutes); lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock until stability is restored. Benzylpenicillin alone is too narrow for empirical paediatric septic shock. (Source: NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway; eTG Paediatrics)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is supportive care only. Admission criteria are SpO2 persistently below 90% (RCH target), feeds less than half normal volume, severe work of breathing, apnoea or social risk. Nasogastric tube feeds at two thirds maintenance are preferred over IV fluids when tolerated. High-flow nasal cannula is a rescue therapy when low-flow oxygen and feeding support fail to maintain saturations or normalise work of breathing.
key_points: Bronchiolitis is supportive: oxygen if SpO2 below 90% (RCH target), feeding support if intake under half
Bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics not routinely indicated
Nasogastric feeds at two thirds maintenance preferred to IV fluids
High-flow nasal cannula is rescue therapy, not first line
explanation.pearls: Apnoea risk is highest in infants under 6 weeks corrected age or with prematurity; admit for observation regardless of work of breathing.

options.rationale: Bronchodilators and corticosteroids have no proven benefit in classic viral bronchiolitis under 12 months and are not recommended; supportive feeding and oxygen are the mainstays. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Sustained SpO2 below 90% (RCH target), feeding less than half normal volume, and increased work of breathing meet admission criteria; nasogastric or intravenous hydration plus titrated oxygen is the supportive standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Hypoxia at rest below 92 percent, tachypnoea above 60 and reduced oral intake all argue against discharge; safety-net advice does not substitute for inpatient support. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
High-flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen or persistent severe distress; routine first-line use does not change outcomes and overtreats. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

RSV-positive bronchiolitis with no toxic features does not require sepsis workup or empirical antibiotics; secondary bacterial pneumonia would warrant focal findings and rising inflammatory markers. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice thresholds depend on postnatal age in hours, gestation and risk factors such as haemolysis or sepsis. DAT-positive ABO incompatibility places the infant in the high-risk category. RCH guidance uses age-in-hours nomograms; for a term infant at 60 hours, total bilirubin around 290 micromol/L crosses the phototherapy threshold. Intensive phototherapy is started and bilirubin is rechecked at 4 to 6 hours. IVIG is reserved for impending exchange.
key_points: Phototherapy thresholds depend on age in hours, gestation and risk factors
DAT-positive haemolysis lowers the threshold for treatment
Continue breastfeeding during phototherapy
IVIG is adjunct, not first line
explanation.pearls: Exchange transfusion threshold at 60 hours in a term infant without high risk factors is above 450 micromol/L; bilirubin doubling above this needs urgent NICU transfer.

options.rationale: DAT-positive ABO incompatibility with bilirubin 290 micromol/L at 60 hours crosses standard phototherapy thresholds; deferring 24 hours risks reaching exchange transfusion levels. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in neonates)

Withholding breastfeeding is not first line; haemolytic jaundice requires phototherapy not formula substitution, and breastfeeding should be supported throughout. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in neonates)

Bilirubin 290 micromol/L at 60 hours of age with DAT-positive haemolysis crosses the RCH phototherapy threshold for a term infant; intensive phototherapy is initiated and bilirubin rechecked at 4 to 6 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in neonates)
Exchange transfusion thresholds at 60 hours are above 450 micromol/L for a term low-risk neonate; intensive phototherapy is tried first and reassessed. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in neonates)

IVIG is reserved as adjunct for haemolytic disease when bilirubin is rising despite intensive phototherapy or approaches exchange threshold; it does not replace initial phototherapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in neonates)

explanation.summary: Febrile infants under 3 months have a higher risk of occult invasive bacterial infection including meningitis even when clinically well-appearing. Standard Australian practice is to admit, obtain blood, urine (suprapubic aspirate or catheter) and CSF cultures, and start empirical antibiotics covering Listeria monocytogenes (benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin), group B Streptococcus and gram-negative organisms (gentamicin plus a third-generation cephalosporin). De-escalation occurs at 36 to 48 hours based on cultures and clinical course.
key_points: Febrile infants under 3 months: full septic workup including LP
Empirical antibiotics cover Listeria, GBS and gram-negatives
Bag urine is unreliable below 12 months
De-escalate at 36 to 48 hours based on cultures
explanation.pearls: Cefotaxime is preferred over ceftriaxone in neonates under 28 days due to risk of bilirubin displacement and biliary sludge; switch to ceftriaxone after 28 days.

options.rationale: Infants under 3 months with temperature 38 or above require admission and full septic workup regardless of clinical appearance; outpatient management is not standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

Empirical antibiotics are mandatory in febrile infants under 3 months pending culture results, regardless of clinical wellness, because of bacteraemia and meningitis risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)
Flucloxacillin monotherapy does not cover Listeria or Escherichia coli, the dominant causes in this age group; broader empirical cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Febrile infant 1 to 3 months requires full septic workup including lumbar puncture and immediate empirical cover for invasive bacterial infection including Listeria, group B Streptococcus and gram negatives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Bag-collected urine is unreliable for diagnosis under 12 months due to contamination; oral antibiotics are inadequate for suspected invasive sepsis in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management balances correction of dehydration and acidosis with minimisation of cerebral oedema risk. Initial fluid resuscitation is conservative: 10 mL/kg of isotonic saline over 30 to 60 minutes only if signs of shock, with reassessment. Deficit replacement is calculated as 5 to 10 percent of body weight and given evenly over 48 hours. Insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour starts 1 hour after fluid commencement. Bicarbonate is avoided. Potassium is added to maintenance fluid once urine output is established.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg isotonic saline only if shocked
Deficit replaced evenly over 48 hours
Insulin 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour starts 1 hour after fluid
Bicarbonate contraindicated in routine DKA
explanation.pearls: Cerebral oedema warning signs include headache, declining GCS, bradycardia and pupillary changes; treat with 2.7% saline 5 mL/kg or mannitol 1 g/kg over 15 minutes.

options.rationale: Insulin is started 1 hour after fluid resuscitation in paediatric DKA to reduce cerebral oedema risk; rapid concurrent infusion increases osmolar shift. (Source: ISPAD/APEG DKA Guidelines)
Hypotonic fluid for resuscitation increases cerebral oedema risk; long-acting subcutaneous insulin during active DKA is not first line and bypasses titration. (Source: ISPAD/APEG DKA Guidelines)
Bicarbonate is contraindicated in routine paediatric DKA: it is associated with increased cerebral oedema risk and worsens intracellular acidosis. (Source: ISPAD/APEG DKA Guidelines)

Large rapid boluses without re-assessment are associated with cerebral oedema; standard is 10 mL/kg over 30 to 60 minutes only if shocked, with frequent re-assessment. (Source: ISPAD/APEG DKA Guidelines)

Cautious 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline addresses perfusion, then ongoing deficit replacement is calculated and given over 48 hours; insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour starts 1 hour after fluid resuscitation. (Source: ISPAD/APEG DKA Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe paediatric asthma escalation follows a stepped pathway: oxygen, burst-dose salbutamol with ipratropium and oral or IV steroid in the first hour. If severity persists, IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes is the standard next step. Aminophylline and IV salbutamol are reserved for ICU-level escalation. Intubation is for exhaustion, hypercapnia or arrest; ketamine RSI minimises bronchoconstriction.
key_points: First hour: oxygen, burst salbutamol/ipratropium, systemic steroid
IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg is the standard second step
Aminophylline and IV salbutamol are ICU escalation
Intubation for exhaustion, rising pCO2 or arrest
explanation.pearls: A normal or rising pCO2 in severe asthma is a sign of failing respiratory effort and impending arrest; do not be reassured by a 'normal' venous gas.

options.rationale: After first-hour burst-dose salbutamol, ipratropium and systemic steroid have failed, IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes is the next step in severe paediatric asthma before further escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)
Aminophylline is reserved for failure of magnesium and is used in ICU due to narrow therapeutic window; it is not the next step in standard escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

Subcutaneous adrenaline is used for anaphylaxis, not pure asthma exacerbations; routine use risks tachyarrhythmia without addressing bronchospasm better than nebulised beta-agonist. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

Intubation is reserved for exhaustion, hypercapnia or imminent arrest in severe asthma; the patient is still alert with normocapnia and IV magnesium has not been trialled. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)
Ceasing bronchodilators during active severe asthma is unsafe; high-flow nasal cannula is adjunctive support, not a substitute for pharmacological escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when fever 5 days or more occurs with fewer than 4 classic features but coronary artery abnormality on echocardiography (Z score 2.5 or above) OR 3 or more supportive lab criteria. Supportive labs include CRP 30 or above, ESR 40 or above, anaemia for age, platelets 450 x10^9/L or above after day 7, albumin 30 g/L or below, ALT raised, and sterile pyuria. First-line treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours plus high-dose aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg per day in divided doses until afebrile for 48 hours, then low-dose aspirin. Steroids are added in Kobayashi-positive high-risk cases.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: 5 days fever + coronary echo OR 3 supportive labs
First-line: IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin
Steroids adjunctive in Kobayashi-positive cases
Infliximab reserved for IVIG-refractory disease
explanation.pearls: Untreated coronary aneurysm rate is 25 percent; IVIG within 10 days of fever onset reduces this to under 5 percent.

options.rationale: Coronary involvement on echocardiography with fever 5 days or more and supportive laboratory criteria confirms incomplete Kawasaki; delaying immunoglobulin while awaiting cultures risks aneurysm progression. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Coronary artery Z score above 2.5 plus fever 5 days or more with supportive labs (CRP raised, albumin low, ALT raised, platelets high, sterile pyuria) meets American Heart Association incomplete Kawasaki criteria; IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin is first-line. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement)
Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first line; the Kobayashi protocol adds steroid to IVIG in high-risk patients but does not replace it. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement)
Infliximab is reserved for IVIG-refractory Kawasaki disease; it is not first-line for newly diagnosed cases with coronary involvement. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement)

Low-dose aspirin alone without IVIG fails to reduce coronary aneurysm risk; the 25 percent untreated aneurysm rate drops to under 5 percent with IVIG plus aspirin. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement)

explanation.summary: Asthma control in children aged 6 to 11 is assessed over the previous 4 weeks: daytime symptoms more than twice a week, reliever use more than twice a week, any nocturnal waking, or any activity limitation indicates poor control. Step-up from low-dose ICS in this age group is to medium-dose ICS as the preferred option, with montelukast or LABA combinations reserved for failure of medium-dose ICS. Technique, adherence, trigger exposure and alternative diagnoses must be checked at every step.
key_points: Children 6 to 11 step-up: low-dose ICS to medium-dose ICS first
ICS/LABA combination reserved for failure of medium-dose ICS in this age group
Reassess control, technique, adherence and triggers at every step
Document a written action plan at every escalation
explanation.pearls: Budesonide 200 micrograms twice daily is the medium-dose threshold for children 6 to 11; fluticasone propionate equivalent is 200 micrograms twice daily.

options.rationale: Poor control on low-dose ICS in a child aged 6 to 11 with good technique warrants step-up to medium-dose ICS as the preferred next step before combination therapy. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)
Montelukast is an add-on option but is less effective than increasing inhaled corticosteroid dose or adding a long-acting beta-agonist in this age group. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

Combination ICS/LABA is reserved for children aged 6 to 11 only after medium-dose ICS has failed; jumping directly from low-dose ICS to ICS/LABA is not the recommended step. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

Maintenance oral corticosteroids carry growth and adrenal suppression risk and are reserved for severe refractory asthma after specialist review, not for routine step-up. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

Three to four reliever uses weekly, nocturnal cough and a recent steroid-requiring exacerbation define poorly controlled asthma; continuing without escalation accepts ongoing morbidity. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

explanation.summary: Iron-deficiency anaemia in toddlers most commonly reflects excess cow's milk intake (which inhibits iron absorption and causes occult GI blood loss) and inadequate iron-rich solids. Workup shows microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin and transferrin saturation. First-line management is dietary advice (cow's milk under 500 mL/day, iron-rich solids including red meat or fortified cereals) plus oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day. Reassess Hb at 4 to 6 weeks; expect a 10 g/L rise.
key_points: Toddler iron deficiency: limit cow's milk to under 500 mL/day
Oral ferrous sulfate 3 to 6 mg elemental iron/kg/day first line
Expect 10 g/L Hb rise at 4 weeks of treatment
Defer haemoglobin electrophoresis until iron-replete
explanation.pearls: Continue oral iron for 3 months after Hb normalises to replete stores; ferritin should rise above 30 microg/L.

options.rationale: Iron-deficiency anaemia in a toddler with excess cow's milk intake requires both dietary modification and elemental iron at 3 to 6 mg/kg/day; recheck FBC in 4 to 6 weeks to confirm response. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

Classic microcytic hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin and risk factors for iron deficiency does not require bone marrow examination; empirical iron with diet change and recheck is first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)
Intravenous iron is reserved for malabsorption, intolerance or non-adherence to oral iron after a trial; first-line is oral iron with dietary advice. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)
Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia with haemodynamic compromise or Hb under 60 to 70 g/L in a sick child; this stable toddler does not meet criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

Haemoglobin electrophoresis is unreliable during iron deficiency and is deferred until iron repletion; ferritin under 12 with low transferrin saturation is diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Pertussis in infants under 6 months carries the highest mortality, often from apnoea or secondary pneumonia. Diagnosis is by nasopharyngeal PCR. Macrolides (azithromycin preferred under 1 month) reduce infectivity and shorten symptoms if started within 3 weeks of cough onset. Chemoprophylaxis with azithromycin is offered to all close household contacts regardless of vaccination, ideally within 14 to 21 days of first exposure, because waning vaccine immunity allows transmission even in vaccinated family members. Notification to public health is mandatory.
key_points: Pertussis PCR diagnosis; azithromycin first line under 1 month
All household contacts get azithromycin prophylaxis regardless of vaccination
Treatment within 21 days of cough reduces transmission
Notifiable disease; public health unit contact required
explanation.pearls: Azithromycin in neonates carries a small risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; counsel parents about projectile vomiting at 3 to 5 weeks of life.

options.rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is contraindicated under 2 months due to kernicterus risk; symptom-based prophylaxis misses the asymptomatic infectious period. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
Amoxicillin has no role in pertussis; macrolides are first-line, and chemoprophylaxis extends to all close household contacts not just infants. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Antibiotics reduce infectivity even when started late and prevent ongoing transmission; vaccination alone is too slow to protect contacts within the incubation window. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Azithromycin is first-line for pertussis treatment under 1 month and chemoprophylaxis is offered to all household contacts regardless of vaccination because vaccine effectiveness wanes and infants are at highest mortality risk. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Treating only the infant misses the household reservoir and waiting for sibling testing delays prophylaxis beyond the effective window of 21 days from index exposure. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Intussusception typically presents in infants 3 months to 3 years with episodic crying, drawing up of legs, bile-stained vomiting and red-currant-jelly stool late in the course. Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice, showing the target or doughnut sign. Pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction succeeds in 80 to 95 percent of stable cases without peritonitis or perforation. Surgical management is reserved for failed reduction, signs of perforation, or shock. Recurrence after enema is 10 percent and usually occurs within 48 hours.
key_points: Ultrasound target sign confirms diagnosis
Air or contrast enema is first-line reduction in stable child
Surgery for failed enema, perforation or shock
Recurrence rate 10 percent, mostly within 48 hours
explanation.pearls: A pathological lead point (Meckel diverticulum, Peyer patch hypertrophy, lymphoma) is more likely in children over 2 years or with recurrence and warrants further imaging.

options.rationale: Confirmed intussusception in a stable child without peritonitis or perforation is reduced by air or contrast enema with surgical standby; success rate is around 80 to 95 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Antibiotics alone do not reduce intussusception; delaying enema risks bowel ischaemia, perforation and the need for surgical resection. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Surgical reduction is reserved for failure of pneumatic or hydrostatic reduction, peritonitis, perforation or shock; first attempt should be radiological in stable children. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Untreated intussusception progresses to ischaemia and perforation within hours; discharge of a confirmed case is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Bowel rest does not reduce intussusception; mechanical reduction by enema is required and delay increases bowel-resection risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: The RCH Melbourne UTI CPG states most children do not require further imaging after a first UTI. A renal tract ultrasound during admission is appropriate for infants under 6 months without antenatal scans, for recurrent UTI, or when atypical features are present. The DMSA-at-4-to-6-months pathway is a NICE NG224 recommendation that RCH has not adopted. MCUG is reserved for recurrent UTI, ultrasound dilatation, or atypical features.
key_points: RCH Melbourne: no routine imaging after first typical UTI once acute renal tract ultrasound is normal or shows non-progressive minor change
DMSA at 4 to 6 months is a NICE construct, not part of the RCH cascade
MCUG reserved for recurrent UTI or abnormal ultrasound
Long-term prophylaxis only for proven high-grade reflux or recurrent UTI
explanation.pearls: An atypical UTI per RCH is one with non-E. coli organism, septicaemia, raised creatinine, poor urine flow, abdominal mass, or failure to respond within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics.

options.rationale: MR urography is a second-line modality for selected complex anomalies and is not part of the RCH Melbourne post-UTI pathway after a typical first febrile UTI. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

RCH Melbourne does not recommend routine MCUG after a first UTI; MCUG is reserved for recurrent UTI, dilatation on ultrasound, or atypical features. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Would be correct only when following NICE NG224 rather than the local RCH Melbourne pathway; the RCH CPG does not include routine DMSA in the post-UTI imaging cascade. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

The RCH Melbourne CPG states that most children do not require further imaging after a first UTI once an acute renal tract ultrasound has excluded obstruction and significant dilatation; mild non-progressive pelvis change alone does not warrant DMSA or MCUG. Parents are counselled to present promptly for any future febrile illness. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Long-term prophylaxis is reserved for proven high-grade reflux or recurrent UTI; first UTI without proven reflux is not an RCH-recommended indication. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: ANZCOR guidance for foreign body airway obstruction depends on age and cough effectiveness. Effective cough (forceful, vocalising, conscious): encourage cough and observe. Ineffective cough (silent, stridor, cyanosis, decreasing consciousness) in conscious patient: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts in infants under 1 year; 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts in children over 1 year, with abdominal thrusts as second-line in older children. Unconscious patient: start CPR with chest compressions and inspect the airway during ventilation. Blind finger sweeps are contraindicated.
key_points: Effective cough: encourage and observe
Ineffective cough conscious: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts
Abdominal thrusts not used under 1 year
Unconscious: commence CPR and inspect airway during ventilation
explanation.pearls: After successful expulsion, all children with peanut or similar high-risk aspiration require bronchoscopy assessment because residual fragments cause delayed pneumonitis.

options.rationale: Abdominal thrusts are reserved for children over 1 year as a second-line manoeuvre after back blows fail; primary use in a young toddler risks abdominal organ injury. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

Encouragement only applies when the cough is effective and the child can vocalise; an ineffective cough with stridor and desaturation requires immediate airway clearance manoeuvres. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)
Blind finger sweeps are contraindicated because they can push the object deeper or cause oedema; only remove if visible and easily graspable. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

Conscious infant or toddler with ineffective cough and airway obstruction is managed by alternating 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts are not used under 1 year due to liver injury risk and are second-line in older children. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation with compressions is started only after the child loses consciousness from obstruction; in a conscious child, airway-clearance manoeuvres are first. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with overflow soiling requires a two-phase approach: disimpaction followed by maintenance. Disimpaction uses high-dose oral macrogol (1 to 1.5 g/kg/day for 3 to 7 days) until clear stools; maintenance uses lower-dose daily macrogol titrated to one soft stool daily. A behavioural toilet-sitting program (after meals for 5 to 10 minutes) and dietary advice (fibre, fluids) accompany medication. Red flags warranting further workup include delayed meconium passage, failure to thrive, abdominal distension, abnormal neurological findings or sacral dimple.
key_points: Disimpaction before maintenance to stop overflow
Macrogol 1 to 1.5 g/kg/day for disimpaction, lower dose for maintenance
Behavioural toilet program after meals essential
Maintenance for at least 6 months and weaned slowly
explanation.pearls: Maintenance laxatives are often required for many months; relapse rates exceed 50 percent if weaned within 6 months of symptom resolution.

options.rationale: Docusate alone is insufficient and skipping disimpaction means overflow soiling continues; without clearing the impacted mass, laxative titration fails. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Functional constipation with overflow soiling requires disimpaction first (high-dose macrogol over 3 to 7 days) followed by maintenance laxative plus a toilet-sitting program; treating the maintenance phase without disimpaction prolongs soiling. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Hirschsprung disease typically presents with delayed meconium passage and failure to thrive; a toilet-trained 6-year-old with classic functional pattern does not require biopsy as a first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Phosphate enemas carry risks of hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia in children and are not first-line; oral macrogol is safer and equally effective for disimpaction. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Behavioural therapy alone fails when an impacted rectal mass causes ongoing overflow; pharmacological disimpaction and maintenance are needed together with the behavioural program. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Autism is a clinical diagnosis based on persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour or interests across multiple settings. Red flags by age 2 years include no two-word phrases, no joint attention, no pointing to show, lack of pretend play, lack of social reciprocity. Hearing assessment is mandatory to exclude hearing loss as a cause of language delay. Multidisciplinary diagnostic assessment, NDIS application and evidence-based early intervention (speech, OT, behavioural) should commence in parallel rather than sequentially.
key_points: Multidisciplinary assessment is gold standard for diagnosis
Hearing assessment mandatory to exclude hearing loss
Early intervention before age 5 has strongest evidence
NDIS funding from diagnosis supports intervention access
explanation.pearls: Under 9 years, NDIS access is available via the early childhood approach without a formal diagnosis if developmental delay is documented, accelerating intervention access.

sources.label: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

options.rationale: Isolated speech therapy without diagnostic assessment misses the broader social communication and restricted-repetitive behaviour phenotype and delays NDIS access. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment)
source_refs: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

options.rationale: Watchful waiting beyond 2 years for language delay with social communication concerns delays diagnosis and access to NDIS-funded early intervention which has the strongest evidence under 5 years of age. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment)
source_refs: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

options.rationale: Dietary interventions including omega-3 have no robust evidence for autism management and delay access to evidence-based behavioural therapy. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment)
source_refs: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

options.rationale: Genetic testing has a role in autism workup but is not the gatekeeper; multidisciplinary assessment and early intervention should commence in parallel, not wait for results. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment)
source_refs: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

options.rationale: Persistent receptive and expressive language delay with social communication concerns warrants audiology to exclude hearing loss and parallel referral for multidisciplinary autism assessment plus early intervention; delaying referral wastes the critical intervention window. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment)
source_refs: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

explanation.summary: Cyanotic breath-holding spells are reflex anoxic episodes triggered by frustration, anger or pain in toddlers aged 6 months to 4 years. The child cries, holds breath in expiration, becomes cyanotic and may lose consciousness for under 60 seconds with rapid full recovery. Distinguishing features from seizures include the consistent emotional trigger, absence of post-ictal phase and absence of stereotyped jerking. Iron deficiency anaemia worsens frequency, so checking ferritin is reasonable; supplementation only helps when deficiency is present. Reassurance with simple first-aid (lay child on side, avoid mouth interference, reinforce that spells are not harmful) is the cornerstone.
key_points: Reflex syncope triggered by emotion, not epilepsy
Check ferritin; treat only if deficient
EEG reserved for atypical features
Cardiac workup only if exertional trigger or family sudden death
explanation.pearls: Resolution by age 5 years occurs in over 90 percent; persistence beyond 6 years or new exertional triggers warrant cardiology review for long QT or catecholaminergic polymorphic VT.

options.rationale: Cyanotic breath-holding spells are a benign reflex phenomenon peaking at 6 to 18 months with normal investigations; reassurance and basic safety advice are the primary management. (Source: RCH CPG: Apparent life-threatening event)

Anticonvulsants are not indicated for breath-holding spells which are reflex syncope not epileptic seizures; sodium valproate carries teratogenic and hepatotoxic risks unwarranted here. (Source: RCH CPG: Apparent life-threatening event)

EEG is reserved for episodes with seizure features (jerking, prolonged unresponsiveness, post-ictal phase) which are absent here; routine EEG yields false positives in normal toddlers. (Source: RCH CPG: Apparent life-threatening event)

Cardiac referral is reserved for syncope with exertional or postural triggers, abnormal ECG or family history of sudden death; reflex triggers with normal ECG do not warrant escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Apparent life-threatening event)

Iron supplementation reduces spell frequency only when iron deficiency is present; this child has normal ferritin and supplementation risks constipation without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Apparent life-threatening event)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in children is largely viral; bacterial cases involve S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis. Immediate antibiotics in Australia are reserved for under 6 months, under 2 years with bilateral disease, severe systemic features (T 39 or above, severe pain, vomiting), suppurative complications, or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children at higher risk of complications. Otherwise watchful waiting 48 hours with safety-netting. Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg 8-hourly for 5 days is first-line. Augmentin reserved for treatment failure or recurrent. Analgesia is mandatory regardless of antibiotic decision.
key_points: Watchful wait OR immediate amoxicillin based on age, severity, risk group
Under 2 with bilateral disease = treat immediately
Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg 8-hourly for 5 days
Analgesia regardless of antibiotic decision
explanation.pearls: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children with acute otitis media have an 8-10 times higher rate of progression to chronic suppurative otitis media and hearing loss, so eTG recommends immediate antibiotic treatment for all acute OM in this population regardless of age or severity.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is appropriate for non-severe unilateral otitis media in children over 2 years with mild symptoms; under 2 years with bilateral disease meets the threshold for immediate antibiotics. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media)
Topical antibiotics are for otitis externa or chronic discharging ears, not acute otitis media with intact tympanic membrane; oral amoxicillin is first-line. (Source: RCH CPG)

AU guidelines (RCH, eTG) recommend immediate oral amoxicillin in children under 2 years with bilateral acute otitis media, severe symptoms (severe pain, T 39 or above, vomiting), or systemic features. Dose 30 mg/kg 8-hourly for 5 days. Analgesia is essential. (Source: RCH CPG; eTG)
Cefuroxime is reserved for amoxicillin failure or non-severe penicillin allergy; amoxicillin is first-line. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)
Tympanostomy referral is for recurrent (3 or more in 6 months or 4 or more in 12 months) or chronic OM with effusion lasting over 3 months, not a single acute episode. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in children under 12 months with viral lower respiratory tract symptoms. RSV is the commonest cause (60-70 percent). Management is supportive: gentle nasal saline, minimal handling, oxygen if SpO2 below 90% (RCH target), fluids via NG or IV if oral intake below 50 percent normal, and apnoea monitoring in younger infants. Salbutamol, corticosteroids, adrenaline, hypertonic saline, and antibiotics are NOT routinely indicated. Escalation criteria: persistent hypoxia despite oxygen, exhaustion, recurrent apnoeas, severe distress.
key_points: Supportive care only - oxygen, feeds, observation
No salbutamol, no steroids, no adrenaline routinely
Admission if SpO2 below 92, feeds below 50 percent, apnoeas, severe distress
Antibiotics only if secondary bacterial infection
explanation.pearls: Apnoeas occur most commonly in infants under 6 weeks or preterm with bronchiolitis and may be the presenting feature even before respiratory distress is severe; cardiopulmonary monitoring is mandatory in this group regardless of initial SpO2.

options.rationale: Salbutamol is not effective in children under 12 months with bronchiolitis (no smooth muscle to act on, no benefit shown in trials); RCH recommends against routine use. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Bronchiolitis in infants is a supportive management diagnosis. RCH CPG recommends nasal saline, oxygen if SpO2 below 90% (RCH target), NG or IV fluids if oral intake below 50 percent, and no routine salbutamol, steroids, adrenaline or antibiotics. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
HFNC is escalation for moderate-severe distress not maintained on standard low-flow; not routine first-line. (Source: RCH CPG)
Corticosteroids are not effective in bronchiolitis (no benefit shown in multiple large RCTs). (Source: RCH CPG; Cochrane)
Nebulised adrenaline shows no benefit in routine bronchiolitis and may cause rebound; reserved for severe cases with failure of supportive measures. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Infant dyschezia and the widely spaced soft stools of an established breastfed infant are both normal developmental patterns that are frequently mislabelled as constipation. Constipation is defined by the consistency and the difficulty of the stool, not by its frequency: a soft stool passed after straining, in a thriving infant who passed meconium within 48 hours and has a normal abdomen, anus and spine, needs no laxative. The straining reflects the infant learning to coordinate abdominal effort with pelvic floor relaxation and settles by three to four months. Treating it with macrogol exposes the infant to an unnecessary medicine and teaches the family that normal variation is disease. Red flags that change this are delayed meconium, hard or pellet stools, blood, abdominal distension, vomiting, faltering growth or an abnormal spine or anus. In context, functional constipation is common from the toddler years onwards but genuinely uncommon in an exclusively breastfed infant, so the first job is to decide whether there is a problem at all.
key_points: Constipation is about stool consistency and difficulty, not frequency.
Breastfed infants can normally stool once a week from about six weeks.
Meconium within 48 hours and normal growth argue strongly against organic disease.
Red flags include delayed meconium, distension, vomiting and faltering growth.
explanation.pearls: The question to ask is what the stool looks like when it finally arrives: a large soft stool after straining is dyschezia, while a hard pellet stool is constipation even if it comes daily.

options.rationale: Breastfed infants beyond the first month may stool once a week; provided the stool is soft, growth is tracking and meconium passed within 48 hours, no treatment is needed and reassurance with clear return advice is the management. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Constipation)
Macrogol is the treatment for functional constipation with hard painful stools or faecal loading, and is not recommended under one month of age. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

Rectal biopsy is indicated when delayed meconium beyond 48 hours, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting or faltering growth suggest an aganglionic segment. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Constipation)

A hydrolysed formula trial is considered for a formula-fed infant with constipation plus other features of cow milk protein allergy such as eczema or blood in the stool. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Constipation)
Rectal measures are reserved for a distressed infant with a hard impacted stool that oral treatment has failed to clear. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia affects 8-10 percent of Australian toddlers; risk factors include excessive cow's milk (over 500 mL/day), early cow's milk introduction before 12 months, low iron-containing solids, prolonged breastfeeding without iron supplementation, prematurity, and Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background. Diagnostic markers: microcytic hypochromic anaemia, low ferritin (below 12 mcg/L), low transferrin saturation. Treatment: oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg/day for 3 months minimum, reduce cow's milk to below 500 mL/day, dietary modification, FBC and ferritin at 8 weeks. Iron deficiency without anaemia (low ferritin alone) still warrants treatment given developmental risk.
key_points: Most common cause of microcytic anaemia in toddlers
Cow's milk excess is the main modifiable factor
Oral iron 3 mg/kg/day elemental for 3 months
Recheck FBC at 8 weeks; Hb rise of 10 g/L or more confirms adequate response
explanation.pearls: Iron deficiency in the second year of life is associated with measurable IQ deficits up to 10 points and impaired motor development that may persist even after iron repletion; the window for prevention is more important than the rapidity of correction.

options.rationale: Iron deficiency anaemia at 22 months requires active treatment and dietary modification; untreated risks cognitive and developmental impact. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
Lead toxicity is rare in Australian children without risk factors; not standard initial workup. Iron deficiency is the typical cause of microcytic anaemia in this age. (Source: RCH CPG)
B12 deficiency causes macrocytic not microcytic anaemia; the FBC pattern points to iron deficiency. (Source: AMH)
Iron supplementation without dietary modification is incomplete; cow's milk excess (over 500 mL/day) is a major driver and must be addressed. (Source: RCH CPG)

RCH guidelines: oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg/day for 3 months, reduce cow's milk to below 500 mL/day, encourage iron-rich foods (red meat, fortified cereals, legumes), and recheck at 8 weeks expecting Hb rise of 10 g/L or more. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Fever in infants under 3 months requires systematic evaluation because clinical signs are unreliable for identifying serious bacterial infection (SBI, around 10 percent prevalence). AU practice: full septic screen (blood cultures, urine via catheter or suprapubic aspirate, LP) and empiric IV antibiotics. Standard regimen IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (or amoxicillin plus gentamicin) covers E. coli, Group B Streptococcus, Listeria monocytogenes, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Add aciclovir if HSV suspected. Admit for at least 48 hours pending culture results.
key_points: Fever under 3 months - full septic screen plus empiric IV antibiotics
Empiric: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (covers Listeria plus neonatal pathogens)
Add aciclovir if HSV concern (vesicles, seizures, hepatitis)
Admit minimum 48 hours
explanation.pearls: Suprapubic aspirate is the gold standard urine collection in infants under 6 months when clean-catch is not feasible because bag samples have around a 25 percent contamination rate; ultrasound-guided SPA increases first-pass success to around 95 percent.

options.rationale: In infants under 3 months with fever, the threshold for serious bacterial infection workup and empiric antibiotic cover is low; sepsis cannot be excluded clinically. The RCH approach is full septic screen (blood culture, urine catheter or SPA, LP) and empiric IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin, covering E. coli, Listeria, Group B strep, and other neonatal pathogens. (Source: RCH CPG; eTG)
Oral therapy is inappropriate in febrile infants under 3 months; sepsis evaluation and IV therapy are mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG)

Ceftriaxone alone covers most enterics but does not reliably cover Listeria, which is important in this age group; AU empiric regimen includes benzylpenicillin or ampicillin for Listeria. (Source: eTG)
Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is inappropriate for septic febrile infant; risks delayed source control and bilirubin displacement in neonates. (Source: AMH)
Withholding antibiotics in a febrile young infant is dangerous; outcomes worsen markedly with each hour of delay. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a self-limited medium-vessel vasculitis of young children (peak age under 5) with major sequelae being coronary artery aneurysms in 25 percent of untreated cases. Diagnostic criteria: fever 5 or more days PLUS 4 or more of: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral changes (strawberry tongue, red cracked lips), polymorphous rash, peripheral extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy. Atypical or incomplete KD requires lab criteria (CRP, ESR, anaemia, platelets over 450, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria). Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg single dose within 10 days reduces aneurysm risk to under 5 percent, plus high-dose aspirin transitioning to low-dose. Echocardiogram at baseline, 2 weeks and 6-8 weeks.
key_points: 5 day fever plus 4 of 5 criteria = classic Kawasaki
IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion within 10 days
Aspirin high-dose acutely, then low-dose for 6-8 weeks pending echo
Echo at baseline, 2 weeks, 6-8 weeks
explanation.pearls: Incomplete or atypical Kawasaki disease should be considered in any child under 6 months or over 5 years with 5 or more days of unexplained fever; coronary aneurysm risk is paradoxically highest in infants under 6 months despite often having fewer classic clinical criteria.

options.rationale: This presentation meets full Kawasaki disease criteria (fever over 5 days plus four of five principal features); antibiotics alone risk progression to coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Scarlet fever does not typically include conjunctivitis or extremity changes; testing for Kawasaki and treating now is essential. (Source: RCH CPG)

Kawasaki disease (fever 5 or more days plus 4 of 5: bilateral conjunctivitis, oral changes, polymorphous rash, peripheral extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy) requires IVIG 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary aneurysm risk from 25 percent to under 5 percent; combined with aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses until afebrile, then 3-5 mg/kg/day until echo confirms no aneurysm. (Source: RCH CPG; AHA 2017)
Steroid monotherapy is reserved for IVIG-resistant cases as second-line; not first-line in Australia. (Source: RCH CPG)
Failure to recognise and treat KD risks coronary aneurysms; this child has multiple criteria for KD. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is the most common childhood vasculitis (peak 4-7 years), classically following upper respiratory infection. Tetrad: palpable purpura on dependent areas (universal), abdominal pain (60-80 percent), arthralgia or arthritis (60-80 percent), and renal involvement (20-50 percent). Renal involvement (nephritis with haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension) is the major long-term concern, occurring weeks to months after rash onset, and is the determinant of long-term outcome. Standard monitoring: urinalysis and BP weekly for 4 weeks, fortnightly to 12 weeks, 3-monthly to 12 months. Refer to nephrology if persistent proteinuria, raised BP, or rising creatinine.
key_points: Palpable purpura on dependent areas, post-infectious context
Renal involvement may develop weeks to months later - structured monitoring
Schedule: weekly 4w, fortnightly 12w, 3-monthly 12m
Steroids reduce abdominal pain duration but not nephritis incidence
explanation.pearls: Persistent proteinuria beyond 6 months from HSP onset, even at low levels, is the strongest predictor of long-term chronic kidney disease in adulthood and warrants paediatric nephrology referral for consideration of renal biopsy and immunosuppressive therapy.

options.rationale: Insufficient surveillance; nephritis can develop weeks to months after rash and is the major long-term morbidity. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

AU paediatric guidelines (RCH) recommend urinalysis and BP weekly for first 4 weeks (when nephritis is most likely to manifest), fortnightly to 12 weeks, then 3-monthly to 12 months. Refer to paediatric nephrology if persistent proteinuria, haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, or rising creatinine. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP; KHA-CARI Paediatric)
Daily home urinalysis is impractical and not evidence-based; structured schedule per guideline is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG)
Renal biopsy is reserved for persistent significant proteinuria, declining renal function, or atypical features; not routine. (Source: KHA-CARI)
Single late check misses early nephritis when intervention may matter; insufficient. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in any neonate is a paediatric surgical emergency that must be assumed to be malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. Volvulus produces midgut ischaemia from torsion around the superior mesenteric artery axis; total midgut infarction can occur within 4-6 hours. Stable infants undergo upper GI contrast study (definitive: abnormally positioned duodenojejunal flexure right of midline, corkscrew duodenum). Shocked or rapidly deteriorating infants go directly to laparotomy. Necrotising enterocolitis (typical in preterm, days 2-3 of life, pneumatosis on AXR) is a differential but the diagnostic approach in a shocked term neonate with bilious vomiting prioritises surgical exploration over imaging.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in neonate = volvulus until proven otherwise
Shocked infant = immediate laparotomy, no imaging delay
Stable infant = urgent upper GI contrast series
Window to prevent total midgut infarction: 4-6 hours
explanation.pearls: The Ladd procedure for malrotation involves derotating the volvulus anticlockwise, dividing Ladd's bands, broadening the mesentery, returning the small bowel to the right and colon to the left of the abdomen, and performing prophylactic appendicectomy because the appendix is left in the left upper quadrant.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Frequent observation in a shocked neonate with bilious vomiting is unsafe; volvulus may be present and demands immediate exploration. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Upper GI contrast study delays definitive surgical management in a shocked infant; bilious vomiting in neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise and warrants exploration; imaging is reserved for stable infants. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Conservative management with observation in a shocked infant with bilious vomiting risks bowel necrosis from volvulus; surgical consultation is the immediate priority. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: CT abdomen exposes the neonate to significant radiation and delays surgery; not first-line investigation in suspected midgut volvulus in a shocked infant. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in any neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. In a shocked infant, imaging delays surgery; the standard of care is resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, immediate paediatric surgical consult and operative exploration without waiting for upper GI contrast. Delayed exploration risks total midgut infarction within 4-6 hours. (Source: RCH CPG; APSA; ANZNN)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

explanation.summary: Febrile urinary tract infection in young children is treated empirically after urine collection; the choice of oral agent depends on local resistance patterns and oral tolerance. RCH lists cefalexin as the first-line oral antibiotic for paediatric urinary tract infection: cystitis 20 mg/kg three times daily, pyelonephritis 25 mg/kg three times daily in children 12 months or older (25 mg/kg four times daily under 12 months). A 7-day course is standard for upper-tract urinary tract infection in well children. Trimethoprim is reserved for sensitivity-confirmed therapy or stepdown.
key_points: Empiric oral cefalexin first-line per RCH urinary tract infection guideline
12 months or older with pyelonephritis: 25 mg/kg three times daily
Intravenous therapy reserved for unwell, under 3 months, or vomiting
Trimethoprim only when local resistance is acceptable and sensitivities support it
Do not delay empirics for culture in a symptomatic confirmed urinary tract infection
explanation.pearls: Twice-daily cefalexin is not RCH dosing for paediatric urinary tract infection; the guideline consistently lists three times daily (or four times daily under 12 months in pyelonephritis).

options.rationale: Amoxicillin clavulanate has broader gram-negative cover than needed and higher rates of diarrhoea compared with the first-line agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Delay in treatment of a confirmed febrile urinary tract infection increases the risk of renal scarring; empiric therapy is started after the urine sample is taken. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)
Trimethoprim resistance of 28 percent locally exceeds the 20 percent ceiling for reliable empiric cover in febrile urinary tract infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Cefalexin is the RCH first-line oral agent for paediatric urinary tract infection. In children 12 months or older with febrile urinary tract infection the dose is 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 7 days. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

Intravenous therapy is reserved for children who are unwell, vomiting, under 3 months, or unable to tolerate oral feeds; this child is well enough for oral therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

explanation.summary: Pertussis postexposure prophylaxis aims to interrupt household transmission and protect high-risk contacts. AU CDNA SoNG defines high-risk contacts as infants under 6 months, women in the last month of pregnancy, and unvaccinated childcare workers. When a high-risk contact is identified all household members receive prophylaxis regardless of immunisation status. Azithromycin is the macrolide of choice for infants over 1 month due to lower hypertrophic pyloric stenosis risk than erythromycin.
key_points: Azithromycin first-line for all ages including infants over 1 month
All household contacts treated if any high-risk contact present
High-risk: infant under 6 months, last month of pregnancy
Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole only if macrolide-intolerant and over 2 months
explanation.pearls: Maternal pertussis vaccination in pregnancy from 20 weeks provides passive protection but does not eliminate the need for household prophylaxis when a confirmed case is identified.

options.rationale: Selective prophylaxis to the infant alone leaves household transmission via the other contacts unaddressed during the infectious period. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)
Pertussis transmits from up to 6 days before cough onset; absence of symptoms in contacts does not exclude infection or transmission risk. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)
AU guidance recommends prophylaxis for all household contacts when a high-risk contact is present such as a young infant or a third-trimester pregnant woman. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)
Restricting prophylaxis omits the father and 4-year-old brother who can transmit to both high-risk contacts within the household. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)
Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole is a second-line agent in pertussis prophylaxis reserved for macrolide-intolerant individuals over 2 months of age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Croup is treated according to a severity score with oral dexamethasone the AU first-line for mild to moderate cases. Stridor at rest with mild recession indicates moderate severity warranting steroid and observation but not adrenaline. Nebulised adrenaline is added for severe disease with marked recession, cyanosis, or altered mental state and always with concurrent steroid. Disposition depends on response at 4 hours after steroid: stable children can usually go home.
key_points: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose first-line
Adrenaline only for severe distress and always with steroid
Budesonide nebulised only if oral intake not possible
Discharge after 4 hours if no stridor at rest
explanation.pearls: Onset of benefit from oral dexamethasone in croup is 30 to 60 minutes with peak at 6 hours; this matches the typical 4-hour ED observation window before safe discharge.

options.rationale: Budesonide is reserved for children unable to tolerate oral steroid; this child is alert and accepting oral medications. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
AU practice supports a single oral dexamethasone dose of 0.15 mg/kg for moderate croup with onset of benefit within 30 to 60 minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Salbutamol does not treat the subglottic oedema responsible for croup and delays definitive steroid therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Adrenaline is reserved for severe distress as it acts for 1 to 2 hours and requires steroid co-administration to avoid rebound. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Dexamethasone is the preferred AU first-line agent due to longer half-life and single-dose efficacy; prednisolone is an alternative only if dexamethasone is unavailable. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis treatment in children is repeated IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh every 5 minutes for persistent severe features. The AU ASCIA weight bands prescribe 150 micrograms for 10 to 20 kg, 300 micrograms for 20 to 50 kg, and 500 micrograms for over 50 kg with simultaneous fluid resuscitation. Refractory shock after 2 or 3 IM doses prompts an adrenaline infusion at 0.1 to 1 microgram/kg/min titrated to response with continuous cardiac monitoring. Antihistamines and steroids are not first-line in acute anaphylaxis.
key_points: IM adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg up to 500 micrograms every 5 minutes
Weight bands: 150 for 10-20 kg, 300 for 20-50 kg, 500 for over 50 kg
IV infusion only when refractory after 2-3 IM doses
Fluids 20 mL/kg crystalloid alongside adrenaline for shock
explanation.pearls: Persistent shock after 2 IM doses indicates impending refractory anaphylaxis; commence an adrenaline infusion early at 0.1 microgram/kg/min and call for senior airway support rather than escalating IM dose.

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is an adjunct for stridor but does not address shock or lower airway anaphylaxis and does not replace systemic IM dosing. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
Subcutaneous absorption is unreliable during shock; intramuscular anterolateral thigh is the recommended route in anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
The 150 microgram dose corresponds to children between 10 and 20 kg and underdoses a 32 kg child experiencing persistent severe anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
IV bolus adrenaline outside cardiac arrest risks malignant arrhythmia and hypertensive crisis and is reserved for refractory shock as an infusion. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

AU ASCIA guidance prescribes 10 micrograms/kg IM up to 500 micrograms with repeat dosing every 5 minutes for persistent severe anaphylaxis; in a 32 kg child the rounded dose is 300 micrograms IM. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Late-onset neonatal sepsis in a community setting is empirically covered with benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin and a third-generation cephalosporin at meningitic dose to cover group B streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria with CNS penetration. Aciclovir is added if features suggest possible HSV. Antibiotics must not be delayed for lumbar puncture in a haemodynamically unstable infant; the LP is performed when the patient is stabilised. Ceftriaxone may be used in term, non-jaundiced neonates over 1 week when cefotaxime is unavailable.
key_points: Late-onset community sepsis: benzylpenicillin + gentamicin + cefotaxime or ceftriaxone
Add aciclovir empirically in late-onset neonatal sepsis with CNS features
Antibiotics first, LP when stable
Ceftriaxone acceptable substitute in term non-jaundiced neonates
explanation.pearls: Maternal HSV history is often absent in neonatal disseminated herpes; empiric aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours in a septic neonate has minimal downside and prevents catastrophic delay.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis in the neonate

options.rationale: Cefazolin lacks reliable CNS penetration; aciclovir is added empirically in any late-onset neonate with sepsis features even without seizures. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis in the neonate

options.rationale: Broad cover with vancomycin and meropenem is reserved for nosocomial late-onset sepsis or proven resistance; community late-onset is treated with first-line regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Late-onset sepsis with shock and full fontanelle requires meningitic third-generation cephalosporin cover not only beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis in the neonate

options.rationale: Late-onset neonatal sepsis with septic shock requires immediate triple antimicrobial cover with meningitic ceftriaxone dose; LP is deferred until cardiovascular stability is achieved. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis; ANZCOR)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis in the neonate

options.rationale: LP must not delay antibiotics in a shocked neonate; antibiotics are given immediately after blood cultures and LP is performed when safe. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis in the neonate

explanation.summary: Weight faltering in infancy is most commonly multifactorial, with inadequate intake the leading cause when there are no organic red flags. Evaluation starts with a feeding history, three-day diet diary, and observation of a feed before laboratory testing. Investigations are guided by red flags such as diarrhoea, vomiting, recurrent infection, dysmorphism, or developmental regression.
