Solids should be established with iron-rich foods around six months in addition to milk feeds.
key_points: Crossing two centiles downward triggers structured assessment
Feeding observation and diet diary precede investigations
Coeliac and other serology reserved for red flags or non-response
NG feeds reserved for severe or unresponsive cases
explanation.pearls: An observed breastfeed in clinic typically lasts 10 to 40 minutes; transfer volumes under 60 mL in a 9-month-old over a sustained feed flag low effective intake before any blood test is sent.

options.rationale: Admission and NG feeds are reserved for severe weight faltering with dehydration, organic disease, or failed community escalation; this child is alert and developing normally. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth)
Detailed feeding assessment and observed feed remain the first-line evaluation for non-organic weight faltering before any investigation cascade. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth)
Targeted bloods are reserved for children with red flags or no improvement after dietary and feeding optimisation; this child has none. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth)
There is no evidence-based reason to stop breastfeeding; mixed feeding decisions follow assessment, not precede it. (Source: NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines)
Crossing two major centile lines downward warrants assessment rather than reassurance, even when development is preserved. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Immunisation Program moved to a single-dose Gardasil 9 schedule for healthy adolescents aged 9 to under 26 years in 2023. Three doses remain for those with moderate to severe immunocompromise. The program is delivered in Year 7 to maximise pre-exposure efficacy and uptake. Vaccination does not replace cervical screening, which begins at age 25 under the renewed National Cervical Screening Program.
key_points: Single-dose Gardasil 9 for healthy 9 to under 26 years
Three doses retained for moderate to severe immunocompromise
Delivered in Year 7 by school-based programs
Does not replace cervical screening from age 25
explanation.pearls: Gardasil 9 covers HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 and is the only HPV vaccine available on the Australian schedule since 2018.

options.rationale: The two-dose schedule was replaced in 2023 by a single-dose schedule for healthy adolescents aged 9 to under 26 years. (Source: ATAGI; Australian Immunisation Handbook)
Healthy adolescents aged 9 to under 26 years receive a single dose of Gardasil 9 under the AU schedule since 2023. (Source: ATAGI; Australian Immunisation Handbook)
There is no clinical reason to delay; immunogenicity and program uptake are highest in early Year 7. (Source: ATAGI; Australian Immunisation Handbook)
Three doses are only required for moderately to severely immunocompromised adolescents, not healthy 12-year-olds. (Source: ATAGI; Australian Immunisation Handbook)
Vaccination and screening are complementary; vaccination prevents most oncogenic HPV exposure that screening later detects. (Source: NCSP; Cancer Council Australia)

explanation.summary: Paraphimosis occurs when a retracted foreskin cannot be returned over the glans and creates a constricting band leading to oedema and risk of ischaemia. Initial management uses topical anaesthesia, sustained manual compression of the glans to reduce oedema, and gentle reduction. If reduction fails or the glans becomes dusky, urgent urology review for dorsal slit is required. This contrasts with physiological phimosis, where the foreskin is simply non-retractable in a well child without entrapment.
key_points: Paraphimosis is a urological emergency, not phimosis
First step: topical anaesthesia and manual reduction
Failed reduction or dusky glans needs urgent urology review
Never forcibly retract a physiologically tight foreskin
explanation.pearls: Most physiological phimosis resolves by age 10 without any intervention; only 1 percent of boys still have a non-retractile foreskin at age 16.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: This is paraphimosis with an entrapped foreskin, which is a urological emergency rather than physiological phimosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin conditions)
Topical anaesthesia with sustained glans compression to reduce oedema followed by manual reduction is the first-line management of paraphimosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin conditions)
Definitive surgery is not the first step; the entrapment must be reduced urgently to avoid glans ischaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin conditions)
Topical steroid is treatment for symptomatic phimosis, not for an acute paraphimosis with entrapment. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin conditions)
There is no retention or infection; catheterisation does not address the foreskin entrapment. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin conditions)

explanation.summary: Suspected airway foreign body in a toddler with witnessed choking, focal wheeze, and unilateral air trapping on inspiration-expiration films is a definitive indication for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia. Bronchodilators, back blows, and CT all delay treatment. Children with peanut, seed, or hard food inhalation can present with a quiet asymptomatic phase before secondary pneumonia. Initial assessment focuses on whether the airway is patent and whether the child can phonate and cough effectively.
key_points: Witnessed choking with focal findings = bronchoscopy
Expiration film air trapping is a key radiological clue
Back blows only for complete obstruction in a basic life support sequence
Avoid bronchodilators or CT delays
explanation.pearls: Right main bronchus is the most common site for inhaled peanut in toddlers because of its more vertical orientation; ipsilateral air trapping on expiration film is the most sensitive radiographic sign.

options.rationale: Bronchodilators do not move a fixed obstructing foreign body and may delay definitive removal. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)
Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is the definitive intervention for suspected airway foreign body with focal signs and air trapping. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)
Back blows are part of basic life support for complete airway obstruction, not for a stable child with focal signs. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)
CT may delay definitive bronchoscopy when the clinical picture and inspiration-expiration films already support a foreign body. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)
Discharge risks delayed pneumonia, atelectasis, and irreversible airway injury from a retained foreign body. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

explanation.summary: Oesophageal button battery is a time-critical emergency because alkali generation begins within two hours and full-thickness injury within four hours. Australian guidance supports oral honey 10 mL every 10 minutes in children older than 12 months presenting within 12 hours, awaiting endoscopic removal as the definitive treatment. Sucralfate suspension is an alternative in hospital. Imaging shows the characteristic double-rim halo on PA view and step-off on lateral, distinguishing battery from coin.
key_points: Time-critical: tissue injury within 2 to 4 hours
Honey 10 mL every 10 min if over 12 months and within 12 hours
Definitive treatment is endoscopic removal under anaesthesia
Never induce vomiting or attempt blind NG dislodgement
explanation.pearls: On PA chest X-ray a button battery shows a double-rim halo whereas a coin shows a single uniform edge; the lateral film shows a step-off at the negative pole that points to the side of greatest mucosal injury.

options.rationale: Oral honey within 12 hours of ingestion in a child over 12 months reduces oesophageal alkali injury severity pending endoscopic removal. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery; NCPP)
Local endoscopy is not available; oral nil by mouth alone offers no tissue protection during the transport delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery)
Induced vomiting risks aspiration, further mucosal injury, and is contraindicated for button battery ingestion. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)
Charcoal does not bind battery alkali leakage and adds aspiration risk without altering tissue injury. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)
Blind NG manipulation risks oesophageal perforation and is not part of any current guideline. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery)

explanation.summary: Global developmental delay in a child without dysmorphism, regression, or seizures still has a high yield genetic basis. Chromosomal microarray is the first-tier genetic investigation in Australia, detecting clinically significant copy number variants in approximately 15 percent of unexplained cases. Fragile X testing is concurrent or sequential. Exome sequencing follows if first-tier testing is negative or if specific syndromic features emerge. Neuroimaging is reserved for focal neurological signs, microcephaly, regression, or seizures.
key_points: Microarray is first-tier for unexplained global delay
Fragile X testing is concurrent or sequential
Exome sequencing is second-tier after negative first-tier
Neuroimaging only if focal signs, microcephaly, regression, or seizures
explanation.pearls: Chromosomal microarray has a diagnostic yield of about 15 percent in non-syndromic global developmental delay versus about 3 percent for karyotype, which is why it has replaced karyotype as first-tier in Australian practice.

sources.label: HGSA: Genetic testing in developmental delay

options.rationale: Karyotype is reserved for suspected Down or Turner syndrome; it has lower yield than microarray for non-syndromic delay. (Source: RACP; HGSA)
source_refs: HGSA: Genetic testing in developmental delay

options.rationale: Chromosomal microarray is the first-line genetic test for unexplained global developmental delay or intellectual disability and detects copy number variants with about 15 percent yield. (Source: RACP; HGSA)
source_refs: HGSA: Genetic testing in developmental delay

options.rationale: MRI is useful if there are focal neurological findings, microcephaly, regression, or seizures; otherwise yield is lower than microarray. (Source: RACP)
Exome is a second-tier test in Australia after a normal microarray and fragile X, or when a specific syndrome is suspected. (Source: HGSA)
source_refs: HGSA: Genetic testing in developmental delay

options.rationale: EEG is reserved for suspected seizures or regression; routine EEG is not part of the workup for global delay. (Source: RACP)

explanation.summary: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is diagnosed in Australia using the Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD, which requires either three sentinel facial features (short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip vermilion) with confirmed or unknown prenatal alcohol exposure, OR severe neurodevelopmental impairment across three of ten domains with confirmed exposure. Multidisciplinary assessment is mandated. Early identification opens access to NDIS support, structured behavioural therapy, and educational accommodations. Stimulants may help comorbid attentional symptoms after diagnosis but are not the first response.
key_points: Three sentinel facial features plus exposure suffice for diagnosis of FASD with three sentinel features
Without all three facial features, severe impairment in 3 of 10 neurodevelopmental domains plus confirmed exposure is required
Growth restriction is supportive but not required for diagnosis
Multidisciplinary assessment is mandatory in the Australian framework
Early diagnosis unlocks NDIS and educational supports
explanation.pearls: Smooth philtrum and thin upper vermilion are scored against the University of Washington lip-philtrum guide, with rank 4 or 5 counting as a sentinel feature.

sources.label: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.rationale: Genetic testing is reserved for atypical features, additional dysmorphism, or when other syndromes are competing on the differential; the sentinel triad with confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure makes broad genetic testing low yield as the first step. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.rationale: Australian diagnostic criteria require multidisciplinary assessment confirming three sentinel facial features and severe impairment in three or more neurodevelopmental domains, alongside documented prenatal exposure. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.rationale: Stimulant trials may be considered after formal diagnosis and behavioural strategies have failed, not as a diagnostic shortcut in a 4-year-old with developmental concerns. (Source: RCH CPG: ADHD)

Routine MRI is not part of the diagnostic pathway when the clinical picture and prenatal exposure are typical; imaging is reserved for focal neurology or seizures. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.rationale: Delaying assessment misses the early-intervention window that improves long-term outcomes when neurodevelopmental impairment is already evident. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease presents in approximately 90 percent within the neonatal period with delayed meconium beyond 48 hours, abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. The classic squirt sign on rectal examination is highly suggestive. Suction rectal biopsy is the diagnostic gold standard. Contrast enema may identify a transition zone but is unreliable in neonates because the aganglionic segment has not yet hypertrophied proximally. Enterocolitis is the most dangerous early complication and warrants empiric antibiotics and rectal washouts.
key_points: Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours is a red flag
Suction rectal biopsy is the diagnostic test of choice
Histology shows absent ganglion cells with hypertrophic nerve trunks
Contrast enema sensitivity is limited in the neonatal period
Enterocolitis is the leading cause of mortality before surgery
explanation.pearls: Rectal biopsies must be taken at least 2 cm above the dentate line to avoid the physiologically hypoganglionic zone and a false-positive result.

options.rationale: Surgery is the definitive treatment after histological confirmation; proceeding without a confirmed diagnosis risks unnecessary laparotomy in alternative causes such as meconium plug or ileal atresia. (Source: RCH CPG: Hirschsprung disease)

Contrast enema is supportive but neonates often lack a mature transition zone; its sensitivity in the first weeks is limited and it does not establish histological diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Hirschsprung disease)

Suction rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells with hypertrophic nerve trunks is the definitive diagnostic test in neonates and can be done cot-side without anaesthesia. (Source: RCH CPG: Hirschsprung disease)
Stool softeners do not address aganglionic obstruction and risk worsening proximal distension with enterocolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Hirschsprung disease)
Sweat testing is unreliable before 2 weeks of age and the explosive release of stool on rectal examination is classic for Hirschsprung rather than meconium ileus. (Source: RCH CPG: Cystic fibrosis)

explanation.summary: The 2015 revised Jones criteria split populations into low-risk and high-risk. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from northern Australia are categorised as high-risk, in whom polyarthralgia counts as a major criterion and monoarthritis (with high-grade fever and elevated inflammatory markers) can also count. Two major, or one major plus two minor, manifestations plus evidence of streptococcal infection fulfils definite disease. Echocardiography is mandatory for severity grading and may upgrade clinical carditis or detect subclinical carditis. Lifelong benzathine penicillin G is the keystone of secondary prevention.
key_points: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from northern Australia are high-risk for application of Jones criteria
High-risk thresholds count polyarthralgia and monoarthritis as major manifestations
Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (ASOT, anti-DNase B, swab) is required
Echocardiography is mandatory for severity and may detect subclinical carditis
Benzathine penicillin G every 21-28 days is the standard secondary prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: ESR over 60 mm/hr or CRP over 30 mg/L counts as a minor criterion in the high-risk threshold; together with raised temperature over 38 degrees this scenario also satisfies two minor criteria.

options.rationale: In high-risk populations the revised Jones criteria allow polyarthralgia plus carditis (auscultatory mitral regurgitation murmur) as two major manifestations, with elevated ASOT confirming preceding streptococcal infection. (Source: RHDAustralia 3rd edition guideline)

Clinical carditis on auscultation contributes a major criterion even before echocardiogram, although echocardiography should still be obtained urgently for severity assessment. (Source: RHDAustralia 3rd edition guideline)
Subcutaneous nodules are uncommon and not required; the case already meets the high-risk threshold for definite disease. (Source: RHDAustralia 3rd edition guideline)
Reactive arthritis would not produce a new murmur or ESR over 60, both of which fulfil rheumatic fever criteria. (Source: RHDAustralia 3rd edition guideline)
Septic arthritis is monoarticular and severely tender with a single hot joint; the migratory polyarthropathy and systemic features here do not fit. (Source: RHDAustralia 3rd edition guideline)

explanation.summary: Atopic eczema flares follow a stepwise approach: liberal emollients, low-potency topical corticosteroid, moderate-potency steroid with or without wet wraps, then specialist input for phototherapy or systemic therapy. Wet-wrap therapy uses a moist tubular layer over the steroid plus emollient to enhance penetration, cool the skin, and improve sleep. It is suitable for short courses of 3 to 5 nights. Steroid phobia is best addressed by demonstrating the fingertip unit and explaining that under-treatment causes more skin damage than appropriate steroid use.
key_points: Step up potency rather than persisting with an inadequate strength steroid
Methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 percent is moderate-potency and once-daily
Wet wraps amplify steroid penetration and reduce excoriation
Oral corticosteroids cause rebound and are avoided in routine eczema
Calcineurin inhibitors are best for sensitive areas or maintenance
explanation.pearls: Methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 percent applied once daily is approximately equivalent in potency to twice-daily betamethasone valerate 0.05 percent and is preferred in young children for the lower potency-to-effect ratio.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Atopic dermatitis

options.rationale: Mild steroid has failed after a full week; persisting risks ongoing skin damage and steroid phobia. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)
Systemic immunosuppression is reserved for severe disease refractory to a moderate-potency topical steroid trial with wet wraps. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)
Oral corticosteroids cause rebound flare on cessation and are not recommended for routine atopic eczema flares. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

Moderate-potency steroid plus wet wraps is the recommended escalation for moderate to severe flares not controlled on mild steroid, with rapid response and good safety in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)
Calcineurin inhibitors are indicated for sensitive areas or as steroid-sparing once a flare has settled; they are too slow as the primary flare treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis is the most important long-term complication of HSP and can develop weeks after the rash and joint symptoms have resolved. All children require monthly urinalysis and blood pressure monitoring for 6 months because nephritis can develop late. Mild urinary abnormalities are followed; nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, acute kidney injury, or persistent moderate proteinuria warrant nephrology referral and biopsy. Treatment is guided by ISKDC histology grade and may include corticosteroids with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide for crescentic disease.
key_points: Monthly urinalysis and BP for 6 months after HSP onset
Nephrotic-range proteinuria is urine protein creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol
Rising creatinine, nephrotic range proteinuria or hypertension trigger nephrology referral
Biopsy directs immunosuppressive intensity
Late onset of nephritis up to 6 months after rash is well-recognised
explanation.pearls: ISKDC grade 3 or higher crescentic HSP nephritis is the histological threshold above which Australian centres typically add mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide to prednisolone.

options.rationale: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with rising creatinine and hypertension is not benign and demands urgent specialist input rather than community follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Steroids alone do not reliably prevent progression of established nephritis and starting without renal biopsy planning misses the diagnostic step that guides therapy. (Source: KHA-CARI: HSP nephritis)
Aspirin does not address established nephritis and the joint symptoms have already resolved. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)
Ultrasound rarely changes management in HSP nephritis and weekly GP monitoring fails to act on already established nephrotic-range disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypertension and an acute creatinine rise meets Australian criteria for urgent paediatric nephrology referral and biopsy to guide immunosuppression. (Source: KHA-CARI: HSP nephritis)

explanation.summary: Non-IgE mediated cow milk protein allergy commonly presents in the first 6 months with proctocolitis (blood-streaked mucousy stools in an otherwise well infant), enteropathy, or chronic GORD-like symptoms. Skin prick test is negative because it is non-IgE mediated. In breastfed infants, maternal cow milk exclusion is first line for at least 2 to 4 weeks with dietetic input and calcium plus vitamin D supplementation. If symptoms persist or the infant is formula-fed, extensively hydrolysed formula is next; amino acid formula is reserved for failure or severe disease. Cow milk should be reintroduced at 9 to 12 months to assess tolerance.
key_points: Non-IgE CMPA is diagnosed clinically; skin prick test is negative
Maternal dairy exclusion in breastfed infants is first line
Extensively hydrolysed formula is next when not breastfed
Amino acid formula is reserved for failure or severe disease
30 percent cross-react with soy; soy is not first line
explanation.pearls: Reintroduce cow milk at 9 to 12 months using the milk ladder to assess tolerance; up to 80 percent of children with non-IgE CMPA tolerate cow milk by age 3 years.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

options.rationale: Non-IgE cow milk protein allergy in a breastfed infant is managed by complete maternal dairy elimination for a minimum 2 to 4 weeks before judging response, with calcium and vitamin D supplementation. (Source: ASCIA: Cow milk allergy)
Cessation of breastfeeding is not required and is harmful when maternal elimination can be trialled successfully in non-IgE disease. (Source: ASCIA: Cow milk allergy)
Amino acid formula is reserved for severe enteropathy, anaphylaxis history, or failure of extensively hydrolysed formula. (Source: ASCIA: Cow milk allergy)

Inflammatory bowel disease is rare in this age group and the clinical picture fits non-IgE cow milk protein allergy; endoscopy is reserved for failure of elimination. (Source: ASCIA: Cow milk allergy)
Up to 30 percent of infants with cow milk protein allergy will also react to soy, so it is not a recommended first-line alternative. (Source: ASCIA: Cow milk allergy)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is most likely in infants under 12 months and carries the highest coronary aneurysm risk if missed. Diagnosis requires fever for at least 5 days plus 2 or 3 of the classical criteria, with supplemental laboratory criteria substituting for absent clinical features. IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion plus aspirin (high or moderate dose) should be given by day 10 to minimise coronary risk. Echocardiography is performed at diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6 to 8 weeks. High-risk infants may benefit from concomitant corticosteroid or infliximab.
key_points: Infants under 12 months often present incompletely and have the highest coronary risk
Supplemental criteria: CRP, ESR, albumin, anaemia, late platelet rise, pyuria, ALT
IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin by day 10 is the standard treatment
Echocardiography at baseline, 2 weeks, and 6 to 8 weeks
Adjunct steroid or infliximab is considered in high-risk infants
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria in a febrile infant beyond day 5 is a classic Kawasaki clue and should not be misattributed to a partially-treated urinary tract infection.

sources.label: American Heart Association: Kawasaki disease scientific statement

options.rationale: Persisting bacterial therapy alone delays Kawasaki recognition and increases the risk of coronary aneurysm beyond day 10. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Discharge before excluding Kawasaki disease in a febrile infant beyond day 5 is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Infants under 12 months with prolonged unexplained fever and at least 3 supplemental laboratory criteria (CRP >=30, ESR >=40, anaemia, platelets >=450 after day 7, albumin <=30, sterile pyuria, raised ALT) meet incomplete Kawasaki criteria and receive IVIG plus aspirin; echo guides surveillance. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first line; adjunctive steroids are considered alongside IVIG in high-risk children, not as a stand-alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
CT chest does not address the most likely diagnosis and exposes the infant to unnecessary radiation. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Paediatric OSA is graded by the obstructive apnoea-hypopnoea index: 1 to 5 mild, 5 to 10 moderate, above 10 severe. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the leading cause. Adenotonsillectomy is first-line for moderate and severe disease in otherwise well children, with cure rates of around 70 to 80 percent. Children with persistent symptoms after surgery, contraindications, or syndromic airways need CPAP. Untreated OSA causes daytime inattention, behavioural disturbance, growth faltering (from disrupted growth hormone secretion), enuresis, and in severe cases pulmonary hypertension.
key_points: OAHI 5 to 10 is moderate paediatric OSA
Adenotonsillectomy is first line in tonsillar hypertrophy
Intranasal steroid is for mild OSA, not moderate or severe
CPAP is second line after surgery failure or contraindication
Growth faltering can reverse after successful surgery
explanation.pearls: Children under 3 years, severe OSA, or significant comorbidity warrant overnight inpatient monitoring after adenotonsillectomy because of higher rates of respiratory complications.

options.rationale: An obstructive apnoea-hypopnoea index above 5 with tonsillar hypertrophy is moderate paediatric OSA and Australian guidelines support adenotonsillectomy as first-line surgical management. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

Intranasal corticosteroid is reserved for mild OSA (OAHI 1 to 5) or as adjunct in persistent symptoms after surgery; it is not appropriate for moderate OSA. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

CPAP is the option when adenotonsillectomy is contraindicated, declined, or unsuccessful; it is not first-line in a typical child with tonsillar hypertrophy. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

Airway MRI is reserved for complex craniofacial syndromes or post-surgical persistent OSA, not initial assessment of typical adenotonsillar hypertrophy. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)
Positional therapy is inadequate for moderate disease with daytime symptoms and growth faltering. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

explanation.summary: ABO haemolytic disease with DAT-positive haemolysis in a term infant produces rapidly rising unconjugated bilirubin. At 60 hours of age, total serum bilirubin 410 micromol/L approaches exchange transfusion thresholds on Australian nomograms. Management is intensive multi-bank phototherapy plus IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg in haemolytic disease, ensuring hydration, and active preparation for double-volume exchange transfusion in a tertiary neonatal unit if bilirubin does not fall or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy develop. Always plot age in hours against current bilirubin chart.
key_points: Plot bilirubin against postnatal age in hours, not days
Intensive multi-bank phototherapy first-line for severe hyperbilirubinaemia
IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg in DAT-positive haemolytic disease near exchange threshold
Acute bilirubin encephalopathy signs trigger immediate exchange
explanation.pearls: In a DAT-positive ABO haemolytic newborn at 60 hours with TSB approaching the exchange line, give IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg over 2 hours alongside intensive phototherapy rather than waiting for the next bilirubin to fail therapy - IVIG reduces exchange need substantially in isoimmune haemolysis.

sources.label: NICE CG98 Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days 2010 (updated)

options.rationale: Bilirubin 410 micromol/L at 60 hours of age with positive DAT and ABO incompatibility approaches the exchange transfusion threshold; outpatient management is unsafe. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline Neonatal Jaundice 2022)

Brief formula supplementation may be considered in dehydration but ceasing breastfeeding is not first-line for hyperbilirubinaemia and does not lower bilirubin rapidly enough. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline Neonatal Jaundice 2022)

Intensive phototherapy and close re-check are appropriate, but at TSB 410 micromol/L at 60 hours of age with DAT-positive haemolysis, immediate exchange criteria are likely already met under Australian charts; preparation should be active rather than contingent. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline Neonatal Jaundice 2022)

Australian and NICE guidance recommend intensive phototherapy plus IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg for haemolytic disease when TSB approaches exchange thresholds, with active preparation for double-volume exchange in a tertiary unit if rapid response is not achieved. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline Neonatal Jaundice 2022)

Phenobarbital enzyme induction is not standard acute management for neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia in Australia and is not effective rapidly enough for this urgent presentation. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline Neonatal Jaundice 2022)

explanation.summary: Intussusception in a previously well infant or toddler presents with intermittent inconsolable crying with leg-drawing, vomiting, lethargy between episodes and the late sign of red-currant-jelly stool. Ultrasound confirms with the target or pseudo-kidney sign. After IV access and fluid resuscitation, definitive management is air (pneumatic) enema reduction performed by paediatric radiology with paediatric surgery on standby. Reduction is successful in 80-90% without perforation. Surgery is required for perforation, peritonitis, shock, failed reduction, or a pathological lead point.
key_points: Triad: intermittent inconsolable crying, vomiting, red-currant-jelly stool (late)
Ultrasound first-line for diagnosis (target / pseudo-kidney sign)
Air enema reduction first-line definitive treatment
Surgery for perforation, peritonitis, failed reduction or pathological lead point
explanation.pearls: In an 11-month-old with ileocolic intussusception confirmed on ultrasound and no perforation, transfer for air enema rather than barium - pneumatic reduction has a 80-90 percent success rate with lower perforation risk, and tertiary radiology can usually accommodate within hours.

sources.label: NSW Health Paediatric Clinical Practice Guideline Acute Abdominal Pain 2019

options.rationale: Untreated intussusception progresses to bowel ischaemia, perforation and shock; observation off-site is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception 2020)
Imaging has already confirmed the diagnosis; broad-spectrum antibiotics without reduction does not treat the obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception 2020)

Confirmed ileocolic intussusception without perforation or peritonitis is treated by air enema reduction in a tertiary or paediatric centre after resuscitation; paediatric surgery is on standby for perforation or failed reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception 2020)
Non-operative reduction by air enema succeeds in 80-90% of cases without perforation or peritonitis and is the first-line definitive management. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception 2020)
Air enema is preferred over barium because of lower perforation risk and cleaner imaging; barium delay is not part of current Australian practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception 2020)

explanation.summary: Pertussis in young infants is a notifiable disease in Australia and admission is required for infants under 6 months with apnoea, cyanosis or feeding difficulty. Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally once daily for 5 days is the first-line antimicrobial for pertussis in infants under 1 month and is preferred over erythromycin because of lower risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Macrolides reduce transmission but do not modify illness once the paroxysmal phase is established. Post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts including unimmunised infants is indicated. The lymphocytosis is characteristic.
key_points: Azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day x 5 days - first line, especially under 1 month
Erythromycin in young infants risks hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Notifiable to public health
Admission for under-6-month-olds with apnoea or feeding compromise
explanation.pearls: In any infant under 1 month with suspected pertussis, prescribe azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days rather than erythromycin to avoid infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis - the absolute risk on erythromycin is increased about 10-fold.

options.rationale: Amoxicillin has no activity against Bordetella pertussis; macrolides are the antimicrobial of choice in pertussis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019 - Pertussis)

Azithromycin is first-line antimicrobial therapy for pertussis in infants under 1 month and is preferred over erythromycin because of lower risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days is the standard Australian regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)

Erythromycin in infants under 1 month carries increased risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; azithromycin is preferred. Even in older infants the shorter azithromycin course is favoured. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)
TMP-SMX is an alternative in macrolide intolerance only and is contraindicated in infants under 2 months because of kernicterus risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)
Fluoroquinolones are not active against Bordetella pertussis and are not used for this indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)

explanation.summary: Pyloric stenosis classically presents at 3-6 weeks with non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds in a hungry infant. The metabolic derangement is hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid loss. Surgical correction is semi-urgent; the priority before anaesthesia is to correct hypoperfusion (20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus), then to replace chloride and potassium with 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose plus KCl 20-40 mmol/L at 1.5 x maintenance, with serial VBG and electrolytes until Cl >100, HCO3 <30 and K >3.5. Uncorrected alkalosis predisposes to post-anaesthetic apnoea.
key_points: Correct fluid and electrolyte derangement before surgery
Bolus 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg if hypoperfused, then 0.45% saline + 5% dextrose + KCl at 1.5 x maintenance
Target Cl >100 mmol/L, HCO3 <30 mmol/L before theatre
Avoid bicarbonate; the alkalosis is the problem
explanation.pearls: Aim for serum chloride above 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L before pyloromyotomy rather than rushing to theatre - uncorrected hypochloraemic alkalosis raises postoperative apnoea risk substantially and is the single most modifiable peri-operative variable.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guideline Paediatric IV fluids 2021

options.rationale: Surgery for pyloric stenosis is a semi-urgent rather than emergency procedure; the priority is correcting hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis before anaesthesia to reduce apnoea risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis 2019)

Dextrose without sodium and chloride fails to correct the hypochloraemic alkalosis and worsens hyponatraemia risk; balanced sodium chloride containing fluid is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis 2019)

RCH guidance: 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus for hypoperfusion, then 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose and KCl 20-40 mmol/L at 1.5 x maintenance, with surgery once Cl >100 mmol/L and HCO3 <30 mmol/L because uncorrected alkalosis predisposes to post-anaesthetic apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis 2019)
Giving bicarbonate worsens existing metabolic alkalosis and is contraindicated; the alkalosis resolves with chloride and potassium replacement. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis 2019)
Continued oral feeds will worsen vomiting and electrolyte derangement; NPO with NG drainage and IV resuscitation is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis 2019)

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia in paediatric oncology is a medical emergency. Australian COSA and eviQ guidance is to draw blood cultures (peripheral and from line) and start empiric antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg IV) within 60 minutes of presentation. Vancomycin is added for haemodynamic instability, severe mucositis, suspected line infection, MRSA colonisation, or proven Gram-positive isolate. Carbapenems are reserved for escalation. Source control of the central venous catheter is reassessed when there is persistent bacteraemia despite appropriate therapy.
key_points: Door-to-antibiotic time within 60 minutes
First line: piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg IV after cultures
Add vancomycin for shock, mucositis, line infection or MRSA risk
Escalate to carbapenem for clinical deterioration or resistant isolate
explanation.pearls: Aim for door-to-antibiotic time under 60 minutes with piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg IV after blood cultures - every additional hour of delayed empiric antibiotic therapy is associated with measurable increases in paediatric febrile neutropenia mortality.

options.rationale: Australian paediatric oncology febrile neutropenia protocols recommend piperacillin-tazobactam as first-line empiric monotherapy after cultures, with vancomycin added for shock, mucositis, MRSA risk or proven line infection. (Source: COSA/eviQ Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia 2020)

Outpatient oral antibiotics are reserved for selected low-risk febrile neutropenia in older children with predicted short neutropenia, not for a 6-year-old with haemodynamic compromise. (Source: COSA/eviQ Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia 2020)

Ceftriaxone has limited Pseudomonas activity and is not recommended as monotherapy in febrile neutropenia in Australia; antipseudomonal beta-lactam is required. (Source: COSA/eviQ Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia 2020)

Carbapenems are reserved for escalation, suspected ESBL or septic shock not responding to first-line therapy; routine empirical use risks resistance. (Source: COSA/eviQ Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia 2020)

Withholding empiric antibiotics in suspected febrile neutropenia substantially increases mortality; empiric therapy must start within 60 minutes of presentation. (Source: COSA/eviQ Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia 2020)

explanation.summary: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis classically presents in obese pre-adolescent males (10-14 years) with knee or thigh pain, antalgic gait and externally rotated lower limb. Drehmann sign (obligate external rotation when the hip is flexed) and disruption of the Klein line on AP pelvis x-ray are diagnostic. SUFE is a surgical emergency requiring non-weight-bearing on diagnosis, admission and urgent in-situ percutaneous single-screw fixation. Prophylactic contralateral fixation is considered for high-risk patients (endocrine disease, very young, very obese). Avascular necrosis risk rises with weight-bearing and instability.
key_points: Obese pre-adolescent male with externally rotated limb and limp
Drehmann sign and Klein line disruption are diagnostic
Non-weight-bearing immediately on diagnosis
Urgent in-situ single-screw fixation; consider prophylactic contralateral fixation
explanation.pearls: When SUFE is confirmed radiographically, instruct strict non-weight-bearing in the clinic that same visit and arrange same-day orthopaedic admission - the rate of avascular necrosis rises substantially with continued ambulation in an unstable slip.

sources.label: AOA Position Statement: Paediatric hip emergencies 2019

options.rationale: SUFE is a surgical emergency; delaying definitive fixation risks progression and avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE 2019)
Anti-inflammatory and physiotherapy management is inappropriate for SUFE; mobilisation increases risk of further slip and AVN. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE 2019)

SUFE diagnosis on imaging requires immediate non-weight-bearing, admission and urgent in-situ percutaneous single-screw fixation to prevent progression and AVN; prophylactic contralateral fixation is considered for high-risk individuals. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE 2019)
Plain radiographs already confirm the diagnosis; MRI is not required and delays definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE 2019)
Perthes typically presents in younger children (4-8 years) and has a different radiographic pattern; bracing is incorrect management for SUFE. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE 2019)

explanation.summary: A previously well neonate who becomes encephalopathic on day two or three of life with hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis), no acidosis, no ketosis and ammonia greater than 200 micromol/L (often >500) is highly suspicious for a urea cycle disorder, most commonly ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency in males. Emergency management is to stop protein intake, reverse catabolism with high concentration IV dextrose with insulin if needed and intralipid, give ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate, arginine) per state metabolic team protocol, and arrange emergency haemodialysis when ammonia exceeds 400-500 micromol/L or fails to fall. Neurodevelopmental outcome correlates closely with duration and peak of hyperammonaemia.
key_points: Urea cycle disorders present with encephalopathy + respiratory alkalosis + hyperammonaemia + no ketosis
Stop protein, reverse catabolism with high IV dextrose and lipid
Sodium benzoate + sodium phenylbutyrate + arginine as scavengers
Haemodialysis at NH3 >400-500 micromol/L or rising
explanation.pearls: Trigger haemodialysis at ammonia 400-500 micromol/L or any rising trend despite scavengers rather than waiting for clinical deterioration - neurodevelopmental outcome correlates more tightly with duration of NH3 above 200 micromol/L than peak level.

options.rationale: Protein loading worsens hyperammonaemia in urea cycle disorders by adding nitrogen substrate; protein must be stopped acutely. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia 2020)
Each hour at ammonia >500 micromol/L worsens neurodevelopmental outcome; empirical treatment must begin before diagnostic confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia 2020)
Lactulose has no role in inborn-error hyperammonaemia; this is a urea cycle disorder, not portosystemic shunting. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia 2020)

Australian metabolic services manage acute hyperammonaemia by stopping protein, reversing catabolism with high-dose IV dextrose and lipid, giving ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate, arginine) and triggering haemodialysis at ammonia 400-500 micromol/L or rising; this is the time-critical sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia 2020)
Mannitol is reserved for raised intracranial pressure as adjunct in cerebral oedema and does not lower ammonia; it is not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia 2020)

explanation.summary: Croup is a clinical diagnosis based on barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor. Severity is assessed using the Westley score or by clinical features such as stridor at rest, recession, oxygen saturation and conscious state. All severities receive a single dose of oral or intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram (or prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram in mild cases). Severe croup with stridor at rest, significant recession, or hypoxia requires nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 for rapid relief. Recurrence after adrenaline within 4 hours warrants admission for observation.
key_points: Croup is a clinical diagnosis; bloods and imaging not required
All severities get corticosteroid (dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram is standard)
Severe croup adds nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000
Observe for at least 4 hours after adrenaline for rebound
explanation.pearls: For severe croup with stridor at rest in a child under five, give nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 immediately plus single dose oral or intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram and observe for 4 hours before discharge consideration.

options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest and recession warrants immediate nebulised adrenaline for rapid relief plus oral dexamethasone for sustained anti-inflammatory effect, with anaesthetic escalation pathway prepared. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

In severe croup with stridor at rest, nebulised adrenaline is required for rapid airway relief; prednisolone alone is acceptable in mild croup but not for severe presentations. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Croup, not epiglottitis, is the working diagnosis given barking cough, hoarse voice and stridor; Hib-vaccinated child without drooling makes epiglottitis very unlikely and antibiotics are not first-line therapy here. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Salbutamol is for lower airway bronchospasm and has no role in croup; heliox is at most an adjunct after first-line adrenaline and corticosteroid have been administered. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Humidified air has no evidence of benefit in croup; severe presentations require admission, corticosteroid and adrenaline, not discharge home. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: All febrile infants under 3 months require admission for full septic workup including blood culture, lumbar puncture and catheter or suprapubic aspirate urine, with empirical intravenous antibiotic cover for likely pathogens (commonly benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime, plus aciclovir if HSV is suspected). Bag urine is unsuitable for diagnosis because of contamination. UTI is the single most common serious bacterial infection in this age group and meningitis must be actively excluded. Risk stratification (Rochester, Step-by-Step) may be applied to selected well-appearing infants but is not used to defer workup at this age.
key_points: All febrile infants under 3 months: admit, full septic workup, empirical IV antibiotics
Catheter or suprapubic aspirate urine; bag urine not used
Lumbar puncture mandatory before empirical antibiotics where feasible
Empirical cover: benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime
explanation.pearls: For any febrile (>=38.0) infant under 3 months, admit and complete blood culture plus lumbar puncture plus clean-catch or suprapubic aspirate urine before commencing empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime rather than discharging on oral antibiotics.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

options.rationale: Febrile infants under 3 months are at high risk of bacteraemia and meningitis and require admission and full septic workup; bag urine has high contamination rates and is not used. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

options.rationale: Febrile infants under 3 months require full septic workup including blood cultures, lumbar puncture and catheter or suprapubic aspirate urine, with immediate empirical intravenous antibiotics pending cultures regardless of clinical appearance. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

options.rationale: Vaccine-associated fever does not explain fever above 38 degrees in a 6-week-old; serious bacterial infection must be excluded before attribution to vaccination. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

options.rationale: Empirical oral antibiotics for an infant under 3 months without lumbar puncture and blood cultures risks missing meningitis or bacteraemia; intravenous antibiotics in hospital are required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

options.rationale: Identifying a viral cause does not eliminate the risk of serious bacterial infection in this age group; full septic workup and empirical antibiotics are still required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a clinical diagnosis requiring fever for 5 or more days plus 4 of 5 principal features (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy at least 1.5 cm). Untreated disease leads to coronary artery aneurysm in around 25% of children. Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kilogram over 10 to 12 hours within 10 days of fever onset reduces aneurysm risk to under 5%. High-dose aspirin is given until afebrile and inflammatory markers normalise, then continued at low antiplatelet dose for 6 to 8 weeks pending echocardiogram. Corticosteroids are added in high-risk or IVIG-resistant disease.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis: fever >=5 days plus 4 of 5 principal features
IVIG 2 g per kilogram within 10 days of fever onset
Aspirin 30 to 50 mg per kilogram per day until afebrile, then low-dose
Echocardiography at diagnosis, 2 weeks and 6 to 8 weeks
explanation.pearls: When fever has lasted 5 or more days with 4 of 5 Kawasaki features, give IVIG 2 g per kilogram plus aspirin within day 10 of fever onset rather than awaiting coronary aneurysm formation; this reduces aneurysm risk from 25% to under 5%.

options.rationale: Delaying treatment until day 10 to await coronary artery aneurysm formation forfeits the window in which IVIG prevents aneurysms; treatment is recommended within 10 days of fever onset on clinical criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome presents with shock and a desquamating rash rather than the constellation of features here; failure to give IVIG within 10 days of fever onset increases coronary aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Kawasaki disease meeting at least five of five principal features warrants intravenous immunoglobulin within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk, plus high-dose aspirin until afebrile and CRP normalises. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Corticosteroids are an adjunct for IVIG-resistant disease or high-risk Kawasaki, not a substitute for IVIG as first-line therapy in standard presentations. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Discharge of suspected Kawasaki disease delays IVIG and risks coronary aneurysm formation; admission and treatment within 10 days of fever onset is the standard of care. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (HSP) is the most common childhood vasculitis. Around 30 to 50% develop renal involvement, usually within four weeks of onset, ranging from isolated haematuria through to crescentic glomerulonephritis. All affected children require weekly urinalysis and blood pressure measurement for at least 6 weeks. Microscopic haematuria alone is observed. Persistent or significant proteinuria, hypertension or rising creatinine requires urgent paediatric nephrology referral and consideration of biopsy and immunosuppressive therapy. Long-term renal follow-up is required because hypertension and CKD can develop years later.
key_points: 30 to 50% of HSP develop renal involvement, usually within 4 weeks
All require weekly urinalysis and BP for at least 6 weeks
Proteinuria, hypertension or rising creatinine = urgent nephrology referral
Long-term follow-up because hypertension and CKD can develop years later
explanation.pearls: For HSP with urine PCR >250 mg/mmol, hypertension above the 95th centile, or rising creatinine, refer to paediatric nephrology within 48 hours rather than continuing observation, because crescentic disease can progress rapidly to end-stage kidney disease.

options.rationale: Severe HSP nephritis with hypertension and rising creatinine cannot wait two weeks for review; urgent nephrology referral is essential to prevent permanent renal injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

Microscopic haematuria alone may be observed, but nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension and rising creatinine reflect severe nephritis requiring urgent specialist involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

Empirical corticosteroids without specialist guidance are inadequate for severe HSP nephritis; biopsy guides selection of pulsed corticosteroid plus other immunosuppressive agents. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

HSP nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension and rising creatinine constitutes severe nephritis warranting paediatric nephrology referral, biopsy consideration and immunosuppressive therapy in selected cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

Cyclophosphamide is an immunosuppressive option in crescentic HSP nephritis but only under specialist nephrology supervision after biopsy; it is not appropriate to commence in general practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

explanation.summary: Severe combined immunodeficiency presents with severe and recurrent infections (especially Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, persistent thrush and chronic diarrhoea), failure to thrive and lymphopenia for age, often with positive family history of early infant death. BCG given at birth can disseminate without local reaction. Immediate management is protective isolation, avoidance of live vaccines, avoidance of non-irradiated and non-CMV-negative blood products, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis and IVIG support, with urgent referral to a paediatric immunology centre for confirmation by lymphocyte subsets and genetic testing. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative and is most effective before significant infection burden.
key_points: Red flags: Pneumocystis pneumonia, thrush after 2 months, lymphopenia, family history
BCG can disseminate without local reaction
Avoid live vaccines and non-irradiated blood products
Definitive treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation
explanation.pearls: If a young infant has Pneumocystis pneumonia plus failure to thrive plus absolute lymphocyte count under 1.5 with positive family history, treat as SCID until disproven by placing in isolation, ordering only irradiated CMV-negative blood, withholding live vaccines and contacting paediatric immunology the same day for transplant pathway planning.

sources.label: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement
BMJ Best Practice: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency

options.rationale: Antifungal prophylaxis alone does not address the underlying immunodeficiency; immunology referral and definitive haematopoietic stem cell transplant planning are urgent. (Source: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement)
source_refs: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement

options.rationale: Rotavirus and MMR are live vaccines and are absolutely contraindicated in suspected SCID due to risk of disseminated vaccine-strain infection. (Source: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement)
source_refs: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement

options.rationale: Non-irradiated blood in SCID can cause fatal transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease; only irradiated CMV-negative blood products are used. (Source: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement)
source_refs: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement

options.rationale: Three serious infections including Pneumocystis pneumonia, failure to thrive, lymphopenia and family history are red flag features for primary immunodeficiency, not normal variation. (Source: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement)
source_refs: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement

options.rationale: The clinical and family pattern, lymphopenia, Pneumocystis pneumonia and BCG-without-reaction strongly suggest severe combined immunodeficiency; live vaccines and non-irradiated blood products risk graft-versus-host disease, and definitive treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. (Source: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement)
source_refs: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement

explanation.summary: Paediatric asthma maintenance should be stepped down once control has been sustained for at least 3 months on the current regimen. The typical approach is to halve the ICS dose while preserving the regimen architecture, then reassess at 2 to 3 months. Complete cessation of preventer therapy is reserved for children who have remained on the lowest dose with excellent control for at least 12 months. Spirometry, symptom diaries, and reliever frequency are all useful objective markers when titrating.
key_points: Step-down trialled after at least 3 months of sustained well-controlled asthma
Halve ICS dose rather than removing LABA partner first when on combination
Review at 2 to 3 months with spirometry and symptom assessment
Maintain a written asthma action plan throughout any step-down
explanation.pearls: In a child on low-dose ICS-LABA with sustained control for at least 3 months, the recommended step-down is to halve the ICS-LABA dose while keeping twice-daily dosing intact, then reassess at 3 months before considering further reduction.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - Asthma in Children
BMJ Best Practice - Asthma in Children

options.rationale: Switching to a higher-equivalent-dose ICS as a single agent escalates total ICS exposure and is the opposite of step-down in a child with sustained control. Fluticasone 250 micrograms twice daily is a high paediatric dose by Australian conventions. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook - Children)

Prolonged continuation of an ICS-LABA in a child with sustained excellent control unnecessarily exposes him to growth velocity effects and adrenal suppression risk. After 3 months of stable control, step-down should be actively trialled rather than deferred. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook - Children)

Abrupt cessation of preventer therapy in a child with confirmed asthma risks loss of control and exacerbation. SABA-only therapy is no longer recommended for any asthma above intermittent severity given the mortality signal in studies such as SABINA. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook - Children)

Montelukast is less effective than ICS for paediatric asthma control and carries a TGA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric adverse effects. It is not a recommended step-down from a well-tolerated ICS-LABA in a child with confirmed responsive disease. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook - Children)

After at least 3 months of well-controlled asthma on a low-dose ICS-LABA, step-down by approximately 50% is appropriate, with review at 2 to 3 months to confirm sustained control. Halving the daily ICS dose while maintaining twice-daily dosing is the recommended step-down for paediatric stable asthma. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook - Children)

explanation.summary: Initial management of paediatric DKA in Australia favours cautious fluid resuscitation due to the well-documented risk of cerebral oedema. A 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 to 60 minutes is the standard initial step when there is clinical dehydration without shock. Insulin is commenced at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour around 1 to 2 hours after fluids begin to avoid rapid glucose drops. Potassium is added to ongoing fluids once urine output is established and serum potassium is known.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 to 60 minutes in non-shocked paediatric DKA
Insulin infusion commenced 1 to 2 hours after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour
Bicarbonate restricted to life-threatening hyperkalaemia or pH below 6.9 with shock
Cerebral oedema risk peaks 4 to 12 hours into treatment, especially in new-onset diabetes under 5 years
explanation.pearls: In paediatric DKA the initial 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus is given over 30 to 60 minutes, not as a rapid push, and insulin is deliberately delayed by 1 to 2 hours to lower the risk of cerebral oedema.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines - DKA

options.rationale: Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia or pH below 6.9 with cardiovascular compromise. It paradoxically worsens intracellular acidosis and increases cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

A 20 mL/kg rapid bolus exceeds the cautious volume recommended for paediatric DKA and is associated with increased cerebral oedema risk in this age group. Insulin is also typically commenced 1 to 2 hours after fluids are started, not concurrently with the initial bolus. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

A clinically dehydrated child with venous pH 7.18 and tachycardia requires an initial resuscitation bolus, not maintenance-only fluid. Waiting for further electrolytes to act would worsen her acidosis and perfusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

Half-normal saline with dextrose is the typical rehydration fluid AFTER the initial resuscitation bolus and once glucose has fallen, not the first-hour resuscitation choice. Starting dextrose immediately at glucose 32 mmol/L is also inappropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

Australian paediatric DKA guidance recommends a cautious initial resuscitation bolus of 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 to 60 minutes for a child with clinical dehydration but without shock, given the risk of cerebral oedema with aggressive fluid loading. Perfusion is reassessed before any further bolus. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease must be considered in any infant with prolonged unexplained fever, even when only two or three classical features are present. Supportive laboratory criteria include CRP above 30, ESR above 40, platelets above 450, albumin below 30, ALT elevation, and sterile pyuria. BCG site reactivation is a highly suggestive sign in Australian infants. Treatment with immunoglobulin within 10 days of fever onset cuts coronary aneurysm rates from around 25% to under 5%.
key_points: Infants under 12 months have the highest coronary aneurysm risk and atypical phenotype
Five supportive labs convert a two-feature infant into a treatable incomplete Kawasaki case
Immunoglobulin 2 g/kg single infusion plus high-dose aspirin is the Australian standard
BCG site reactivation is a useful Australian-specific clinical clue
explanation.pearls: In an infant under 12 months with fever for 5 or more days and 2 to 3 classical features, immunoglobulin 2 g/kg should be given within the first 10 days of fever to bring coronary aneurysm risk from around 25% down to under 5%.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement - Diagnosis Treatment and Long-term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.rationale: Infants under 12 months frequently present with incomplete Kawasaki phenotype and have the highest risk of coronary artery aneurysm. With prolonged fever, BCG site reactivation, sterile pyuria, hypoalbuminaemia and thrombocytosis, treatment must not wait for full clinical criteria. Echocardiography defines baseline coronary status while immunoglobulin reduces aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Coronary aneurysm risk rises sharply after day 10 of untreated fever in infants, and this child is on day 8 already. Watchful waiting in this high-risk demographic is dangerous when supportive laboratory features of incomplete Kawasaki are present. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Broad-spectrum antibiotics do not treat Kawasaki disease and delay definitive immunoglobulin therapy. Two courses of amoxicillin have already failed to defervesce; the laboratory pattern is inflammatory, not bacterial. Doxycycline is also contraindicated under 8 years for non-life-threatening indications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Corticosteroids may be added to immunoglobulin in selected high-risk Kawasaki cases but are not first-line monotherapy in Australia. Steroid-only treatment misses the proven aneurysm-protective effect of immunoglobulin. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

There are no features of meningoencephalitis, and the clinical and laboratory picture is dominated by systemic inflammation with mucocutaneous signs. Aciclovir and lumbar puncture do not address the leading diagnosis and delay immunoglobulin therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Anti-c is a clinically significant non-D Rh antibody capable of causing severe haemolytic disease of the newborn. Cord DAT positivity, early jaundice within 24 to 36 hours, and rapid rise of bilirubin warrant intensive phototherapy and pre-emptive exchange preparation. The Australian phototherapy and exchange thresholds are age-in-hours and gestation-adjusted, with haemolysis lowering the trigger by approximately 35 micromol/L. Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 to 1 g/kg may also be considered as an adjunct in isoimmune haemolysis approaching exchange thresholds.
key_points: Anti-c can cause severe haemolytic disease equivalent in severity to anti-D
Phototherapy and exchange thresholds are lowered by approximately 35 micromol/L when haemolysis is confirmed
Intensive multi-light phototherapy delivers higher irradiance than single-bank
Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 to 1 g/kg can reduce the need for exchange in isoimmune cases
explanation.pearls: In confirmed isoimmune haemolytic jaundice approaching the exchange line, intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 to 1 g/kg given alongside intensive phototherapy reduces the need for exchange transfusion by more than 50%.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-c in Pregnancy
NICE NG98 - Jaundice in Newborn Babies under 28 Days

options.rationale: Discharging a term infant with confirmed isoimmune haemolysis and bilirubin 318 micromol/L at 28 hours risks rapid kernicterus. The trajectory of antibody-driven haemolysis is unpredictable and demands inpatient management. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Serum bilirubin of 318 micromol/L at 28 hours of age in a term infant with confirmed isoimmune haemolysis crosses the intensive phototherapy threshold on the Australian gestational-age-adjusted graph and approaches the exchange line. Anti-c is a clinically significant antibody causing haemolytic disease similar in pattern to anti-D. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Conventional single-light therapy is insufficient when bilirubin is approaching the exchange threshold with active haemolysis. Intensive multi-light phototherapy delivers more irradiance and is appropriate for high-risk haemolytic jaundice. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Phenobarbital is not an accepted treatment for established neonatal haemolytic jaundice in Australia. The infant needs immediate light therapy and possibly exchange, not enzyme induction. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Once total serum bilirubin has confirmed a level crossing the phototherapy threshold in a high-risk infant, treatment must commence immediately. Transcutaneous values are unreliable above 250 micromol/L and after phototherapy starts. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Brief resolved unexplained events are stratified into lower and higher risk based on age, gestation, episode features, and prior medical history. Lower-risk infants must be over 60 days, term, with a single episode under 1 minute, and no concerning history or examination. All infants under 60 days automatically fall into the higher-risk group regardless of how well they appear. Higher-risk infants warrant a period of monitored observation, paired saturations, glucose, ECG, and sometimes admission for further workup.
key_points: Age under 60 days is an automatic higher-risk criterion in BRUE
Lower-risk discharge requires age over 60 days, term gestation, single episode under 1 minute, normal exam, no prior BRUE
Higher-risk infants need monitored observation for at least 4 hours plus ECG and paired saturations
Family CPR education and clear safety-net advice are part of every BRUE disposition
explanation.pearls: Any infant under 60 days with a brief resolved unexplained event is automatically higher-risk by Australian and AAP definitions and needs at least 4 hours of monitored observation, regardless of how well they look in the emergency department.

options.rationale: A well infant without fever, lethargy, or focus does not require empiric sepsis treatment based on a single brief episode. Routine LP and broad antibiotics are not part of BRUE evaluation. (Source: RCH CPG: BRUE)

Lower-risk BRUE discharge applies only to infants over 60 days who meet all low-risk criteria. This 6-week-old infant does not qualify regardless of how reassuring the current examination appears. (Source: RCH CPG: BRUE)

Although her episode meets brief resolved unexplained event criteria, she is under 60 days old, which automatically places her in the higher-risk category and warrants a period of monitored observation. A 4-hour observation period with cardiorespiratory monitoring is the recommended minimum in Australian paediatric emergency protocols. (Source: RCH CPG: BRUE)

Outpatient EEG without admission is not appropriate for an under-60-day infant with an unexplained event. The yield of unprovoked EEG is low and observation in the higher-risk group should be inpatient. (Source: RCH CPG: BRUE)

Holter monitoring is not the standard first investigation for BRUE in the absence of suspected arrhythmia or family history of long QT. The age-based higher-risk classification mandates inpatient monitoring, not outpatient cardiology. (Source: RCH CPG: BRUE)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the commonest cause of hospitalisation in infants under 12 months and is managed almost entirely with supportive care. AU paediatric guidance frames admission decisions around hypoxia, feeding adequacy, and work of breathing rather than imaging or laboratory testing. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics are not recommended in routine bronchiolitis because the underlying pathology is mucosal oedema and debris rather than bronchospasm or bacterial infection. The shift in oxygen target from 94% to 90% (RCH target) in recent AU guidelines was driven by evidence that the lower threshold reduces length of stay without increasing safety events.
key_points: SpO2 90% (RCH target) in room air is the AU admission threshold for bronchiolitis
Feeding under 50% of usual or significant work of breathing also mandates admission
Bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics have no routine role
Nasogastric feeds and minimal handling are preferred over IV fluids when tolerated
explanation.pearls: RCH CPG sets bronchiolitis oxygen target at 90% (RCH target) and admits feeds below 50% of normal; bronchodilator trials add no value under 12 months.

options.rationale: AU paediatric guidance is to admit infants with bronchiolitis when SpO2 is below 90% (RCH target) in room air or feeding is below 50% of normal; oxygen is titrated to maintain SpO2 90% (RCH target) and hydration is supported by nasogastric or small-volume oral feeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Bronchodilators are not recommended in infants under 12 months with bronchiolitis as the wheeze reflects small-airway oedema rather than smooth-muscle bronchospasm; trials show no meaningful response. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Inhaled corticosteroids have no role in acute bronchiolitis and do not modify illness duration; a primary-care review at 48 hours would also miss the existing hypoxia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
Hypertonic saline shows inconsistent benefit and is not part of routine AU paediatric care; oral corticosteroids do not alter outcomes in viral bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Routine antibiotics are not indicated as bronchiolitis is viral; bacterial co-infection rates are low and discharge with hypoxia is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Croup is a clinical diagnosis based on the barking cough and stridor in a young child following a viral prodrome. AU paediatric guidance recommends a single dose of oral dexamethasone for all severities, including mild, because it reduces symptom duration, return visits and need for adrenaline. Nebulised adrenaline is added for moderate to severe disease, defined by stridor and recession at rest. Imaging is not required and may worsen distress.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg per kg orally is given for all severity grades of croup
Mild croup is defined by no stridor and no recession at rest
Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate/severe croup or impending respiratory failure
Antibiotics have no role unless there is suspicion of bacterial tracheitis
explanation.pearls: AU paeds dose of dexamethasone in croup is 0.15 mg per kg orally as a single dose; observe until stridor at rest settles (typically 1-2 hours) before discharge if mild.

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate to severe croup with stridor and recession at rest; this child is mild with no rest stridor. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

A single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg per kg is recommended for all severities of croup, including mild, and reduces re-presentation; observation of around until stridor at rest settles (typically 1-2 hours) before discharge confirms stability. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Humidified air has no evidence base in croup; discharge without dexamethasone misses an opportunity to reduce illness duration and re-presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Imaging is not required to diagnose croup or exclude epiglottitis in a settled child; the clinical picture is diagnostic and imaging may distress and decompensate the airway. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Croup is viral and antibiotics are not indicated; this also omits dexamethasone which is the only proven therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis with peak incidence in children under 5; untreated, around a quarter develop coronary artery aneurysms. The first-line therapy is intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg given within day 10 of fever combined with aspirin. IVIG resistance, defined as persistent or recrudescent fever 36 hours after IVIG, occurs in 10 to 20% and significantly increases aneurysm risk; AU guidance recommends a second IVIG dose plus pulsed methylprednisolone in this scenario, with infliximab as third-line. Echocardiographic surveillance is repeated at 2 and 6 weeks regardless of initial findings.
key_points: IVIG resistance = persistent or recurrent fever 36 hours after first IVIG
Coronary artery involvement at baseline raises the threshold for prompt second-line therapy
Second-line = repeat IVIG 2 g/kg plus IV methylprednisolone in AU
Infliximab is reserved for third-line when steroids and repeat IVIG fail
explanation.pearls: Persistent fever beyond 36 hours after IVIG 2 g per kg in Kawasaki defines resistance and warrants repeat IVIG plus IV methylprednisolone in Australia.

options.rationale: Persistent fever and CRP at 36 hours after IVIG defines IVIG resistance in Kawasaki disease and warrants prompt second-line therapy as coronary aneurysm risk rises. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Aspirin dose adjustment does not address IVIG resistance; second IVIG or corticosteroid is required to reduce ongoing vasculitis and aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Cultures should be drawn but the clinical picture meets Kawasaki criteria with documented coronary changes; antibiotics alone do not treat the underlying vasculitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

IVIG resistance is defined as persistent or recurrent fever 36 hours after the first IVIG dose; the AU recommendation is a second IVIG dose at 2 g per kg with methylprednisolone, given the documented coronary involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Clopidogrel monotherapy is not appropriate and oral prednisolone alone does not match the second-line evidence base for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki with coronary involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management balances correction of dehydration and acidosis against the catastrophic risk of cerebral oedema, which carries 20 to 25% mortality. Fluid resuscitation beyond an initial 10 mL per kg bolus is gradual: total deficit plus maintenance over 48 hours, with frequent neurological observations. Insulin is started after at least 1 hour of fluids at a low rate; bicarbonate, rapid sodium swings, and excessive fluid administration are independent risk factors for cerebral oedema. Dextrose is added when glucose falls toward 14 to 17 mmol/L to allow ongoing insulin infusion without hypoglycaemia.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg only unless shocked; further boluses raise cerebral oedema risk
Deficit replaced over 48 hours, not 24, in paediatric DKA
Insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h started 1 hour after fluids
Bicarbonate is generally avoided
explanation.pearls: AU paediatric DKA: 5 to 7% deficit replaced over 48 hours with saline+KCl; insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h started after 1 hour, bicarbonate avoided.

options.rationale: Aggressive bolusing beyond initial resuscitation increases cerebral oedema risk in paediatric DKA; replacement fluid is calculated and given more slowly. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guideline)
Insulin is started 1 to 2 hours after fluids in paediatric DKA to allow for circulating volume restoration and to reduce the risk of cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Bicarbonate is associated with worsened cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA and is reserved for severe acidaemia with haemodynamic instability after appropriate fluid resuscitation. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guideline)
Dextrose is added only when blood glucose falls below 14 to 17 mmol/L; switching prematurely worsens hyperglycaemia and delays acidosis correction. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guideline)
