AU paediatric DKA guidance replaces an assumed deficit (5 to 7% for moderate, up to 10% for severe) over 48 hours alongside maintenance using saline with potassium once urine output established; insulin starts at 0.05 to 0.1 units per kg per hour after 1 hour to reduce cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for over 90% of paediatric chronic constipation and is managed with a disimpaction phase followed by maintenance. AU paediatric guidance recommends oral macrogol with electrolytes as first-line for both phases; disimpaction uses escalating daily doses over 3 to 7 days then steps down to a maintenance dose titrated to one soft motion per day. Behavioural toileting after meals (using the gastrocolic reflex) and stool diaries support adherence. Red flags for organic causes (delayed meconium, failure to thrive, abdominal distension) prompt specialist referral.
key_points: Oral macrogol is first-line for disimpaction and maintenance
Overflow soiling indicates impaction and mandates disimpaction first
Senna is added as a second agent if macrogol alone is insufficient
Red flags for Hirschsprung include delayed meconium and infantile onset
explanation.pearls: Macrogol disimpaction at escalating daily doses over 3 to 7 days followed by maintenance dosing is the AU first-line paediatric constipation strategy.

options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease typically presents in infancy with delayed meconium and abdominal distension; manometry referral is not first-line for a 5-year-old with classic functional constipation. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Diet alone is insufficient when impaction is present and overflow soiling is occurring; pharmacological disimpaction is required first. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Oral macrogol is preferred over enemas in children because of acceptability and equal efficacy; phosphate enemas have a small risk of electrolyte disturbance. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Functional constipation with faecal impaction and overflow soiling is treated with oral macrogol disimpaction over 3 to 7 days followed by maintenance dosing, alongside toileting and behavioural advice. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Stimulant laxatives are used in addition to macrogol when response is poor; they are not first-line monotherapy and skipping disimpaction perpetuates overflow. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Adolescent self-harm and suicidality is assessed across intent, plan, means, prior attempts, mental disorder, and protective factors. A specific plan with cached means, particularly paracetamol, and prior self-harm with limited treatment response confers high acute risk that exceeds community management. AU paediatric guidance supports inpatient admission with urgent specialist review (CAMHS/CYMHS) and concrete means-restriction. Safety contracts have no evidence base and have been replaced by collaborative safety planning involving the young person, family, and clinical team.
key_points: Cached method (especially paracetamol) raises acute risk substantially
Verbal safety contracts have no evidence and are not used
Inpatient admission is appropriate for high-risk plans with limited community supports
Means restriction is a core part of every disposition
explanation.pearls: Cached paracetamol with a written plan in an adolescent with prior self-harm meets RCH criteria for inpatient admission and urgent CYMHS review.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

options.rationale: Active suicide plan with method, cached tablets, and limited treatment response is not adequately mitigated by community safety planning alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

options.rationale: Increasing antidepressant dose without acute assessment misses the urgency of a planned ingestion and provides inadequate immediate safety. (Source: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

options.rationale: Adolescents often minimise on direct questioning; basing admission on second-interview disclosure underestimates risk after a concrete plan with cached means. (Source: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

options.rationale: Verbal contracts of safety lack evidence and are no longer recommended; phone follow-up after 72 hours does not address acute risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

options.rationale: Concrete plan, cached means, repeated self-harm and inadequate antidepressant response warrant inpatient admission for safety and urgent CYMHS review with collaborative means restriction planning before discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

explanation.summary: Acute viral gastroenteritis is one of the commonest paediatric ED presentations. AU paediatric guidance recommends oral rehydration solution as first-line for mild to moderate dehydration, delivered as small frequent volumes totalling around 50 mL per kg over 4 hours, with clinical reassessment. Nasogastric ORS is preferred over intravenous fluid if oral intake fails, as IV access is more invasive and not superior. Antiemetics are not routine; ondansetron is reasonable when vomiting prevents ORS uptake.
key_points: ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours is first-line for mild to moderate dehydration
Nasogastric ORS precedes IV fluid in failed oral trials
Single dose ondansetron may rescue persistent vomiting
Gut rest and dilute juice are not routine
explanation.pearls: RCH CPG: 50 mL per kg ORS over 4 hours in frequent small volumes is the AU paediatric standard for mild to moderate dehydration.

options.rationale: Mild to moderate dehydration is managed with oral rehydration solution at 50 mL per kg over 4 hours in frequent small volumes; clinical reassessment guides escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
IV rehydration is reserved for failed oral or nasogastric trial, shock, persistent vomiting, or severe dehydration; jumping to IV violates the AU stepwise approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
Bolusing without first trialling oral or nasogastric ORS in a non-shocked child is not the AU first step and exposes the child to cannulation unnecessarily. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Ondansetron is reasonable for persistent vomiting, but routine admission irrespective of response is unnecessary if oral intake resumes; AU guidance favours discharge with ORS once tolerance returns. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
Gut rest is not recommended in paediatric gastroenteritis; dilute apple juice has slightly higher relapse compared with structured ORS in moderate cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Childhood asthma management follows a stepwise escalation guided by symptom frequency, reliever use, night waking and prior flares. Children under 12 starting at low-dose ICS who remain poorly controlled despite adherence and good technique are stepped up to medium-dose ICS (typically by doubling), with reassessment at 4 to 6 weeks. Add-on LTRA, fixed combination ICS-LABA, and biologics are subsequent options. Salbutamol use 3 or more days a week or night waking once a week or more indicates poor control.
key_points: Low-dose ICS to medium-dose ICS is the preferred first step in children
MART is not routinely used in children under 12 in Australia
Reliever use 3+ days/week or nocturnal cough = poor control
Always recheck technique and adherence before escalation
explanation.pearls: AU Asthma Handbook in children under 12: double low-dose ICS first before MART or biologics; review at 4 to 6 weeks.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Add-on LTRA is an option for partial control but the AU paediatric preferred next step in children with poor control on low-dose ICS is to increase ICS or add LABA above age 5. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: In children with poor symptom control on low-dose ICS the AU preferred step is to double the ICS to medium dose with technique recheck and review at 4 to 6 weeks. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: MART is established in adolescents and adults but not the AU preferred approach in children under 12; consider combination ICS-LABA in fixed dosing when escalation is needed. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Stopping preventer in poorly controlled asthma is unsafe; oral steroid courses do not replace ongoing preventer therapy. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Omalizumab is reserved for severe IgE-mediated asthma uncontrolled on high-dose ICS plus LABA in specialist clinics; this is premature at low-dose ICS. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: Henoch Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) typically affects children under 10 with a triad of purpura, arthritis and abdominal pain; renal involvement develops in around a third and largely declares within 6 months. AU paediatric guidance is weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first month, fortnightly to 3 months, and monthly to 6 months. New or persistent proteinuria, hypertension, or rising creatinine triggers urgent paediatric nephrology referral for UPCR, eGFR, and biopsy consideration. Long-term proteinuria and hypertension are managed with RAAS blockade.
key_points: Surveillance urinalysis and BP for 6 months catches late nephritis
New proteinuria + hypertension = urgent nephrology referral
Biopsy indications include crescentic disease and persistent significant proteinuria
Routine steroids do not prevent nephritis
explanation.pearls: Urinalysis surveillance for 6 months and a urine protein:creatinine ratio above 100 mg per mmol prompt urgent paediatric nephrology referral in HSP.

options.rationale: New significant haematuria and proteinuria with elevated blood pressure require urgent paediatric assessment, not routine follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)
Steroid initiation in HSP nephritis with proteinuria requires paediatric nephrology input on biopsy and treatment intensity; starting alone is not appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)
Persistent or new proteinuria with hypertension after HSP requires urgent paediatric nephrology referral; UPCR and eGFR guide need for renal biopsy and immunosuppression. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)
RAAS blockade may be used for persistent proteinuria but only after specialist assessment, biopsy where indicated, and confirmation of injury pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)
Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for biopsy-proven severe crescentic nephritis or rapidly progressive disease, not initial assessment of significant urinalysis change. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)

explanation.summary: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a complication of bacterial tonsillitis classically presenting with trismus, muffled voice, severe unilateral throat pain and uvular deviation. AU first-line management combines drainage (needle aspiration or incision and drainage) with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus metronidazole to cover oral anaerobes, switching to oral therapy once afebrile. Dexamethasone may be added to reduce pain and swelling. Tonsillectomy is reserved for recurrent disease or as an acute Quinsy tonsillectomy in selected cases. Airway compromise (drooling, stridor) is the cue to mobilise anaesthesia and ENT immediately.
key_points: Trismus + muffled voice + uvular deviation = peritonsillar abscess
Drainage + IV benzylpenicillin + metronidazole is first-line
Steroids are adjunctive, not substitutive
CT neck is reserved for deeper space concerns
explanation.pearls: Quinsy: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6 hourly plus metronidazole 500 mg 8 hourly, with bedside drainage by experienced ED or ENT clinician.

options.rationale: Established peritonsillar abscess requires drainage in addition to antibiotics; antibiotics alone rarely resolve a fluctuant collection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Imaging is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected deeper space involvement; ultrasound is already confirmatory and CT delays definitive drainage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Acute tonsillectomy is not first-line; needle aspiration or incision and drainage with intravenous antibiotics is the AU first step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) requires needle aspiration or incision and drainage by an ENT or experienced ED clinician, plus intravenous benzylpenicillin and metronidazole pending culture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Steroids are an adjunct to drainage and antibiotics, not a substitute; relying on steroids alone risks airway compromise as the abscess enlarges. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Paediatric atopic eczema is managed primarily with emollients applied liberally and topical corticosteroids matched to severity and site. Steroid phobia is a major barrier and education on safe potency-by-site (mild for face, moderate to potent for body), the fingertip unit, and duration is essential. Calcineurin inhibitors are second-line steroid-sparing for face/eyelids or maintenance. Bleach baths and intermittent proactive twice-weekly steroid application reduce flare recurrence in moderate disease. Systemic therapy and biologics are specialist domains.
key_points: Emollient + appropriate-potency steroid is first-line in flares
Moderate potency (methylprednisolone aceponate) suits non-facial flexural eczema
Topical calcineurin inhibitors are second-line steroid-sparing agents
Antihistamines and routine antibiotics have no flare-control role
explanation.pearls: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan supports methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% once daily for 1 to 2 weeks for moderate flexural flare, alongside generous emollient.

options.rationale: Dietary elimination is not first-line in eczema without IgE-confirmed food trigger and skipping topical steroid undertreats inflammation, perpetuating itch and infection risk. (Source: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan)

Topical calcineurin inhibitors are second-line steroid-sparing agents; for flare control in a steroid-naive flexural eczema, an appropriate-potency topical corticosteroid is first. (Source: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan)
High-potency steroids and wet wraps are reserved for severe or refractory disease; an appropriate-potency step is preferred and wet wrap is short-term only. (Source: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan)
Antihistamines do not treat the underlying inflammation; topical antibiotics are reserved for impetiginised eczema, not routine flares. (Source: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan)

AU paediatric guidance recommends thick emollients applied liberally plus a moderate-potency topical steroid such as methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% once daily to the flare areas for 1 to 2 weeks, with education to address steroid phobia. (Source: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan)

explanation.summary: Toddler iron deficiency anaemia frequently reflects excess cow's milk intake (over 600 mL daily reduces iron absorption and displaces iron-rich solids), low dietary iron, and ongoing physiological demand. AU paediatric guidance is oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg per kg daily for 3 months alongside dietary modification (cow's milk under 500 mL per day, iron-rich foods, vitamin C-rich drinks); recheck haemoglobin and ferritin at 4 to 6 weeks. Parenteral iron, transfusion and haematology referral are reserved for failures or red flags. Screening also covers maternal mental health and developmental milestones since chronic iron deficiency affects neurodevelopment.
key_points: Oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day is first-line
Cow's milk under 500 mL/day reduces ongoing displacement of iron-rich solids
Recheck Hb and ferritin at 4 to 6 weeks
Continue iron 3 months after Hb normalises to replete stores
explanation.pearls: RCH guidance: oral iron 3 to 6 mg per kg per day plus cow's milk under 500 mL per day; recheck Hb and ferritin at 4 to 6 weeks.

options.rationale: There is no clinical evidence of infection and a CRP of 4 is normal; antibiotics are not indicated and delay iron correction. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)
Parenteral iron is reserved for failed oral therapy or malabsorption; oral elemental iron is first-line in most paediatric cases with dietary modification. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)
Classic dietary iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler with high milk intake and no red flags does not require haematology referral or marrow biopsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

First-line treatment for paediatric iron deficiency anaemia is oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg per kg daily combined with dietary advice to limit cow's milk below 500 mL per day; recheck haemoglobin and ferritin at 4 to 6 weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)
Transfusion is reserved for severe symptomatic anaemia with cardiovascular compromise; this child is haemodynamically stable and responds to oral iron. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE) typically presents in obese adolescents between 10 and 15 years with chronic groin or referred knee pain and obligate external rotation on hip flexion. Bilateral disease occurs in up to 40% and risk factors include obesity and endocrine conditions (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency). Definitive management is urgent in situ pinning to prevent slip progression and avascular necrosis; the child is kept strictly non-weight bearing until surgery. Perthes disease affects younger children (4 to 10) and has a different radiographic pattern.
key_points: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion in an adolescent = SUFE until proven otherwise
Pain may refer to the knee and delay diagnosis
Make strictly non-weight bearing; urgent orthopaedic referral; AP + frog-leg lateral views
Up to 40% of cases are bilateral over time
explanation.pearls: Obligate external rotation in adolescent hip flexion is the cardinal SUFE sign; AP + frog-leg lateral X-rays confirm and surgery prevents progression.

options.rationale: Irritable hip rarely affects adolescents over 10 and typically resolves quickly; the obligate external rotation sign and risk profile make this presentation surgically urgent. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)
Active orthopaedic pathology with mechanical signs needs prompt surgical evaluation rather than deferred rheumatology assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)
Plain radiographs (AP and frog-leg lateral) are the imaging of choice; bone scan is not first-line and delays definitive surgical fixation. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)
Aspiration is indicated for suspected septic arthritis; this presentation is not febrile, CRP is low, and the obligate external rotation sign supports a mechanical aetiology. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

Obligate external rotation in an overweight adolescent with chronic groin pain referred to the knee is slipped upper femoral epiphysis until proven otherwise; non-weight bearing and urgent orthopaedic referral with AP and frog-leg lateral views is the AU standard to prevent slip progression and avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia is assessed against AU age-specific nomograms which plot serum bilirubin against postnatal hours; treatment lines are adjusted for gestational age and risk factors (haemolysis, sepsis, prematurity). Intensive phototherapy uses higher irradiance (>=30 microwatts per cm2 per nm) over a broad surface area and is monitored with repeat serum bilirubin at 6 to 12 hour intervals. Continued breastfeeding is encouraged; formula supplementation is reserved for inadequate feeding. Exchange transfusion remains the rescue therapy for severe hyperbilirubinaemia or acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
key_points: Use AU nomograms plotting bilirubin against postnatal age in hours
Intensive phototherapy is the first-line intervention at threshold
Continue breastfeeding during phototherapy
Repeat serum bilirubin every 6 to 12 hours during phototherapy
explanation.pearls: Serum bilirubin at threshold on the AU nomogram triggers intensive phototherapy plus repeat measurement at 6 to 12 hours; continue breastfeeding.

sources.label: NICE NG98 Jaundice in newborn babies

options.rationale: Term infants at 72 hours with serum bilirubin around the phototherapy threshold on AU nomograms require intensive phototherapy and a repeat serum bilirubin within 6 to 12 hours to monitor response. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)
Routine formula supplementation is not first-line in breastfed infants; phototherapy is the intervention and continued breastfeeding is encouraged. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)
Sunlight exposure is unsafe and ineffective; discharge near the phototherapy threshold without intervention risks acute bilirubin neurotoxicity. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)
Exchange transfusion is reserved for levels above the exchange threshold or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy; it is not first-line at this concentration. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)
Physiological jaundice peaks at days 3 to 5 but levels near the phototherapy threshold mandate intervention and serial monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Infants under 6 months with febrile urinary tract infection require admission for intravenous antibiotics in Australia due to the risk of bacteraemia and renal scarring. First-line cover is gentamicin (single daily dose) plus benzylpenicillin or ampicillin, transitioning to a narrow-spectrum oral agent once afebrile and sensitivities known, for a total course of 7 to 10 days. A renal tract ultrasound is recommended after the first febrile UTI under 6 months; further imaging (MCUG, DMSA) depends on the ultrasound findings and clinical course.
key_points: Febrile UTI under 6 months: admit for IV gentamicin + benzylpenicillin/ampicillin
Ultrasound urinary tract after first febrile UTI in this age group
Switch to oral once afebrile and sensitivities known
Beware enteric gram-negative resistance to trimethoprim
explanation.pearls: AU first-line for febrile UTI under 6 months: IV gentamicin + benzylpenicillin/ampicillin then oral switch on sensitivities for a 7 to 10 day total course.

options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with febrile UTI require intravenous antibiotic initiation in Australia until clinically stable and afebrile; oral monotherapy is unsafe at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

Febrile UTI in infants under 6 months requires admission and intravenous therapy; AU first-line is gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin or ampicillin pending culture and sensitivity. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

Ceftriaxone is reserved when first-line cover is inadequate or sepsis is severe; gentamicin and penicillin remain first-line for uncomplicated febrile UTI in young infants. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Trimethoprim has significant resistance and is not first-line for febrile UTI in young infants; the AU pathway requires IV therapy at this age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate tissue levels for pyelonephritis; it is reserved for older children with uncomplicated cystitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Severe bronchiolitis in infants is the commonest reason for paediatric ICU admission with viral illness. AU practice tiers respiratory support from oxygen via nasal prongs, to HFNC, to non-invasive ventilation (in selected sites), to intubation; HFNC failure markers include rising CO2, reducing GCS, increasing work of breathing, and tachycardia. Once HFNC failure is recognised, the treating team should escalate to PICU rather than uptitrate flow indefinitely. The paediatric retrieval service should be contacted early to facilitate inter-hospital transfer.
key_points: HFNC failure markers: rising CO2, reducing GCS, persistent tachypnoea and tachycardia
Escalation pathway is to NIV or intubation, not higher HFNC
Engage paediatric retrieval services early for inter-hospital transfer
Bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics have no role even in severe bronchiolitis
explanation.pearls: Rising pCO2 above 8 kPa with reducing GCS on HFNC in bronchiolitis is an indication for intubation and PICU transfer, not further HFNC uptitration.

options.rationale: HFNC has clearly failed with rising CO2 and altered mental state; further uptitration delays definitive ventilatory support. (Source: ANZICS Paediatric Respiratory Support Guidance)
Bronchodilators have no place in bronchiolitis and do not address the central failure of ventilation in this scenario. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Bronchiolitis with rising CO2, reduced mental state and HFNC failure has an indication for intubation and PICU transfer; AU paediatric retrieval services should be engaged early. (Source: ANZICS Paediatric Respiratory Support Guidance)

BiPAP can be a bridge in some centres, but with reducing GCS and ongoing rise in CO2 a controlled intubation is preferred before deterioration. (Source: ANZICS Paediatric Respiratory Support Guidance)
Steroids do not modify bronchiolitis and empirical antibiotics are not indicated without a clear focus; the immediate problem is ventilatory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Doctors in all Australian states and territories are mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse. Spiral or metaphyseal fractures, posterior rib fractures, multiple fractures of different ages, torn frenulum in non-mobile infants, and bruising in non-mobile infants are sentinel injuries that warrant immediate child protection involvement. Workup includes skeletal survey, head imaging (CT or MRI), ophthalmology fundoscopy, baseline coagulation studies, and consultation with the local child protection team. The threshold to report is reasonable suspicion, not proof.
key_points: Spiral femoral fracture in a non-mobile infant is a sentinel injury
Mandatory reporting threshold is reasonable suspicion, not proof
Workup: skeletal survey, head imaging, fundoscopy, coags
Specialist child protection team should be consulted early
explanation.pearls: Sentinel injuries (bruise/torn frenulum/spiral fracture in a non-mobile infant) trigger mandatory reporting AND a structured medical safeguarding workup.

options.rationale: Spiral femoral fractures in non-mobile infants are highly suspicious for inflicted injury; discharge without further safeguarding assessment is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)
Metabolic workup may be considered later but should not delay child protection processes; the clinical picture mandates immediate safeguarding action. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

The injury pattern in a non-mobile infant warrants immediate mandatory reporting and specialist child protection involvement, irrespective of subsequent family account. (Source: State Mandatory Reporting Legislation)

Spiral femur fracture in a non-mobile infant with additional bruising and torn frenulum is highly suspicious for non-accidental injury; the doctor is a mandatory reporter, the child requires admission with skeletal survey, ophthalmology fundoscopy review and child protection consultation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse; State Mandatory Reporting Legislation)
Orthopaedic management alone misses the child protection imperative; admission must include safeguarding processes including skeletal survey and statutory notification. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Newborn bloodspot screening for cystic fibrosis in Australia uses elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen followed by reflex CFTR genotyping; positive screens are referred to a tertiary CF centre for confirmatory sweat chloride testing. Multidisciplinary care begins in the neonatal period with respiratory clearance education, nutritional review, pancreatic insufficiency screening (faecal elastase), and CFTR modulator eligibility assessment. The diagnosis is confirmed when sweat chloride exceeds 60 mmol per L; values of 30 to 59 prompt repeat testing and ongoing follow-up. Newborn diagnosis improves nutritional and pulmonary outcomes substantially.
key_points: Sweat chloride >60 mmol/L confirms CF in symptomatic and screen-positive infants
Two CFTR mutations support but do not replace sweat test confirmation
Tertiary multidisciplinary care starts in the neonatal period
Faecal elastase guides need for pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy
explanation.pearls: Sweat chloride above 60 mmol/L confirms CF diagnosis in the AU newborn screening pathway, with multidisciplinary tertiary care from the neonatal period.

options.rationale: Confirmation of CFTR dysfunction is required regardless of mutation class; deferring to 6 months is unsafe and not consistent with the AU pathway. (Source: Royal Childrens Hospital CF Pathway)

PERT is initiated after demonstrating pancreatic insufficiency through faecal elastase plus clinical assessment; it is not the only step and does not confirm CF. (Source: Royal Childrens Hospital CF Pathway)
Genetic counselling is essential but presymptomatic CF management is the AU standard; deferring care worsens outcomes. (Source: Royal Childrens Hospital CF Pathway)
Two CFTR mutations support but do not yet replace a sweat test in the AU pathway; azithromycin prophylaxis is not initiated at 3 weeks. (Source: Royal Childrens Hospital CF Pathway)

Positive newborn screening with two CFTR mutations is confirmed by sweat chloride testing in an accredited CF centre, followed by tertiary multidisciplinary review including respiratory, gastroenterology, dietetics, physiotherapy, social work and genetic counselling. (Source: Royal Childrens Hospital CF Pathway)

explanation.summary: Tinea capitis in children is typically caused by Trichophyton or Microsporum species and presents with patchy alopecia, scaling, broken hair shafts and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by mycology of skin scraping and plucked hairs (more sensitive than scrape alone). Systemic therapy is required for hair-shaft penetration: oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for 4 to 8 weeks. Adjunctive antifungal shampoo reduces spore shedding and household transmission. Untreated disease may produce kerion (boggy inflammatory mass) or scarring alopecia.
key_points: Topical antifungals alone are inadequate for tinea capitis
Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for 4 to 8 weeks is the AU first-line
Antifungal shampoo (selenium sulfide or ketoconazole) reduces spread
Steroids alone risk tinea incognito
explanation.pearls: Tinea capitis requires oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for 4 to 8 weeks plus antifungal shampoo; topical alone is inadequate for hair-shaft penetration.

options.rationale: Tinea capitis requires systemic antifungal therapy (oral griseofulvin or terbinafine) for adequate hair-shaft penetration; an antifungal shampoo (selenium sulfide or ketoconazole) reduces spore shedding and household spread. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)
Topical antifungals alone do not penetrate the hair shaft and are inadequate as monotherapy for tinea capitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)
There is no evidence of impetiginisation; antibiotics do not treat dermatophyte infection and delay definitive antifungal therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)
Steroids may worsen tinea capitis (tinea incognito) by suppressing inflammation without treating the dermatophyte. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)
Untreated tinea capitis progresses to scarring alopecia and continues to transmit; treatment is required to prevent permanent hair loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Paediatric headache red flags that mandate urgent neuroimaging include progressive course, morning headache with vomiting, change in personality or school performance, focal neurological deficits, papilloedema, headache worsened by Valsalva, and headache in children under 3 years. MRI is preferred in stable patients due to better posterior fossa visualisation and no radiation; CT is reserved for acute deterioration or when MRI is unavailable. Lumbar puncture is deferred until imaging excludes a mass lesion.
key_points: Morning headache + vomiting + focal signs + papilloedema = same-day imaging
MRI is preferred unless acutely unstable or MRI unavailable
Avoid LP until imaging excludes a mass lesion
Outpatient imaging delays are unsafe in red-flag paediatric headache
explanation.pearls: RCH paediatric headache red flags: morning headache, vomiting, focal signs and papilloedema mandate same-day specialist review and imaging.

options.rationale: Daily morning headaches with vomiting, focal neurology and papilloedema are red flags incompatible with primary headache; starting prophylaxis without imaging is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

Progressive morning headache with vomiting, focal neurological deficit and papilloedema indicates raised intracranial pressure; AU paediatric guidance is urgent same-day specialist review and neuroimaging, preferring MRI over CT in stable patients. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
Outpatient delays of a week are unsafe for raised intracranial pressure red flags; same-day assessment is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
Triptans are inappropriate when red flags suggest secondary headache; they neither diagnose nor treat the underlying lesion. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
Lumbar puncture before imaging is contraindicated in suspected mass lesion due to coning risk; imaging precedes LP when red flags are present. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

explanation.summary: Paediatric anaphylaxis requires immediate intramuscular adrenaline at 10 micrograms/kg, drawn from a 1:1000 ampoule and delivered into the anterolateral mid-thigh through clothing if needed. For a 10 to 20 kg child the standard dose is 0.15 mg, escalating to 0.3 mg above 20 kg and 0.5 mg in adolescents and adults. Antihistamines, corticosteroids, and bronchodilators are second-line adjuncts only. After the first dose the child should remain supine with the legs elevated if hypotensive; the dose can be repeated every 5 minutes for ongoing or recurrent symptoms.
key_points: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg is first-line in paediatric anaphylaxis
Subcutaneous and intravenous routes are NOT the standard initial route
Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway or circulatory compromise
Repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes if no clinical response
explanation.pearls: For a 10 to 20 kg paediatric patient the ASCIA IM adrenaline dose is 0.15 mg from a 1:1000 ampoule into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes as needed.

options.rationale: Oral antihistamines treat cutaneous symptoms only and have no role as primary treatment in anaphylaxis; their use risks delaying adrenaline in a patient with airway and circulatory involvement. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

Corticosteroids have no demonstrated effect on the acute phase of anaphylaxis and do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions; their administration must not precede intramuscular adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg up to 0.5 mg into the anterolateral thigh is the immediate treatment in paediatric anaphylaxis; a 10 to 20 kg child receives 0.15 mg, with repeat doses every 5 minutes if no response. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

Subcutaneous adrenaline is no longer used in anaphylaxis because absorption is slow and unpredictable when peripheral vasoconstriction has occurred; intramuscular delivery into the thigh is essential. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

Nebulised bronchodilators are adjuncts for residual bronchospasm after adrenaline but must never be primary treatment when angioedema, urticaria, and circulatory features confirm systemic anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

explanation.summary: Weight-led faltering growth in a toddler with preserved height and head circumference points to inadequate intake or malabsorption rather than endocrine or neurological pathology. The history of bulky pale stools and post-gluten bloating raises coeliac disease as the leading organic differential, requiring tissue transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA to avoid missing selective IgA deficiency. The first-line work-up also captures iron deficiency, renal causes, occult urinary infection, and thyroid dysfunction. Endocrine, genetic, and imaging investigations are reserved for short stature, dysmorphism, or neurological features.
key_points: Weight crossing two centiles down with bulky pale stools suggests malabsorption
Coeliac screen needs tissue transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA
Baseline FBC, ferritin, UEC, TSH and urine MCS capture common organic causes
Endocrine and genetic workup is for short stature or syndromic features, not weight-led faltering growth
explanation.pearls: Always order total IgA with tissue transglutaminase IgA; an isolated tissue transglutaminase IgA in IgA-deficient children is falsely negative and misses coeliac disease.

options.rationale: An 18-month-old with weight faltering, bulky pale stools, and food avoidance after gluten introduction requires coeliac screening with tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA to exclude selective IgA deficiency, alongside baseline FBC, ferritin, UEC, TSH, and urine culture to capture the common organic causes. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering Growth)

Endocrine investigations are reserved for short stature with preserved weight or proportionate growth failure; in weight-led faltering growth with normal height and head, endocrine workup is low yield and delays nutrient-deficiency identification. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering Growth)

Neuroimaging is indicated when head circumference is abnormal or growth failure is paired with neurological signs; isolated weight crossing centiles with preserved head circumference does not warrant MRI. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering Growth)

Genetic testing is appropriate for proportionate short stature with dysmorphic features or developmental concern; this child has normal milestones and weight-led faltering growth, not syndromic short stature. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering Growth)

Dietetic input is part of management once organic causes are excluded; commencing energy supplements before excluding coeliac or other malabsorption risks masking the diagnosis without resolving it. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering Growth)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception in infants between 3 months and 3 years presents with episodic colic, vomiting, redcurrant jelly stool, and a sausage-shaped abdominal mass. Bedside ultrasound showing a target or doughnut sign confirms the diagnosis. After fluid resuscitation, image-guided pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction in the radiology suite with surgical standby is the standard of care, with surgery reserved for failed reduction, peritonitis, perforation, or a pathological lead point. Bilious vomiting is common with prolonged intussusception and does not by itself mandate primary laparotomy.
key_points: Target sign on USS confirms ileocolic intussusception
First-line management is fluid resuscitation then pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction
Surgery is reserved for failed reduction, peritonitis, perforation, or a pathological lead point
Recurrence rate after enema reduction is 5 to 10 percent
explanation.pearls: Even infants with established bilious vomiting and lethargy can usually be reduced by air enema if there is no peritonism; primary laparotomy is the exception, not the rule.

options.rationale: Ileocolic intussusception without peritonitis is treated with hydrostatic or pneumatic enema reduction after fluid resuscitation; success rates exceed 80 percent and surgical standby is required for failed reduction or perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Surgery is reserved for failed enema reduction, peritonitis, perforation, or a pathological lead point; primary laparotomy is unnecessary and exposes the child to avoidable risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Observation alone allows progression to bowel ischaemia and perforation; the child has confirmed ileocolic intussusception that requires active reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Antibiotics are not indicated for intussusception; treating presumed gastroenteritis misses the diagnosis and delays reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Ultrasound has confirmed the diagnosis; meal and follow through is not the diagnostic tool of choice and adds delay without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until imaging proves otherwise. Even in a well-appearing infant the diagnosis is time critical because volvulus can cause irreversible bowel necrosis within hours. The diagnostic investigation of choice is an upper gastrointestinal contrast study, which demonstrates the duodenojejunal flexure position and any corkscrew appearance of the duodenum. Concurrent management is nil by mouth, nasogastric drainage, intravenous fluids, and immediate referral to paediatric surgery. Plain films and abdominal ultrasound are adjuncts that do not exclude the diagnosis.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in the newborn equals malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise
Upper GI contrast study is the primary investigation
Even a well infant needs urgent imaging because volvulus progresses quickly
Initial care includes NBM, NG drainage, IV fluids and paediatric surgical referral
explanation.pearls: Bile is green. A normal abdominal exam in a green-vomiting neonate does not exclude volvulus. Move directly to the contrast study, not the AXR.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: A plain abdominal film cannot reliably exclude malrotation with midgut volvulus; relying on it risks missing an evolving volvulus that progresses to bowel necrosis within hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise; an upper GI contrast study is the diagnostic investigation of choice and must be expedited as delay risks irreversible bowel ischaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Cow's milk protein allergy does not present with bilious vomiting in the first week; trialling formula change delays the urgent diagnosis of a surgical cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Symptomatic antiemetic therapy without investigation is dangerous in any neonate with bilious vomiting; the diagnostic priority is to exclude volvulus by contrast study. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Doppler ultrasound of the SMA and SMV relationship may suggest malrotation but is operator dependent and is not the primary investigation; an upper GI contrast study remains the standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

explanation.summary: Prophylaxis is indicated in paediatric migraine when there are 4 or more attacks per month, significant school absence, or abortive failure. First-line options in Australia are pizotifen or propranolol, both started at low dose and titrated. Lifestyle interventions including regular sleep, hydration, meal timing, and screen-time review are essential adjuncts. Amitriptyline and topiramate are second-line and require closer monitoring for adverse effects. Imaging is reserved for red flags. Treatment success is measured by attack frequency, severity, and functional impact, not by symptom abolition alone.
key_points: Prophylaxis threshold in paediatric migraine is 4+ attacks per month or significant school absence
First-line agents are pizotifen and propranolol
Lifestyle measures are core, not optional adjuncts
MRI is for red flags only
explanation.pearls: Pizotifen 0.5 mg nocte titrated to 1.5 mg is a reasonable starting prophylactic in paediatric migraine; counsel about weight gain and somnolence.

options.rationale: Attack frequency above 4 per month with school absence meets the threshold for prophylaxis in paediatric migraine; ongoing acute therapy alone underservices her. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

MRI is indicated for red flags such as new neurological signs, morning vomiting, occipital location with neck pain, or rapidly escalating severity; routine prophylaxis decisions do not require imaging in the absence of red flags. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

Amitriptyline at 25 mg in an 11-year-old is an excessive starting dose with cardiac and anticholinergic risk; AU paediatric guidance favours pizotifen or propranolol first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
Triptans are appropriate adjunct abortive therapy in adolescents but do not address the frequency that drives school absence; prophylaxis is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

Paediatric migraine prophylaxis is indicated for 4 or more attacks per month or significant school absence; pizotifen 0.5 mg nocte plus lifestyle measures is an Australian first-line option, with review at 8 weeks for response and adverse effects. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

explanation.summary: Acute immune thrombocytopenia in children typically follows a viral illness and presents with isolated thrombocytopenia and cutaneous bleeding signs in a well-looking child. Spontaneous remission occurs in approximately 80 percent within 6 months. Management is conservative when bleeding is cutaneous only, regardless of platelet count, with bleeding precautions and avoidance of contact sports. Indications for pharmacological therapy include mucosal or major bleeding, with IVIG, corticosteroids, or anti-D as first-line options. Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding. Bone marrow examination is required only with atypical features such as cytopenias in other lineages or non-response to first-line treatment.
key_points: Paediatric ITP with cutaneous-only bleeding is observed, not treated
Pharmacological treatment is reserved for mucosal or major bleeding
Platelet transfusion is ineffective except in life-threatening bleeding
Bone marrow is needed only for atypical features or treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Platelet count alone does not drive treatment in paediatric ITP; bleeding severity does. A well child with petechiae and a count of 5 is still managed conservatively.

options.rationale: IVIG is reserved for clinically significant bleeding or platelet counts below 20 with mucosal bleeding; this child has cutaneous signs only and a count of 8 alone does not mandate IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

Corticosteroids are an alternative pharmacological treatment when intervention is needed but are not first-line in well-appearing children with cutaneous-only ITP. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

Routine bone marrow examination is not required in typical paediatric ITP with isolated thrombocytopenia and normal red and white cells; it is reserved for atypical features or non-response to first-line therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

Paediatric ITP with cutaneous-only bleeding is managed conservatively because spontaneous remission occurs in approximately 80 percent within 6 months; treatment is reserved for clinically significant bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)
Platelet transfusion is ineffective in ITP because transfused platelets are also destroyed, and it is reserved for life-threatening bleeding only. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

explanation.summary: Raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation in a child after head injury is identified by the Cushing reflex of hypertension and bradycardia, irregular respiration, falling GCS, anisocoria, and focal signs. Immediate care is airway protection through rapid sequence intubation, head-up 30 degrees, and a hypertonic saline 3 percent bolus, alongside expedited CT head and definitive neurosurgical care. Mannitol is an alternative osmotic agent but hypertonic saline is increasingly preferred in paediatric protocols. Hyperventilation is used only briefly as a temporising measure for herniation, and lumbar puncture is contraindicated.
key_points: Cushing reflex (hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing) signals impending herniation
Airway protection precedes osmotherapy
Hypertonic saline is increasingly preferred over mannitol in paediatric protocols
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated until imaging excludes mass effect
explanation.pearls: Head-up 30 degrees and 3 percent hypertonic saline 3 to 5 mL/kg is the immediate paediatric osmotherapy of choice; mannitol remains an alternative when sodium loading is contraindicated.

options.rationale: Falling GCS with anisocoria, the Cushing reflex of hypertension and bradycardia, and respiratory irregularity indicates raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation; standard care is RSI with head-up positioning, hypertonic saline 3 percent bolus, and urgent imaging with definitive neurosurgical care. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

Lumbar puncture in a patient with focal signs and likely raised intracranial pressure risks cerebral herniation and is absolutely contraindicated until imaging excludes mass effect. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

There is no fever, neck stiffness, rash, or history suggestive of meningitis; treating bacterial meningitis here delays the actual diagnosis of intracranial haemorrhage. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

Aggressive hyperventilation to low PaCO2 risks ischaemic injury through vasoconstriction; PaCO2 is normalised at 35 to 40 mmHg with brief targeted reduction only for impending herniation as a temporising measure. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

Mannitol may be used for raised intracranial pressure but is not the immediate single intervention; airway protection precedes osmotherapy and hypertonic saline is increasingly preferred in paediatric protocols. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

explanation.summary: Iron poisoning has five recognised phases: gastrointestinal in the first 6 hours, a latent phase from 6 to 24 hours, shock and metabolic acidosis from 12 to 48 hours, hepatic injury, and late gastrointestinal scarring. Activated charcoal does not bind iron and is not used. Whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol is the preferred decontamination when radio-opaque tablets remain in the gut. Serum iron at 4 to 6 hours guides deferoxamine therapy, with treatment initiated for serum iron above 90 micromol/L, shock, altered conscious state, or persistent acidosis. Even asymptomatic children with iron ingestion above 40 mg/kg require observation through the latent phase.
key_points: Activated charcoal does not bind iron
Whole-bowel irrigation is the decontamination of choice when tablets remain in the gut
Serum iron at 4 to 6 hours guides deferoxamine therapy
The latent phase from 6 to 24 hours masks deterioration; observe through it
explanation.pearls: A deferoxamine threshold of serum iron 90 micromol/L plus the trigger of shock or persistent acidosis covers nearly all cases; clinical state always trumps a borderline number.

options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not bind iron and adds no benefit while increasing aspiration risk; it has no role in iron poisoning. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Iron)

Deferoxamine is reserved for serum iron above 90 micromol/L taken 4 to 6 hours post ingestion, shock, altered conscious state, or persistent acidosis; empirical treatment is unnecessary in a well child with imaging visible tablets. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Iron)

Gastric lavage is not routinely used in iron overdose and risks aspiration and oesophageal injury; whole-bowel irrigation is the preferred decontamination when tablets remain visible. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Iron)

Iron ingestion above 40 mg/kg requires observation for 6 hours and a serum iron at 4 to 6 hours because the latent phase between gastrointestinal symptoms and shock can lull clinicians into a false reassurance. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Iron)

With residual radio-opaque tablets and ingestion above 40 mg/kg of elemental iron, polyethylene glycol whole-bowel irrigation clears the gut, while serum iron at 4 to 6 hours guides deferoxamine, which is started for iron above 90 micromol/L, shock, altered conscious state, or persistent acidosis. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Iron)

explanation.summary: Neuroblastoma is the commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood and arises from sympathetic neural crest tissue. It typically presents in children under 5 years with an abdominal mass that crosses the midline, distinguishing it from Wilms tumour which usually remains confined to one side. Periorbital ecchymoses or so called raccoon eyes reflect orbital metastases, while subcutaneous blueberry muffin nodules and bone marrow involvement complete the syndrome. Urinary catecholamines and MIBG scintigraphy are diagnostic. Treatment depends on stage and risk stratification, including INSS stage, MYCN amplification, and age. Low-risk disease may regress spontaneously, while high-risk disease requires multimodal therapy including surgery, chemotherapy, autologous stem cell transplant, and immunotherapy with anti-GD2.
key_points: Neuroblastoma crosses midline; Wilms typically does not
Bilateral periorbital ecchymoses without trauma signal orbital metastasis
Urinary catecholamines plus MIBG scintigraphy clinch the diagnosis
Risk-adapted management is determined by stage, MYCN, and age
explanation.pearls: Bilateral racoon eyes without trauma in a toddler plus an abdominal mass crossing midline equals neuroblastoma until proven otherwise; do not biopsy the kidney.

options.rationale: The mass crosses the midline and shows MIBG-avid metastases with elevated catecholamines, consistent with neuroblastoma not Wilms tumour; primary nephrectomy is the wrong operation. (Source: eviQ Paediatric Neuroblastoma)

The combination of abdominal mass, MIBG-positive skull deposits, and elevated catecholamines indicates metastatic neuroblastoma; corticosteroid trial for autoimmune cytopenia is inappropriate and delays oncology care. (Source: eviQ Paediatric Neuroblastoma)

Bilateral periorbital ecchymoses in the absence of clear trauma plus a fixed abdominal mass are red flags for metastatic neuroblastoma; reassurance and delay are unsafe. (Source: eviQ Paediatric Neuroblastoma)

The presentation of a midline-crossing abdominal mass with bilateral periorbital ecchymoses (raccoon eyes), MIBG-avid skull metastases, and elevated catecholamines is metastatic neuroblastoma; urgent oncology referral for tissue diagnosis, staging, and risk-adapted treatment is the standard of care. (Source: eviQ Paediatric Neuroblastoma)
Wilms tumour does not typically cross the midline, lacks MIBG avidity, and does not produce catecholamines; renal biopsy targets the wrong diagnosis. (Source: eviQ Paediatric Neuroblastoma)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA fluid management balances volume restoration against cerebral oedema risk. A single 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus is given only for circulatory compromise. Dehydration is estimated at 7 to 8 percent and replaced evenly over 48 hours alongside maintenance, with insulin started 1 hour after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h. Bicarbonate is contraindicated outside arrest.
key_points: Bolus only for shock; single 10 mL/kg dose then reassess
Deficit replaced over 48 hours, not 24
Insulin starts 1 hour after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h
Bicarbonate worsens outcomes in paediatric DKA
explanation.pearls: Australian APEG paediatric DKA protocol: 10 mL/kg saline bolus only if shocked, then maintenance plus 7 to 8 percent deficit over 48 hours, insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h starting 1 hour after fluids.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA

options.rationale: Aggressive 20 mL/kg boluses in non-shocked paediatric DKA increase cerebral oedema risk; bolus volumes are reserved for circulatory shock and given as 10 mL/kg with reassessment. (Source: APEG/RCH Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Australian paediatric DKA protocols use a single 10 mL/kg bolus only when perfusion is impaired, then estimate dehydration at 7 to 8 percent and replace the deficit evenly over 48 hours alongside maintenance to minimise cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG/RCH Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Large volume Hartmann boluses risk dilutional fall in osmolality and rapid bicarbonate correction with cerebral oedema; insulin started before intravascular volume restoration accelerates the osmotic shift. (Source: APEG/RCH Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Oral rehydration is inadequate in vomiting children with significant acidosis; intravenous access and controlled deficit replacement with insulin infusion are mandatory. (Source: APEG/RCH Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Bicarbonate is not indicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia or cardiac arrest; routine use worsens intracellular acidosis and increases cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG/RCH Paediatric DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe croup is defined by stridor at rest plus retractions or agitation. Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL gives rapid relief within 10 minutes lasting around 60 minutes, and oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg provides sustained corticosteroid effect. Children must be observed for 3 hours (RCH minimum) after-adrenaline because of potential rebound stridor before discharge can be considered.
key_points: Stridor at rest plus retractions = severe croup
Adrenaline acts in 10 minutes; effect wanes by 60 minutes
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO for severe disease
Observe 3 hours (RCH minimum) post-adrenaline for rebound
explanation.pearls: Severe croup: nebulised 1:1000 adrenaline 5 mL plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, observe 3 hours (RCH minimum) minimum because rebound stridor follows the 60-minute adrenaline window.

options.rationale: Oral dexamethasone is correct for mild to moderate croup, but severe croup with stridor at rest plus retractions warrants concurrent nebulised adrenaline for rapid relief. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Stridor at rest with retractions defines severe croup; nebulised adrenaline gives rapid relief lasting 30 to 60 minutes and a single corticosteroid dose extends effect, with mandatory observation post-adrenaline for rebound. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Bronchodilators target lower airway bronchospasm and have no benefit in viral laryngotracheitis where the obstruction is subglottic oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Empiric ceftriaxone with ENT is the pathway for suspected epiglottitis where the child is toxic, drooling, and sitting in tripod position; the barking cough and coryza here are typical viral croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Cochrane reviews show humidified air provides no benefit in croup and delays effective treatment; severe croup mandates adrenaline and steroid without delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Nephritis in HSP can present up to 6 months after the initial rash, and around one third of children develop urinary abnormalities. The Australian surveillance schedule includes weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first month, then monthly to 6 months, with a final review at 12 months. Persistent proteinuria, hypertension, or declining function trigger nephrology referral and potential biopsy.
key_points: Nephritis may appear up to 6 months after rash
Surveillance: weekly to 4 weeks, monthly to 6 months, then 12 months
Steroids do not prevent or treat nephritis prophylactically
Biopsy thresholds: nephrotic proteinuria, persistent significant proteinuria, or declining GFR
explanation.pearls: Even with normal initial urinalysis, HSP requires weekly BP and dipstick to 4 weeks then monthly to 6 months and review at 12 months because nephritis can present late.

sources.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Glomerular Diseases

options.rationale: Nephritis can present up to 6 months after initial rash even when urinalysis is initially normal; the recommended surveillance is weekly to 4 weeks then monthly to 6 months with a final review at 12 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Renal ultrasound is not part of routine HSP surveillance and does not detect early nephritis; urinalysis and blood pressure are the screening tools that pick up significant proteinuria first. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

A single 4-week urinalysis misses the delayed nephritis window; up to 30 percent develop renal involvement within 6 months and weekly then monthly surveillance is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)
Routine corticosteroids do not prevent nephritis or reduce long-term renal sequelae and are not justified solely to influence rash duration. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Biopsy is reserved for nephrotic-range proteinuria, persistent significant proteinuria over 4 weeks, or rapidly deteriorating function; isolated microscopic haematuria does not warrant invasive investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in well non-Indigenous Australian children over 2 years with unilateral disease and intact tympanic membrane is managed with analgesia and review at 48 hours. Antibiotics are reserved for children under 2, bilateral AOM, perforation with discharge, systemic illness, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander background, or failure to improve at 48 hours. When indicated the first-line agent is amoxicillin.
key_points: Watchful waiting suits non-toxic non-Indigenous unilateral AOM over 2
Amoxicillin first line when antibiotics indicated
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is second line for treatment failure or discharge
Antibiotics indicated in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children due to higher complication rates
explanation.pearls: Therapeutic Guidelines indications for immediate antibiotics in AOM: under 2 years, bilateral, perforation with discharge, systemic illness, immunocompromise, or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander background.

options.rationale: Routine immediate antibiotics are not first line in a non-toxic non-Indigenous child over 2 years with unilateral AOM and intact tympanic membrane; analgesia with 48-hour observation is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Otitis media)

Therapeutic Guidelines support a watchful-waiting approach with analgesia in well non-Indigenous children over 2 with unilateral AOM and intact tympanic membrane, reserving antibiotics for failure to improve at 48 hours, perforation, or systemic illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Otitis media)

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure after amoxicillin or perforation with discharge; first-line antibiotic when indicated is amoxicillin alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Otitis media)
Corticosteroids and decongestants have no demonstrated benefit in AOM and risk harm; analgesia is the cornerstone of supportive care. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Otitis media)
Tympanocentesis is not routine and is reserved for atypical, recurrent, or complicated cases not responding to standard care. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Otitis media)

explanation.summary: Complex febrile seizures are those lasting more than 15 minutes, recurring within 24 hours, or focal. A well child who returns to baseline requires investigation of the febrile source and a period of observation, but routine imaging, EEG, and anticonvulsant prophylaxis are not indicated. LP and imaging are reserved for clinical suspicion of meningitis, altered consciousness, focal neurology, or signs of raised ICP. Recurrence risk after first febrile seizure is about 30 percent overall.
key_points: Complex = under 15 min, recurrent in 24 h, or focal
Investigate source of fever; do not routinely image
LP only if clinically suspicious for meningitis or not back to baseline
No role for anticonvulsant prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Complex febrile seizure with full recovery and no focal signs: investigate the fever source, observe, and discharge with safety-netting. No routine CT, EEG, or anticonvulsants.

sources.label: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile Seizures

options.rationale: Routine CT and EEG are not indicated in a fully recovered well child with prolonged febrile seizure and no focal neurology, raised ICP signs, or persistent altered consciousness. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

A complex febrile seizure in a child who has fully returned to baseline without focal signs requires investigation of the febrile source and observation only; brain imaging and EEG are not routinely required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

Universal LP in children under 24 months is no longer supported; LP is indicated when meningitis is clinically suspected, when the child has not returned to baseline, or when pretreatment with antibiotics could mask features. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

Long-term anticonvulsant prophylaxis is not indicated for febrile seizures because the recurrence and subsequent epilepsy risk does not justify medication adverse effects. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

ICU admission and EEG monitoring are not indicated after a self-terminating febrile seizure in a child who has returned to baseline; this overtreats a benign syndrome. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants is managed primarily with supportive care: hydration via nasogastric or intravenous route as needed and oxygen titrated to maintain saturations above 92 percent. When low-flow oxygen is insufficient, heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min reduces escalation to ICU compared with standard oxygen (PARIS trial). Salbutamol, steroids, hypertonic saline, and antibiotics are not routinely recommended.
key_points: Saturations target above 92 percent
HFNC 2 L/kg/min reduces ICU escalation (PARIS trial)
No role for salbutamol, steroids, antibiotics in typical bronchiolitis
Hydration: NG or IV when feeds dropping
explanation.pearls: PARIS trial: heated humidified HFNC at 2 L/kg/min reduces ICU escalation in infant bronchiolitis when low-flow oxygen fails; saturations target above 92 percent.

sources.label: PARIS trial - High-flow oxygen therapy in infants with bronchiolitis

options.rationale: Hypertonic saline does not change duration of hospitalisation in bronchiolitis; rising oxygen requirement on low-flow nasal cannula indicates escalation to high-flow rather than nebuliser strategies. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Salbutamol has no demonstrated benefit in bronchiolitis under 12 months and is not recommended; the appropriate response is escalation of oxygen support. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Intramuscular adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis, not bronchiolitis; intubation may be needed later but is not the immediate next step before non-invasive escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min is the recommended escalation when low-flow oxygen fails to maintain saturations above 92 percent in moderate bronchiolitis; the PARIS trial demonstrated reduced escalation to ICU compared with standard oxygen. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Corticosteroids have no proven benefit in bronchiolitis under 12 months and should not be used routinely; rising oxygen requirement signals escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric functional constipation with faecal impaction requires disimpaction before maintenance. Escalating macrogol over 3 to 7 days is the first-line oral agent and avoids the risks of phosphate enemas. Maintenance dose macrogol is continued for months alongside scheduled toilet sits after meals, fibre and fluid optimisation, and reward systems. Stimulant laxatives are reserved for breakthrough. Red flags (delayed meconium, ribbon stools, sacral abnormality, faltering growth, abnormal lower limb neurology) warrant specialist work-up.
key_points: Disimpact first with escalating macrogol then maintain
Phosphate enemas carry hyperphosphataemia risk; avoid
Behavioural toileting after meals is essential
Red flags trigger specialist referral
explanation.pearls: Macrogol PEG with electrolytes escalating regimen is first-line disimpaction in paediatric functional constipation; do not skip disimpaction or overflow soiling will persist.

sources.label: NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN evidence-based recommendations on functional constipation

options.rationale: Hirschsprung presents in infancy with delayed meconium and tight rectum on PR; a 5-year-old with classic functional constipation and overflow soiling does not require surgical work-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Maintenance therapy without disimpaction in a child with palpable faecal loading risks ongoing overflow soiling and does not address the impacted faecal mass. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Stimulant laxatives have a role as add-on therapy, but they should not be used as monotherapy in impacted constipation, and disimpaction with osmotic laxatives is the first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Phosphate enemas carry hyperphosphataemia risk in children and are reserved for failed oral disimpaction; macrogol-based oral disimpaction is the standard first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Escalating macrogol (polyethylene glycol with electrolytes) is the recommended first-line disimpaction agent for paediatric functional constipation with faecal loading, with subsequent maintenance and behavioural toileting to prevent recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: IDMs, LGA, SGA and late-preterm infants are routinely screened for hypoglycaemia from 2 hours of age after a feed. The operational threshold in Australia is 2.6 mmol/L; below this in an asymptomatic infant, treat with feed plus 200 mg/kg buccal 40 percent dextrose gel and recheck in 30 minutes. Symptomatic hypoglycaemia or persistent low readings escalate to IV dextrose. Earlier glucose checks pick up physiological nadir at 1 hour and prompt unnecessary escalation.
key_points: Risk groups: IDM, LGA, SGA, late preterm, perinatal stress.
Screen at 2 h after first feed, then pre-feed during 12 to 24 h.
Threshold 2.6 mmol/L; gel 200 mg/kg + feed for asymptomatic.
IV 10 percent dextrose if symptomatic or refractory.
explanation.pearls: The 2.6 mmol/L threshold and 2-hour-after-feed timing are the most commonly missed numbers; buccal dextrose gel 200 mg/kg is given with a feed, never instead of it.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia in Neonates

options.rationale: Australian NHMRC and Queensland Clinical Guideline schedules for IDM and large-for-gestational-age neonates screen at 2 hours after a feed (not earlier, as transient nadir at 1 hour is physiological), then before subsequent feeds with an operational threshold of 2.6 mmol/L. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn Hypoglycaemia)

IDM and LGA neonates require glucose screening from 2 hours regardless of symptoms because severe asymptomatic hypoglycaemia is well documented in this population during the first 12 hours. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn Hypoglycaemia)

Immediate screening captures a physiological postnatal nadir and the 3.3 mmol/L threshold is not the Australian operational cut-off; routine intravenous dextrose without enteral feed trial is excessive in an asymptomatic feeding IDM. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn Hypoglycaemia)

Buccal dextrose gel is indicated when the screening glucose is below 2.6 mmol/L in an asymptomatic infant alongside a feed, not as universal prophylaxis irrespective of measured glucose. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn Hypoglycaemia)

Prophylactic intravenous dextrose is reserved for symptomatic infants or those failing to respond to enteral and buccal dextrose strategies; routine admission separates mother and baby unnecessarily in an asymptomatic IDM. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Pyloric stenosis classically presents at 3 to 8 weeks with progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting in a hungry feeder, palpable olive, and hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Ultrasound is the first-line confirmatory test in Australia using thresholds of muscle thickness at least 3 mm and channel length at least 15 mm. Management is resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline plus potassium to correct the alkalosis before Ramstedt pyloromyotomy. Family history (especially affected parent) increases risk substantially.
key_points: Classic 3-8 week age, hungry vomiter, projectile non-bilious.
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis is biochemical hallmark.
Ultrasound thresholds: muscle 3+ mm, channel 15+ mm.
Resuscitate alkalosis before surgery; not a surgical emergency.
explanation.pearls: Surgical referral waits for the bicarbonate to fall below 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L; operating on uncorrected alkalosis predisposes to post-operative apnoea.

sources.label: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons paediatric resources

options.rationale: Ultrasound is the first-line confirmatory imaging in Australia; diagnostic thresholds are pyloric muscle thickness 3 mm or greater and channel length 15 mm or greater, with sensitivity above 95 percent and no radiation. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

Contrast studies have been superseded by ultrasound in Australian paediatric centres because of radiation exposure and aspiration risk in a vomiting hypovolaemic infant; reserved for atypical presentations after a non-diagnostic ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

Endoscopy is not indicated in infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; it carries anaesthetic risk in a metabolically deranged infant and ultrasound is non-invasive and definitive. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

Plain films are non-specific and neither confirm nor exclude pyloric stenosis; relying on them delays surgical referral and exposes the infant to ionising radiation unnecessarily. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

The presentation is already classic and biochemistry shows the typical hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; delaying imaging prolongs dehydration and surgical correction. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception in the 3 month to 3 year age range is managed by pneumatic reduction under fluoroscopy as the first-line definitive intervention when the child is haemodynamically stable, without peritonism, and without free air. Surgical team must be available for immediate laparotomy in case of perforation or failed reduction. Recurrence after pneumatic reduction occurs in approximately 10 percent and these are usually managed by repeat reduction. A pathological lead point (Meckel diverticulum, lymphoma, polyp) should be considered in children over 3 years or with recurrent episodes.
key_points: Pneumatic reduction is first-line for stable cases.
Contraindications: perforation, peritonism, shock.
Surgical backup essential during reduction.
Consider lead point in >3 y or recurrent cases.
explanation.pearls: Maximum air pressure for reduction is 120 mmHg under fluoroscopy; perforation rate is under 1 percent, and post-reduction the child stays for 24 hours observation.

options.rationale: Antibiotics alone do not reduce an intussusception; perforation has not occurred and broad-spectrum cover is not the initial intervention in a confirmed ileocolic intussusception without sepsis. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Surgery is reserved for failed pneumatic reduction, perforation, peritonism, or shock; primary operation in a stable child denies an 80 to 90 percent chance of avoiding laparotomy. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Air contrast has replaced barium in Australian paediatric practice because air carries lower peritoneal contamination risk on perforation and higher reduction pressures are achievable safely. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Spontaneous reduction is uncommon and delay risks ischaemia, perforation, and increased need for bowel resection; non-operative reduction should not be delayed in a confirmed case. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Pneumatic (air contrast) reduction is the first-line definitive intervention in haemodynamically stable ileocolic intussusception without perforation or peritonism, with success rates of 80 to 90 percent and surgical backup mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Australian newborn screening uses raised IRT plus reflex CFTR variant detection; any infant with positive bloodspot screen is referred for sweat chloride testing at an accredited CF centre at 4 to 6 weeks of age. Sweat chloride 60 mmol/L or greater confirms CF, 30 to 59 mmol/L is intermediate (CRMS/CFSPID, needing ongoing follow-up), and under 30 mmol/L excludes CF. Diagnosis triggers entry to a multidisciplinary paediatric CF service for surveillance, enzyme assessment, airway clearance education, and CFTR-modulator eligibility consideration.
key_points: Sweat chloride cutoffs: <30 normal, 30-59 intermediate, >=60 CF.
Test by pilocarpine iontophoresis at accredited centre.
Single variant after screen needs sweat test, not reassurance.
Multidisciplinary CF service for confirmed diagnoses.
explanation.pearls: Sweat chloride should be paired (both arms) with at least 75 mg of sweat collected per arm; insufficient sweat is the commonest cause of an unsatisfactory test and warrants repeat at 4 to 6 weeks of age.

options.rationale: Pancreatic insufficiency is treated once confirmed by faecal elastase or weight faltering after diagnosis; empiric enzyme therapy in an asymptomatic infant pre-diagnosis is inappropriate. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Diagnosis Guidelines)

Sequencing is the second-tier test when sweat chloride is intermediate or when a single variant complicates classification; it is not the immediate next test ahead of sweat chloride. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Diagnosis Guidelines)

Australian newborn screening programs refer all infants with raised IRT and one or more CFTR variants for sweat testing because the bloodspot panel does not exhaustively detect every CF-causing variant. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Diagnosis Guidelines)
