Radiological imaging is not part of the diagnostic pathway in an asymptomatic newborn screen positive infant and carries radiation exposure with no diagnostic yield at this stage. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Diagnosis Guidelines)

The gold standard confirmatory test after positive newborn screening is sweat chloride by pilocarpine iontophoresis at an accredited paediatric CF centre, with chloride 60 mmol/L or greater diagnostic, 30 to 59 intermediate, and under 30 normal in infants. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Diagnosis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Red Nose Australia's six core safe-sleep messages are: sleep baby on back; head and face uncovered; smoke-free environment before and after birth; safe sleeping environment day and night; sleep baby in own safe sleep space in same room as parent or carer for the first 6 to 12 months; breastfeed if possible. Bed-sharing, particularly on couches with sleep-deprived parents and soft surfaces, dramatically increases SUDI risk. Positioners, bumpers, soft bedding, and loose blankets are hazards.
key_points: Supine sleep is highest-impact single intervention.
Room-share (not bed-share) for first 6-12 months.
Firm flat mattress, no bumpers/positioners/loose bedding.
Smoke-free environment, breastfeed if possible.
explanation.pearls: Use an Australian Standard AS/NZS 2172-compliant cot with a firm mattress, fitted sheet only, and feet-to-foot positioning; document safe sleep counselling at every well-baby check until 12 months.

sources.label: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations
RACGP Guidelines for Preventive Activities in General Practice

options.rationale: Prone (tummy) sleeping is the single largest modifiable SUDI risk factor; supine sleeping cuts SUDI risk by more than half and is the strongest individual counselling point. (Source: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations)
source_refs: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations

options.rationale: Bed-sharing (especially on couches, with sleep-deprived adults, smokers, or with soft bedding) increases SUDI risk; room-sharing on a separate sleep surface is the recommended arrangement. (Source: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations)
source_refs: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations

options.rationale: Smoking exposure is an important SUDI risk factor and cessation is recommended, but in this family the most modifiable and highest-impact risks are prone sleeping and unsafe couch co-sleeping with maternal fatigue. (Source: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations)
source_refs: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations

options.rationale: Supine sleep is the cornerstone of SUDI prevention and pairs with own-surface room-sharing (not bed-sharing) for at least 6 months in the Red Nose evidence-based recommendations. (Source: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations)
source_refs: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations

options.rationale: Side sleeping is unstable (baby can roll prone) and positioners themselves are SUDI hazards; Red Nose advises against any anti-roll or sleep-positioning device. (Source: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations)
source_refs: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations

explanation.summary: Kocher criteria differentiate septic arthritis from transient synovitis in a child with hip pain: non-weight-bearing, temperature above 38.5, ESR above 40, WCC above 12 x10^9/L. The probability of septic arthritis is 3 percent (0 of 4), 40 percent (1 of 4), 62 percent (2 of 4), 93 percent (3 of 4), and 99 percent (4 of 4). Aspiration under image guidance is the diagnostic and therapeutic step; antibiotics (flucloxacillin in Australia, plus cefotaxime if under 3 months or risk of MRSA) are given immediately after cultures. CRP and Caird modifications add prognostic value.
key_points: Kocher 4 criteria: NWB, T>38.5, ESR>40, WCC>12.
3 of 4 = 93% probability of septic arthritis.
Aspiration before antibiotics where possible.
Empiric flucloxacillin IV; cefotaxime cover in young infants.
explanation.pearls: Hip aspiration in theatre under fluoroscopy or ultrasound prevents the false-negative of a dry tap; if pus is obtained, send for Gram, culture, cell count and crystals, and arrange surgical washout under the same anaesthetic.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.rationale: The Kocher count here is 3 of 4 (refusal to weight-bear, fever above 38.5, WCC above 12), giving a 93 percent probability of septic arthritis and requiring arthrocentesis rather than discharge. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.rationale: A pre-test probability over 90 percent does not justify watchful waiting; ibuprofen also blunts inflammatory markers and can mask deterioration before arthrocentesis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.rationale: MRI is helpful when osteomyelitis or pyomyositis is suspected and the joint is dry on ultrasound; here there is a visible effusion and aspiration takes priority because delayed treatment causes cartilage destruction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are inadequate for septic arthritis (which has a 90+ percent pre-test probability here) and a week of delay risks femoral head avascular necrosis; admission and arthrocentesis are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.rationale: With 3 of 4 Kocher predictors (refusal to weight-bear, fever above 38.5, raised WCC) plus a visible effusion, the probability of septic arthritis is over 90 percent; urgent arthrocentesis under image guidance with antibiotics after cultures is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

explanation.summary: Bacterial tracheitis classically follows a viral URTI with worsening croup that does not respond to nebulised adrenaline or steroids. The child is toxic, febrile, and has purulent tracheal secretions, distinguishing from viral croup (less toxic, dry barking cough) and epiglottitis (sudden onset, drooling, no cough). Management is airway team-led controlled intubation in theatre with simultaneous tracheal toilet, cultures, and intravenous flucloxacillin (Staph aureus is the dominant pathogen in Australia) plus ceftriaxone for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae cover.
key_points: Suspect when croup unresponsive to adrenaline + steroids.
Toxic child, high fever, purulent secretions.
Definitive airway in theatre with anaesthesia + ENT + ICU.
Empirical flucloxacillin + ceftriaxone IV.
explanation.pearls: Tracheal cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus in 50 percent of Australian cases; once intubated, mucus plugs need repeat bronchoscopic toilet and extubation usually proceeds at 3 to 7 days after resolution of secretions and fever.

options.rationale: Failure of two doses of nebulised adrenaline plus dexamethasone in a toxic child with purulent secretions and high fever points away from viral croup; further croup therapy delays definitive airway management. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)
Imaging in a child with imminent airway compromise delays definitive airway control and has no place ahead of expert intubation; airway team activation is the priority. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

Awake examination of the supraglottis in a distressed child with critical upper airway disease risks complete obstruction; airway inspection occurs after controlled anaesthesia in theatre. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

Bacterial tracheitis (a viral croup that does not respond to adrenaline, with toxicity, high fever, and purulent secretions) requires senior airway team-led controlled intubation in theatre, then tracheal toilet, microbiological sampling and empirical antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)
HFNC does not relieve fixed upper airway obstruction from purulent secretions; waiting for steroid effect in a toxic deteriorating child risks loss of the airway. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

explanation.summary: Vaso-occlusive crises require analgesia within 30 minutes of arrival: intranasal fentanyl 1.5 micrograms/kg as a bridge while siting IV access, then IV morphine titrated (typically 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg every 10 to 15 minutes), supported by maintenance fluids (avoid overhydration), warmth, oxygen if SpO2 below 95 percent, and continuous reassessment for acute chest syndrome (new infiltrate plus respiratory symptoms requiring exchange). Pethidine is contraindicated. Exchange transfusion is reserved for stroke, acute chest, multi-organ failure, or priapism.
key_points: Strong opioid within 30 minutes (intranasal fentanyl bridge to IV morphine).
Avoid pethidine - norpethidine lowers seizure threshold.
Maintenance fluids; avoid 20 mL/kg boluses.
Exchange transfusion only for chest, stroke, MOF, priapism.
explanation.pearls: Watch for the emergence of acute chest syndrome within 24 to 72 hours of admission: new infiltrate on CXR with fever, hypoxia, or chest pain triggers urgent haematology review for exchange transfusion.

options.rationale: Oral analgesia has already failed in a child scoring 9 of 10 pain; sickle cell guidelines mandate strong opioid by intranasal or intravenous route within 30 minutes of arrival. (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease)

Australian sickle cell guidelines require strong opioid analgesia within 30 minutes (intranasal fentanyl bridge, then IV morphine titrated), warmth, oxygen if hypoxic, and intravenous maintenance fluids without overhydration, with regular reassessment of pain and respiratory status. (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease)

Exchange transfusion is reserved for acute chest syndrome, stroke, multi-organ failure, or priapism; uncomplicated VOC is managed with analgesia, hydration and warmth. (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease)
Sickle vaso-occlusive crises are not a hypovolaemic state; large fluid boluses risk pulmonary oedema and acute chest syndrome and do not relieve pain. (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease)

Pethidine is contraindicated in sickle cell crises because its metabolite norpethidine accumulates and lowers seizure threshold; IM injections are also painful and slow onset compared with intranasal fentanyl. (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease)

explanation.summary: Pertussis classically progresses through catarrhal (1 to 2 weeks), paroxysmal (2 to 8 weeks) and convalescent phases. Infants under 6 months are at risk of apnoea, pneumonia, seizures and death. Azithromycin (10 mg/kg/day for 5 days) is first-line under 1 month; clarithromycin or azithromycin from 1 month onward. Public health notification is mandatory. Postexposure prophylaxis for high-risk contacts (pregnancy 3rd trimester, household contacts of infant under 6 months) with the same macrolide. Promote maternal pertussis vaccination during each pregnancy from 20 weeks to prevent neonatal infection.
key_points: Infant under 6 months - admit for apnoea monitoring.
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day for 5 days under 1 month.
Erythromycin in neonates linked to pyloric stenosis.
Notifiable disease in Australia.
Maternal vaccination each pregnancy from 20 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Lymphocytosis greater than 50 percent of WCC in young infants with pertussis is associated with pulmonary hypertension and mortality - exchange transfusion or ECMO may be life-saving in severe cases.

options.rationale: Bronchodilators and steroids do not modify pertussis cough paroxysms; treatment is supportive plus a macrolide. (Source: RCH CPG Pertussis)

Antibiotics started in catarrhal or early paroxysmal phase shorten infectivity and may attenuate symptoms; infants under 6 months require admission regardless of treatment for apnoea monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG Pertussis)
Azithromycin is first-line for pertussis in infants under 1 month and over (10 mg/kg/day for 5 days); admission is mandatory under 6 months due to apnoea risk. (Source: RCH CPG Pertussis)
Erythromycin in neonates carries increased risk of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; azithromycin is preferred under 1 month. (Source: RCH CPG Pertussis)
Benzylpenicillin has no useful activity against Bordetella pertussis; macrolide therapy is required. (Source: RCH CPG Pertussis)

explanation.summary: Enterobius vermicularis (threadworm) is common in young children and spreads through household autoinfection. Classic presentation is perianal itch waking the child. Diagnosis is clinical or confirmed by sticky-tape test taken in the early morning. Australian first-line treatment is mebendazole 100 mg as single dose, repeated in 2 weeks, given to all household members regardless of symptoms. Adjuncts include hand hygiene, short fingernails, daily morning showers and hot washing of bed linen and night clothing for the 2 days after each treatment.
key_points: Treat entire household to break cycle.
Mebendazole 100 mg single dose then repeat at 2 weeks.
Hygiene: hand wash, short nails, morning shower, hot wash bedding.
Albendazole is alternative if mebendazole unavailable.
Reassure school - no need to exclude after treatment.
explanation.pearls: Mebendazole is not licensed in Australia for children under 6 months and has limited safety data under 1 year - in infants, consult Therapeutic Guidelines and consider pyrantel pamoate or topical petrolatum as alternatives.

options.rationale: Hygiene alone rarely clears established infection within reasonable time; medication is needed to interrupt the cycle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Threadworm)
Ivermectin is not first-line for threadworm; mebendazole to all household members is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Threadworm)
Mebendazole is the first-line agent in Australia; albendazole is an alternative when mebendazole is unavailable or contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Threadworm)
Treating only the index child leaves household reservoir; reinfection is highly likely without whole-household treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Threadworm)
Therapeutic guidelines recommend treating the entire household with single-dose mebendazole 100 mg repeated in 2 weeks to break the autoinfection cycle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Threadworm)

explanation.summary: Primary nocturnal enuresis is involuntary wetting during sleep without a 6-month dry period, with no daytime symptoms. Treatment is offered from age 6 when child and family are motivated. Alarm therapy is first-line with 60 percent lasting cure rate after 8 to 12 weeks; relapses respond to a further course. Oral desmopressin is second-line for older children or short-term cover (school camps). Reward charts may complement alarm therapy. Look for constipation, daytime symptoms, snoring/OSA, behavioural concerns and diabetes if atypical features present.
key_points: Treat from age 6 with motivated family.
Alarm therapy first-line; 8 to 12 weeks minimum.
Oral desmopressin melt second-line.
Tricyclics reserved for refractory cases.
Screen for constipation, daytime symptoms, OSA, diabetes.
explanation.pearls: Desmopressin tablets/melt should be taken without fluids around the dose - children given desmopressin who drink large volumes overnight are at risk of severe hyponatraemic seizures, which is why the intranasal preparation was withdrawn.

options.rationale: Intranasal desmopressin is no longer recommended in Australia in children due to hyponatraemic seizures; oral melt is used when desmopressin is required, after alarm therapy. (Source: RCH CPG Nocturnal Enuresis)

Enuresis alarm is first-line for motivated children over 5 with primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis; lasting cure rates around 60 percent after 8 to 12 weeks of consistent use. (Source: RCH CPG Nocturnal Enuresis)
Reward charts alone have low success in established nocturnal enuresis; alarm therapy is superior when family-engaged treatment is sought. (Source: RCH CPG Nocturnal Enuresis)
Tricyclics are reserved for refractory cases due to overdose mortality and cardiotoxicity; not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG Nocturnal Enuresis)

Imaging and urodynamics are not indicated in primary monosymptomatic enuresis with normal examination; reserved for daytime symptoms, recurrent UTIs or abnormal findings. (Source: RCH CPG Nocturnal Enuresis)

explanation.summary: Allergic rhinitis is classified by ARIA as intermittent or persistent and mild or moderate-severe. Mild intermittent responds to non-sedating oral antihistamines or saline rinses; moderate-severe persistent (sleep affected, school/work impact) requires regular intranasal corticosteroid as cornerstone therapy. Combination intranasal corticosteroid + intranasal antihistamine sprays improve speed of onset. Saline rinse before sprays improves drug delivery. Allergen immunotherapy is offered if pharmacotherapy fails or to modify long-term disease progression.
key_points: Moderate-severe persistent - regular intranasal corticosteroid.
Mild intermittent - non-sedating antihistamine or saline.
Combine antihistamine + steroid if single agent fails.
Avoid sedating antihistamines and oral steroids.
Immunotherapy after maximal pharmacotherapy failure.
explanation.pearls: Intranasal corticosteroid sprays work best when angled outward toward the lateral wall, not toward the septum - misdirected delivery causes septal irritation and epistaxis without improving symptoms.

options.rationale: Allergen immunotherapy is considered after maximal pharmacological therapy and confirmed allergen sensitisation; not the immediate next step. (Source: ASCIA Allergic Rhinitis)
Sedating antihistamines impair learning and worsen daytime fatigue; non-sedating agents are preferred and addition of intranasal steroid is the priority. (Source: ASCIA Allergic Rhinitis)
Montelukast has modest efficacy and a TGA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects; reserved for cases unresponsive to topical corticosteroids. (Source: ASCIA Allergic Rhinitis)

Intranasal corticosteroid is the most effective single agent for persistent allergic rhinitis and is recommended as add-on or first-line for moderate-severe disease in Australian guidance. (Source: ASCIA Allergic Rhinitis)
Oral steroids are reserved for severe refractory cases; routine use for moderate allergic rhinitis is inappropriate due to systemic side effects. (Source: ASCIA Allergic Rhinitis)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated infant gastro-oesophageal reflux is regurgitation without functional concern; it affects up to 40 percent of healthy infants and resolves spontaneously by 12 to 14 months. Reflux disease (GORD) involves complications: faltering growth, recurrent respiratory symptoms, oesophagitis, food refusal, distressed behaviour. Management is stepwise from parental reassurance, upright positioning, smaller more frequent feeds, thickened formula (not breastfed infants) through to acid suppression only if GORD is confirmed. Red flags (bilious vomiting, blood, bulging fontanelle, abdominal distension) demand urgent assessment for alternative diagnoses.
key_points: Uncomplicated reflux: reassurance, position upright after feeds.
PPIs and H2 blockers offer no benefit without GORD.
Thickened feeds OK for formula-fed infants.
GORD red flags: weight loss, recurrent wheeze, oesophagitis.
Bilious vomit, blood, bulging fontanelle - urgent assessment.
explanation.pearls: Sandifer syndrome (dystonic head/neck posturing during feeds) is a manifestation of GORD that mimics seizures - oesophageal pH/impedance monitoring rather than EEG is the appropriate first investigation.

options.rationale: Formula switch is reserved for suspected cows-milk protein allergy with red flags; not indicated in an exclusively breastfed thriving infant with no allergy features. (Source: RCH CPG Gastro-oesophageal Reflux)
PPIs are ineffective for uncomplicated reflux without oesophagitis and increase infection and fracture risk; not indicated in a well-thriving baby. (Source: RCH CPG Gastro-oesophageal Reflux)
Ranitidine has been withdrawn due to NDMA contamination; H2 blockers are no longer routine for uncomplicated reflux. (Source: RCH CPG Gastro-oesophageal Reflux)

Invasive investigation is reserved for red flags (poor growth, haematemesis, persistent respiratory or neurological symptoms); not for uncomplicated regurgitation. (Source: RCH CPG Gastro-oesophageal Reflux)

Uncomplicated infant gastro-oesophageal reflux is physiological and self-resolves by 12 to 14 months; reassurance and feeding-position advice are first-line. (Source: RCH CPG Gastro-oesophageal Reflux)

explanation.summary: Acute sore throat management in Australia is stratified by ARF risk. High-risk groups include Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, especially in northern Australia, those with personal or family history of ARF and people living in crowded conditions. In high-risk groups, all sore throats with GAS pharyngitis features are treated empirically. Single-dose IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is preferred for adherence; oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg BD for 10 days is an alternative. Low-risk populations may use Centor or FeverPAIN criteria with delayed prescription.
key_points: Risk-stratify by ARF risk.
High-risk: empirical IM benzathine penicillin G.
Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 10 days is alternative.
Macrolides for severe penicillin allergy.
Low-risk: Centor or FeverPAIN-guided delayed prescription.
explanation.pearls: Persistent throat carriage of group A streptococcus after appropriate treatment in a low-risk patient rarely needs eradication - it does not progress to invasive disease and adds antibiotic exposure without benefit.

options.rationale: A single dose of phenoxymethylpenicillin is inadequate; either a 10-day oral course or single IM benzathine dose is required for streptococcal eradication. (Source: RHDAustralia Guidelines)
Macrolides are reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy; resistance is rising and they are not first-line in this scenario. (Source: RHDAustralia Guidelines)

Australian guidelines recommend single-dose IM benzathine benzylpenicillin for sore throat in children at high risk of acute rheumatic fever (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander background, remote community, family history). (Source: RHDAustralia Guidelines)

Oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg daily for 10 days is an alternative if IM benzathine penicillin is unavailable; adherence over 10 days is the challenge in remote settings, hence IM preferred. (Source: RHDAustralia Guidelines)
Watchful waiting is appropriate in low-risk populations but not for high-ARF-risk children where empirical antibiotics are recommended to prevent rheumatic fever. (Source: RHDAustralia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: A tet spell results from acute increase in right ventricular outflow tract obstruction combined with falling systemic vascular resistance, causing right-to-left shunting and profound hypoxia. Immediate management is to settle the child in knee-to-chest (or parental cuddling with knees flexed) plus high-flow oxygen. Pharmacological escalation includes morphine 0.1 mg/kg IM or IV to abolish hyperpnoea, IV phenylephrine to raise SVR, IV propranolol to relax the RVOT, sodium bicarbonate for acidosis and prompt referral for surgical or palliative shunting if recurrent. Quiet murmur indicates near-total RVOT obstruction.
key_points: Knee-to-chest + high-flow O2 are immediate first steps.
Morphine 0.1 mg/kg blunts hyperpnoea.
Phenylephrine raises SVR and reduces shunt.
Propranolol relaxes RVOT muscular obstruction.
Quieter murmur means worse spell.
explanation.pearls: Beta-blockade with propranolol is used both acutely (intravenously) and as outpatient prophylaxis (oral 1 to 2 mg/kg/day) in babies awaiting repair - schedule surgical repair before 6 months when spells start to recur to avoid long-term right ventricular damage.

options.rationale: Adrenaline increases right ventricular outflow tract spasm by beta-agonism and worsens the spell; beta-blockade is the relevant pharmacology. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic Heart Disease)
The child is not in cardiac arrest; aggressive resuscitation without addressing the shunt physiology will not resolve the spell. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic Heart Disease)
Pulmonary vasodilation is not the mechanism in tet spells; the problem is right ventricular outflow tract obstruction with shunt reversal. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic Heart Disease)
Tet spells are not driven by pulmonary oedema; diuresis reduces preload and worsens the shunt. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic Heart Disease)

Knee-to-chest increases systemic vascular resistance, reverses right-to-left shunting and is the immediate first step in a tet spell, with simultaneous high-flow oxygen. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic Heart Disease)

explanation.summary: Classical salt-wasting CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency, most common) presents in the second week of life with vomiting, weight loss, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and shock. Males may not have ambiguous genitalia, making missed diagnosis at delivery common before newborn screen returns. Acute management is IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat (infant) plus IV 0.9 percent saline with 5 percent dextrose 20 mL/kg bolus, then stress-dose hydrocortisone infusion. Once stable, transition to oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone with sodium chloride supplementation. Genitogram, karyotype, ACTH, 17-OHP and renin sent on presentation.
key_points: Second week of life vomiting + weight loss - think CAH.
Biochemistry: low Na, high K, low glucose, metabolic acidosis.
IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat + saline-dextrose bolus.
Fludrocortisone and salt added once stable.
Send 17-OHP, ACTH, renin BEFORE first steroid dose.
explanation.pearls: Sick-day rules: triple the maintenance hydrocortisone dose during fever or vomiting and give IM hydrocortisone if oral dose cannot be retained - parents should be supplied with an emergency injection kit at diagnosis.

options.rationale: Withholding steroid in a shocked baby with the classic biochemistry of salt-wasting CAH risks death; take samples and treat immediately. (Source: RCH CPG Adrenal Crisis)
Oral therapy is inadequate for a shocked vomiting infant; intravenous hydrocortisone is required and fludrocortisone is started later when stable. (Source: RCH CPG Adrenal Crisis)

Calcium is indicated when hyperkalaemia produces ECG changes; the immediate priority is steroid replacement plus volume resuscitation, which itself corrects the potassium. (Source: RCH CPG Adrenal Crisis)

Acute adrenal crisis in suspected salt-wasting CAH requires immediate parenteral hydrocortisone (stress dose) and isotonic dextrose-containing fluid to correct shock, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia simultaneously. (Source: RCH CPG Adrenal Crisis)

Hypertonic saline is reserved for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia with seizures; rapid correction here risks osmotic demyelination and does not treat the underlying adrenal crisis. (Source: RCH CPG Adrenal Crisis)

explanation.summary: Down syndrome is associated with congenital heart disease in about 45 percent of children, atrioventricular septal defect being the most common, followed by VSD, ASD and PDA. Early echocardiography in the first 4 to 6 weeks identifies lesions before pulmonary vascular disease develops; surgical repair of AVSD is typically performed by 6 months. Other screening on the Down syndrome health check schedule includes hearing assessment at birth and 6 months, ophthalmology at 6 to 12 months, thyroid function annually, coeliac screen, atlantoaxial assessment before contact sport, sleep study if obstructive symptoms, and developmental surveillance.
key_points: About 45 percent CHD - AVSD most common.
Echocardiogram at 4 to 6 weeks regardless of pulse oximetry screen.
AVSD repair typically before 6 months.
Thyroid screening annually.
Atlantoaxial assessment before contact sports.
explanation.pearls: Atrioventricular septal defects in Down syndrome have early-onset pulmonary vascular disease compared with non-Down AVSD - elective repair is brought forward to 3 to 6 months to avoid Eisenmenger physiology.

sources.label: Down Syndrome Australia Health Care Guide

options.rationale: CXR and ECG cannot exclude septal defects; echocardiography is required. (Source: RCH CPG Down Syndrome)

Around 45 percent of infants with Down syndrome have congenital heart disease and pulse oximetry screen misses non-cyanotic lesions like AVSD and VSD; transthoracic echocardiogram is recommended in the first weeks of life. (Source: RCH CPG Down Syndrome)
Pulse oximetry misses non-cyanotic CHD common in Down syndrome (AVSD, VSD, PDA); formal echocardiography is required. (Source: RCH CPG Down Syndrome)
MRI is reserved for select complex lesions; echocardiography is the first-line non-invasive screen for CHD in Down syndrome. (Source: RCH CPG Down Syndrome)
Awaiting symptoms risks irreversible pulmonary vascular disease in undiagnosed AVSD; early echocardiography is mandatory in trisomy 21. (Source: RCH CPG Down Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Posterior urethral valves are the commonest cause of severe lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants. Antenatal findings include bilateral hydronephrosis, dilated bladder and keyhole sign of dilated posterior urethra. Postnatally, suspect in any boy with weak stream, palpable bladder or anuria. Immediate management is catheter decompression with a small feeding tube (urethral catheter balloons can lodge in dilated posterior urethra), correction of electrolytes and prophylactic antibiotics. Definitive surgery is cystoscopic valve ablation. Long-term complications include chronic kidney disease, bladder dysfunction and need for transplantation in around 30 percent.
key_points: Suspect in boy with weak stream + palpable bladder + AKI.
Catheter decompression first - use feeding tube without balloon.
Send creatinine, electrolytes, USS post-decompression.
Cystoscopic valve ablation is definitive.
Long-term CKD risk - lifelong urology and nephrology follow-up.
explanation.pearls: Post-obstructive diuresis is common after relief of bilateral obstruction - replace urine output 1:1 with 0.45 percent saline plus dextrose for 24 to 48 hours to prevent profound electrolyte and volume disturbance.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Paediatric Surgery

options.rationale: Aspiration alone does not relieve bladder outlet obstruction; ongoing obstruction continues to damage the kidneys and bladder. (Source: RCH CPG Posterior Urethral Valves)
Volume loading without relieving obstruction risks bladder injury and worsening hydronephrosis; catheter decompression is required first. (Source: RCH CPG Posterior Urethral Valves)
Furosemide does not relieve mechanical obstruction; outflow must be established first by catheterisation, and dehydration may worsen the picture. (Source: RCH CPG Posterior Urethral Valves)

MCUG is required to confirm the diagnosis but only after the bladder is decompressed and the baby is stabilised; not the first step in an obstructed septic-risk neonate. (Source: RCH CPG Posterior Urethral Valves)

Suspected posterior urethral valves are decompressed urgently with bladder catheterisation, then transferred for paediatric urological assessment and surgical valve ablation. (Source: RCH CPG Posterior Urethral Valves)

explanation.summary: Croup is a viral laryngotracheitis with subglottic oedema causing barking cough and inspiratory stridor. Severity is graded by stridor at rest, retractions, oxygenation and mental status. A single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg shortens duration and prevents readmission across the mild to moderate spectrum. Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with significant respiratory distress; its effect lasts about 2 hours so observation for at least 4 hours after adrenaline is required. Discharge is safe if the child is stridor-free at rest, well hydrated and the parent can return easily.
key_points: Single oral dexamethasone for all mild and moderate croup.
Nebulised adrenaline for severe croup only.
Observe at least 4 hours after adrenaline before discharge.
No role for salbutamol in croup.
Avoid throat examination and IV access if not needed.
explanation.pearls: Choose dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral over prednisolone 1 mg/kg even though both are used; dexamethasone has a longer half-life and is single-dose, reducing risk of bounce-back stridor.

options.rationale: Salbutamol has no role in croup as the obstruction is supraglottic; using it delays effective steroid therapy. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)
Intravenous steroids are unnecessary because oral dexamethasone is rapidly absorbed and equally effective without cannulation distress. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)
A single oral dose of dexamethasone is the standard Australian first-line treatment for mild to moderate croup with rapid onset of effect and durable benefit. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)
Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with marked stridor at rest, retractions and distress; it is not first-line for mild stridor. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)
Discharging without dexamethasone misses the opportunity to shorten symptoms and reduce return rates, even when the child is feeding well. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is a small vessel vasculitis of childhood with palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain and IgA glomerulonephritis. Renal involvement develops in about a third of cases, mostly within 4 to 6 weeks. Weekly home urinalysis is recommended for the first 4 weeks then less frequently for 6-12 months. Significant proteinuria (urine ACR above 30), nephrotic syndrome, hypertension or rising creatinine demand urgent nephrology referral for renal biopsy and treatment. Steroids do not prevent nephritis but reduce abdominal pain and arthritis duration in severe cases.
key_points: Monitor urinalysis weekly for 4 weeks then less frequently 6-12 months.
Refer if proteinuria ACR above 30, BP above 95th centile, or rising creatinine.
Nephritis can develop after rash and arthritis resolve.
Steroids reduce extra-renal symptoms but do not prevent nephritis.
Long-term renal follow-up needed for any nephritis.
explanation.pearls: Confirm hypertension with three separate readings using the correct paediatric cuff size and using the 95th centile threshold for age, height and sex from the AAP nomogram, not adult thresholds.

options.rationale: Significant proteinuria and hypertension above 95th centile require specialist review and further investigation rather than continued observation. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)
Empirical steroid therapy without paediatric nephrology assessment and consideration of biopsy is not standard initial management. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)
Significant proteinuria and elevated BP indicate renal involvement that requires ongoing nephrology surveillance, not discharge. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

Persistent significant proteinuria with hypertension warrants urgent paediatric nephrology referral for biopsy consideration and treatment to preserve kidney function. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)
ACE inhibitors are considered after nephrology assessment; delaying specialist review with significant proteinuria risks irreversible kidney damage. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed by fever for at least 5 days plus 4 of: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips, pharyngitis), polymorphous rash, peripheral changes (erythema, oedema, peeling) and cervical lymphadenopathy at least 1.5 cm. IVIG 2 g/kg given within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25 percent to about 5 percent. High-dose aspirin (30-50 mg/kg/day) is started during the acute phase, transitioning to antiplatelet 3-5 mg/kg/day once afebrile until echocardiography is reassuring. Echocardiography at diagnosis, 2 weeks and 6 weeks tracks coronary changes.
key_points: Diagnosis: fever 5+ days plus 4 of the classical features.
IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm to 5 percent.
High-dose aspirin acutely, then low-dose antiplatelet until echo clear.
Echo at diagnosis, 2 weeks and 6 weeks.
Second IVIG dose or steroids/infliximab if persistent fever 36 h post-IVIG.
explanation.pearls: Incomplete Kawasaki disease (3 features plus fever) is more common in infants under 1 year - presentations may be subtle and CRP above 30 plus ESR above 40 plus other supportive features (anaemia, low albumin, ALT elevation, pyuria, platelets above 450) justify IVIG.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement Diagnosis Treatment and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics treat infection but miss the Kawasaki diagnosis where IVIG within 10 days is critical to prevent coronary aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki Disease)
Aspirin and steroids are adjuncts; IVIG within 10 days is the cornerstone of management to reduce coronary aneurysm risk to about 5 percent. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki Disease)
IVIG 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin given within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25 to about 5 percent. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki Disease)
Topical care and oral antibiotic for presumed bacterial adenitis miss the diagnosis and the time-critical window for IVIG before day 10. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki Disease)
Steroid pulse and infliximab are second-line for IVIG-resistant disease, not first-line treatment for incomplete or complete Kawasaki disease. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Intussusception classically presents in 6-36 month old children with episodic colicky pain, vomiting (initially non-bilious then bilious), redcurrant jelly stool (late sign) and a palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass. Ultrasound shows target or pseudokidney sign. Air or contrast enema reduction in radiology with surgical standby is the standard first-line treatment with success rates of 80-90 percent, contraindicated by peritonism, perforation, hypovolaemic shock or pneumatosis. Surgery is for failed reduction, perforation or pathological lead point. Recurrence is 5-10 percent, mostly within 24 hours.
key_points: Episodic pain, drawing up legs, redcurrant jelly stool, sausage-shaped mass.
Ultrasound confirms with target sign or pseudokidney sign.
Air or contrast enema is first-line for stable child.
Surgery if peritonism, perforation, failure of reduction or pathological lead point.
Recurrence 5-10 percent - admit overnight for observation.
explanation.pearls: In children over 2 years suspect pathological lead point (Meckel's diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma) and arrange follow-up imaging or surgical consultation even after successful enema reduction.

options.rationale: Spontaneous reduction is uncommon and conservative management delays intervention and increases bowel ischaemia risk. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)
Surgery is reserved for failed enema reduction, perforation, peritonism or unstable patient; first-line reduction is non-operative. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)
Hydrostatic or pneumatic enema reduction under radiological guidance is the standard first-line treatment for stable ileocolic intussusception. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)
Outpatient management is unsafe; intussusception is a surgical emergency requiring inpatient resuscitation and prompt reduction. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)
Endoscopy is not indicated; ultrasound has already confirmed the diagnosis and reduction takes priority over lead point investigation. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically presents at 3-6 weeks in first-born males with projectile non-bilious vomiting, hunger between feeds, weight loss and a palpable olive. Ultrasound confirms with pyloric muscle thickness at least 3 mm and length at least 15 mm. Vomiting of gastric HCl causes hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria; this must be corrected before anaesthesia to prevent post-operative apnoea. Resuscitation uses 0.9 percent saline boluses then maintenance with added potassium once urine output established. Ramstedt pyloromyotomy is curative; feeding is reintroduced within hours postoperatively.
key_points: Projectile non-bilious vomiting in 3-6 week first-born male.
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis is classic.
Correct biochemistry before anaesthesia to prevent apnoea.
Aim chloride above 100 and bicarbonate below 30 before theatre.
Ramstedt pyloromyotomy is curative; feed within hours.
explanation.pearls: Add potassium only after urine output is established (above 1 mL/kg/h) and never give as a stat bolus; standard maintenance fluid is 0.9 percent saline with 20-40 mmol/L KCl, never glucose-water alone in alkalosis.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Surgery Guidelines - Pyloric Stenosis

options.rationale: Correction of hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with NaCl and potassium replacement is mandatory before anaesthesia; pyloric stenosis is a medical not surgical emergency. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)
Anaesthesia with metabolic alkalosis causes hypoventilation and apnoea; biochemical correction must precede surgery. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)
Feeding does not resolve mechanical pyloric obstruction; further vomiting worsens dehydration and electrolyte loss. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)
Antiemetics do not treat mechanical obstruction; the diagnosis is confirmed and definitive management is fluid resuscitation then pyloromyotomy. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)
Dextrose alone does not correct chloride and sodium deficits or replace gastric losses; volume and electrolyte replacement are the priorities. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: Australian newborn screening uses immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) on day 2-3 dried blood spot, with elevated IRT (above 99th centile) prompting CFTR mutation panel. A positive screen requires confirmatory sweat chloride at a recognised CF centre by Gibson-Cooke method; chloride at least 60 mmol/L is diagnostic, 30-59 is intermediate (extended CFTR sequencing and clinical correlation needed), under 30 is normal. Early diagnosis and multidisciplinary care (paediatrician, dietitian, physiotherapist, psychologist) improves growth, lung function and survival. Pancreatic enzyme replacement, fat-soluble vitamins, airway clearance and CFTR modulators (in eligible mutations) are core treatments.
key_points: Newborn screening: IRT day 2-3 then CFTR panel if elevated.
Sweat chloride at CF centre is the definitive diagnostic test.
Chloride above 60 mmol/L diagnostic, 30-59 intermediate, under 30 normal.
CF centre coordinates multidisciplinary follow-up.
CFTR modulators (ivacaftor and combinations) transformed prognosis.
explanation.pearls: Suspect CF clinically even with a normal screen if meconium ileus, recurrent chest infections or failure to thrive develops - 1 in 20 CF cases are missed by screening due to rare mutations not on the panel.

sources.label: Australasian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

options.rationale: Positive IRT plus pending CFTR genotyping requires definitive diagnostic confirmation, not repeat screening. (Source: RCH CPG Cystic Fibrosis)
Treatment is not started until diagnosis is confirmed by sweat chloride; empirical therapy is inappropriate. (Source: RCH CPG Cystic Fibrosis)
Imaging is not first-line in asymptomatic CF screen-positive infants; diagnostic confirmation by sweat chloride is required. (Source: RCH CPG Cystic Fibrosis)
Sweat chloride is the gold standard diagnostic test for CF after positive newborn screening; CF centre referral coordinates testing, counselling and surveillance. (Source: RCH CPG Cystic Fibrosis)
Faecal elastase assesses pancreatic function but does not diagnose CF; sweat chloride is the diagnostic standard. (Source: RCH CPG Cystic Fibrosis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in infants under 12 months; investigations are not routinely required. Admission is guided by hypoxia (SpO2 persistently under 92%), feeding under 50% of normal, significant work of breathing, apnoea, or social risk. Therapy is supportive: minimal handling, oxygen if needed and nasogastric or intravenous fluids if feeding is poor. High-flow nasal cannula is escalated when standard oxygen fails. Salbutamol, steroids, hypertonic saline, adrenaline and antibiotics do not change outcomes in routine cases.
key_points: Admit if SpO2 under 92%, feeds under 50% or apnoea episodes.
Supportive care only - no bronchodilators or steroids.
Escalate to high-flow if work of breathing persists on low-flow.
RSV is the most common pathogen, but co-infection is rare.
Chest x-ray is not routine and may prompt unnecessary antibiotics.
explanation.pearls: Apnoea is the dominant deterioration in infants under 6 weeks or ex-premature; admit even with normal saturations if any apnoeic episode is reported by carers.

options.rationale: Salbutamol is not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; trials show no meaningful benefit and may cause tachycardia and desaturation. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)
Corticosteroids have no role in viral bronchiolitis even when wheeze is present; they do not shorten illness or reduce admission. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)
SpO2 below 92%, feeding under 50% baseline and increased work of breathing meet admission criteria; supportive care with oxygen and assisted hydration is standard. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)
Bacterial co-infection is uncommon in confirmed RSV bronchiolitis without focal consolidation or marked fever; antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)
Hypoxia, reduced feeding and increased work of breathing in a 4-month-old preclude discharge; this infant needs inpatient observation. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Meningococcal septicaemia is a time-critical emergency where empirical antibiotics must be given as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, not delayed for investigations or lumbar puncture. Intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg up to 2 g is the agent of choice; IM benzylpenicillin is the field alternative when no IV access exists. Fluid resuscitation should be cautious and reassessed after each bolus because of capillary leak and high risk of pulmonary oedema. Early activation of paediatric retrieval is critical in rural and remote sites. PCR remains positive for up to 72 hours after antibiotics.
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour, never delayed by LP or imaging.
Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg IV is first line.
Reassess after every 10 to 20 mL/kg bolus for fluid overload.
Dexamethasone not used in meningococcal disease.
Notify public health for household chemoprophylaxis.
explanation.pearls: Single-dose ciprofloxacin 500 mg is preferred over rifampicin for adult household chemoprophylaxis because it is a single dose and avoids interactions with oral contraceptives.

options.rationale: LP is contraindicated in suspected meningococcal sepsis with shock or coagulopathy and must never delay antibiotics. (Source: eTG Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

Empirical ceftriaxone within the first hour and titrated fluid resuscitation with early retrieval are the time-critical priorities in suspected meningococcal septicaemia. (Source: eTG Acute Bacterial Meningitis)
IV ceftriaxone is preferred where access exists and gives broader cover; withholding fluid in a shocked child with lactate 4 is dangerous. (Source: eTG Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

Dexamethasone is not recommended in meningococcal disease and any role in pneumococcal meningitis requires steroid with or just before antibiotics, never delaying them. (Source: eTG Acute Bacterial Meningitis)
Antibiotic delay for microbiology is unacceptable in suspected meningococcal sepsis; PCR remains positive after antibiotics are given. (Source: eTG Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid producing a characteristic hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. The kidney initially excretes bicarbonate then switches to a paradoxical aciduria once volume contraction dominates. Pyloromyotomy is a semi-elective procedure that should never proceed until pH is below 7.45, bicarbonate is below 28 and chloride is above 100, because residual alkalosis depresses central respiratory drive after anaesthesia. Resuscitation uses sodium chloride with dextrose; potassium is added after urine output is established. Ultrasound criteria for diagnosis are pyloric muscle thickness above 3 mm and channel length above 15 mm.
key_points: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis is pathognomonic.
Correct biochemistry before surgery to avoid post-op apnoea.
Sodium chloride with dextrose is the resuscitation fluid.
Add potassium only after urine output 1 mL/kg/hour.
Ultrasound: muscle thickness above 3 mm, length above 15 mm.
explanation.pearls: Target pre-operative chloride above 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate below 28 mmol/L; if alkalosis persists despite saline, suspect inadequate volume replacement rather than ongoing vomiting alone.

options.rationale: Pyloromyotomy is never an emergency; metabolic alkalosis must be corrected first to avoid post-anaesthetic apnoea from impaired respiratory drive. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)
Crystalloid is preferred over colloid for paediatric resuscitation; half-normal saline does not adequately replace chloride losses. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)
Hartmann is relatively chloride poor and inadequate to correct the hypochloraemia driving the alkalosis; sodium chloride is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)
Nil oral plus NG drainage without IV replacement worsens dehydration and electrolyte derangement; intravenous fluid is mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)
Resuscitation requires sodium chloride with dextrose to replace chloride and avoid hypoglycaemia, with potassium added safely once renal output is confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: Infant SVT typically presents as a narrow complex tachycardia at 220 to 300 bpm with no rate variability and no visible P waves; the absence of beat-to-beat variation distinguishes it from sinus tachycardia. Acute management of a stable infant follows a stepped algorithm: vagal manoeuvres first (iced water bag to face is most effective in infants), then adenosine 0.1 mg/kg with rapid saline flush, doubling to 0.2 mg/kg, then synchronised cardioversion 1 J/kg if unstable or unresponsive. Verapamil is contraindicated under 12 months. Heart failure features such as hepatomegaly and crackles can develop after prolonged SVT but do not yet mandate cardioversion if perfusion is preserved.
key_points: Infant SVT rate usually 220 to 300, no rate variability.
Iced water diving reflex first, adenosine second.
Verapamil contraindicated under 1 year.
Cardioversion 1 J/kg if unstable or refractory.
Refer to paediatric cardiology after first episode.
explanation.pearls: Wolff-Parkinson-White accounts for around half of infant SVT; once converted, an ECG in sinus rhythm may show a delta wave and short PR indicating accessory pathway.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline 12.2 Paediatric Advanced Life Support

options.rationale: Diving reflex with iced water to the face is first-line vagal manoeuvre in infants and terminates SVT in around 30% with minimal haemodynamic risk. (Source: RCH CPG SVT)
Adenosine is the correct pharmacological choice but vagal manoeuvres should be tried first in a stable infant before drug therapy. (Source: RCH CPG SVT)
Synchronised cardioversion is reserved for haemodynamically unstable SVT or failure of vagal manoeuvres plus adenosine; this infant is still perfusing. (Source: RCH CPG SVT)
Verapamil is contraindicated under 1 year because of profound hypotension and cardiac arrest from negative inotropy. (Source: RCH CPG SVT)
Amiodarone is reserved for refractory or unstable arrhythmia after vagal manoeuvres and adenosine fail; it is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG SVT)

explanation.summary: Suspected physical abuse in infancy requires a structured response: admission, multidisciplinary work-up for occult injury, and statutory notification to child protection. Spiral or metaphyseal corner fractures, rib fractures, and any fracture in a non-mobile infant are high-specificity injuries for abuse. Skeletal survey is the imaging gold standard with repeat at 2 weeks to detect callus formation. Head imaging and ophthalmology assessment screen for occult intracranial injury and retinal haemorrhages of abusive head trauma. Bruising in a child under 4 months who is not yet cruising should always prompt a safeguarding assessment.
key_points: Bruise in a pre-mobile infant requires safeguarding work-up.
Skeletal survey with 2-week repeat is the imaging standard.
Head MRI and retinal review for occult abusive head trauma.
Mandatory notification by all clinicians where abuse is suspected.
Bone fragility work-up does not delay reporting.
explanation.pearls: Bruises in babies who don't cruise should not be ignored - the TEN-4-FACESp clinical decision rule identifies high-risk patterns: bruising on torso, ear, neck in under 4 years or any bruising in infants under 4 months.

sources.label: RACP Position Statement Child Abuse and Neglect

options.rationale: Discharging an infant with a suspicious spiral fracture and unexplained bruising without child protection involvement is a serious safety breach. (Source: RCH CPG Child Abuse)
Bone fragility work-up may be added but does not replace mandatory notification; child protection must be activated first. (Source: RCH CPG Child Abuse)
Imaging and notification must not be delayed pending further history-taking; the fracture pattern is already inconsistent with the given mechanism. (Source: RCH CPG Child Abuse)
A spiral humeral fracture in a non-mobile infant with multiple bruises mandates admission for occult injury work-up and statutory child protection notification. (Source: RCH CPG Child Abuse)
Mandatory reporting cannot be deferred to community follow-up; all clinicians are reporters when abuse is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis is anterior to the orbital septum and presents with eyelid swelling and erythema but no proptosis, no pain on eye movement and preserved vision. Orbital (postseptal) cellulitis extends behind the septum and causes proptosis, painful or restricted eye movement, chemosis and potentially reduced visual acuity or relative afferent pupil defect. Orbital cellulitis is a surgical emergency because subperiosteal abscess and intracranial extension are well-recognised complications. Contrast CT of orbits and sinuses is the imaging modality of choice; treatment is IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering sinus organisms with prompt ophthalmology and ENT involvement.
key_points: Proptosis or eye movement pain defines orbital cellulitis.
Urgent contrast CT orbits and sinuses, not delayed imaging.
Ceftriaxone with flucloxacillin or vancomycin as empirical cover.
Surgical drainage for abscess over 10 mm or vision threat.
Sinus disease is the most common source in children.
explanation.pearls: Reduced colour vision and a relative afferent pupil defect signal optic nerve compromise from orbital pressure and require emergency surgical decompression regardless of antibiotic response.

sources.label: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis
eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

options.rationale: Proptosis, restricted eye movement and pain on gaze meet criteria for orbital cellulitis; oral therapy and discharge are unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis

options.rationale: Flucloxacillin alone does not cover the sinus organisms that complicate orbital infection; imaging cannot be delayed in suspected orbital involvement. (Source: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis

options.rationale: Proptosis and ophthalmoplegia indicate orbital cellulitis; urgent imaging defines abscess or subperiosteal collection and dictates whether surgical drainage is required. (Source: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis

options.rationale: Imaging should not be deferred when proptosis and gaze restriction are already present; delaying CT risks intracranial extension. (Source: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis

options.rationale: Outpatient oral therapy is appropriate only for uncomplicated preseptal cellulitis without orbital signs. (Source: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis

explanation.summary: Nutritional iron deficiency anaemia is the most common haematological problem in Australian toddlers and peaks at 9 to 24 months. Excessive cow's milk intake above 500 to 600 mL daily is a key driver because milk is iron poor, displaces iron rich foods and causes microscopic enteric blood loss. First-line therapy is oral iron 3 mg/kg of elemental iron once daily with vitamin C sources to enhance absorption; once daily dosing is now preferred over divided dosing because it gives better fractional absorption and fewer side effects. Repeat haemoglobin and ferritin after 4 weeks; expect haemoglobin to rise by at least 10 g/L.
key_points: Limit cow's milk to under 500 mL daily after 12 months.
Oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg/kg once daily is first line.
Vitamin C source with iron improves absorption.
Repeat Hb at 4 weeks; expect rise above 10 g/L.
Investigate alternative causes if no response after compliance.
explanation.pearls: Alternate-day iron dosing has equivalent absorption to daily and fewer side effects in adults; in toddlers the practical preference is still once daily because of palatability and parental compliance.

options.rationale: Microcytic anaemia with low ferritin is diagnostic of iron deficiency; electrophoresis is added later only if iron repletion fails to correct anaemia. (Source: RCH CPG Iron Deficiency)
IV iron is reserved for failed oral therapy, malabsorption or non-adherence; first-line is oral with dietary advice. (Source: RCH CPG Iron Deficiency)
Oral iron with dietary modification including milk reduction below 500 mL is first-line therapy in nutritional iron deficiency. (Source: RCH CPG Iron Deficiency)
Three times daily dosing is no more effective than once daily for iron deficiency in children and increases gastrointestinal side effects. (Source: RCH CPG Iron Deficiency)
Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or symptomatic anaemia under 70; this toddler is well-perfused. (Source: RCH CPG Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management balances correction of dehydration and acidosis against cerebral oedema risk, which carries 25% mortality. Bolus fluids are limited to 10 mL/kg unless overt shock; deficit assumed at 5 to 7% and replaced over 48 hours with isotonic fluid. Insulin starts at least 1 hour after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour, never with a bolus. Potassium 40 mmol/L is added after serum potassium is known unless anuric. Bicarbonate is contraindicated. Watch for warning signs of cerebral oedema: headache, falling GCS, hypertension with bradycardia, cranial nerve palsy. Treat suspected oedema with mannitol or hypertonic saline and reduce fluid rate.
key_points: Limit bolus to 10 mL/kg, deficit over 48 hours.
Delay insulin start by at least 1 hour after fluids.
Never bolus insulin; infuse 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour.
Bicarbonate contraindicated except life-threatening hyperkalaemia.
Cerebral oedema warning: headache, falling GCS, hypertension with bradycardia.
explanation.pearls: Effective osmolality (2 x Na plus glucose) should fall by no more than 3 mOsm/kg/hour; faster correction is independently associated with cerebral oedema even with apparently appropriate fluids.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

options.rationale: Rapid bolus and early insulin both increase cerebral oedema risk; bolus is reserved for shock and insulin starts after 1 hour of fluid resuscitation. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

options.rationale: Cautious 10 mL/kg bolus, gradual deficit replacement over 48 hours and delayed insulin start reduce cerebral oedema risk in paediatric DKA. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

options.rationale: Bicarbonate is harmful in paediatric DKA, causing paradoxical CSF acidosis and increased cerebral oedema; it is contraindicated unless life-threatening hyperkalaemia is present. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

options.rationale: Insulin must be delayed at least 1 hour after fluid resuscitation begins; immediate insulin worsens cerebral oedema risk. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid increases free water and worsens cerebral oedema; isotonic sodium chloride is mandatory and rates this high are unsafe. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia is plotted on a gestational-age-specific nomogram to set phototherapy and exchange thresholds. ABO incompatibility lowers the treatment threshold because of ongoing haemolysis. Conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or 20% of total is pathological and requires investigation for biliary atresia or sepsis. Acute bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) presents with lethargy, poor feeding, hypertonia, opisthotonus and a high-pitched cry. Intensive phototherapy reduces unconjugated bilirubin within hours; exchange transfusion is reserved for failure of intensive phototherapy or encephalopathy. Discharge follow-up should include a community SBR check within 24 to 48 hours when risk factors are present.
key_points: Use age-in-hours nomogram for phototherapy thresholds.
ABO incompatibility lowers treatment threshold.
Conjugated bilirubin above 20 needs separate work-up.
Exchange transfusion only for treatment failure or encephalopathy.
Adequate hydration is essential during phototherapy.
explanation.pearls: Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is always pathological - haemolytic disease, sepsis or G6PD deficiency until proven otherwise - and never attributable to physiological or breast milk jaundice.

options.rationale: SBR 320 at 60 hours in a term infant with ABO incompatibility exceeds the phototherapy threshold; treatment is required now. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal Jaundice)
IVIg is an adjunct considered only when intensive phototherapy fails or exchange transfusion is imminent in haemolytic disease. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal Jaundice)
Exchange transfusion is reserved for failure of intensive phototherapy or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy, neither of which is present. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal Jaundice)
Breastfeeding interruption is not first-line; haemolysis is the driver here and lactation support with phototherapy is correct. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal Jaundice)
SBR above the term phototherapy threshold with ABO haemolysis warrants intensive phototherapy with hydration optimisation and short-interval SBR monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary:
Australian paediatric practice escalates acute severe asthma in a fixed order once maximal inhaled therapy and systemic corticosteroid have failed: intravenous magnesium sulfate first, then an intravenous salbutamol load with infusion, then aminophylline, with intubation as a last resort. This boy has had magnesium without response, so the next pharmacological rung is intravenous salbutamol, given with cardiac monitoring and serial potassium, glucose and lactate measurement in a high dependency or intensive care bed.

In context: acute asthma is the commonest reason a school-aged child is escalated in an Australian emergency department. Severity is judged on speech, work of breathing and conscious state rather than on a single saturation reading, and the escalation ladder exists so that each step is trialled and assessed before the next. Knowing where a child sits on that ladder, and what has already been given, is what determines the next drug.
key_points: Order is magnesium, then intravenous salbutamol, then aminophylline
Intravenous salbutamol load 15 micrograms per kilogram over 10 minutes then infusion
Escalation beyond magnesium needs high dependency or intensive care
Intubation is a last resort because of dynamic hyperinflation
explanation.pearls: Ask what rung the child is already on before choosing a drug; the wrong answer in refractory asthma is usually a step that has already been taken or one two rungs ahead.

options.rationale: After magnesium has failed, the RCH acute asthma guideline moves to an intravenous salbutamol loading dose followed by an infusion, in a high dependency or intensive care setting with cardiac monitoring and electrolyte checks. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

Aminophylline sits below intravenous salbutamol in the Australian paediatric sequence and would be right only once both magnesium and intravenous salbutamol have failed, given its arrhythmia and seizure risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

Intramuscular adrenaline is for anaphylaxis, or for asthma so near arrest that inhaled and intravenous access have failed. This boy is alert with intravenous access already in place. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

Non-invasive ventilation is considered in an intensive care setting for a tiring child with rising carbon dioxide after pharmacological escalation, not before the next available bronchodilator has been given. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

Induction with ketamine belongs to the decision to intubate, which is reserved for arrest, exhaustion or refractory hypoxaemia because ventilating hyperinflated lungs is hazardous. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: Most wheeze in the first year of life is viral and not steroid-responsive, even when a parent has atopic asthma. Australian guidance reserves a preventer trial for children over 12 months with frequent episodes, interval symptoms or atopic features. Salbutamol responsiveness should be documented before chronic bronchodilator therapy is prescribed to infants. Parental anxiety is best managed with a written action plan and clear escalation triggers rather than empirical preventers.
key_points: Infant viral wheeze without atopy or salbutamol response does not justify a preventer trial.
Preventer trials become appropriate after 12 months when atopic features or interval symptoms appear.
Document bronchodilator response before prescribing regular salbutamol in any infant.
explanation.pearls: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce neither admissions nor symptom days in non-atopic infants under 12 months with isolated viral wheeze.

options.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids in infants under 12 months with viral wheeze and no atopy do not reduce admission rates and expose the infant to potential growth effects without clear benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)
A single bronchiolitic admission with normal growth and no chronic cough does not raise concern for cystic fibrosis; newborn screening already reduces residual risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

Montelukast has only modest benefit in selected preschool wheezers older than 2 years and is not first-line in infants; behavioural and neuropsychiatric adverse effects further limit routine use. (Source: AMH; eTG: Respiratory)
Regular salbutamol in infants without documented bronchodilator response is unhelpful and may mask deterioration; in this child salbutamol gave no benefit during admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

Under 12 months of age viral wheeze rarely represents atopic asthma and a documented poor salbutamol response confirms the bronchiolitis phenotype; routine preventers are not indicated and watchful waiting with safety-net advice is the standard approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

explanation.summary: Late-onset neonatal sepsis spans the period from 72 hours to 28 days of life. Empiric antibiotic choice in community-acquired disease must cover Group B Streptococcus, Listeria, Escherichia coli and other Gram-negatives, with adequate CNS penetration because meningitis cannot be excluded. The standard Australian neonatal regimen is intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin. Intravenous aciclovir should be added if vesicular rash, seizures, hepatitis or maternal HSV history exists.
key_points: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates under 28 days because of bilirubin displacement.
Cefotaxime is the cephalosporin of choice for neonatal sepsis with meningitis cover.
Add intravenous aciclovir if any HSV red flags are present in a sick neonate.
explanation.pearls: Cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin is first-line for community-acquired neonatal sepsis from day 3 to day 28 of life across Australian neonatal units.

options.rationale: Late-onset community-acquired sepsis in a previously well term neonate is empirically treated with cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin to cover Group B Streptococcus, Listeria and Gram-negatives including meningeal cover. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)
Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates under 28 days because of bilirubin displacement and a risk of kernicterus, particularly with concurrent calcium-containing fluids. (Source: AMH; eTG: Antibiotic)

This combination targets early-onset sepsis pathogens but lacks reliable cover for community-acquired late-onset bacteraemia and meningitis; CNS penetration of gentamicin is poor. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

Broad-spectrum vancomycin and meropenem are reserved for hospital-acquired late-onset sepsis or suspected resistant organisms; community-acquired presentations do not need this breadth empirically. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

Aciclovir requires intravenous administration in suspected neonatal HSV and amoxicillin alone has inadequate Gram-negative cover; this combination undertreats both bacterial and viral targets. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates approximately 1% of paediatric DKA episodes and carries 20 to 25% mortality. Risk peaks in younger children, first presentations, severe acidosis and high urea. Hyperosmolar therapy with intravenous mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg or hypertonic saline 3% at 2.5 to 5 mL/kg, combined with a one-third reduction in fluid rate, is initiated on clinical grounds. Headache, hypertension, bradycardia and falling conscious state form the Cushing triad equivalent in this setting.
key_points: Diagnose cerebral oedema clinically; do not wait for imaging.
Mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg or hypertonic saline 3% at 2.5 to 5 mL/kg are first-line.
Reduce IV fluid rate by one third and elevate the head of bed to 30 degrees.
explanation.pearls: Cushing triad in paediatric DKA - bradycardia, hypertension, falling GCS - means give mannitol 0.5 g/kg now and cut the fluid rate by a third before imaging.

options.rationale: Glucose is falling appropriately and ketosis is improving; increasing insulin further does not address the deteriorating neurology and risks worsening cerebral water shifts. (Source: ISPAD; APEG: Paediatric DKA)

Bradycardia, falling GCS and hypertension after fluid initiation in paediatric DKA define clinical cerebral oedema; mannitol or hypertonic saline plus a fluid rate reduction is the standard emergent response without waiting for imaging. (Source: ISPAD; APEG: Paediatric DKA)

Cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA is a clinical diagnosis; imaging delays definitive therapy and adds no early sensitivity, although CT may follow once the child is stabilised. (Source: ISPAD; APEG: Paediatric DKA)
A further bolus worsens cerebral oedema; the bradycardia here is a brainstem response to raised intracranial pressure, not hypovolaemic shock. (Source: ISPAD; APEG: Paediatric DKA)
Stopping insulin allows ketogenesis to resume and worsens acidosis without treating the cerebral oedema; insulin should continue alongside hyperosmolar therapy. (Source: ISPAD; APEG: Paediatric DKA)

explanation.summary: The Kocher criteria - inability to weight-bear, temperature over 38.5°C (often relaxed to 38°C in Australia), ESR over 40 mm/h and WCC over 12 x10^9/L - guide pretest probability of septic arthritis. Three or four positive criteria correspond to a 93 to 99% probability respectively. Joint aspiration provides immediate diagnostic yield via cell count, Gram stain and culture, and must precede empirical antibiotics whenever possible. Empiric flucloxacillin is then commenced; kingella kingae cover with cefazolin or addition of a second agent may be considered in children under 4 years.
key_points: Four Kocher criteria positive carries roughly 99% probability of septic arthritis.
Aspirate before antibiotics whenever feasible to maximise culture yield.
Empirical flucloxacillin covers Staphylococcus aureus; consider kingella kingae cover under 4 years.
explanation.pearls: A non-weight-bearing febrile child with CRP above 20 mg/L plus ultrasound effusion warrants same-day joint aspiration; transient synovitis remains a diagnosis of exclusion.

options.rationale: With three Kocher criteria positive the probability of septic arthritis is approximately 93% and outpatient management risks rapid joint destruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)
Antibiotics given before aspiration reduce culture yield and delay diagnosis; aspiration must precede empirical antibiotics whenever septic arthritis is plausible. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Four Kocher criteria positive in this child (non-weight-bearing, fever 38.1°C, ESR over 40, WCC over 12 x10^9/L) gives a high pre-test probability of septic arthritis; aspiration is the definitive diagnostic step. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)
MRI is helpful for osteomyelitis or atypical presentations but delays joint sampling in a probable septic hip; ultrasound has already confirmed an effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)
Symptomatic treatment risks masking deterioration in a child with four high-risk features; the priority is definitive sampling not analgesic monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in any infant under 12 months is treated as midgut volvulus until imaging excludes it. Time-to-detorsion correlates directly with bowel survival, so the workup is compressed - nasogastric decompression, IV access, fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics and an immediate paediatric surgical referral run in parallel with imaging. The upper GI contrast study showing a corkscrew or right-sided duodenojejunal junction confirms malrotation; whirlpool sign on ultrasound is supportive. Laparotomy and Ladd procedure are definitive.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in infants is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.
Upper GI contrast study is the definitive imaging test.
Time-to-theatre directly determines bowel survival.
explanation.pearls: In a neonate with green vomiting, call paediatric surgery and book an upper GI contrast study before plain films or ultrasound delay the diagnosis.

sources.label: Paediatric Surgery: malrotation chapter (BMJ Best Practice)

options.rationale: Ultrasound is operator-dependent and only supportive; a negative scan does not exclude malrotation and must not delay the definitive contrast study. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise; an urgent upper GI contrast study to confirm or exclude an abnormal duodenojejunal junction position is the definitive test before laparotomy. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)
Plain films are often normal in malrotation without established volvulus and cannot exclude the diagnosis; relying on them risks missing a surgical emergency. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

Sweat testing investigates cystic fibrosis-related meconium ileus equivalents, which present earlier and without bilious vomiting; it does not address the surgical emergency. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

Hirschsprung disease classically presents with delayed meconium passage and distal obstruction; bilious vomiting points to a proximal obstructive lesion, of which malrotation is the priority diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

explanation.summary: Hypernatraemic dehydration is most often caused by improperly mixed feeds, inadequate breastfeeding or large gastroenteritis losses without free water replacement. Rapid sodium correction draws water back into brain cells and causes cerebral oedema with herniation. The Australian paediatric standard replaces the deficit with isotonic sodium chloride plus dextrose over 48 to 72 hours, aiming to drop sodium no faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour or 10 to 12 mmol/L per day. Boluses are reserved for true shock.
key_points: Hypernatraemic deficit replacement runs over 48 to 72 hours not 24.
Plasma sodium must fall no faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour.
Use isotonic fluids; hypotonic regimens accelerate dangerous sodium shifts.
explanation.pearls: Slow correction with sodium chloride 0.9% plus glucose 5% over 48 hours, capped at a 10 mmol/L sodium drop per day, prevents the cerebral oedema and seizures that follow rapid correction of hypernatraemic dehydration.

options.rationale: Hypernatraemic dehydration requires slow correction with isotonic fluids over 48 to 72 hours; the deficit is replaced gradually so plasma sodium falls no faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour or 12 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)
Hypotonic resuscitation fluids drop plasma sodium too rapidly and risk cerebral oedema; the bolus strength should be isotonic and the correction phase prolonged. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)
Pure glucose for maintenance after the bolus delivers free water too quickly and causes a precipitous sodium drop; correction must be paced over 48 hours minimum. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

A lethargic child with capillary refill of 4 seconds and 7% volume loss requires intravenous resuscitation, although oral therapy is valuable once intravascular volume is restored. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)
Rapid 12-hour correction predisposes to cerebral oedema and seizures despite using an isotonic fluid; rate of sodium fall not total volume is the safety variable. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

explanation.summary: Salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents around day 7 to 14 with vomiting, lethargy, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis. Female infants often have virilised genitalia; male infants have normal genitalia, which can delay recognition.
