Emergency management is intravenous stress-dose hydrocortisone (25 mg in infants under 6 years), isotonic volume with glucose, and correction of hypoglycaemia. Long-term replacement combines hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone and salt supplementation under endocrinology supervision.
key_points: Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg is the stat dose in infants under 6 years with adrenal crisis.
Use isotonic fluids with glucose; avoid dexamethasone in acute crisis because of absent mineralocorticoid effect.
Hyperkalaemia of CAH usually resolves with volume and steroid, not insulin or beta-agonists.
explanation.pearls: Day 7 to 14 vomiting infant with sodium under 130 mmol/L and potassium over 6 mmol/L is salt-wasting CAH until proven otherwise; give intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg now.

options.rationale: An unwell shocked infant in adrenal crisis cannot absorb oral therapy reliably; intravenous hydrocortisone with intravenous resuscitation is the correct route. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis; APEG: CAH)
Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and is the wrong steroid in acute salt-wasting crisis; hypotonic fluids worsen hyponatraemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis; APEG: CAH)

Salt-wasting CAH crisis requires immediate stress-dose hydrocortisone, isotonic volume resuscitation containing glucose to address hypoglycaemia, and urgent specialist involvement to guide ongoing replacement; fludrocortisone is added once enteral therapy is tolerated. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis; APEG: CAH)

The hyperkalaemia of salt-wasting CAH responds rapidly to volume and steroid replacement; insulin is unnecessary and risks profound hypoglycaemia in a glucose-2.1 mmol/L infant. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis; APEG: CAH)

Although a septic workup is reasonable to add in parallel, the diagnosis of salt-wasting CAH is already supported by ambiguous genitalia, raised 17-OHP and the electrolyte pattern; immunoglobulin has no role. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis; APEG: CAH)

explanation.summary: Hand foot and mouth disease is a common coxsackievirus or enterovirus rash with grey-white vesicles on the palms, soles and oral mucosa. The Staying Healthy 5th edition recommends exclusion until the blisters have dried; there is no fixed day count and crusting is not part of the natural history. Hygiene measures and surface cleaning at the childcare centre are the main control strategies, with EV71 surveillance flagged separately for severe disease.
key_points: Exclude from childcare until blisters have dried, not until they have crusted.
There is no fixed day count for return; clinical wellness is required in addition.
Notification is only triggered in clusters with severe neurological involvement suggesting EV71.
explanation.pearls: If a child with HFMD develops ataxia, drowsiness or myoclonic jerks within the first 5 days, escalate urgently because enterovirus 71 brainstem encephalitis is a public health priority.

options.rationale: The Staying Healthy 5th edition advises exclusion of children with HFMD until the blisters have dried, with the child also clinically well; this aligns the duration to actual infectivity and clinical state rather than a fixed day count. (Source: Staying Healthy 5th edition NHMRC)

HFMD is not on the standard national notifiable list and is managed by exclusion plus hygiene; PHU notification is only triggered in clusters of severe disease such as suspected EV71-associated brainstem encephalitis. (Source: CDNA Series of National Guidelines)

HFMD does carry an exclusion period in Australian early childhood settings; absence of fever does not change the recommendation while the vesicles are still moist. (Source: Staying Healthy 5th edition NHMRC)
There is no mandated 21 day exclusion for HFMD; this length applies to no notifiable childhood infection currently listed in the NHMRC schedule. (Source: Staying Healthy 5th edition NHMRC)

This is the rule for varicella, not for hand foot and mouth disease; the vesicles in HFMD do not crust like chickenpox and prolonged exclusion is not required. (Source: Staying Healthy: Preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services)

explanation.summary: Scarlet fever in an Aboriginal child from a remote community sits in the highest-risk group for acute rheumatic fever. The cornerstone of prevention is eradication of Group A Streptococcus from the pharynx with a full ten-day course of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin or a single dose of intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin. Shorter courses settle symptoms but leave organisms behind and do not prevent ARF. Macrolides are reserved for true penicillin allergy.
key_points: Phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for ten days is first-line.
Single dose IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is an alternative when adherence is uncertain.
Shorter courses settle symptoms but do not prevent rheumatic fever.
explanation.pearls: In any Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander child with pharyngitis, treat group A streptococcal infection as a 10-day course or single benzathine dose; do not stop at 5 days even if the child is asymptomatic by day 3.

sources.label: RHDAustralia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of ARF and RHD

options.rationale: Five days is enough to settle symptoms but is insufficient to eradicate Group A Streptococcus from the pharynx and so does not reliably prevent acute rheumatic fever. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Amoxicillin is an acceptable alternative when adherence to penicillin V dosing is a concern, but the AU rheumatic-fever prevention regimens specify a full ten-day duration, not seven. (Source: RHDAustralia guideline)
source_refs: RHDAustralia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of ARF and RHD

options.rationale: In a child from a high acute rheumatic fever risk group, withholding antibiotics is unsafe because rheumatic fever can follow even mild pharyngitis. (Source: RHDAustralia guideline)
source_refs: RHDAustralia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of ARF and RHD

options.rationale: Macrolides are reserved for documented penicillin hypersensitivity; in penicillin-tolerant patients they are not first-line because of increasing macrolide-resistant Group A Streptococcus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

In Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children living in remote communities a full ten-day course of phenoxymethylpenicillin (or single dose IM benzathine benzylpenicillin) is required to prevent acute rheumatic fever, even when symptoms resolve early. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets in Australia is most commonly seen in dark-skinned children with limited sunlight exposure, prolonged exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation, and low dietary calcium. Diagnosis combines hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, elevated ALP and PTH, low 25-OH vitamin D, plus radiographic metaphyseal cupping and fraying. Treatment is several weeks of colecalciferol with adequate calcium intake; bony deformities correct over months without orthopaedic intervention.
key_points: Treatment dose colecalciferol 1000 to 5000 units daily for 12 weeks depending on age.
Calcium 500 mg elemental daily is needed alongside vitamin D in established rickets.
ALP and 25-OH D are followed at 3 months to confirm response.
explanation.pearls: In suspected rickets, an ALP above 1000 U/L with a 25-OH vitamin D below 25 nmol/L is highly suggestive; check PTH to exclude renal forms.

sources.label: APEG: Vitamin D and health in children

options.rationale: 1000 units daily is a maintenance dose; it is too low for established rickets, which requires a treatment dose for several weeks. (Source: APEG vitamin D position statement)
source_refs: APEG: Vitamin D and health in children

options.rationale: Treatment-dose vitamin D (1000 to 2000 units daily under 1 month, 3000 units daily 1-12 months, or 5000 units daily over 12 months) for 12 weeks, combined with adequate calcium intake, is the Australian guideline approach to symptomatic rickets. (Source: APEG vitamin D position statement)
source_refs: APEG: Vitamin D and health in children

options.rationale: Bow legs in nutritional rickets correct over months once vitamin D and calcium are repleted; surgery is not the first step. (Source: APEG vitamin D position statement)
source_refs: APEG: Vitamin D and health in children

options.rationale: High-dose stoss therapy has been associated with hypercalcaemia and is not the AU first-line approach; daily dosing is preferred where adherence allows. (Source: APEG vitamin D position statement)
source_refs: APEG: Vitamin D and health in children

options.rationale: IV calcium is reserved for symptomatic hypocalcaemia (seizures, tetany, prolonged QT); this child has mild biochemical hypocalcaemia and no acute cardiac or neuromuscular features. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypocalcaemia)

explanation.summary: Non-IgE mediated cow milk protein allergy commonly presents in young formula-fed infants with crying, vomiting, mucousy bloody stools and faltering growth. Diagnosis is clinical: a 2 to 4 week trial of an extensively hydrolysed formula should resolve symptoms, with a planned milk challenge between 9 and 12 months. Soy formula is not first-line under 6 months because of cross-reactivity, and lactose-free formula does not remove the offending protein.
key_points: Extensively hydrolysed casein formula is first-line for proven or suspected non-IgE CMPA under 6 months.
Soy formula is avoided as first-line under 6 months due to cross-reactivity.
Specific IgE testing is normal in non-IgE phenotypes and should not gate the trial.
explanation.pearls: Blood-streaked mucous stools plus eczema and slowing weight gain in an infant just after the breast-to-formula switch is classic non-IgE cow milk protein allergy; expect symptoms to resolve within 2 to 4 weeks of extensively hydrolysed formula.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: Lactose-free formula still contains intact cow milk protein and does not treat protein-induced colitis. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: Non-IgE mediated cow milk protein allergy is a clinical diagnosis with normal specific IgE; testing before a dietary trial delays treatment and is rarely diagnostic in this phenotype. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: Up to one in three infants with cow milk protein allergy are also intolerant of soy protein; ASCIA does not recommend soy formula as a first-line substitute under 6 months. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: Acid suppression treats reflux oesophagitis but does not address the immune-mediated colitis suggested by streaks of blood and slowing weight gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux)

Non-IgE mediated cow's milk protein allergy in a young infant with proctocolitis features is managed by a trial of an extensively hydrolysed formula; symptomatic improvement within two to four weeks supports the diagnosis. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

explanation.summary: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis typically presents from day 5 to day 14 of life with mucopurulent discharge in a well-appearing baby. Systemic erythromycin for 14 days is the standard Australian regimen because topical therapy alone does not eradicate organisms from the nasopharynx and predisposes to chlamydial pneumonitis at 4 to 12 weeks. Maternal partner notification, infant pyloric stenosis counselling and contact tracing are integral parts of management.
key_points: Oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 14 days is first-line.
Topical therapy alone is inadequate because of nasopharyngeal colonisation.
Counsel parents about the small risk of infantile pyloric stenosis with macrolides under 6 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Sticky eyes in a 1-2 week old baby with mucopurulent discharge and a well-appearing infant should be treated as chlamydia until PCR proves otherwise; do not stop at topical chloramphenicol.

sources.label: ASHM Sexually transmissible infections in primary care manual

options.rationale: Watchful management without antimicrobials is appropriate for chemical conjunctivitis in the first 24 hours of life, not for a day-7 mucopurulent picture with high suspicion of chlamydia. (Source: STIs in gay men action group AU and Therapeutic Guidelines)

Single-dose ceftriaxone is the regimen for suspected gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum (day 1 to 5, hyperacute purulent discharge); this presentation pattern is typical of chlamydia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Chloramphenicol drops cover bacterial conjunctivitis but do not eradicate chlamydia from the nasopharynx, leaving the baby at risk of pneumonitis at 4 to 12 weeks of age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Azithromycin single dose is the standard for adult genital chlamydia but is not the AU regimen for neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis; the 14-day erythromycin course also reduces pneumonitis risk and infantile pyloric stenosis risk is similar with either macrolide. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis at day 5 to 14 of life is treated with systemic oral erythromycin for 14 days because topical therapy alone does not prevent later chlamydial pneumonitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: ANZBA criteria mandate referral of any partial-thickness burn over 5% total body surface area in a child to a designated paediatric burns service, and any burn involving the face, hands, feet, perineum, joints or circumferential limb burns regardless of size. Pre-transfer wound care is cling film loosely applied, not circumferential, with strong analgesia; topical antimicrobials should be delayed until the receiving service has assessed depth. Parkland-style IV resuscitation is reserved for burns 10% or greater.
key_points: Refer any partial-thickness burn over 5% TBSA in a child.
Cling film loosely applied is the pre-transfer dressing of choice.
Parkland-style IV resuscitation begins at 10% TBSA, not at 5%.
explanation.pearls: In a child with a scald, calculate the burn area using the child's palmar surface (~1% TBSA) and use ANZBA criteria; never apply silver sulfadiazine before the burns unit has assessed depth.

options.rationale: Parkland-style fluid resuscitation is started for paediatric burns of at least 10% TBSA; a 6% scald is below that threshold but still warrants oral hydration and transfer. (Source: ANZBA Burn Patient Management)
Deroofing intact blisters in the community is not advised; it increases pain, infection risk and contamination before burns-service assessment. (Source: ANZBA Burn Patient Management)

ANZBA criteria require referral to a designated paediatric burns service for any partial-thickness burn over 5% TBSA in a child under 16; the AU pre-transfer cover is loose cling film (not circumferential), with effective analgesia. (Source: ANZBA Burn Patient Management 4th edition)
Cooling beyond 20 minutes after a scald is not beneficial and increases hypothermia risk, particularly in a young child with a 6% surface area injury. (Source: ANZBA Burn Patient Management)

Silver sulfadiazine should not be applied before assessment by the receiving burns service because it stains the wound and complicates depth assessment; outpatient management of a 6% burn in a 2-year-old is also outside primary-care scope. (Source: ANZBA Burn Patient Management)

explanation.summary: Mild to moderately dehydrated children with acute gastroenteritis who fail to keep down oral rehydration benefit from a single oral wafer dose of ondansetron, which roughly halves the rate of IV fluid escalation. If oral rehydration after ondansetron fails, NG rehydration is the next step, then IV fluids. Antimotility agents are not used in children and stool studies are reserved for atypical illness.
key_points: Ondansetron 2 mg wafer for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for over 15 kg, single dose.
Trial oral rehydration solution after ondansetron before considering IV or NG.
Avoid loperamide in children.
explanation.pearls: A single ondansetron wafer plus 30 minutes of patient oral rehydration prevents IV cannulation in roughly half of vomiting children with mild dehydration.

options.rationale: IV fluid bolus is reserved for moderate-to-severe dehydration with haemodynamic compromise or failed oral rehydration after ondansetron; this child has only mild dehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
NG rehydration is a reasonable option if oral fluids continue to fail after ondansetron, but it is not the first step in a child not yet trialled on ondansetron. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Stool studies do not change acute management of typical viral gastroenteritis and are reserved for bloody diarrhoea, prolonged or atypical illness, or immunocompromise. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

A single oral ondansetron dose (2 mg for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for over 15 kg) reduces vomiting and the need for IV fluids in mild-moderate dehydration; oral rehydration is then attempted before escalating. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
Antimotility agents are contraindicated in paediatric gastroenteritis because of toxic megacolon and CNS toxicity risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Night terrors are a non-REM parasomnia that occur in the first third of the night, peak between 3 and 7 years of age, and resolve spontaneously. Children appear awake but are unresponsive, have no recall, and should not be roused during the event. Management is reassurance, sleep hygiene and, for clustered episodes, scheduled awakening 15 minutes before the usual time. Investigations and pharmacotherapy are reserved for atypical or injurious episodes.
key_points: Typical onset 90 minutes after sleep, no recall, full recovery between episodes.
First-line management is reassurance and scheduled awakening.
Investigate only if features atypical (daytime, stereotyped, later in night).
explanation.pearls: Scheduled awakening 15 minutes before the expected terror, for two weeks, breaks the non-REM cycle and resolves clusters in most preschoolers.

sources.label: RACGP HANDI: Scheduled awakening for sleep terrors

options.rationale: Night terrors are a non-REM parasomnia that peaks at 3 to 7 years; reassurance, predictable bedtime routine and pre-emptive scheduled awakening for clustered episodes is first-line management, and most children outgrow them by adolescence. (Source: RACGP HANDI: Scheduled awakening for sleep terrors)
source_refs: RACGP HANDI: Scheduled awakening for sleep terrors

options.rationale: Night terrors are not a manifestation of anxiety in toddlers and do not predict psychopathology; psychiatry referral is not indicated based on this history. (Source: RACGP HANDI)
source_refs: RACGP HANDI: Scheduled awakening for sleep terrors

options.rationale: EEG is reserved for atypical features such as stereotyped movements, daytime symptoms, very brief episodes or episodes later in the night; a typical 3-year-old parasomnia in the first third of the night does not need investigation. (Source: RACGP HANDI)
source_refs: RACGP HANDI: Scheduled awakening for sleep terrors

options.rationale: Melatonin has weak evidence for sleep-onset insomnia in children, not for parasomnias, and is not the first-line approach for night terrors. (Source: AAP Clinical Report: Melatonin)

Benzodiazepines are reserved for severe, injury-causing parasomnias in older children after non-drug strategies have failed; routine use in a 3-year-old is not appropriate. (Source: AASM practice parameters)

explanation.summary: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows a streptococcal skin or pharyngeal infection by 1 to 3 weeks and presents with macroscopic haematuria, mild hypertension and periorbital oedema. Diagnosis is supported by low C3 with normal C4, evidence of recent streptococcal infection (ASOT or anti-DNase B), and red-cell casts on microscopy. Management is supportive with admission for BP and fluid monitoring during the first 1 to 2 weeks; complement and urine should normalise by 8 to 12 weeks.
key_points: Low C3, normal C4, red cell casts, positive ASOT or anti-DNase B suggest PSGN.
Inpatient monitoring focuses on BP and pulmonary congestion in the first 1-2 weeks.
Biopsy is reserved for atypical or progressive presentations.
explanation.pearls: If C3 remains low at 12 weeks after presumed PSGN, switch the diagnosis to MPGN or lupus nephritis and refer for biopsy.

options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for atypical features such as persistent low C3 beyond 3 months, normal complement, nephrotic-range proteinuria, or progressive renal impairment; this child has classic PSGN. (Source: KHA-CARI)

Children with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis are at risk of hypertensive encephalopathy and pulmonary oedema during the first 1 to 2 weeks; inpatient observation with salt restriction and short-acting antihypertensives like nifedipine is first-line if hypertension develops. (Source: KHA-CARI Adolescent and adult glomerulonephritis)
Outpatient follow-up alone fails to capture the peak risk of hypertensive encephalopathy and pulmonary oedema in the first 1 to 2 weeks; admission for monitoring is safer. (Source: KHA-CARI)

PSGN is a self-limiting illness; corticosteroids are not part of standard management and are reserved for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis or proven crescentic disease on biopsy. (Source: KHA-CARI)

Antibiotics do not alter the course of established PSGN; if active streptococcal infection persists in a household it is treated for the index case, not as part of PSGN management. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension in adolescents is associated with obesity and certain drugs including isotretinoin, tetracyclines, growth hormone and excess vitamin A. Diagnostic criteria include papilloedema, normal neuroimaging including venogram, and elevated CSF opening pressure with normal constituents. Management is precipitant removal, acetazolamide and weight loss, with surgical options reserved for vision loss despite medical therapy.
key_points: Cease the precipitant drug before starting other therapy.
Acetazolamide is first-line pharmacotherapy.
Serial perimetry monitors visual function; surgery if vision loss progresses.
explanation.pearls: Any teenager on isotretinoin or doxycycline with a new daily headache needs fundoscopy at the first visit; missing papilloedema risks irreversible optic atrophy.

options.rationale: Continuing the precipitant perpetuates the disease and the picture is not migraine; propranolol does not treat IIH. (Source: ANZCNS: Paediatric IIH)
Corticosteroids cause rebound intracranial hypertension on withdrawal and risk weight gain in an obese adolescent; they are not first-line. (Source: ANZCNS: Paediatric IIH)

Stopping the precipitant (isotretinoin, tetracyclines, vitamin A excess), commencing acetazolamide and arranging serial automated perimetry is the standard AU adolescent management of idiopathic intracranial hypertension; surgical CSF diversion is for failing vision or medication-refractory disease. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Child Neurology Society IIH guidance)
Serial therapeutic LPs are not the long-term management; they are uncomfortable and risky and have been replaced by acetazolamide and weight loss. (Source: ANZCNS: Paediatric IIH)
Shunting (lumboperitoneal or ventriculoperitoneal) and optic-nerve sheath fenestration are reserved for vision loss despite optimal medical therapy. (Source: ANZCNS: Paediatric IIH)

explanation.summary: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally aggressive vascular tumour of adolescent males that presents with recurrent unilateral epistaxis and progressive nasal obstruction. A vascular nasopharyngeal mass should never be biopsied without imaging because of the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage. Contrast MRI defines extent and skull-base spread, followed by angiography, preoperative embolisation and endoscopic resection.
key_points: Adolescent male + unilateral epistaxis + nasal obstruction = consider JNA.
Image before any biopsy.
Pre-op angiography and embolisation reduces operative blood loss.
explanation.pearls: Never biopsy a smooth red mass behind the middle turbinate in an adolescent male without imaging first; embolise within 24 to 48 hours of resection to minimise revascularisation.

options.rationale: Direct biopsy of suspected juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma can cause life-threatening haemorrhage; imaging confirms the diagnosis before any tissue sampling. (Source: RANZCO/AAOHNS)
The history of unilateral nasal mass plus progressive obstruction points to a structural lesion, not coagulopathy; further haematology testing will not capture this diagnosis. (Source: RANZCO/AAOHNS)

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in an adolescent male is a vascular tumour that bleeds catastrophically on biopsy; contrast MRI defines extent and intracranial spread, followed by preoperative angiography and embolisation. (Source: RANZCO and AAOHNS combined head and neck guidance)
Plain films are insensitive for soft-tissue tumours of the post-nasal space and cannot define skull-base involvement. (Source: RANZCO/AAOHNS)
Steroid sprays treat allergic rhinitis, not a vascular nasopharyngeal mass, and delay definitive diagnosis. (Source: RANZCO/AAOHNS)

explanation.summary: Beta-thalassaemia major presents in the second half of the first year as fetal haemoglobin production wanes, with progressive anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly and faltering growth. Once the diagnosis is confirmed and the child is symptomatic, regular transfusion at pre-transfusion Hb 95 to 105 g/L suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis and supports growth. Iron chelation is added when ferritin exceeds about 1000 micrograms/L, typically after 10 to 20 transfusions.
key_points: Start regular transfusion when symptoms, growth failure or organomegaly emerge.
Pre-transfusion target Hb 95 to 105 g/L.
Iron chelation begins around 10-20 transfusions or ferritin over 1000.
explanation.pearls: Curative haematopoietic stem cell transplant from an HLA-matched sibling should be discussed early in beta-thalassaemia major to capture the best-outcome window before iron overload.

options.rationale: Hydroxycarbamide is established in sickle cell disease and used in some intermediate thalassaemias; it is not first-line in transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia major. (Source: HSANZ)
Folate alone does not correct the underlying defect; in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, folate is an adjunct, not a definitive treatment, and this child is already symptomatic. (Source: HSANZ)

Withholding transfusion until profound anaemia leads to extramedullary haematopoiesis, severe skeletal changes and growth failure; modern regimens transfuse at pre-transfusion Hb 95 to 105 g/L. (Source: HSANZ)

Confirmed beta-thalassaemia major with symptomatic anaemia, organomegaly and faltering growth meets criteria to start regular transfusion at a pre-transfusion Hb of 95 to 105 g/L; chelation is started later when ferritin rises. (Source: HSANZ: Thalassaemia in Australia)
Splenectomy is deferred until age over 5 years and reserved for excessive transfusion requirements, given infection and thrombosis risks. (Source: HSANZ)

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy is an idiopathic generalised epilepsy that begins between 4 and 10 years with multiple daily brief unresponsive episodes triggered by hyperventilation, and a characteristic 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave EEG. Ethosuximide is the AU first-line monotherapy. Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin and tiagabine should be avoided because they can worsen absences. Most children remit before puberty.
key_points: Ethosuximide first-line, valproate second-line.
Avoid carbamazepine (worsens absences).
Hyperventilation provocation in clinic supports diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: If a child with apparent CAE has additional myoclonic jerks or GTCS, suspect juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and switch from ethosuximide to valproate or lamotrigine.

options.rationale: Carbamazepine can aggravate absence seizures and is contraindicated in idiopathic generalised epilepsies. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Lamotrigine is third-line for absence epilepsy; slow titration and lower response rates make it inferior to ethosuximide or valproate as initial therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Valproate is effective in childhood absence epilepsy but is second-line because of greater attentional side-effects in the CAE trial and the teratogenic risk that becomes relevant later in adolescence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Levetiracetam is not licensed for absence epilepsy in monotherapy and has lower efficacy than ethosuximide or valproate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Ethosuximide is first-line for typical childhood absence epilepsy because it has superior efficacy and a better cognitive profile than valproate in childhood absence epilepsy (CAE) head-to-head trials. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology and Cochrane review of CAE)

explanation.summary: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia commonly presents with bone pain, pallor, petechiae or bruising, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, and recurrent low-grade fevers. Pancytopenia with circulating blasts requires same-day discussion with paediatric oncology and admission for tumour-lysis prophylaxis (hyperhydration, urate-lowering therapy) and bone marrow biopsy. Empirical steroids before diagnosis should be avoided.
key_points: Night bone pain + pallor + petechiae = exclude leukaemia.
Same-day paediatric oncology contact; tumour-lysis prophylaxis is the first inpatient task.
Avoid empirical steroids before tissue diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Use the FBC, film and LDH to triage urgency: any child with night bone pain plus a circulating blast count needs same-day oncology contact, not a 'review in a week' plan.

options.rationale: There is no joint swelling, warmth or limp localisation; the bicompartmental nightly pain in a child with pancytopenia points to marrow infiltration, not infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)
Empirical steroids before tissue diagnosis can mask the marrow picture and delay accurate classification of the leukaemia subtype. (Source: eviQ)
The blood film already shows blasts; deferring action by a week risks tumour lysis, severe sepsis with neutropenia, or bleeding complications. (Source: eviQ)

Pancytopenia, peripheral blasts, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy and biochemical evidence of high cell turnover suggest acute leukaemia; immediate transfer for tumour-lysis prophylaxis (hyperhydration, allopurinol or rasburicase) and bone marrow assessment is mandatory. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL induction)
Night pain that wakes the child, with pallor, petechiae and hepatomegaly, is incompatible with benign growing pains and ibuprofen could worsen bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

explanation.summary: Posterior urethral valves are the commonest cause of severe obstructive uropathy in newborn boys and typically present with antenatal hydronephrosis, oligohydramnios and a distended bladder with weak stream postnatally. Initial management is bladder drainage with a small feeding-tube catheter (Foley balloons can traumatise the prostatic urethra), followed by paediatric urology transfer for MCUG and cystoscopic ablation. Renal function should be monitored as nephrogenic damage may already be established.
key_points: Fine feeding-tube catheter for initial drainage, not a Foley.
Definitive treatment is cystoscopic valve ablation.
Renal failure, pulmonary hypoplasia and bladder dysfunction may persist long-term.
explanation.pearls: Antenatal bilateral hydronephrosis + oligohydramnios + male fetus = plan for postnatal PUV; have a 6 Fr feeding tube ready at birth and paediatric urology on standby.

options.rationale: Initial management of suspected posterior urethral valves is bladder drainage with a small feeding-tube catheter (Foleys may traumatise the prostatic urethra) followed by transfer for micturating cystourethrogram and cystoscopic valve ablation. (Source: APSA and ANZUNS paediatric urology guidance)
Persistent obstruction worsens AKI, electrolyte derangement and bladder damage; drainage is required within hours. (Source: ANZUNS)
Furosemide will not bypass a mechanical obstruction and can precipitate electrolyte derangement; the lesion is anatomical. (Source: ANZUNS)
A 10 Fr Foley balloon catheter can sit in the prostatic urethra and traumatise the valves; a fine feeding tube is preferred until cystoscopic assessment. (Source: ANZUNS)
A single aspiration does not provide ongoing drainage; an infant with PUV needs continuous bladder decompression and definitive surgical valve ablation. (Source: ANZUNS)

explanation.summary: ANZCOR Guideline 4 directs that an infant under 1 year with ineffective cough and severe airway obstruction receives up to five back blows in a head-down prone position, followed by up to five chest thrusts if obstruction persists. Abdominal thrusts are contraindicated under 1 year. If the infant becomes unresponsive, commence infant CPR. Direct laryngoscopy with Magill forceps is the next step if available.
key_points: Back blows then chest thrusts in infants under 1 year.
Abdominal thrusts are contraindicated under 1 year.
Avoid blind finger sweeps.
explanation.pearls: Bradycardia precedes arrest in airway obstruction; treat the obstruction first - oxygen will not bypass a complete mechanical block.

options.rationale: Blind finger sweeps may push the foreign body further into the airway; only remove a foreign body that you can directly visualise. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

While bradycardia in choking is ominous, the immediate priority remains relief of the airway obstruction with back blows then chest thrusts; CPR commences only if the infant becomes unresponsive. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)
Abdominal thrusts are contraindicated under 1 year because they risk visceral and hepatic injury; chest thrusts are used instead after back blows. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

In an infant under 1 year with ineffective cough and obstruction, ANZCOR guidance is to deliver up to five back blows in a head-down prone position followed by up to five chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts are contraindicated in infants. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)
Oxygen cannot reach the alveoli through a fully obstructed airway; mechanical relief of the obstruction is the priority. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

explanation.summary: Nirsevimab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody recommended in Australia for infants entering their first RSV season and for high-risk infants (chronic lung disease of prematurity, haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease) entering their second RSV season. A single weight-based IM dose covers the entire season, replacing monthly palivizumab where funded. Maternal vaccination with RSVpreF is the alternative pathway for healthy term babies whose mothers were eligible antenatally.
key_points: Single-dose nirsevimab covers the whole RSV season.
Eligible: first season for all infants, second season for high-risk infants.
Maternal RSVpreF in pregnancy is an alternative for healthy term infants.
explanation.pearls: If maternal RSVpreF was given in pregnancy at 28-36 weeks, the term infant does not also need nirsevimab; if not, a single nirsevimab dose is the AU default.

options.rationale: Montelukast is not an RSV prophylactic and does not prevent severe RSV bronchiolitis admission. (Source: GINA Australia and Therapeutic Guidelines)
Palivizumab is being replaced by single-dose nirsevimab in Australian jurisdictions because nirsevimab provides season-long protection in one dose. (Source: AIH)

AU NIRP (immunisation handbook) recommends single-dose nirsevimab for high-risk infants under 2 years with chronic lung disease of prematurity or significant CHD entering their first or second RSV season, replacing monthly palivizumab in most jurisdictions. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook NIRP)
Behavioural measures alone are insufficient in an infant with BPD on home oxygen; targeted monoclonal-antibody prophylaxis substantially reduces hospital admission. (Source: AIH)
RSVpreF is a maternal vaccine given antenatally; it is not licensed for direct infant vaccination. (Source: AIH)

explanation.summary: Excessive cow milk intake above 500 mL per day is a leading cause of toddler iron deficiency in Australia because milk displaces iron-rich foods and reduces non-haem iron absorption. The Royal Children's Hospital guideline recommends 3 mg/kg/day of elemental iron orally for at least 3 months, then a further 3 months once Hb normalises to replenish stores. A FBC and ferritin check at 4 to 6 weeks documents response. Dietary modification including red meat, iron-fortified cereals and vitamin C with meals is essential alongside supplementation.
key_points: Cow milk above 500 mL daily is a key dietary risk factor.
Elemental iron dose is 3 mg/kg once daily for three months.
Recheck FBC and ferritin at four to six weeks for response.
IV iron is reserved for oral failure, intolerance or malabsorption.
explanation.pearls: Expect a reticulocyte rise within 5 to 7 days and a Hb rise of about 10 g/L per month on oral iron; failure to respond after 4 weeks should prompt review of adherence, ongoing milk excess, or alternative diagnoses such as coeliac disease.

options.rationale: Multivitamin syrups contain too little elemental iron to correct established deficiency anaemia; a therapeutic iron dose is needed alongside dietary change. (Source: RCH CPG Iron deficiency)
IV iron is reserved for failure of oral therapy, malabsorption or intolerance; uncomplicated nutritional deficiency responds to oral iron and dietary modification. (Source: RCH CPG Iron deficiency)

Australian guidance recommends 3 mg/kg/day of elemental iron for at least 3 months in nutritional iron deficiency, plus cow milk volume below 500 mL to reduce iron antagonism. (Source: RCH CPG Iron deficiency)
The very low ferritin and dietary history give an unambiguous nutritional diagnosis; electrophoresis is reserved if the anaemia fails to respond to iron replacement. (Source: RCH CPG Iron deficiency)
Diet alone is too slow to correct symptomatic anaemia with Hb 84 g/L; oral iron replacement is required in addition to dietary advice. (Source: RCH CPG Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance recommends a stepped-care approach to paediatric atopic eczema starting with generous emollient use plus a topical corticosteroid matched to severity and site. Mild potency steroids such as hydrocortisone 1% are appropriate for the face and flexures of young children, with stronger steroids reserved for thicker plaques or recalcitrant disease. A finger-tip unit guide helps families dose correctly. Antibiotic therapy is reserved for clinical infection rather than colonisation alone.
key_points: Use mild topical steroid for flexural toddler eczema.
Emollients applied liberally several times per day are essential.
Reserve systemic therapy for failure of optimised topical care.
Treat infected eczema with cefalexin or flucloxacillin if oozing or honey-crusted.
explanation.pearls: A single finger-tip unit (about 0.5 g) treats an area equal to two adult palms; under-dosing is the commonest reason for apparent topical steroid failure in toddler eczema.

options.rationale: Established lichenified eczema disturbing sleep needs active anti-inflammatory therapy; emollients alone are inadequate at this stage of the disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Dermatology)

Mild topical corticosteroid plus generous emollient is the stepped-care first-line for paediatric flexural atopic eczema, escalating potency if uncontrolled after a defined trial. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Dermatology)

Systemic corticosteroids are not recommended for routine paediatric eczema due to rebound flare and adverse effects; topical therapy should be optimised first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Dermatology)
Non-sedating antihistamines do not reduce eczema inflammation; the itch in eczema is histamine-independent and responds to topical steroid plus emollient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Dermatology)
Systemic immunomodulators are reserved for severe disease unresponsive to optimised topical therapy; a stepwise trial must be completed first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Dermatology)

explanation.summary: The Australian Immunisation Handbook provides catch-up schedules that respect previously documented doses while bringing children rapidly up to age-appropriate cover. At 12 months MMR, meningococcal ACWY and 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate are due, and 18-month doses include MMRV, DTPa and Hib. Serology before catch-up is not required. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, and those with medical risk conditions, receive additional doses such as hepatitis A and pneumococcal polysaccharide where indicated.
key_points: Accept documented overseas doses; do not restart the schedule.
At 12 months give MMR, MenACWY and PCV13.
Serology is not required prior to catch-up immunisation.
Use the Immunise Australia online catch-up calculator for complex histories.
explanation.pearls: All live parenteral vaccines including MMR, varicella and MMRV can be co-administered on the same day; if not given together they must be separated by at least 4 weeks to avoid blunting the immune response.

options.rationale: Catch-up should bring multiple antigens up to schedule at one visit; deferring leaves the child unprotected against MMR, MenACWY and pneumococcal disease. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
Catch-up schedules do not require pre-vaccination serology; serology delays protection and is not part of routine Australian practice. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Hepatitis A is not on the universal schedule for non-Aboriginal children; varicella alone misses MMR, meningococcal and pneumococcal protection that are now due. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
These are the routine 12-month doses on the Australian schedule and are due now; the 18-month doses are given separately at the next planned visit. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Documented doses received overseas are accepted by the Australian Immunisation Handbook; restarting is unnecessary and causes vaccine wastage and overdosing. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Acute paediatric ITP typically presents 1 to 4 weeks after a viral illness with isolated thrombocytopenia and an otherwise well child. The Royal Children's Hospital guideline reserves active therapy for wet purpura, severe mucosal bleeding or planned procedures; IVIG raises platelets within 24 to 48 hours. Bone marrow examination is needed only when features are atypical, when steroid is being considered without prior marrow review, or when the response is poor. HSP is excluded clinically by the absence of palpable purpura, arthritis and abdominal pain.
key_points: Wet purpura plus platelets under 10 indicates severe ITP needing IVIG.
Platelet transfusion is reserved for catastrophic bleeding only.
Bone marrow is not required for classic acute paediatric ITP.
HSP is distinguished by palpable purpura on lower limbs and buttocks.
explanation.pearls: IVIG 0.8 g/kg as a single dose typically raises platelets above 50 x10^9/L within 48 hours; if no rise occurs by day 3, recheck the diagnosis with a bone marrow aspirate before further immunosuppression.

options.rationale: Wet mucosal purpura with platelets under 10 x10^9/L is severe ITP with a real intracranial bleed risk; IVIG rapidly raises the platelet count and admission is mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG ITP)
Wet purpura is a marker of severe bleeding risk; outpatient management is not appropriate until the platelet count has been raised and bleeding controlled. (Source: RCH CPG ITP)
Steroids are an alternative but slower-acting therapy and bone marrow aspirate is needed before high-dose steroid to exclude leukaemia in atypical presentations. (Source: RCH CPG ITP)
Bone marrow examination is not required in a classic well child with isolated thrombocytopenia, normal blood film and no atypical features; it is reserved for atypical cases. (Source: RCH CPG ITP)
Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding only because autoantibodies destroy transfused platelets rapidly; IVIG or steroid is the standard therapy. (Source: RCH CPG ITP)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance recommends orchidopexy between 6 and 18 months for an undescended testis because surgery before 18 months improves long-term fertility and reduces malignancy risk. Spontaneous descent is uncommon after 6 months, so referral at the 6 to 12-month check should not be delayed. Imaging adds no value for a palpable testis. Endocrine workup is reserved for bilateral non-palpable testes or any sign of disorders of sex development.
key_points: Refer to paediatric surgery once persistence is clear after 6 months.
Operate before 18 months to preserve fertility.
Imaging does not change management for a palpable testis.
Bilateral non-palpable testes warrant endocrine and genetic evaluation.
explanation.pearls: Bilateral non-palpable testes in a newborn are a disorder-of-sex-development emergency until proven otherwise; obtain electrolytes, 17-hydroxyprogesterone and karyotype before assigning sex of rearing.

options.rationale: Spontaneous descent after 6 months is uncommon and delayed surgery worsens fertility and increases later malignancy risk; review at 24 months is too late. (Source: RCH CPG Undescended testis)

Persistent undescended testis after 6 months warrants surgical referral so that orchidopexy is performed before 18 months to preserve spermatogenesis and reduce malignancy risk. (Source: RCH CPG Undescended testis)
Imaging does not change management for a palpable testis and adds delay; surgical referral is based on clinical findings alone. (Source: RCH CPG Undescended testis)

Hormonal induction with hCG is not part of standard Australian care because of poor efficacy and adverse effects; surgical orchidopexy is the recommended approach. (Source: RCH CPG Undescended testis)
Endocrine and genetic studies are reserved for bilateral non-palpable testes or ambiguous genitalia, not a single palpable undescended testis with normal phallus. (Source: RCH CPG Undescended testis)

explanation.summary: Aspirin in Kawasaki disease has two distinct jobs at two distinct doses. The anti-inflammatory dose of 30 to 50 mg/kg per day in divided doses runs alongside immunoglobulin while the child is febrile. Once she has been afebrile for 48 to 72 hours the dose falls to an antiplatelet dose of 3 to 5 mg/kg once daily, which covers the reactive thrombocytosis that peaks in the second and third weeks and continues for six to eight weeks until repeat echocardiography is normal. Children with persisting coronary abnormalities stay on low-dose aspirin indefinitely, with anticoagulation added for giant aneurysms. In context, Kawasaki disease is a self-limiting medium-vessel vasculitis of early childhood whose whole management is built around preventing coronary artery aneurysms, so every treatment decision after the acute illness is a coronary risk decision rather than a fever decision.
key_points: High-dose aspirin is anti-inflammatory and stops 48 to 72 hours after defervescence.
Low-dose aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily is antiplatelet and runs six to eight weeks.
Platelet counts peak in weeks two and three, which is why cover continues.
Persisting coronary abnormalities mean indefinite low-dose aspirin.
explanation.pearls: The dose change is driven by the fever chart, not by the calendar: 48 to 72 hours afebrile is the trigger, and the duration is then set by the six to eight week echocardiogram.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Once a child has been afebrile for 48 to 72 hours, aspirin drops from the anti-inflammatory dose to an antiplatelet dose of 3 to 5 mg/kg once daily, continued for six to eight weeks until repeat imaging confirms normal coronary arteries. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: The anti-inflammatory dose would be continued only while fever persists; prolonged high-dose salicylate adds gastritis, tinnitus and hepatitis risk without further coronary benefit. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Stopping antiplatelet cover altogether would be reasonable only after repeat imaging at six to eight weeks shows normal coronary arteries, because platelet counts peak in the third week. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: A two-week course would stop antiplatelet therapy during the thrombocytosis peak; the low dose runs until follow-up imaging is normal, or indefinitely if aneurysms persist. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Clopidogrel substitutes for aspirin when there is true salicylate intolerance, or is added to aspirin for larger aneurysms, neither of which applies here. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

explanation.summary: A neonate with cyanosis and failed hyperoxia in the first 48 hours of life has duct-dependent congenital heart disease until proven otherwise. Prostaglandin E1 reopens or maintains the ductus arteriosus and restores pulmonary or systemic blood flow until echocardiography defines anatomy and surgical or catheter intervention is arranged. Side effects to anticipate during prostaglandin therapy include apnoea, hypotension and fever. Septic workup and broad spectrum antibiotics may be added because sepsis can mimic duct-dependent collapse.
key_points: Failed hyperoxia means SpO2 stays under 85% on 100% oxygen.
Start prostaglandin E1 at 10 nanograms/kg/min and titrate.
Anticipate apnoea, hypotension and fever as side effects.
Echocardiography defines the lesion and guides intervention.
explanation.pearls: Prostaglandin E1 causes apnoea in about 10 to 15 percent of neonates; have a clinician at the bedside able to intubate before starting infusion, particularly during interhospital retrieval.

options.rationale: Failed hyperoxia with cyanosis in the first 48 hours indicates a duct-dependent cyanotic lesion; prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency until definitive diagnosis and surgery. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic neonate)

Persistent cyanosis on 100% FiO2 over 10 minutes is the failed hyperoxia test diagnostic of cyanotic congenital heart disease; oxygen alone will not address the lesion. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic neonate)

Sepsis can mimic this presentation but failed hyperoxia and metabolic acidosis with hepatomegaly suggest a duct-dependent lesion that needs immediate prostaglandin therapy. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic neonate)
Bicarbonate does not treat the underlying ductal-dependent circulation; restoring ductal patency with prostaglandin corrects perfusion and resolves acidosis. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic neonate)
Inotropes do not restore ductal-dependent pulmonary blood flow and may worsen the shunt; prostaglandin E1 is the priority intervention with cardiology input. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic neonate)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome arises from the abrupt intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium driven by insulin release when carbohydrate is reintroduced after prolonged starvation. Adolescents with severe restrictive eating disorders and weight loss exceeding 15% are at highest risk. Prophylaxis with thiamine 100 to 300 mg daily and replacement of phosphate, magnesium, and potassium before and during early feeding prevents the cardiac, neurological, and respiratory complications. Initial feed volume is started low (around 20 kcal/kg/day) and titrated up over 7 to 10 days with daily electrolyte checks.
key_points: Refeeding risk highest with weight loss above 15%, prolonged starvation, or BMI under 14
Thiamine 100 to 300 mg daily before any carbohydrate load prevents Wernicke encephalopathy
Phosphate, magnesium, and potassium replaced prophylactically even when baseline levels appear normal
Initial feed at around 20 kcal/kg/day advancing over 7 to 10 days with daily electrolytes
explanation.pearls: Thiamine must precede any glucose or feed in severe malnutrition: a single intravenous bolus of dextrose into a thiamine-deplete adolescent can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy within hours.

sources.label: NICE NG69 - Eating Disorders Recognition and Treatment

options.rationale: Prolonged starvation worsens cardiac and metabolic instability. Cautious feeding with concurrent prophylaxis is preferred over further fasting, which increases mortality in this cohort. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Refeeding Guidelines)

In severe malnutrition with prolonged starvation, prophylactic thiamine before any carbohydrate load prevents Wernicke encephalopathy, and pre-emptive electrolyte replacement covers the anticipated refeeding shifts even when baseline levels are within normal range. Australian eating disorder guidelines recommend this prophylactic bundle for high-risk refeeding before commencing nutrition. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Refeeding Guidelines)

Starting at 40 kcal/kg/day in a severely malnourished adolescent without prophylaxis precipitates classical refeeding syndrome with phosphate, magnesium, and potassium crashes. Australian guidelines advise starting low and advancing cautiously with prophylactic micronutrients. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Refeeding Guidelines)

A rapid carbohydrate load in a thiamine-deplete malnourished patient is a recognised trigger for both Wernicke encephalopathy and acute refeeding syndrome. Thiamine and electrolyte cover must precede any carbohydrate. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Refeeding Guidelines)

Parenteral nutrition does not lower refeeding risk and carries additional line and metabolic complications. Cautious enteral nutrition with prophylactic thiamine and electrolytes is the Australian standard. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Refeeding Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperammonaemia is a metabolic emergency typically due to urea cycle disorders or organic acidaemias. The classical pattern is a previously well term neonate who deteriorates 24 to 72 hours after feeding establishes, with lethargy, tachypnoea, and respiratory alkalosis from central ammonia stimulation. Plasma ammonia above 200 micromol/L in a sick neonate prompts urgent metabolic workup and treatment, and above 400 micromol/L triggers preparation for renal replacement therapy. The therapeutic bundle is stop protein, give anabolic dextrose with intralipid, give scavenger drugs (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate) where available, and dialyse.
key_points: Urea cycle disorders present with respiratory alkalosis; organic acidaemias with metabolic acidosis and anion gap
Ammonia above 400 micromol/L mandates urgent haemodialysis
Protein must be stopped within 24 to 48 hours; anabolic IV dextrose plus intralipid supports caloric needs
Family history of unexplained neonatal death is a strong clue for inherited metabolic disease
explanation.pearls: A previously well term neonate who deteriorates after 36 hours of successful feeding with respiratory alkalosis and ammonia above 200 micromol/L should be assumed to have a urea cycle disorder until proven otherwise, with dialysis prep at ammonia 400 micromol/L.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Suspected Inborn Error of Metabolism

options.rationale: Plasma ammonia above 400 micromol/L in a neonate with encephalopathy is a metabolic emergency consistent with a urea cycle disorder or organic acidaemia, with respiratory alkalosis driven by central ammonia toxicity. Immediate protein withdrawal, anabolic dextrose support, and dialysis are required to halt neurotoxicity. Family history of neonatal death increases the prior probability of an inborn error. (Source: HGSA - Metabolic Emergency Guidelines)

Protein loading in a neonate with hyperammonaemia accelerates ammonia generation and worsens encephalopathy. Protein must be withdrawn for 24 to 48 hours while ammonia falls. (Source: HGSA - Metabolic Emergency Guidelines)

Aciclovir is appropriate empirically when HSV encephalitis is suspected, but the combination of normal CRP, profound hyperammonaemia, respiratory alkalosis, and family history strongly indicates an inborn error. Treatment of the metabolic emergency cannot be deferred for an HSV workup. (Source: HGSA - Metabolic Emergency Guidelines)

The blood gas shows respiratory alkalosis, not acidosis - bicarbonate is contraindicated and worsens the alkalaemia. The therapeutic priority is ammonia removal and anabolic support. (Source: HGSA - Metabolic Emergency Guidelines)

Phenobarbital treats clinical seizures but does not address the underlying hyperammonaemia, which is the primary driver of neurological injury. Without ammonia clearance, irreversible neurotoxicity progresses within hours. (Source: HGSA - Metabolic Emergency Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Exertional heatstroke is defined by core temperature above 40 degrees C with central nervous system dysfunction occurring during physical exertion. Mortality rises sharply for every minute spent above 40 degrees C, so the maxim is cool first, transport second. Cold-water immersion is the gold standard with cooling rates of approximately 0.2 degrees C per minute. Adjunct measures (cooled IV fluids, evaporative cooling, ice packs to groin and axillae) are added if immersion is not immediately available. Complications include rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC, hepatic failure, and ARDS.
key_points: Exertional heatstroke: core above 40 degrees C plus CNS dysfunction during exertion
Cold-water immersion cools at around 0.2 degrees C per minute, faster than any other method
Stop active cooling at 39 degrees C to avoid rebound hypothermia
Rhabdomyolysis, AKI and DIC are predictable complications and require admission to a high-acuity unit
explanation.pearls: Antipyretics like paracetamol do not work in heatstroke because the hypothalamic set-point is normal and the elevated core temperature is from environmental load, not endogenous fever - the only effective treatment is rapid external cooling, ideally cold-water immersion.

sources.label: Sports Medicine Australia - Hot Weather Guidelines

options.rationale: Gastric lavage achieves much slower cooling than immersion and carries aspiration risk in an obtunded patient. It is at best an adjunct, never a primary strategy. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.4 - Heat-Induced Illness)

Tepid sponging cools too slowly to prevent multi-organ injury in exertional heatstroke. Antipyretics do not work in heatstroke because the hypothalamic set-point is normal, and dantrolene has no proven role outside malignant hyperthermia. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.4 - Heat-Induced Illness)

In exertional heatstroke, every minute above 40 degrees C drives multi-organ injury, and cold-water immersion is the most rapid cooling method, lowering core temperature by approximately 0.2 degrees C per minute. Cooling targets cessation at 39 degrees C to avoid rebound hypothermia. Airway and circulation are supported in parallel rather than sequentially. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.4 - Heat-Induced Illness)

Cooled IV fluids contribute only modest cooling rates compared with immersion. Aggressive fluid loading also risks pulmonary oedema in an adolescent with normal cardiac function and threatens cooling target overshoot. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.4 - Heat-Induced Illness)

Cooling must commence immediately; mortality rises with every minute above 40 degrees C. Intubation and central access proceed in parallel with cold-water immersion, not before it. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.4 - Heat-Induced Illness)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in children under 12 months driven by viral lower respiratory tract infection. The Royal Children's Hospital guideline targets SpO2 of at least 90% (not 92%) and admits for sustained SpO2 below 90%, severe work of breathing, feeding under 50% of normal, apnoea, or social concerns. Standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen is the first-line respiratory support; high-flow nasal cannula therapy is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen after at least 2 hours with persistent SpO2 below 90% and no improvement. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics are not part of the standard pathway.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target is at least 90% in uncomplicated bronchiolitis
Standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen is the first-line respiratory support
High-flow is reserved for failure of low-flow after at least 2 hours with persistent SpO2 below 90%
Feeding under 50% triggers nasogastric support
Bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics are not routine
explanation.pearls: RSV-positive infants under 3 months and those born before 32 weeks are at highest risk of apnoea; admit even if SpO2 appears adequate, because apnoea may be the first sign of severe disease in this group.

options.rationale: Salbutamol does not improve outcomes in viral bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months and is not recommended in the Australian paediatric pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Systemic corticosteroids do not shorten bronchiolitis or reduce admission length and are not recommended by Australian guidelines. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

RCH targets SpO2 of at least 90% in uncomplicated bronchiolitis and uses standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen first-line when SpO2 falls below this on room air. Feeding under 50% triggers nasogastric support. High-flow oxygen is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen after at least 2 hours with persistent SpO2 below 90% and no clinical improvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

RCH reserves high-flow nasal cannula therapy for failure of standard low-flow oxygen, defined as persistent SpO2 below 90% after at least 2 hours of low-flow oxygen with no respiratory improvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
There is no clinical evidence of bacterial co-infection and empirical antibiotics are not part of the bronchiolitis pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Croup severity is graded clinically as mild (stridor with activity), moderate (stridor at rest with mild recession) or severe (stridor at rest with marked distress or altered mental state). Australian first-line treatment for moderate croup is a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg followed by 4-hour observation. Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe disease and bridges the time to dexamethasone onset. Antibiotics, bronchodilators and intubation are not used in uncomplicated viral croup.
key_points: Stridor at rest without severe distress defines moderate croup.
Single-dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is first-line.
Observe for 4 hours after steroid and discharge if stable.
Reserve adrenaline for severe croup or impending failure.
explanation.pearls: Rebound at 4 to 6 hours after a single adrenaline dose is well described; never discharge a child who needed nebulised adrenaline without 4 hours of clear observation after administration, regardless of how well they look immediately afterwards.

options.rationale: Salbutamol treats lower airway bronchospasm rather than the upper airway narrowing of croup and does not relieve stridor. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)
Nebulised adrenaline is indicated for severe croup with marked respiratory distress or impending failure, not moderate disease with preserved alertness. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)
Bacterial tracheitis presents with high fever and toxic appearance; this child is well between cough bouts and antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

Moderate croup with stridor at rest but no severe distress is treated with a single dose of oral dexamethasone and 4-hour observation; most children improve and are safely discharged. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)
Intubation is reserved for impending or actual respiratory failure with cyanosis, exhaustion or reduced responsiveness, none of which is present. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

explanation.summary: Therapeutic Guidelines recommend immediate antibiotic therapy for acute otitis media in children with bilateral disease under 2 years, perforation with discharge, systemic illness, immunosuppression or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background. Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days is first-line; amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours. Adequate analgesia with paracetamol and ibuprofen is core to management irrespective of antibiotic decision. Watchful waiting suits uncomplicated unilateral disease in older children.
key_points: Children under 2 with bilateral disease need antibiotics now.
Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days is first-line.
Analgesia is essential regardless of antibiotic choice.
Switch to amoxicillin-clavulanate if no improvement at 48-72 h.
explanation.pearls: Recurrent acute otitis media (three or more episodes in 6 months or four in 12 months) prompts ENT referral for grommet consideration; mastoiditis presents with post-auricular swelling, tenderness and downward-and-outward displacement of the pinna and warrants urgent admission.

options.rationale: Bilateral acute otitis media in a child under 2 years with high fever and severe pain warrants immediate amoxicillin; 30 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days is the Therapeutic Guidelines recommendation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Watchful waiting suits unilateral mild disease in children over 2 years, not bilateral disease with high fever in a child under 2. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Topical antibiotic drops have no role in middle-ear infection through an intact tympanic membrane; they target external otitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Decongestants do not reduce middle-ear effusion or shorten illness and carry significant adverse effects in young children. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Systemic steroids are not part of acute otitis media management in Australian guidelines and may mask deterioration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with faecal loading is the commonest paediatric bowel complaint in Australia. Royal Children's Hospital and RACGP advice favour macrogol 3350 first-line for both disimpaction and maintenance. Disimpaction uses escalating sachet doses for up to 7 days, then maintenance is titrated to achieve one soft stool per day. Long-term success depends on toileting routine, reward charts and continued maintenance for at least 6 months after symptom resolution.
key_points: Macrogol 3350 is first-line for disimpaction and maintenance.
Disimpaction escalates over 7 days; maintenance follows.
Maintain therapy for at least 6 months after symptoms resolve.
Reserve surgery referral for organic red flags.
explanation.pearls: Beware of stopping macrogol the moment stools normalise; relapse rates are high without 6 months of maintenance, and many families need explicit permission to keep dosing once everything looks better.

options.rationale: Lactulose is acceptable but Australian guidelines now recommend macrogol 3350 first-line because of higher disimpaction success and better palatability. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

Macrogol disimpaction with up to 8 sachets per day for up to 7 days followed by maintenance is the first-line Australian regimen for functional constipation with faecal loading. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)
Stimulants are added if osmotics alone fail; routine first-line use can cause cramping and is not standard for initial therapy. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)
Surgical referral is reserved for organic causes such as Hirschsprung disease or anorectal malformation; none of these features are present here. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)
Routine PR therapy is invasive, traumatising for young children and not first-line for typical functional constipation in well children. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

explanation.summary: Pertussis remains a serious risk in young infants, with mortality concentrated in those under 6 months. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines indicate chemoprophylaxis for all close household contacts when an infant under 6 months lives in the home, irrespective of vaccination status. Azithromycin is first-line because of short course and good compliance. The index case is notifiable and the public health unit will trace wider contacts, but treatment should not be delayed for notification.
key_points: Index case requires treatment and notification.
All household contacts get prophylaxis when an infant under 6 months lives in the home.
Azithromycin is the first-line chemoprophylaxis agent.
Vaccination alone does not protect close contacts in time.
explanation.pearls: Infants under 6 months can present with apnoea before cough, especially if exposed to a coughing adult at home; admit for monitoring at the threshold of any apnoea, cyanosis or feeding change even if pertussis PCR has not yet returned.

options.rationale: Pertussis spreads readily within households; chemoprophylaxis is indicated for all contacts when an infant under 6 months lives in the home regardless of vaccination status. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Vaccination does not provide rapid post-exposure protection; chemoprophylaxis is required for vulnerable contacts within the household. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Pre-test triage delays prophylaxis and risks transmission to the infant during the 24- to 48-hour wait for swab results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Public health notification is mandatory, but commencing prophylaxis should not wait; treatment of contacts within 21 days of exposure to an infant is time-critical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

When an infant under 6 months lives in the household, azithromycin chemoprophylaxis is given to all close household contacts to prevent severe and fatal infant pertussis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Suspected meningococcal disease in the community is a time-critical diagnosis. Australian guidelines indicate immediate intramuscular or intravenous benzylpenicillin if there is any delay establishing intravenous access. Survival correlates inversely with time to first antibiotic dose. After the first dose, urgent retrieval and supportive resuscitation with fluids and oxygen are arranged. Public health notification and ciprofloxacin prophylaxis for close contacts follow once the index case is stabilised.
key_points: Intramuscular benzylpenicillin in clinic if no intravenous access.
Do not delay first antibiotic dose for transfer or imaging.
Notify the public health unit on the same day.
Ciprofloxacin prophylaxis for household and kissing contacts.
explanation.pearls: Petechiae are a late sign; in early meningococcaemia the leg pain, cold mottled peripheries, and prolonged capillary refill precede the rash by hours and are the cues to act on suspicion alone.

options.rationale: Suspected meningococcaemia in a community setting warrants immediate intramuscular benzylpenicillin while awaiting transfer; intramuscular is acceptable when intravenous access is not yet available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Delaying antibiotics in suspected meningococcaemia worsens mortality; intramuscular benzylpenicillin should be given immediately when intravenous access is not yet established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Steroid alone has no role and antibiotic delay is dangerous; dexamethasone in meningitis is given with or shortly after the first antibiotic dose in hospital. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Prophylaxis for contacts is given once the index case is stabilised; it does not treat the index patient and must not delay her own antibiotic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Pre-hospital antibiotic improves survival in meningococcaemia and outweighs the modest reduction in culture yield; cultures can still be taken on arrival. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Preschool wheeze is divided into episodic viral and multi-trigger phenotypes. Episodic viral wheeze without atopic background is managed with as-needed salbutamol via spacer during exacerbations and red flag advice. Maintenance inhaled corticosteroid is reserved for multi-trigger wheeze, persistent inter-episode symptoms or strong atopic background. Oral steroids in this age group are restricted to moderate or severe acute exacerbations.
key_points: Salbutamol via spacer is first-line during viral wheeze episodes.
Maintenance inhaled steroid only if multi-trigger or atopic.
Avoid oral steroid for mild episodic viral wheeze.
Review phenotype if episodes become more frequent.
explanation.pearls: A spacer with a face mask delivers more drug to the small airways than a nebuliser in a wriggly toddler; switching from nebuliser to spacer often improves practical response and reduces tachycardia from systemic absorption.

options.rationale: Maintenance inhaled corticosteroids do not reduce viral-only wheeze episodes in preschoolers without atopic features and risk growth and adrenal effects. (Source: National Asthma Handbook)
Daily montelukast is not first-line for episodic viral wheeze and carries a black-box neuropsychiatric warning that limits use in young children. (Source: National Asthma Handbook)

Episodic viral wheeze in a young preschooler without atopic features is managed with as-needed salbutamol via spacer; maintenance inhaled steroid is reserved for multi-trigger or atopic phenotypes. (Source: National Asthma Handbook)
Skin prick testing is reserved for suspected allergic asthma or multi-trigger phenotypes and is not needed for typical episodic viral wheeze. (Source: National Asthma Handbook)
Oral steroids are reserved for moderate to severe acute wheeze; routine prophylactic courses are not recommended in mild episodic viral wheeze. (Source: National Asthma Handbook)

explanation.summary: The Kocher criteria stratify the probability of septic arthritis of the hip in a child with limp: fever above 38.5, refusal to weight bear, WCC above 12 and ESR above 40. With all four present probability exceeds 95 percent. Australian practice favours urgent surgical aspiration and washout with empirical intravenous flucloxacillin pending cultures. Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion in a well, afebrile child with normal inflammatory markers and rapid improvement on rest.
key_points: Four Kocher criteria give over 95 percent probability of septic arthritis.
Aspiration in theatre obtains cultures and decompresses the joint.
Empirical flucloxacillin covers the commonest organisms.
Transient synovitis requires normal inflammatory markers.
explanation.pearls: Kingella kingae is now the commonest cause of culture-positive septic arthritis in children under 4 in Australia and is fastidious; if Gram stain is negative and the child is under 4, ask the laboratory to inoculate paediatric blood culture bottles with the joint aspirate to improve yield.

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics and outpatient care will fail to clear an established septic joint and risk femoral head osteonecrosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Serial imaging delays definitive treatment; the four Kocher criteria together give a very high probability of septic arthritis and warrant urgent joint aspiration. (Source: RCH CPG Septic Arthritis)
Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion in a well child; the combination of fever, raised inflammatory markers and refusal to weight bear makes this unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG Septic Arthritis)
Antibiotics before joint aspiration reduce culture yield and delay the source-control surgery that is required for septic arthritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Four positive Kocher criteria (fever above 38.5, refusal to bear weight, WCC above 12, ESR above 40) give over 95 percent probability of septic arthritis; aspiration, washout and intravenous antibiotics are the standard of care. (Source: RCH CPG Septic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: Around a third of paediatric type 1 diabetes presentations occur without ketoacidosis. These children still require hospital admission for insulin initiation because the underlying insulin deficiency will progress without treatment. Inpatient education by the paediatric diabetes team covers dose adjustment, hypoglycaemia recognition, ketone monitoring and sick-day rules. Discharge without these supports is a leading cause of early readmission with diabetic ketoacidosis.
key_points: Diabetic ketoacidosis is defined by venous pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15 with ketones above 3.0 mmol/L
Subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin is the initial regimen for non-ketoacidotic presentations in Australia
Inpatient diabetes education is part of initial management, not an optional add-on
Metformin and oral hypoglycaemics have no role in type 1 diabetes initiation
A documented sick-day plan with ketone testing thresholds is required before discharge
explanation.pearls: Capillary ketones above 0.6 mmol/L with a glucose above 14 mmol/L on a sick day triggers extra rapid-acting insulin every 2 hours under the APEG sick-day rule.

options.rationale: An insulin infusion is the diabetic ketoacidosis pathway and is not indicated when venous pH and bicarbonate are normal and ketones are only mildly elevated; it carries unnecessary risk of hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes Mellitus)

Withholding insulin in new-onset hyperglycaemia perpetuates ketogenesis and lipolysis and will worsen the metabolic picture; insulin is the definitive treatment for hyperglycaemia with ketosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines)

New-onset hyperglycaemia without acidosis is managed with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin and inpatient education by a paediatric diabetes service; this is the Australian standard and prevents readmission with diabetic ketoacidosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines)

Metformin is not appropriate for new-onset type 1 diabetes; the clinical picture of rapid weight loss and ketones points to insulin deficiency, and oral hypoglycaemics will not arrest progression to ketoacidosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines)

Basal insulin alone will not cover prandial glycaemic excursions and ketosis, and discharging without structured education and a sick-day plan risks early readmission with diabetic ketoacidosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia is the most common nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers, driven by excessive cow's milk intake and selective eating.
