Oral elemental iron at 3 mg/kg once daily with dietary modification corrects the deficit in the majority of well children. A rise in haemoglobin of at least 10 g/L by four weeks confirms response; failure to respond prompts review for malabsorption, ongoing blood loss or alternative diagnoses. Persistent iron deficiency in this age group is associated with cognitive and motor delay.
key_points: Cow's milk above 500 mL daily in toddlers displaces dietary iron and causes occult enteric blood loss
Ferritin under 12 micrograms/L is diagnostic of iron deficiency in children when the C-reactive protein is normal
Oral iron once daily improves absorption versus divided dosing because of hepcidin kinetics
Reticulocytosis at 7 to 10 days confirms early response and haemoglobin rise at 4 weeks confirms cure
Intravenous iron is second line and reserved for treatment failure or intolerance
explanation.pearls: Once-daily oral iron given on alternate days may improve fractional absorption versus thrice-daily dosing because hepcidin remains elevated for 24 hours after each dose.

options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia or haemoglobin below 70 g/L with cardiovascular compromise; this child is haemodynamically stable and responds to oral iron. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

Excess cow's milk intake displaces iron-rich foods and causes occult gut blood loss; oral iron with dietary modification corrects iron deficiency anaemia and the haemoglobin should rise by at least 10 g/L within a month. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

The ferritin, microcytosis and dietary history are diagnostic of iron deficiency in this context; further haematology workup is reserved for failure to respond to a trial of oral iron. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

Intravenous iron is reserved for malabsorption, oral iron intolerance or treatment failure; first-line therapy in a well toddler is oral iron with dietary adjustment. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)
A ferritin under 12 micrograms/L with microcytic anaemia is not physiological and untreated iron deficiency in toddlers causes long-term neurodevelopmental harm. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Atopic eczema management is a stepped ladder anchored on emollients and soap substitutes, with topical corticosteroid potency matched to flare severity. Hydrocortisone 1% is sufficient for mild flares on the face; moderate body or flexural flares need a moderate-potency steroid such as methylprednisolone aceponate. A short defined course of stronger steroid is safer and more effective than prolonged low-potency steroid. Parental steroid phobia is a major driver of undertreatment and persistent flare.
key_points: Topical corticosteroid potency should match flare severity, not patient age in isolation
Methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% is a moderate-potency steroid safe for short courses in children
Antibiotics are added only when bacterial superinfection is clinically suspected
Topical calcineurin inhibitors are second line, particularly for sensitive sites or maintenance
Systemic corticosteroids are avoided because of rebound flares on withdrawal
explanation.pearls: The fingertip unit covers one adult fingertip from the distal interphalangeal joint to the tip and treats an area equal to two adult palms; this gives parents a reproducible dosing measure.

options.rationale: Failure of 1% hydrocortisone in a moderate flare warrants topical step-up rather than indefinite continuation; biologics are reserved for severe disease refractory to standard topical care. (Source: ACD Atopic Dermatitis Position Statement)
Systemic corticosteroids cause rebound flares on cessation and are not used for atopic eczema in children outside specialist supervision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

There is no honey-coloured crust, pustule or systemic feature to suggest staphylococcal superinfection; antibiotics will not address the underlying inflammatory flare. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

A moderate-potency topical corticosteroid is the next step when low-potency steroid fails; a defined two-week course with emollients restores skin barrier function and matches Australian dermatology advice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Topical calcineurin inhibitors are second line for steroid-sparing maintenance or for sensitive sites such as eyelids, not for inducing remission in an actively weeping flare. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Febrile urinary tract infection in young children is treated empirically once a clean-catch urine sample has been collected, because untreated infection risks renal scarring. The RCH urinary tract infection guideline lists oral cefalexin as first-line empirical therapy: 20 mg/kg/dose three times daily for cystitis, and 25 mg/kg three times daily for pyelonephritis in children 12 months or older (25 mg/kg four times daily under 12 months). Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is only used once sensitivities confirm susceptibility. Intravenous gentamicin is reserved for infants under 3 months, sepsis, vomiting, or inability to tolerate oral antibiotics.
key_points: Cefalexin is first-line empirical oral therapy for paediatric urinary tract infection per RCH
Pyelonephritis dose in 12 months or older: 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 7 days
Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole only after sensitivities confirm susceptibility
Amoxicillin alone is not used because of community E. coli resistance
Intravenous antibiotics are reserved for under-3-month infants, sepsis, or oral intolerance
explanation.pearls: Recurrent febrile urinary tract infections or abnormal initial ultrasound trigger paediatric nephrology referral; the RCH cascade does not include routine DMSA or routine micturating cystourethrogram.

options.rationale: Cefalexin is the RCH first-line empirical oral antibiotic for paediatric urinary tract infection; for a child 12 months or older with febrile urinary tract infection the dose is 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 7 days. She is alert and tolerating oral intake so oral therapy is appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Intravenous therapy is reserved for infants under 3 months, suspected pyelonephritis with sepsis, vomiting, or inability to tolerate oral antibiotics; this child is well perfused and tolerating oral intake. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is reasonable only once urine culture sensitivities confirm susceptibility; it is not RCH first-line empirical therapy because of background community Escherichia coli resistance. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

Amoxicillin alone has unacceptably high resistance among community Escherichia coli isolates in Australia and is not first-line empirical therapy for paediatric urinary tract infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A positive nitrite and leucocyte dipstick in a febrile child under 2 years is sufficient to commence empirical antibiotics; deferring treatment risks progression to pyelonephritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura is an immunoglobulin A small-vessel vasculitis that follows an upper respiratory infection in school-aged children. The classical tetrad is palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain and renal involvement. Significant abdominal pain warrants admission for analgesia and observation for intussusception, which is typically ileoileal in this disease. Corticosteroids shorten the abdominal pain but do not alter the renal trajectory; long-term surveillance is mandated because nephritis can emerge over months.
key_points: Palpable purpura over buttocks and lower limbs with arthralgia is highly suggestive of HSP
Intussusception in HSP is typically ileoileal rather than ileocolic and may be missed by enema
Significant abdominal pain is shortened by oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg daily
Steroids do not prevent or alter the course of HSP nephritis
Weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for 6 months is required to detect late nephritis
explanation.pearls: Renal involvement may appear up to 6 months after the initial rash, so surveillance with urinalysis and blood pressure is continued even after symptoms resolve.

options.rationale: Bowel wall oedema from the vasculitis can mimic obstruction, but the ultrasound excludes intussusception and there is no peritonism; laparotomy is not indicated without surgical findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

Pulse intravenous methylprednisolone is reserved for severe nephritis with crescents or rapidly progressive renal failure; this child has only mild proteinuria and no acute kidney injury. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP Nephritis Guideline)

Significant abdominal pain warrants admission for analgesia, hydration and observation for intussusception; ongoing renal surveillance is also required to detect late nephritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)
Cytotoxic therapy is reserved for biopsy-proven severe nephritis; it is not indicated for abdominal pain with mild proteinuria. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP Nephritis Guideline)

Significant abdominal pain in vasculitis is shortened by oral corticosteroids without changing renal outcomes; weekly surveillance for nephritis is required because renal involvement may emerge over the following 6 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood and the leading cause of acquired heart disease in Australian children. The diagnosis requires at least 5 days of fever plus 4 of 5 clinical features: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes, polymorphous rash, peripheral changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg plus aspirin within the first 10 days of fever reduces coronary artery aneurysm rates from around 25% to under 5%. Sterile pyuria, raised transaminases and low albumin support the diagnosis even when classical features are partial.
key_points: Five days of fever plus 4 of 5 clinical criteria establishes complete Kawasaki disease
Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg plus aspirin reduces aneurysm rates from around 25% to under 5%
Treatment within the first 10 days of fever is the key prognostic determinant for coronary outcomes
Sterile pyuria, raised liver enzymes and low albumin are supportive features
Refractory disease at 36 hours after IVIG triggers a second dose plus corticosteroid escalation
explanation.pearls: Adjunctive corticosteroids are considered up front for children with predicted IVIG resistance based on the Kobayashi or Sano scores in Japanese cohorts, although routine use in Australian children remains case-by-case.

options.rationale: The clinical picture and a negative throat swab do not support streptococcal infection; antibiotics will not address the underlying vasculitis or prevent coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Five days of fever plus four of the five clinical criteria meet the threshold for Kawasaki disease and inflammatory markers support active vasculitis; discharge risks untreated coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Treatment is not contingent on echocardiographic findings; delaying intravenous immunoglobulin past day 10 increases the risk of coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

He meets clinical criteria for complete Kawasaki disease; intravenous immunoglobulin within the first 10 days of fever plus low-dose aspirin reduces coronary artery aneurysm rates from approximately 25% to under 5%. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Corticosteroids are an adjunct considered for IVIG resistance or high-risk patients, not as monotherapy; standard initial treatment is intravenous immunoglobulin with aspirin. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice plotted against postnatal hours on the Australian phototherapy nomogram is the basis of management decisions. ABO incompatibility with a positive direct antiglobulin test is an acceleration risk and lowers the threshold for intensive phototherapy. Exchange transfusion is reserved for levels above the exchange line, signs of bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction or failure of intensive phototherapy. Intravenous immunoglobulin reduces the need for exchange transfusion in isoimmune disease when bilirubin is climbing toward the exchange line.
key_points: Bilirubin must always be plotted against postnatal hours on a treatment nomogram
ABO incompatibility with positive direct antiglobulin test is a risk factor for rapid haemolysis
Intensive phototherapy is first-line and exchange transfusion is reserved for failure or extreme levels
Intravenous immunoglobulin is adjunctive in isoimmune haemolytic disease at high bilirubin levels
Hydration with breast or expressed milk is continued throughout phototherapy whenever possible
explanation.pearls: A rise of more than 8.5 micromol/L per hour or failure to respond to intensive phototherapy is the trigger to consider intravenous immunoglobulin and prepare for exchange transfusion.

options.rationale: His bilirubin sits well above the Australian phototherapy threshold for a well term baby at 38 hours, and ABO incompatibility raises the risk of rapid bilirubin acceleration; observation alone is unsafe. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal Jaundice)

Routine cessation of breastfeeding is not indicated for haemolytic jaundice; supplementation may be considered for hydration but the underlying ABO incompatibility still requires phototherapy. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal Jaundice)

His bilirubin exceeds the phototherapy line on the term low-risk nomogram at 38 hours, and the positive direct antiglobulin test with ABO mismatch is a risk factor for rapid rise; intensive phototherapy with hydration is standard. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal Jaundice)

Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin levels above the exchange line, signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy or rapid rise on intensive phototherapy; the first step is intensive phototherapy. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal Jaundice)

Intravenous immunoglobulin is an adjunct considered only when bilirubin continues to rise despite intensive phototherapy and approaches the exchange transfusion line, not as an initial intervention. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Simple febrile convulsions are generalised seizures under 15 minutes that occur once in 24 hours in a developmentally normal child aged 6 months to 5 years during a febrile illness. They do not require investigation, neuroimaging or prophylaxis. Recurrence occurs in roughly a third of children, usually within a year, and the risk of later epilepsy is only slightly above the population baseline. Family education on first-aid positioning and a clear ambulance threshold at five minutes is the core intervention.
key_points: A simple febrile convulsion is generalised, under 15 minutes, and occurs once in 24 hours in a well child
Neuroimaging and electroencephalogram have no role in simple febrile convulsions
Recurrence is around 30% and the risk of later epilepsy is only marginally raised
Continuous antiepileptic prophylaxis is not recommended
Ambulance should be called for any febrile convulsion lasting over 5 minutes
explanation.pearls: Buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg can be supplied for at-home rescue only when a child has a documented prolonged febrile convulsion over 5 minutes.

options.rationale: EEG and neuroimaging are not indicated for a first simple febrile convulsion with normal neurological examination and recovery; they yield no useful prognostic information in this setting. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizures)

A simple febrile convulsion in a developmentally normal child needs no investigation; parental reassurance, recurrence counselling and an ambulance plan for seizures lasting over five minutes is the entire required management. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizures)
Continuous antiepileptic prophylaxis is not used for simple febrile convulsions because the modest reduction in recurrence does not outweigh the medication risks. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizures)
Empiric antibiotics and lumbar puncture are not warranted in a well child with a clear viral source and no meningism; reflexive sepsis workup is overtreatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizures)

Intermittent prophylactic benzodiazepines at fever onset do not reliably prevent febrile convulsions and risk sedation that can confound assessment of a sick child. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizures)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media is the most common bacterial infection of childhood. Australian guidelines advise immediate antibiotics for children under 2 years with bilateral disease or with unilateral disease plus systemic features, for any child with ear discharge from acute perforation, and for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children. Other children with mild disease may be observed for 48 hours with analgesia. High-dose oral amoxicillin remains first line.
key_points: Immediate antibiotics for under 2 years with unilateral disease and systemic features
High-dose amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for five days is first line in non-allergic children
Cefalexin and macrolides have inferior pneumococcal coverage
Topical antibiotics do not penetrate an intact tympanic membrane
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children receive immediate antibiotics at all ages because of perforation risk
explanation.pearls: Australian guidelines advise switching to amoxicillin-clavulanate if there is no improvement at 48 to 72 hours on high-dose amoxicillin.

options.rationale: Children under 2 years with unilateral acute otitis media and systemic features benefit from immediate amoxicillin per Australian guidelines; the higher dose covers intermediate-resistance pneumococcus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Watchful waiting is reserved for children over 2 years with mild unilateral disease; under 2 years with systemic features Australian guidelines advise immediate antibiotic treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Cefalexin has poor pneumococcal cover compared with amoxicillin and is not the first-line agent for acute otitis media in non-allergic children. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Without mastoid tenderness, post-auricular swelling, or systemic toxicity, mastoiditis is unlikely and outpatient oral therapy is appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media)

Topical antibiotics are used for otitis externa or grommet-related discharge; they do not penetrate an intact tympanic membrane to treat acute otitis media. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the most common reason for hospital admission in Australian infants under one year. Management is supportive: oxygen for hypoxia, nasogastric or intravenous fluids for reduced feeding, and observation for apnoea. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics and chest x-rays are not part of routine care. Admission thresholds include oxygen saturation under 92%, tachypnoea over 60, feeding under half normal, parental concern, apnoea, and high social risk.
key_points: Admission criteria include SpO2 under 92%, feeding under half normal, apnoea or moderate respiratory distress
Salbutamol, corticosteroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated
Nasogastric fluids are preferred over intravenous when tolerated
High-flow nasal oxygen is reserved for those failing standard oxygen
Apnoea risk is greatest in infants under 6 weeks of age
explanation.pearls: High-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min reduces escalation to intensive care in moderately severe bronchiolitis but is reserved for failure of standard oxygen, not first-line.

options.rationale: Reduced feeding to under half normal and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air meet admission thresholds for bronchiolitis in Australia; discharge home is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Admission criteria are met by tachypnoea over 60, hypoxia under 92% on room air and feeding under half normal; supportive care with hydration and oxygen is the mainstay of bronchiolitis management. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Salbutamol does not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis under 12 months because bronchospasm is not the predominant pathology; routine bronchodilator use is discouraged. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Corticosteroids have no role in viral bronchiolitis and routine chest x-ray adds radiation without changing management in classical disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Routine antibiotics are not indicated in classical bronchiolitis with a known viral cause and no focal consolidation or persistent fever. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for over 90% of paediatric constipation. Treatment proceeds in two stages: disimpaction with high-dose oral macrogol over three to seven days, followed by ongoing maintenance for at least three months after a normal bowel pattern is established. A scheduled post-meal toileting program, age-appropriate dietary fibre, adequate fluids and reward charts support the medication. Red flags requiring further investigation include onset before 4 weeks of age, failure to pass meconium, ribbon stools, severe failure to thrive, abnormal neurological exam or sacral abnormalities.
key_points: Disimpaction with oral macrogol precedes maintenance therapy
Maintenance laxatives continue for at least three months after a normal bowel pattern returns
Rectal enemas are reserved for failure of oral disimpaction
Imaging and bloods are not required when no red flags are present
Toileting routine after meals leverages the gastrocolic reflex
explanation.pearls: Macrogol 3350 disimpaction dose escalates over three days from 4 sachets per day to 8 sachets per day for children 5 to 11 years.

options.rationale: Functional constipation is a clinical diagnosis when red flags are absent; imaging and routine coeliac serology add cost without benefit and delay disimpaction. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

First-line management of paediatric functional constipation is oral macrogol disimpaction followed by maintenance, combined with a scheduled toileting routine; rectal interventions are second line. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Rectal enemas are reserved for failure of oral macrogol disimpaction; they are invasive and risk electrolyte disturbance in children. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Dietary and behavioural measures alone are insufficient once impaction has formed; macrogol is required to clear retained faecal mass before maintenance. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Stimulant laxatives are added to macrogol if response is inadequate; they are not first-line monotherapy in paediatric chronic constipation. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Croup severity is graded by clinical features rather than oxygen saturation, which often remains preserved until late. Mild croup has barking cough without stridor at rest, moderate croup has stridor at rest with minimal recession, and severe croup has stridor at rest with marked recession and distress. All severities receive corticosteroid because it reduces return visits and shortens illness duration. Nebulised adrenaline gives rapid relief in moderate to severe disease, with onset in 10 minutes and effect lasting up to two hours, so observation for at least three to four hours catches rebound.
key_points: Severity is clinical, not based on oxygen saturation
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally is used in moderate and severe croup
Nebulised adrenaline is added for stridor at rest with significant recession
Observe at least 3 to 3 hours (RCH minimum) after adrenaline for rebound
Avoid distressing the child to prevent acute airway compromise
explanation.pearls: Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.5 mL/kg up to 5 mL acts in under 10 minutes but rebounds within 2 hours, hence the mandatory observation window.

options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession requires nebulised adrenaline for immediate relief plus dexamethasone for sustained effect; the four-hour observation captures the rebound at one to two hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Low-dose oral dexamethasone alone is appropriate for mild croup without rest stridor; severe croup with rest stridor and recession needs nebulised adrenaline and extended observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
There is no drooling, trismus or toxic appearance to suggest epiglottitis; imaging delays adrenaline and exposes the child to upset that risks airway decompensation. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Salbutamol targets lower airway bronchospasm and has no role in upper airway oedema of croup; relying on it delays effective treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Most severe croup responds to nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone; primary intubation is reserved for impending failure unresponsive to medical therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of death in paediatric DKA and is linked to rapid fluid shifts. Australian APEG and RCH guidelines therefore standardise resuscitation to a single 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus unless the child is in shock, followed by calculated deficit replacement spread over 48 hours and maintenance using a two-bag system with potassium. Insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour begins after the first hour of fluids. Bicarbonate, large repeated boluses and accelerated correction are explicitly avoided.
key_points: Initial bolus is 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline unless shocked
Deficit is replaced over 48 hours, not 24
Insulin starts at least one hour after fluid resuscitation begins
Bicarbonate is not used in paediatric DKA
Cerebral oedema risk peaks 4 to 12 hours after treatment start
explanation.pearls: A sudden headache, altered conscious state or bradycardia after starting therapy mandates immediate 3% saline 5 mL/kg bolus and reduction of fluid rate for suspected cerebral oedema.

options.rationale: Australian paediatric DKA guidelines use a single 10 mL/kg bolus followed by deficit replacement over 48 hours; this approach minimises rapid osmolar shifts that precipitate cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Large repeated boluses and accelerated maintenance increase the risk of cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA; current Australian practice restricts bolus to 10 mL/kg unless shocked. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)
Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA because it worsens intracellular acidosis and increases cerebral oedema risk without changing outcome. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Insulin without preceding fluid resuscitation worsens dehydration and precipitates hypokalaemia; fluid is started first and insulin is added after the first hour. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)
Dextrose-containing fluid is added later when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L; initial resuscitation uses isotonic crystalloid to restore intravascular volume. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Bruising in a non-mobile infant, or bruising in protected sites such as ears, mandible, neck, torso, buttocks or genitalia at any age, is a sentinel injury for non-accidental injury. The rule "those who don't cruise rarely bruise" highlights how rare any bruise is before independent mobility. Investigation includes skeletal survey, neuroimaging, retinal exam, coagulation studies and consideration of metabolic bone disease. Statutory mandatory reporting to child protection is triggered by suspicion and is independent of investigation results.
key_points: Any bruise in a non-mobile infant is concerning until proven otherwise
Bruising of ears, mandible, neck and torso is high specificity for inflicted injury
Skeletal survey plus neuroimaging plus retinal review forms the standard workup
Mandatory reporting is triggered by suspicion, not confirmation
A normal coagulation panel does not exclude inflicted injury
explanation.pearls: Up to 30% of children later confirmed as physically abused have a recognised sentinel injury in the preceding weeks that was not reported, so escalation of any single suspicious bruise is the inflection point for prevention.

options.rationale: Bruising in a non-mobile infant or in protected sites such as ears and mandible is a sentinel injury and requires admission, full non-accidental injury workup and statutory child protection notification. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)
Normal coagulation does not exclude inflicted injury; the location and mechanism profile mandate workup and notification regardless of laboratory results. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)
Bruising in non-mobile infants is rare and never normal; reassurance is unsafe and misses a sentinel injury that predicts escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

Delaying notification while awaiting metabolic workup is not safe; mandatory reporting is triggered by suspicion alone and proceeds in parallel with investigation. (Source: RACGP Child Protection Resource)
Community follow-up alone for an infant with a sentinel injury risks serious further harm; statutory notification and acute admission are required. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Febrile infants under 90 days have a significantly higher rate of serious bacterial infection than older children and clinical appearance is unreliable. Australian guidelines mandate a full septic screen including urine collected by catheter or supra-pubic aspirate, blood culture, lumbar puncture, FBE, CRP and consideration of viral PCR. Empiric intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin covers Listeria, group B Streptococcus and E coli, the most common pathogens at this age. Cefotaxime is added if meningitis is suspected.
key_points: Under 90 days, clinical appearance does not exclude serious bacterial infection
Full septic workup includes blood culture, urine, and lumbar puncture
First-line empiric therapy is intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin
Cefotaxime replaces ceftriaxone in neonates because of bilirubin displacement
Viral PCR may shorten antibiotic course if positive and infant clinically improves
explanation.pearls: Cefotaxime is preferred over ceftriaxone in the first 28 days of life because ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin and risks kernicterus.

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics in a febrile infant under 3 months are inadequate cover for occult bacteraemia or meningitis and the infant requires admission with parenteral therapy and full workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

Australian guidelines mandate full sepsis evaluation including lumbar puncture and empiric intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin for any febrile infant under 3 months without a clear viral focus. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)
A limited workup misses occult meningitis and bacteraemia in this age group; the full septic screen plus empiric antibiotics is the standard of care under 3 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)
Delaying empiric antibiotics in a young febrile infant is unsafe because clinical appearance is a poor predictor of serious bacterial infection at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

Ceftriaxone alone misses Listeria cover required under 3 months, and lumbar puncture is part of the standard workup in this age group regardless of clinical appearance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed clinically when fever lasts five or more days with at least four of five principal features (conjunctivitis, oral changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy over 15 mm). Untreated, coronary artery aneurysms develop in around 25% of children. IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin given before day 10 reduces this to under 5%. Baseline echocardiography and follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks track coronary involvement.
key_points: Diagnosis requires fever 5 or more days plus 4 of 5 principal features in classic Kawasaki disease
IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin should be given before day 10 of illness
Coronary aneurysm risk falls from around 25% to under 5% with timely IVIG
Baseline echocardiogram is performed at diagnosis with follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks
Incomplete Kawasaki disease may be treated on fewer criteria if inflammatory markers and supportive features are present
explanation.pearls: Children under 12 months often present with incomplete Kawasaki disease and have the highest coronary aneurysm risk; CRP over 30 mg/L plus albumin under 30 g/L lowers the diagnostic threshold to 2 of 5 criteria.

options.rationale: A solitary 17 mm node with multisystem mucocutaneous findings and sterile pyuria does not fit bacterial adenitis; antibiotic delay risks coronary aneurysm formation. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Five days of fever plus four of five principal criteria meet the diagnostic threshold; IVIG given before day 10 of illness reduces coronary artery aneurysm risk from roughly 25% to under 5%. Baseline echocardiography establishes a comparator for coronary surveillance. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

A 48-hour observation period beyond day 6 of fever wastes the IVIG efficacy window; viral mimics rarely produce this combination of mucosal, extremity and laboratory findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Australian first-line treatment is IVIG plus aspirin; corticosteroid monotherapy is not standard initial therapy and is reserved for IVIG-resistant or high-risk subgroups. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Discharge would miss the IVIG window; the constellation of findings beyond five days of fever meets clinical Kawasaki disease criteria and mandates inpatient treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Australian neonatal jaundice management uses gestation-and-age-specific phototherapy and exchange thresholds plotted against postnatal hours. Term infants with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia above the phototherapy line need intensive phototherapy and continued breastfeeding. A repeat bilirubin at 4 to 6 hours assesses response and excludes ongoing rise toward exchange. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia above 20% or 20 micromol/L always prompts a separate cholestasis workup.
key_points: Phototherapy and exchange thresholds vary by gestation and hours of age in Australian nomograms
Intensive phototherapy plus continued breastfeeding is first-line above the phototherapy line
Repeat serum bilirubin at 4 to 6 hours to confirm downward trend
Negative direct antiglobulin test plus normal haemoglobin and reticulocytes argues against isoimmune haemolysis
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is always pathological and prompts cholestasis workup
explanation.pearls: A conjugated bilirubin over 20 micromol/L or over 20% of total in any jaundiced infant at any age mandates same-day investigation for biliary atresia because Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes deteriorate sharply after 60 days of life.

options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin at or above the exchange threshold or for signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy; this baby is well below exchange. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)
Routine formula top-ups are not indicated when feeding is adequate and weight loss is under 10%; this delay risks crossing the exchange threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Serum bilirubin sits above the phototherapy threshold for this gestation and age; intensive phototherapy with ongoing breastfeeding is first-line and a 6-hour repeat captures rebound or treatment failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

IVIG is used for proven isoimmune haemolytic disease with a rapidly rising bilirubin; the direct antiglobulin test is negative and there is no evidence of haemolysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)
Discharge with a bilirubin above the phototherapy threshold risks bilirubin neurotoxicity; treatment is required before community follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is treated with prompt intramuscular adrenaline 1:1000 dosed by weight band, with supine posture for hypotension and crystalloid resuscitation. ASCIA dosing is 0.15 mg (0.15 mL) for 7.5 to 20 kg, 0.3 mg (0.3 mL) for over 20 kg, repeating every 5 minutes if symptoms persist. Antihistamines and corticosteroids do not save the airway or restore blood pressure and must not delay adrenaline. After two doses persistent shock requires an adrenaline infusion in a monitored setting.
key_points: IM adrenaline 1:1000 lateral thigh is first-line by weight band: 0.15 mg under 20 kg, 0.3 mg over 20 kg
Repeat every 5 minutes if symptoms persist or recur
Lay the patient flat with legs elevated for hypotension; never sit upright with shock
Crystalloid 20 mL/kg bolus for hypotension that does not respond to first adrenaline
Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only and never replace adrenaline
explanation.pearls: Two or more IM adrenaline doses or any persistent hypotension is the threshold to start an adrenaline infusion at 0.1 to 1 micrograms/kg/min and call retrieval if the child is in a non-tertiary centre.

options.rationale: Antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory features; nebulised adrenaline is adjunctive for upper airway oedema only and never replaces IM adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

0.30 mL of 1:1000 is the adult dose, twice the band for a 16 kg child; hydrocortisone has no role in acute resuscitation and delays definitive measures. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

IV adrenaline bolus risks severe hypertension and arrhythmia in an unmonitored child; an IV infusion at 0.1 to 1 micrograms/kg/min is the correct escalation, not a bolus. Upright posture worsens distributive shock. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

Persistent anaphylaxis after one EpiPen Jr requires a repeat dose; the paediatric weight-band for under 20 kg is 0.15 mg (0.15 mL of 1:1000) IM. Supine positioning with legs elevated and crystalloid expansion treats distributive shock. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

Anaphylaxis with persistent hypotension and airway features mandates repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes until resolved; withholding risks death from distributive shock or airway obstruction. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

explanation.summary: Pertussis in infants under 6 months presents with apnoea, paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting, often without the classic whoop. Admission for cardiorespiratory monitoring is standard, and azithromycin is the preferred macrolide because erythromycin in neonates increases pyloric stenosis risk. Household contacts including pregnant women and other infants require post-exposure prophylaxis. Maternal pertussis vaccination at 20 to 32 weeks of every pregnancy is the most effective prevention.
key_points: Infants under 6 months with pertussis often present without the classic whoop
Apnoea, lymphocytosis and post-tussive vomiting are the key clues
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days is the first-line antibiotic in young infants
Erythromycin in neonates is associated with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Maternal pertussis vaccination at 20 to 32 weeks is the most effective infant prevention
explanation.pearls: A peripheral white cell count over 20 x10^9/L with marked lymphocytosis (over 50% lymphocytes) in an infant with paroxysmal cough has a high positive predictive value for pertussis and is associated with severe disease and pulmonary hypertension.

options.rationale: Treatment should be empiric for infants with clinically compatible pertussis; awaiting PCR delays therapy that reduces transmission and may worsen the apnoea risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Amoxicillin has no useful activity against Bordetella pertussis; an infant with witnessed apnoea cannot be safely managed at home. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Erythromycin in infants under one month carries a recognised pyloric stenosis risk and is poorly tolerated; azithromycin is preferred in this age group in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Benzylpenicillin does not cover pertussis; the lymphocytosis, paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting fit pertussis far better than meningitis and a lumbar puncture is not justified here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Infants under 6 months with suspected pertussis and apnoea require admission for monitoring; azithromycin is first-line in this age group and reduces transmission. Household contacts including the pregnant aunt warrant prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Reye syndrome is a mitochondrial encephalopathy classically triggered by aspirin during viral illness, particularly varicella and influenza. The picture is hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with hepatic dysfunction, hypoglycaemia and cerebral oedema, but jaundice is characteristically absent. Mortality is high and treatment is supportive: cease the inciting drug, correct glucose, lower intracranial pressure with hypertonic saline and PICU-level care. Inherited fatty acid oxidation disorders such as MCAD deficiency can mimic Reye and should be excluded once stable.
key_points: Hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with raised ALT and AST but normal or near-normal bilirubin is the Reye picture
Aspirin during viral illness, especially varicella and influenza, is the classic trigger in children
Hypoglycaemia and cerebral oedema dominate the early presentation
Treatment is supportive: stop aspirin, give dextrose, hypertonic saline and PICU care
Inherited metabolic disorders such as MCAD deficiency mimic Reye and require post-stabilisation workup
explanation.pearls: Aspirin is contraindicated under 16 years of age in Australia outside Kawasaki disease and specific cardiology indications; any child presenting with encephalopathy after a viral illness needs salicylate, paracetamol and ammonia levels in the first hour.

options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine treats paracetamol toxicity and has unproven benefit here; withholding dextrose in hypoglycaemia worsens cerebral oedema and a ward bed is unsafe with GCS 11. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Liver Failure)

The clinical picture is Reye-like encephalopathy from salicylate exposure during varicella: hyperammonaemia, hypoglycaemia, transaminitis without jaundice and cerebral oedema. Aspirin must stop, dextrose corrects hypoglycaemia, hypertonic saline lowers intracranial pressure, and PICU manages the airway and pressure monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Liver Failure)

There is no fever or meningism, varicella lesions are crusted and CT shows diffuse oedema without focal lesion making encephalitis unlikely; lumbar puncture risks coning with raised intracranial pressure. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Liver Failure)

Charcoal is not indicated 5 days after the last dose; urinary alkalinisation is for acute salicylate poisoning, not for Reye-like mitochondrial injury at a level of 1.8 mmol/L. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Watchful waiting with raised intracranial pressure, hypoglycaemia and INR 2.4 is unsafe; an inherited metabolic disorder is in the differential but does not change the immediate resuscitation priorities. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Liver Failure)

explanation.summary: HSP is a small-vessel IgA vasculitis where extra-renal features usually resolve in weeks but nephritis can develop or worsen over the following 6 months. Australian practice is structured urinalysis and blood pressure surveillance at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 12 months from diagnosis. Nephrology referral is triggered by persistent proteinuria, hypertension, or rising creatinine. Renal biopsy and immunosuppression are reserved for severe or rapidly progressive nephritis.
key_points: HSP nephritis can develop or worsen for up to 6 months after the rash resolves
Structured urinalysis and BP at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 12 months is standard surveillance
Refer to paediatric nephrology for persistent proteinuria, hypertension or raised creatinine
Routine corticosteroids do not prevent or treat established HSP nephritis
ACE inhibitors are the preferred antihypertensive when proteinuria is present, started under specialist guidance
explanation.pearls: Sustained proteinuria over 6 months or any nephrotic-range proteinuria in HSP triggers same-day nephrology referral because biopsy-proven crescentic disease has the highest long-term risk of chronic kidney disease.

options.rationale: Persistent haematuria with proteinuria above 20 mg/mmol and hypertension after HSP defines significant nephritis that requires paediatric nephrology review and 12-month surveillance per RCH guidance. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)
Up to a third of HSP nephritis develops within 6 weeks; discharge without urinalysis surveillance misses progressive renal disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

Routine prednisolone does not prevent or treat established HSP nephritis with this level of proteinuria and is not indicated without nephrotic syndrome or rapidly progressive disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)
Parental observation cannot detect persistent microscopic haematuria or low-grade proteinuria; structured urinalysis at defined intervals is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

Specific antihypertensive choice and dose in HSP nephritis should be decided by paediatric nephrology after biopsy decisions; ACE inhibitors are preferred when proteinuria is the driver. (Source: KHA-CARI Paediatric Nephrology Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian gastroenteritis management starts with structured oral rehydration solution given in small frequent aliquots, with breastfeeding continued. Mild to moderate dehydration is treated with 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance. Ondansetron and nasogastric rehydration are reserved for failure of oral therapy. Intravenous fluids are second-line for severe dehydration or failure of enteral routes. Antidiarrhoeals are not used in children.
key_points: Oral rehydration solution 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance is first-line for mild to moderate dehydration
Continue breastfeeding throughout rehydration
Ondansetron is reserved for children unable to tolerate oral fluids due to vomiting
Nasogastric or intravenous fluids escalate when oral fails or dehydration is severe
Loperamide and other antidiarrhoeals are contraindicated in children
explanation.pearls: Bloody diarrhoea, prolonged duration over 10 days, or recent travel triggers a stool culture and PCR including shiga-toxin producing E. coli, because empirical antibiotics in E. coli O157 increase haemolytic uraemic syndrome risk.

options.rationale: Ondansetron is reserved for children who cannot retain oral fluids due to vomiting; this child has not vomited in the past several hours and tolerates sips. The bolus rate suggested is also faster than guideline. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

IV fluids are second-line after failed oral or nasogastric rehydration in mild dehydration; first-attempt cannulation is unnecessarily invasive when oral fluid is tolerated. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Australian guidelines recommend oral rehydration as first-line for mild to moderate dehydration with 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance, continuing breastfeeding throughout. Review at 4 hours assesses fluid intake and tolerance. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
NG rehydration is appropriate when oral feeding fails despite encouragement; this child has not yet been trialled on oral rehydration solution in titrated aliquots. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
Antidiarrhoeals are contraindicated in young children due to ileus and toxic megacolon risk; high-sugar fluids worsen osmotic diarrhoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Australian newborn screening uses raised immunoreactive trypsinogen followed by a second-tier CFTR genotype panel; two mutations strongly suggest cystic fibrosis but sweat chloride remains the confirmatory test. Early referral to a tertiary CF clinic enables sweat testing, family counselling, dietitian and physiotherapy linkage and surveillance microbiology. Pancreatic enzyme replacement and CFTR modulator decisions occur after confirmation. Time to diagnosis matters: early intervention improves growth and lung function.
key_points: IRT plus two CFTR mutations on newborn screening is highly suggestive but not diagnostic
Sweat chloride over 60 mmol/L confirms cystic fibrosis
Urgent referral to a tertiary CF clinic with multidisciplinary team is the next step
Pancreatic enzymes start after confirmation and evidence of malabsorption
CFTR modulators such as elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor are increasingly used from young ages in eligible genotypes
explanation.pearls: Sweat chloride values of 30 to 59 mmol/L are equivocal in infants under 6 months and require repeat testing and CF specialist input; values 60 mmol/L and above confirm diagnosis even with only one or no identified CFTR mutation.

sources.label: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement

options.rationale: A 6-week non-CF-specific review misses the early-intervention window; sweat testing within the first weeks of life is the Australian standard after a positive screen. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement

options.rationale: Two pathogenic CFTR mutations on the second-tier panel makes false positivity extremely unlikely; delay risks pancreatic insufficiency presenting as failure to thrive. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement

options.rationale: Pancreatic enzymes are started after sweat test confirmation and evidence of fat malabsorption; routine chest imaging in an asymptomatic neonate is not indicated. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement

options.rationale: Two CFTR mutations on the newborn screen still require sweat chloride confirmation and multidisciplinary CF clinic linkage; early diagnosis improves nutritional and respiratory outcomes. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement

options.rationale: Azithromycin and surveillance swabs are introduced later in CF care under specialist guidance; they are not the first step at diagnosis confirmation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: The RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis CPG places standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen as the first-line respiratory support, titrated to maintain SpO2 at least 90%. HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen, defined as persistent SpO2 below 90% or no respiratory improvement after a minimum 2-hour low-flow trial. Salbutamol, nebulised hypertonic saline, and corticosteroids are not routinely recommended.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis: at least 90%
First-line respiratory support: low-flow nasal prong oxygen
HFNC reserved for low-flow failure (SpO2 persistently below 90% or no improvement after at least 2 hours)
Salbutamol, hypertonic saline, corticosteroids not routinely used
explanation.pearls: The 92% SpO2 target is a NICE figure; the RCH CPG explicitly uses 90% and notes that brief desaturations below 90% alone are not an indication to start supplemental oxygen.

options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis CPG specifies standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen as the first-line respiratory support, titrated to maintain SpO2 at least 90%, with HFNC reserved for persistent SpO2 below 90% or no respiratory improvement after a minimum 2-hour low-flow trial. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)
The RCH CPG advises against routine salbutamol and nebulised hypertonic saline in bronchiolitis as neither alters disease course. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

The RCH CPG reserves HFNC for failure of low-flow oxygen defined as persistent SpO2 below 90% or no respiratory improvement after at least 2 hours; bypassing the low-flow trial is not RCH-aligned. The 92% target is a NICE figure, not the RCH 90% target. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Intubation is reserved for failure of escalating non-invasive support; the RCH ladder is low-flow first, then HFNC if low-flow fails, then PICU input for further escalation. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Would be correct only after a documented failure of low-flow oxygen (persistent SpO2 below 90% or no improvement after at least 2 hours); HFNC is not the RCH first-line respiratory support. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Croup severity is graded by stridor and recession; stridor at rest with moderate recession defines moderate-severe disease and triggers nebulised adrenaline plus a single dose of dexamethasone. Adrenaline acts within 30 minutes and effects wane by 2 hours, so observation for 3 hours (RCH minimum) after the dose detects rebound stridor. Dexamethasone benefits all severities of croup and reduces re-presentation. Humidified air, antibiotics and bronchodilators are not recommended in viral croup. Children who remain stridor-free at rest after 3 hours (RCH minimum) can be discharged with safety-net advice.
key_points: Stridor at rest defines moderate-severe croup
Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL acts within 30 minutes and wanes by 2 hours
Single oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg covers all severities
3 hours (RCH minimum) after adrenaline to detect rebound
Avoid lateral neck X-ray in suspected epiglottitis-resembling presentations
explanation.pearls: Recurrent or atypical croup under 6 months or over 6 years warrants ENT review for subglottic stenosis or anatomical narrowing; dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose is non-inferior to 0.6 mg/kg in mild croup at the lower dose.

options.rationale: Stridor at rest with moderate recession is at least moderate croup; corticosteroid alone without nebulised adrenaline misses the rapid airway benefit and discharge at four hours is too early after adrenaline-eligible disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))
Bronchodilators target lower airway smooth muscle and have no role in supraglottic-subglottic oedema of croup. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Moderate-severe croup with stridor at rest mandates nebulised adrenaline plus a single dexamethasone dose; the benefit of adrenaline wanes by 2 hours so a 3 hours (RCH minimum) observation window screens for rebound. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

Imaging delays definitive treatment and provokes distress; classic prodrome, barking cough and absence of drooling or toxic appearance argue against epiglottitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))
Humidified air alone is no longer recommended and delays effective therapy that meaningfully reduces stridor and admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

explanation.summary: After a typical first febrile urinary tract infection in an infant with a good response to treatment and a normal antenatal renal tract on anomaly scanning, the RCH guideline does not mandate any imaging. Imaging during the acute illness is reserved for atypical urinary tract infection (seriously unwell, poor urine flow, non-E. coli organism, raised creatinine, sepsis, or no response within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics). Infants under 6 months without complete antenatal monitoring, or those with recurrence, get a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound. Routine DMSA and micturating cystourethrogram are NICE constructs not adopted by RCH.
key_points: Most children need no imaging after a first urinary tract infection per RCH
Ultrasound during illness is reserved for atypical urinary tract infection
Under-6-month infants with absent antenatal scans or recurrence get a renal tract ultrasound
Routine DMSA and micturating cystourethrogram are NICE-based and not in RCH cascade
Computed tomography is not first-line in paediatric urinary tract infection
explanation.pearls: Atypical urinary tract infection criteria that escalate imaging: seriously unwell appearance, poor urine flow, non-E. coli organism, raised creatinine, sepsis, or failure to respond to appropriate antibiotics within 48 hours.

options.rationale: The RCH urinary tract infection guideline reserves ultrasound during the acute illness for atypical urinary tract infection; with normal antenatal scans and a typical responsive first urinary tract infection at 5 months it is not routinely required. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

Royal Children's Hospital guidance states that most children do not require any imaging after a first urinary tract infection; ultrasound during illness is reserved for atypical urinary tract infection, and a renal tract ultrasound is only mandatory for infants under 6 months when antenatal monitoring was incomplete or there is recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

DMSA and routine micturating cystourethrogram are part of the NICE algorithm and are not in the RCH cascade after a single uncomplicated treatment-responsive first urinary tract infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection; NICE NG224)

Computed tomography is not first-line imaging in paediatric urinary tract infection because of radiation exposure; ultrasound is the appropriate modality when imaging is indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

Prophylaxis is reserved for recurrent urinary tract infection or significant reflux and is not used routinely after an uncomplicated first urinary tract infection in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

explanation.summary: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected meningococcal disease when there is shock, coagulopathy, rapidly evolving purpura, focal neurology, GCS under 13 or signs of raised intracranial pressure. Antibiotics should never be delayed for an LP in a deteriorating child. Blood culture, blood meningococcal PCR and skin lesion PCR have high yield in invasive meningococcal disease without requiring CSF. LP can be performed later once the child has stabilised and contraindications have resolved.
key_points: Shock, coagulopathy, GCS under 13 and rapidly evolving purpura contraindicate LP
Empirical ceftriaxone must not be delayed for any LP
Blood and skin PCR retain meningococcal diagnostic yield
Routine CT before LP does not reliably exclude raised ICP
LP can be deferred and performed once contraindications resolve
explanation.pearls: In paediatric meningococcal sepsis, fluid resuscitation past 40 mL/kg without haemodynamic response is the trigger for intubation, vasopressor support and admission to intensive care; dexamethasone is not given when the dominant picture is sepsis without proven bacterial meningitis.

sources.label: NICE NG143 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease in under 16s

options.rationale: Shock, coagulopathy and rapidly progressive purpura are contraindications to immediate LP in suspected meningococcal disease; blood and skin biopsy PCR retain diagnostic yield. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal disease)
Intubation does not remove the LP contraindications of coagulopathy and shock; antibiotics should not be delayed for any LP in this scenario. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Routine CT before LP does not exclude raised intracranial pressure and adds delay without changing the immediate threshold for LP. (Source: NICE NG143 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease in under 16s)
source_refs: NICE NG143 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease in under 16s

options.rationale: Shock, coagulopathy (INR 1.6, fibrinogen 1.0), rapidly evolving purpura and GCS under 13 are all contraindications to LP; PCR on blood and skin biopsy plus blood culture obtains the microbiological diagnosis without delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal disease)

Empirical ceftriaxone is the cornerstone of paediatric meningococcal sepsis therapy; switching to vancomycin plus aciclovir is not indicated in this clinical pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Suspected non-accidental injury in a pre-mobile infant requires a structured workup including skeletal survey, neuroimaging, fundoscopy by ophthalmology, baseline bloods and a statutory report. Frenular tears, posterior trunk bruising and spiral long-bone fractures in non-mobile infants are sentinel injuries with a high yield for occult injury. Mandatory reporting obligations apply to all medical practitioners in every Australian jurisdiction. Care planning and discharge decisions are made jointly with the child protection authority and not by the treating team alone.
key_points: Frenular tear, posterior bruising and spiral fracture in a non-mobile infant are sentinel for abuse
Workup is skeletal survey, neuroimaging, fundoscopy and baseline bloods
Mandatory reporting to the state child protection authority is required
Metabolic bone disease evaluation does not delay protective action
Discharge planning is joint with child protection
explanation.pearls: A skeletal survey repeat at 11-14 days improves yield for healing rib and metaphyseal fractures that are occult on the first set; classic metaphyseal lesions and posterior rib fractures are highly specific for non-accidental injury.

sources.label: RACGP: Child Abuse Identification and Management

options.rationale: Spiral long-bone fractures, frenular tear and unexplained multi-age bruising in a non-mobile infant mandate full child protection workup including skeletal survey, neuroimaging, fundoscopy and a statutory report. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)
source_refs: RACGP: Child Abuse Identification and Management

options.rationale: Discharge home in suspected non-accidental injury before completing the workup and statutory report places the child at ongoing risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

Limiting imaging and deferring statutory reporting until family consent is obtained breaches mandatory reporting obligations and risks missed occult injury. (Source: RACGP: Child Abuse Identification and Management)
source_refs: RACGP: Child Abuse Identification and Management

options.rationale: Metabolic bone disease is exceptionally rare and should not delay the standard non-accidental injury workup or mandatory reporting in this clinical pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)
Occult abusive head trauma occurs without external signs; fundoscopy and neuroimaging are part of the routine workup, not symptom-triggered. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management is built around cautious volume restoration and slow correction over 48 hours to reduce the risk of cerebral oedema. Initial boluses are typically 10 mL/kg unless there is shock, with the deficit estimated at 5-7% and replaced together with maintenance over 48 hours. Insulin is started after at least 1 hour of fluid at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour. Potassium is added once urine output is established. Bicarbonate is avoided.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline unless shocked
Replace 5-7% deficit plus maintenance over 48 hours
Insulin 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour starting after 1 hour of fluids
Potassium added with first maintenance bag once urine output is present
Avoid bicarbonate; monitor for cerebral oedema with hourly neuro obs
explanation.pearls: Risk factors for cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA include age under 5 years, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis (pH under 7.1), bicarbonate therapy and rapid fluid administration over 50 mL/kg in the first 4 hours.

options.rationale: Rapid 20 mL/kg boluses and immediate insulin (before 1 hour of fluid replacement) increase the risk of paediatric cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG paediatric DKA guideline)
Insulin should not start until at least 1 hour of intravenous fluids has been delivered in paediatric DKA. (Source: APEG paediatric DKA guideline)

Paediatric DKA replacement uses cautious boluses (10 mL/kg) and a 48-hour deficit-plus-maintenance approach with insulin started after 1 hour and at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour to minimise cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG paediatric DKA guideline)
Potassium replacement starts with the initial maintenance bag once urine output is present; awaiting gas normalisation prolongs ketosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)
Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA and a 12-hour rapid correction increases cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG paediatric DKA guideline)

explanation.summary: Suspected foreign body aspiration in a child with effective cough or stridor at rest is partial airway obstruction and is managed by minimising distress, supplemental oxygen as tolerated and urgent rigid bronchoscopy under anaesthetic. Back blows and chest thrusts are reserved for the child with ineffective cough or unconsciousness. Plain radiographs are insensitive for organic foreign bodies and should not delay ENT referral. Inhaled peanut is the commonest organic foreign body in toddlers.
key_points: Partial airway obstruction is managed by keeping the child calm with parents
Rigid bronchoscopy by ENT in theatre is the standard intervention
Back blows and thrusts are for ineffective cough or unconscious patients
Plain X-ray can be normal in radiolucent foreign bodies
Bronchodilators and corticosteroids do not treat foreign body aspiration
explanation.pearls: Asymmetric breath sounds, persistent unilateral wheeze or new-onset chronic cough in a toddler with a witnessed choking event are red flags for retained foreign body even with a normal radiograph; bronchoscopy under anaesthetic is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

options.rationale: Effective coughing and ongoing stridor indicate partial obstruction; back blows and thrusts risk converting partial to complete obstruction. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4 Airway)
Sudden onset while eating and asymmetric breath sounds suggest foreign body, not viral croup, and bronchodilators or steroids do not address aspiration. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled foreign body)
Normal radiographs do not exclude foreign body aspiration; ENT referral should not be deferred for imaging in an evolving airway presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled foreign body)
Awake direct laryngoscopy in a stridorous toddler risks complete obstruction; rigid bronchoscopy by ENT in theatre with anaesthetic support is the standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled foreign body)

Partial airway obstruction from a suspected foreign body is managed by minimising distress, keeping the child upright in the parent's lap and arranging urgent rigid bronchoscopy under anaesthetic with ENT. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled foreign body)

explanation.summary: Crossing 2 or more major centile lines in infancy meets the definition of faltering growth and warrants stepped assessment in primary care. The first step is a structured feeding history, observed feed with lactation support, a comprehensive examination and a baseline investigation panel. Inpatient or specialist evaluation is reserved for severe deficit, red flags or failure to respond. Reassurance without assessment risks missing breastfeeding difficulties, coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis or other treatable causes.
key_points: Crossing 2 major centiles defines faltering growth
First-line is feeding assessment and outpatient baseline screen
Baseline screen: FBC, iron, UEC, LFT, TFT, urinalysis, coeliac
Lactation support precedes formula top-up in breastfeeding infants
Specialist referral is for red flags or failed first-line management
explanation.pearls: Red flags that bypass the staged outpatient workup and trigger admission include weight under 70% of expected, severe undernutrition signs, suspected child protection concerns, dysmorphic features or atypical examination findings.

options.rationale: Inpatient metabolic workup is reserved for atypical features or no response to standard feeding interventions; first-line management focuses on feeding optimisation and a stepped outpatient workup. (Source: RACGP Red Book Faltering Growth)

Australian guidance recommends a structured feeding assessment, observed feed and baseline screen (FBC, iron, UEC, LFT, TFT, urinalysis, coeliac) before escalating to inpatient or specialist workup in non-organic faltering growth. (Source: RACGP Red Book Faltering Growth)
Endoscopy and stool elastase are second-line tests after a baseline screen and feeding assessment have failed to identify a cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth)

Formula top-ups are introduced only after a structured feeding assessment confirms inadequate breastmilk transfer; routine introduction overrides maternal preference and undermines lactation. (Source: NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines)
Crossing 2 or more centile lines is faltering growth and warrants structured assessment; reassurance without further evaluation misses treatable causes. (Source: RACGP Red Book Faltering Growth)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation in children is the cause of over 90% of presentations. Diagnosis is clinical (Rome IV criteria: 2+ of 2 or fewer defecations per week, history of retentive posturing, history of painful or hard motions, large diameter stools, faecal mass on exam, soiling in toilet-trained child). Red flags suggesting organic cause include delayed meconium past 48 hours, failure to thrive, fever, vomiting, abnormal anal exam or neurology, sacral abnormalities. Management is disimpaction with oral PEG (Movicol Junior, escalating doses), then maintenance for at least 3 months, plus toileting behavioural program. Avoid rectal interventions where possible.
key_points: Functional constipation: clinical diagnosis (Rome IV), 90% of cases
Red flags: delayed meconium, FTT, abnormal anal exam, neurology
Disimpaction: Movicol Junior 4-8 sachets daily over 3-7 days
Maintenance: Movicol 1-2 sachets daily for at least 3 months
Behavioural: regular toileting after meals, reward charts
explanation.pearls: Premature cessation of maintenance laxatives in the first 6 months is the single most common cause of relapse; counsel families that hard-stool memories take months to fade and that staying on maintenance through a painless interval is the actual treatment, not just a dose.

sources.label: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people

options.rationale: Dietary advice alone in the presence of demonstrable faecal impaction is insufficient; disimpaction with osmotic laxatives is recommended first to break the cycle. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Hirschsprung's disease typically presents in infancy with delayed meconium passage; functional constipation does not require biopsy unless red flags are present. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Oral disimpaction with high-dose polyethylene glycol is preferred over invasive rectal interventions in children, which can be traumatic and worsen stool-withholding behaviour. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

RCH guidance recommends oral disimpaction with high-dose Movicol Junior (escalating regimen until impaction clears) followed by maintenance therapy with sustained Movicol for 3+ months alongside behavioural toileting program. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Disimpaction must precede maintenance; lactulose alone without disimpaction or behavioural intervention in the setting of faecal impaction is inadequate. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is the commonest small-vessel vasculitis of childhood. Diagnosis is clinical: palpable purpura with at least one of arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, biopsy-proven IgA deposition or renal involvement. Renal involvement (microscopic haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, nephritis) occurs in 20 to 40% and is the major long-term morbidity. Most cases self-resolve. Monitoring: urinalysis and BP weekly for 1-2 months, then 3-monthly for 12 months. Refer to nephrology if nephrotic-range proteinuria (UPCR over 200 mg/mmol or ACR over 250 mg/mmol), persistent significant proteinuria, hypertension, eGFR decline or significant haematuria/casts. Steroids do not prevent nephritis but are used for severe symptoms.
key_points: HSP: palpable purpura + arthritis/abd pain/IgA biopsy/renal involvement
Renal involvement in 20-40%; major long-term morbidity
Monitoring: urinalysis + BP weekly for 1-2 months then 3-monthly for 12 months
Steroids: severe abdominal pain, scrotal involvement, established nephritis
Refer nephrology: nephrotic-range, persistent significant proteinuria, hypertension, eGFR decline
explanation.pearls: Scrotal involvement in HSP can mimic testicular torsion; bedside ultrasound showing scrotal wall oedema with normal testicular Doppler flow supports HSP scrotal involvement and avoids unnecessary surgical exploration.

sources.label: Royal College of Paediatrics: HSP guideline

options.rationale: ACR 18 mg/mmol with blood 2+ is not nephrotic-range and does not warrant biopsy or pulsed steroids; HSP nephritis is monitored with urine and BP at follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis))

Typical HSP with mild renal findings is managed with home follow-up; serial urinalysis and BP are recommended weekly for 1-2 months then 3-6 monthly for at least 12 months to detect delayed nephritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis))

Palpable purpura in HSP is a vasculitic eruption not meningococcal sepsis; the child is well, afebrile with characteristic distribution. Septic workup and broad antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis))

HSP can cause intussusception (typically ileoileal) but it is not the most likely cause of mild abdominal pain in this child; routine US is not indicated unless pain is severe, persistent or there is bilious vomiting or PR bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis))

Steroids do not prevent or alter incidence of HSP nephritis; they are reserved for severe symptoms (significant abdominal pain, scrotal involvement, severe arthralgia, established nephritis with crescents). (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis))

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice is common; in term well infants without haemolysis the AAP/RCH 2022 nomogram thresholds for phototherapy at 72 hours are approximately 290 to 300 micromol/L (with thresholds adjusted lower with risk factors: gestational age under 38 weeks, isoimmune haemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, sepsis, significant lethargy or temperature instability). Exchange transfusion thresholds at 72 hours are around 425 micromol/L for term infants without risk factors. Phototherapy is given with intensive blue spectrum, feeding maintained, repeat TSB in 4 to 6 hours. Investigate prolonged jaundice (over 14 days term, 21 days preterm) for cholestasis, infection, hypothyroidism, metabolic causes.
key_points: Term well 72h: phototherapy at TSB approx 290-300 micromol/L
Adjust lower with risk factors: gestation under 38wk, haemolysis, G6PD, sepsis
Exchange transfusion term 72h: TSB approx 425 micromol/L
IVIG: Coombs-positive haemolysis approaching exchange
Investigate prolonged jaundice over 14 days term
explanation.pearls: Visual estimation of jaundice severity is unreliable past the umbilicus; always confirm with TSB or transcutaneous bilirubinometer (TcB) and plot on age-in-hours nomogram - the trajectory matters more than the static number.

sources.label: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperbilirubinemia in Newborn Infant 2022

options.rationale: TSB 290 at 72 hours in a term infant crosses the phototherapy threshold per AAP/RCH nomograms; deferral risks further rise toward exchange-transfusion territory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Exchange transfusion threshold in a term infant at 72 hours is around 425 micromol/L (AAP) with no risk factors; 290 is below exchange threshold and warrants phototherapy first. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Breastfeeding-related jaundice and ABO setoff are reasonable considerations; investigations are useful but should not delay initiation of phototherapy at this level. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

IVIG is used for isoimmune haemolytic disease (Rh or ABO) with positive Coombs and rising bilirubin despite phototherapy approaching exchange threshold; Coombs is negative here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

TSB 290 at 72 hours crosses the phototherapy threshold for a term infant without risk factors; intensive phototherapy, ongoing feeding support and repeat TSB in 6 hours are recommended. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Preschool wheeze (under 5 years) is heterogeneous - episodic viral-induced wheeze (no interval symptoms, no atopy) versus multi-trigger wheeze (likely asthma trajectory, often atopic). Acute moderate exacerbation: salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer (12 puffs for over 6 years) every 20 minutes for 3 doses with oxygen titrated to keep SpO2 over 94%. Oral prednisolone (1-2 mg/kg up to 50 mg) for moderate/severe exacerbations is recommended in Australian guidance even for preschool age presenting to ED. Ipratropium adds benefit in severe/life-threatening. ICS preventer use in pure viral-induced wheeze is debated; consider after 3+ episodes in a year, family history of asthma, or interval symptoms. Spacer technique is critical.
key_points: Acute moderate preschool wheeze: salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer q20min x3
Oral prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg (max 50 mg) for moderate/severe exacerbation
Ipratropium: add for severe/life-threatening
Spacer with mask under 4 years, mouthpiece from 4-5 years
ICS preventer: consider after 3+ episodes, atopy or interval symptoms
explanation.pearls: An infant under 12 months with a first wheeze illness is bronchiolitis not asthma until proven otherwise; reaching for salbutamol there is not evidence-based, but in a toddler with recurrent wheeze responding to bronchodilator, the phenotype tips toward asthma even before formal diagnosis.

sources.label: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.rationale: Salbutamol via spacer (6 puffs at this size) is preferred over nebuliser; oral prednisolone is preferred over IV in moderate exacerbation tolerating oral; routine ipratropium is reserved for severe disease. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia))
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.rationale: SpO2 92% with moderate work of breathing requires in-department observation with bronchodilator and oxygen titration before considering discharge; not an immediate discharge candidate. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia))
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.rationale: Moderate preschool wheeze responds to salbutamol via spacer (6 puffs) every 20 minutes for 3 doses; oral prednisolone in modest episodes in children with a clear viral-induced wheeze pattern who present to ED is now supported in Australian guidance.
