(Source: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia))
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.rationale: ICS preventer in pure viral-induced preschool wheeze without interval symptoms or atopy has limited benefit; initiation should be considered after 3+ episodes when guided by phenotype, and not as the acute ED intervention. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia))
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is for stridor in croup, not for lower-airway wheeze; this is not appropriate for viral-induced wheeze. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia))
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

explanation.summary: Infants of diabetic mothers are at high risk of transient hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia from in-utero glucose exposure. Australian pathways treat asymptomatic BGL between 1.0 and 2.5 mmol/L with a 5 mL/kg feed of expressed breast milk or formula and a 30-minute recheck. Persistent low levels then trigger 40% dextrose gel (200 mg/kg = 0.5 mL/kg) plus a feed. Intravenous 10% dextrose is for symptomatic infants, BGL under 1.0, or failure of feed plus gel. The target threshold for treatment in the first 48 hours is 2.6 mmol/L.
key_points: IDM, LGA, SGA, late preterm are at-risk groups requiring screening
Treatment threshold first 48h: BGL under 2.6 mmol/L
First line: feed 5 mL/kg EBM or formula, recheck 30 min
Second line: 200 mg/kg of 40% dextrose gel buccally plus feed
IV 10% dextrose if symptomatic, under 1.0 mmol/L, or persistent failure
explanation.pearls: Buccal 40% dextrose gel dose is 0.5 mL/kg (200 mg/kg) given with a feed, not instead of one - this single dose has reduced NICU admission in the Sugar Babies trial.

options.rationale: A BGL under 2.0 mmol/L in any at-risk infant always triggers active management and a 30-minute recheck after feeding, not passive observation until the next routine feed time. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn hypoglycaemia)

Intravenous 10% dextrose is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia, BGL under 1.0 mmol/L, or persistent BGL under 2.6 mmol/L after feed plus buccal gel; an asymptomatic 1.8 mmol/L at first measurement is treated with feed first. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn hypoglycaemia)

Buccal 40% dextrose gel is used in combination with a feed, not instead of one, and only after the first low BGL persists or as second-line for the next low reading per the Sugar Babies and Queensland pathway. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn hypoglycaemia)

ASID and Queensland Health newborn hypoglycaemia pathways treat an asymptomatic BGL of 1.0 to 2.5 mmol/L with an immediate feed of 5 mL/kg expressed colostrum or formula and a recheck 30 minutes after; persistent levels below 2.6 mmol/L then trigger 40% dextrose gel and senior review. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn hypoglycaemia)

A critical hypoglycaemia screen is appropriate when BGL stays below 2.6 mmol/L despite adequate feeds at over 48 hours of age, not at the first reading at 2 hours of life in an infant of a diabetic mother. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Moderate croup is defined as stridor at rest with mild to moderate recession. First-line treatment is single-dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (or prednisolone 1 mg/kg if dexamethasone unavailable). Nebulised adrenaline (0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000, max 5 mL) is added for severe disease with marked recession, tracheal tug, agitation or hypoxia. Children are observed for at least 4 hours post-steroid (or 4 hours post-last-adrenaline) before discharge. Antibiotics, imaging and routine humidification are not recommended.
key_points: Croup severity: mild (barking cough, no stridor at rest), moderate (stridor at rest, mild recession), severe (marked recession, tracheal tug, agitation)
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for all moderate or severe croup
Add nebulised adrenaline for severe croup
Observe 4 hours post-treatment before discharge
Croup is a clinical diagnosis - no routine imaging
explanation.pearls: A child with croup who becomes drooling, very still and toxic should raise suspicion of bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis - call ENT/anaesthetics for theatre intubation before any throat examination.

options.rationale: RCH and Therapeutic Guidelines recommend single-dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as first-line for moderate croup with at-least 4 hours of observation; nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe disease with marked recession or tracheal tug. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with marked sternal recession, tracheal tug or hypoxia; mild recession with stridor at rest is moderate and treated with steroid alone in most cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

Croup is a clinical diagnosis and routine imaging or viral PCR delays treatment without changing management; steroids should be given promptly on clinical grounds alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

Croup is viral so antibiotics are not indicated; humidified oxygen is unhelpful in an infant with saturations of 97% and may distress the child further. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

Even mild croup benefits from a single dose of oral dexamethasone to reduce relapse and re-presentation; discharge without steroid is suboptimal in stridor-at-rest disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

explanation.summary: Any febrile infant under 3 months of age requires a full septic workup. RCH defines this as urinalysis and culture by catheter or suprapubic aspirate, blood culture, FBC, CRP, and lumbar puncture (unless contraindicated). Empirical IV benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) plus gentamicin covers Group B streptococcus, Listeria and Gram negatives; cefotaxime replaces gentamicin if meningitis suspected. The infant is admitted pending cultures. Well-appearance does not exclude serious bacterial infection in this age group.
key_points: Under 1 month: always full septic workup plus admit on empirical IV antibiotics
1-3 months: full septic workup unless very well and low-risk per Rochester/Step-by-Step
Empirical IV penicillin plus gentamicin (cefotaxime if meningitis suspected)
Urine: catheter or SPA only, not bag
Renal tract US after confirmed UTI in infants under 6 months
explanation.pearls: Listeria monocytogenes covers the rationale for adding ampicillin/amoxicillin to gentamicin in neonates - it is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins.

options.rationale: Imaging is not done before empirical antibiotics; renal tract US in confirmed UTI is arranged later per KHA-CARI and RCH timelines. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Bag urine has a high contamination rate and is not acceptable for diagnosing UTI in infants; oral antibiotics and outpatient management are inappropriate for any febrile infant under 3 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)
Well-appearance is unreliable in infants under 3 months and serious bacterial infection prevalence is 5 to 10 percent; observation alone is inadequate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)
Urine dipstick is unreliable in young infants and oral antibiotics are not first-line; full septic workup and IV antibiotics are mandated. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

RCH and the Therapeutic Guidelines treat a febrile infant under 3 months as full septic workup including catheter urine, blood culture, LP and empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (cefotaxime if LP delayed) regardless of well appearance. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is diagnosed when there is any acute onset of typical skin or mucosal change PLUS either respiratory or cardiovascular involvement, or any hypotension after a known allergen. First-line treatment is IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 (10 mcg/kg, max 0.5 mg) into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes as needed. Supine positioning, high flow oxygen and IV fluid 20 mL/kg if hypotensive complete the bundle. Observation for at least 4 hours post symptom resolution is required, with adrenaline autoinjector script, action plan and allergy referral on discharge.
key_points: IM adrenaline first - always first - 0.01 mg/kg 1:1000 IM mid anterolateral thigh, max 0.5 mg
Repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes if no response
Supine with legs elevated unless pregnant (left lateral) or vomiting (lateral)
Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only
Observe at least 4 hours post symptom resolution
explanation.pearls: For a 22 kg child the IM dose is 0.22 mg, but ASCIA pre-calibrates by age band: 0.15 mg for under 20 kg, 0.30 mg for 20 to 50 kg and 0.5 mg for over 50 kg - the band is appropriate here despite slight under-dose.

options.rationale: Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only and never replace adrenaline for any feature of anaphylaxis; delaying IM adrenaline increases mortality. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses with persistent shock and senior clinician supervision; first-line is always IM adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

ASCIA action plan: IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 (max 0.5 mg) into the mid anterolateral thigh, with supine positioning, high flow oxygen and a minimum 4-hour observation after symptom resolution before discharge with an adrenaline autoinjector and follow up. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

Inhaled salbutamol treats wheeze but not airway oedema or hypotension; nebulised adrenaline is for severe upper airway oedema as an adjunct only, never replacing IM adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

Anaphylaxis is diagnosed by any combination of skin, airway or breathing involvement after exposure regardless of blood pressure; IM adrenaline is given immediately rather than awaiting hypotension. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed clinically by fever for at least 5 days plus 4 of 5 principal features: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, mucosal changes (cracked lips, strawberry tongue), extremity changes (palmar/plantar erythema or oedema, periungual desquamation), polymorphous rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy of at least 1.5 cm. Treatment with single-dose IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm rates from 25 percent to under 5 percent. Aspirin is dosed at 30 to 50 mg/kg/day until 48 hours afebrile, then 3 to 5 mg/kg/day until echo follow up at 6 to 8 weeks.
key_points: Diagnose by 5+ days fever plus 4 of 5 criteria (or incomplete KD by criteria plus echo)
Treat within 10 days of fever onset: IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin
Baseline echo, repeat at 6 to 8 weeks
Steroid added upfront for high-risk (Kobayashi score) or IVIG resistance
Long-term cardiology follow up if z-score abnormal
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria, raised CRP, anaemia of inflammation and a normal-to-rising platelet count by week 2 are supportive markers used in incomplete KD scoring.

sources.label: American Heart Association: Kawasaki disease scientific statement

options.rationale: Delaying treatment beyond day 10 of fever loses the window of maximal IVIG efficacy in preventing coronary aneurysm; treat as soon as Kawasaki criteria are met. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

The combination of fever for 6 days plus 4 of 5 principal criteria fulfils Kawasaki disease; staphylococcal scalded skin would not give bilateral conjunctivitis and strawberry tongue with this lymph node pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Single dose IVIG 2 g/kg infused over 8 to 12 hours plus high or moderate dose aspirin started within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25 percent to under 5 percent; baseline echo establishes coronary z-scores. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Steroid monotherapy is not first line; high-risk Kawasaki may receive IVIG plus steroid combination (Kobayashi-style risk stratification), but never steroid without IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Low-dose aspirin is the maintenance antiplatelet dose used after fever resolves; the acute high-inflammation phase always requires IVIG plus moderate-to-high dose aspirin until day 14 or 48 hours afebrile. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is the most common childhood malignancy, typically presenting between 2 and 5 years with marrow failure (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia), bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms. Circulating blasts on film are diagnostic until proven otherwise. Tumour lysis risk increases with WCC over 50, raised LDH, urate over 0.45 mmol/L and bulky disease; intravenous hyperhydration at twice maintenance plus allopurinol (or rasburicase if very high risk) is started before induction. Tertiary transfer for marrow aspirate, immunophenotyping and minimal residual disease assessment guides risk-stratified chemotherapy.
key_points: Triad: marrow failure + organomegaly + bone pain in pre-school child
Film: circulating blasts trigger urgent transfer
Tumour lysis: hydrate twice-maintenance plus allopurinol or rasburicase
Avoid transfusion before diagnostic marrow if possible
Australian protocols via eviQ; cure rate over 90 percent in standard-risk B-ALL
explanation.pearls: Mediastinal mass on chest X-ray in T-cell ALL can compress trachea or great vessels; lying flat for procedures becomes hazardous and dictates early imaging.

sources.label: Children's Cancer and Leukaemia Group: ALL guidance

options.rationale: Excisional lymph node biopsy is appropriate for suspected lymphoma without circulating blasts; here marrow examination is faster and definitive. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL - Induction)
Transfusion without first taking diagnostic marrow may confound flow cytometry; outpatient delay risks progressive cytopenia and tumour lysis. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL - Induction)

Although febrile neutropenia management is needed if a fever spikes, the immediate priority is diagnosis with bone marrow aspirate and tumour lysis prophylaxis; abx are not first-line in stable apyrexial neutropenia. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL - Induction)

Circulating blasts on film with pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and raised LDH require urgent transfer for diagnostic bone marrow plus tumour lysis prophylaxis given the WCC and urate; ALL is the most likely diagnosis. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL - Induction)
Viral serology has a place but never delays urgent tertiary referral when circulating blasts and a leukaemoid white cell count are present. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL - Induction)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is a small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis of children with palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain and nephritis. Renal involvement determines long-term prognosis. Australian and KDIGO pathways monitor blood pressure and urinalysis weekly for 4 weeks then monthly to 6 months. Indications for nephrology referral and biopsy include nephrotic-range proteinuria, persistent PCR over 100 to 250 mg/mmol, hypertension, raised creatinine or AKI, or atypical features. Biopsy ISKDC class guides treatment: class II-IIIA may have RAAS blockade alone; IIIB+ get steroids; class IV-V and crescentic disease often need pulse methylprednisolone plus cyclophosphamide or MMF.
key_points: Monitor urine and BP weekly for 4 weeks, then monthly to 6 months after diagnosis
PCR over 100 to 250 mg/mmol, hypertension, AKI or nephrotic syndrome trigger nephrology referral
Biopsy stratifies treatment per ISKDC class
RAAS blockade is the cornerstone of proteinuria control
Long-term follow up because late progression to CKD can occur
explanation.pearls: Normal complement is the rule in IgA vasculitis nephritis - low complement should redirect workup toward post-infectious glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis instead.

sources.label: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

options.rationale: Trace haematuria alone may resolve, but PCR over 100 mg/mmol with hypertension represents progressive nephritis that requires nephrology input rather than continued primary care monitoring. (Source: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis)
source_refs: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

options.rationale: Persistent heavy proteinuria (PCR over 250 mg/mmol or nephrotic-range) with hypertension at 4 weeks after IgA vasculitis onset triggers nephrology referral for biopsy; ISKDC class II to V guides steroid plus immunosuppression decisions. (Source: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis)
source_refs: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

options.rationale: Empirical steroid without biopsy classification is not first-line for HSP nephritis at this severity; KDIGO and RCH guide biopsy-stratified therapy rather than blind community steroid courses. (Source: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis)
source_refs: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide is considered only after biopsy demonstrates crescentic or class IV-V disease and after steroid trial; empirical use is inappropriate. (Source: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis)
source_refs: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

options.rationale: Clinical picture of preceding palpable purpura with normal complement is classical IgA vasculitis nephritis, not ANCA-associated vasculitis; serology should be confirmatory but not delay biopsy referral. (Source: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis)
source_refs: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

explanation.summary: Mitochondrial disease presents at any age but in infancy and toddlers classically features developmental regression, hypotonia, lactic acidosis, multisystem involvement (cardiomyopathy, deafness, retinopathy, hepatic and renal tubular dysfunction) and characteristic MRI patterns. Leigh syndrome shows symmetric T2 hyperintensities in basal ganglia, brainstem and cerebellum with raised brain or CSF lactate. Initial management is referral to tertiary metabolic genetics, mitochondrial cofactor support (riboflavin, thiamine, coenzyme Q10, biotin, levocarnitine) and strict avoidance of mitochondrial toxins including sodium valproate, metformin, linezolid, aminoglycosides and propofol infusions. Genetic diagnosis via mitochondrial DNA panel plus nuclear gene exome sequencing guides prognosis and family counselling.
key_points: Symmetric basal ganglia lesions + lactic acidosis + regression = Leigh syndrome until proven otherwise
Cofactor cocktail: riboflavin, thiamine, CoQ10, levocarnitine, biotin
Avoid valproate (fatal hepatotoxicity in POLG), metformin, aminoglycosides
Genetic confirmation by mtDNA panel + nuclear WES
Multidisciplinary care: neurology, cardiology, ophthalmology, audiology, dietetics
explanation.pearls: POLG mutations cause Alpers syndrome and are exquisitely sensitive to sodium valproate, which can precipitate fulminant hepatic failure - a key reason mitochondrial disease must be excluded before valproate in early-life epilepsy.

sources.label: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

options.rationale: MLD is a leukodystrophy with white matter lesions, not symmetric grey-matter basal ganglia pattern; discharge before treatment risks metabolic decompensation with intercurrent illness. (Source: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline)
source_refs: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is unlikely with symmetric metabolic-pattern lesions on MRI and persistent lactic acidosis; the clinical and imaging pattern points to mitochondrial disease. (Source: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline)
source_refs: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

options.rationale: Gastroenteritis would not produce a persistent lactic acidosis with developmental regression, ptosis and basal ganglia lesions; the presentation is metabolic. (Source: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline)
source_refs: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

options.rationale: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in suspected mitochondrial disease (especially POLG-related) due to risk of fatal hepatotoxicity; ictal-eye movements should not be empirically treated this way. (Source: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline)
source_refs: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

options.rationale: Symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem T2 lesions with lactic acidosis and a hypotonic regression suggest Leigh syndrome or mitochondrial disease; tertiary referral, mitochondrial cofactor cocktail and avoidance of mitochondrial-toxic drugs are recommended pending genetic diagnosis. (Source: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline)
source_refs: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

explanation.summary: Disposition in bronchiolitis is driven by sustained SpO2, work of breathing, feeding adequacy, apnoeas and carer factors rather than by interventions of unproven benefit. This infant meets all RCH discharge criteria after simple suction and a feed. Hypertonic saline, bronchodilators, antibiotics and routine imaging are not indicated. Safe discharge requires a clear action plan and short-interval review.
key_points: Discharge thresholds: SpO2 at or above 92% in air sustained 30 minutes, feeds at or above 50% baseline, no apnoea, mild work of breathing
Hypertonic saline and salbutamol are not recommended in routine bronchiolitis under 12 months
Antibiotics and chest x-ray only with focal signs, persistent high fever or severe disease
Carer reliability, distance to care, and follow-up plan are part of the disposition decision
explanation.pearls: If SpO2 sits at 92% in air after suction and feed in an otherwise well infant with reliable carers, discharge with a written action plan and GP review within 24 hours is correct - admitting to escalate to high-flow is over-treatment.

options.rationale: Routine chest imaging and empirical antibiotics are not indicated in uncomplicated bronchiolitis without focal signs or persistent high fever; both increase harm without altering outcomes in this clinical picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

She meets discharge criteria: SpO2 at or above 92% in air sustained for at least 30 minutes, mild work of breathing, feeding above 50% of baseline, no apnoeas, reliable carer and access to review; an action plan with red-flag advice and short-interval GP review is standard practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Routine nasogastric feeding is reserved for infants taking under 50% of usual oral intake or in respiratory distress that precludes safe oral feeding, neither of which applies here. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

High-flow nasal cannula is an escalation therapy for infants with persistent hypoxia or severe work of breathing despite low-flow oxygen, not a pre-discharge screening test for a stable, normoxic infant. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Nebulised hypertonic saline and trial salbutamol are not recommended in routine bronchiolitis management in infants under 12 months and do not change the disposition decision in a stable child meeting discharge criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance supports watchful waiting in non-Aboriginal children over 6 months with uncomplicated, non-severe acute otitis media. Analgesia alone and review at 48 hours is the first step; antibiotics are reserved for at-risk groups, bilateral disease under 2 years, perforation with discharge, severe systemic illness, or failure to improve. Immediate amoxicillin would be appropriate in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children given the high rate of complicated otitis. Choosing parenteral antibiotics or ENT review is overreach in this clinical picture.
key_points: Watchful waiting with analgesia and 48-hour review for uncomplicated AOM in non-Aboriginal children over 6 months
Antibiotics from outset: under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander child, perforation with discharge, severe illness, or bilateral disease under 2 years
First-line antibiotic: amoxicillin; amoxicillin-clavulanate if non-response or recent amoxicillin
Tympanocentesis or parenteral antibiotics only if complicated (mastoiditis, sepsis, intracranial involvement)
explanation.pearls: In a non-Aboriginal, fully immunised, well-looking child over 6 months with first-episode unilateral AOM, regular paracetamol plus ibuprofen and 48-hour review beats amoxicillin from the door - antibiotics in this group reduce pain by less than a day and the number needed to treat is high.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media

options.rationale: In a previously well, fully immunised non-Aboriginal child over 6 months with uncomplicated acute otitis media, watchful waiting with analgesia and 48-hour review is the preferred initial approach reserving antibiotics for failure to improve. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media

options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is second-line if there has been recent amoxicillin or non-response, and grommet referral is for recurrent or persistent disease, not a first uncomplicated episode in a previously well child. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media

options.rationale: Immediate antibiotics are reserved for under-6-months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children, bilateral disease under 2 years, perforation with discharge, or systemic illness; none apply to this otherwise well child meeting watchful-waiting criteria. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media

options.rationale: Routine tympanocentesis and same-day ENT review are not indicated in uncomplicated first-episode acute otitis media; analgesia and 48-hour reassessment guide management at primary care level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media

options.rationale: He has no features of meningitis, sepsis or mastoiditis: a well child with a bulging tympanic membrane and low-grade fever does not require parenteral antibiotics, blood cultures or lumbar puncture. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute otitis media)

explanation.summary: Paediatric asthma discharge requires SpO2 above 94% in air, salbutamol stretched to at least 3-hourly with sustained effect, minimal work of breathing and tolerating oral intake. Discharge is paired with oral steroid completion, ongoing preventer, a written action plan and short-interval GP review. Admission, IV magnesium and montelukast are reserved for ongoing severity or unresolved features, not as routine. Over-prolonged ED stays add cost without clinical gain.
key_points: Discharge criteria: SpO2 above 94% air, salbutamol every 3 to 4 hours sustained, no recession, oral intake tolerated
Prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for total 3 days in exacerbations needing systemic steroid
IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes is for severe or life-threatening attacks failing first-line therapy
Asthma action plan and GP review within 48 to 72 hours are mandatory on discharge
explanation.pearls: Stretching salbutamol to 3-hourly with no recession and SpO2 above 94% in air is the practical gate for safe discharge; do not wait for 6-hourly intervals or order IV magnesium for a child who is clinically improved.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook

options.rationale: A salbutamol interval of 3 to 4 hours sustained with stable observations is the accepted discharge threshold; insisting on a 6-hourly interval before discharge is more conservative than guidelines and prolongs ED length of stay without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

Routine addition of montelukast is not recommended for an acute exacerbation; preventer step-up is determined at outpatient review, not driven by a single ED episode in a child already on appropriate preventer therapy. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook

options.rationale: Intravenous magnesium is for severe or life-threatening exacerbations failing to respond to first-line therapy; this child has clinically improved and has no indication for magnesium or HDU admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

Sustained 3-hourly salbutamol with stable saturations and minimal work of breathing supports safe discharge; admission for routine overnight observation in this scenario is overuse of inpatient resources. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook

options.rationale: He meets discharge criteria: SpO2 above 94% in air, salbutamol stretched to at least 3-hourly with sustained response, no recession, and tolerating oral intake; a 3-day prednisolone course, written action plan and short-interval review complete the package. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook

explanation.summary: Simple febrile seizures last under 15 minutes, are generalised, and are not followed by focal neurology or recurrence within 24 hours. In a developmentally normal child older than 6 months with an identifiable febrile source and a normal examination, routine workup is not required. Counselling covers recurrence risk (about 30%), reassurance that simple febrile seizures do not cause brain injury or developmental harm, basic first-aid, and that antipyretics do not prevent recurrence. Maintenance anti-seizure medication after simple febrile seizures is not recommended.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure: under 15 minutes, generalised, not recurrent within 24 hours, normal neuro exam
Recurrence risk around 30%, higher with first event under 18 months or low fever threshold
Lumbar puncture if under 6 months, meningism, partially treated with antibiotics or persistent altered mental state
No role for maintenance anti-seizure medication or routine EEG/imaging after simple febrile seizure
explanation.pearls: Antipyretics provide comfort but do not reduce the risk of seizure recurrence; written parental advice on duration, recovery position, and when to call for help is the highest-yield intervention you offer at discharge.

options.rationale: Lumbar puncture after a simple febrile seizure is reserved for children under 6 months, those with persistent altered mental state, meningism, or who are partially treated with antibiotics; none of these apply here. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

Inpatient video EEG and admission are not warranted after a single simple febrile seizure; her clinical picture and family history do not raise concern for an underlying epilepsy syndrome requiring inpatient workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

She has a simple febrile seizure with a clear viral focus and a normal neurological examination; routine investigations and admission are not indicated and a structured parental education and safety-net discharge is correct. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

Maintenance anti-seizure medication after simple febrile seizures does not reduce future febrile or unprovoked seizures and carries significant adverse effects; it is not recommended for prevention after a first event. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

Routine neuroimaging and EEG are not indicated after a single simple febrile seizure in a developmentally normal child with a normal neurological examination and an obvious infective source. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

explanation.summary: Classic intussusception in an infant under 2 years presents with paroxysmal pain, vomiting (often bilious late), and redcurrant jelly stool; ultrasound shows a target or doughnut sign. Without peritonism, perforation or shock, management is resuscitation, decompression, intravenous antibiotic cover, and image-guided air enema reduction with surgical standby. Operative reduction is reserved for failed enema, peritonism, perforation, or shock. CT adds nothing in classic ileocolic disease and should be avoided.
key_points: Air enema reduction success rate approaches 80 to 90% in uncomplicated ileocolic intussusception
Absolute contraindications to enema: perforation, peritonism, shock; relative: persistent ileus, lead point identified
Bilious vomiting in an infant should always prompt urgent surgical assessment
Recurrence after air enema reduction occurs in around 10%, usually within 48 hours, and a second air enema is acceptable if no peritonism
explanation.pearls: Surgical standby during the air enema is non-negotiable: if perforation occurs during reduction or the enema fails, operative reduction must follow within minutes - book the radiologist and theatre in parallel, not sequentially.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Surgical - Paediatric abdominal emergencies

options.rationale: Watchful waiting risks bowel ischaemia and perforation; ultrasound-confirmed intussusception with classic clinical features warrants prompt air enema reduction rather than observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Confirmed ileocolic intussusception without perforation or peritonism is managed with resuscitation, decompression, intravenous antibiotic cover and image-guided air enema reduction performed with surgical standby in case of perforation or failed reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Primary operative reduction is reserved for failed enema reduction, peritonism, perforation or shock; he has none of these and a non-operative air enema is the first-line therapy with high success rates. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Ultrasound is the diagnostic modality of choice in paediatric intussusception with high sensitivity and specificity; routine CT adds ionising radiation without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Spontaneous reduction is unreliable and delays risk ischaemic complications; analgesia is appropriate but does not replace urgent air enema or surgical reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Sentinel injuries in a non-ambulant infant - bruising in patterned distributions, torn frenulum, scalp haematoma, burns - have a high specificity for inflicted injury. The RCH and statewide child protection pathways require admission for structured workup (CT brain, skeletal survey within 24 hours, dilated fundoscopy, coagulation screen) alongside specialist consultation and statutory notification. Mandatory reporting obligations apply to all Australian medical practitioners; you do not need certainty, only a reasonable suspicion. Failing to act risks fatal recurrence.
key_points: Bruising in a non-ambulant infant is highly suspicious for inflicted injury until proven otherwise
Recognised sentinel injuries: torn frenulum, ear bruising, patterned bruises, burns, scalp haematoma in non-ambulant infant
Workup: CT brain, skeletal survey at 0 and at 11 to 14 days, fundoscopy, coagulation, LFTs, amylase/lipase
Mandatory reporting in all Australian jurisdictions; reasonable suspicion is the threshold, not proof
explanation.pearls: Bruises in those who do not cruise are a red flag - in a non-ambulant infant, a single unexplained bruise warrants the full sentinel injury workup, and any combination as here mandates inpatient admission and statutory notification before discharge.

sources.label: AIFS: Mandatory reporting of child abuse and neglect

options.rationale: Multiple sentinel injuries in a non-ambulant infant (torn frenulum, patterned bruising, scalp haematoma, healing burn) mandate a structured non-accidental injury workup and statutory child protection notification under all Australian mandatory reporting frameworks. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

A normal CT brain does not exclude abusive injury or skeletal fractures; skeletal survey, fundoscopy and inpatient child protection team review are part of the recognised package of investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Community escalation alone is insufficient when sentinel injuries are present; the threshold for inpatient workup and statutory notification is met and cannot be delegated to outpatient services. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Discharge without statutory notification or imaging in a non-ambulant infant with multiple sentinel injuries breaches mandatory reporting obligations and risks repeat injury including life-threatening abusive head trauma. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Sentinel injuries in a non-ambulant infant require workup and notification regardless of how plausibly the history is rephrased; pre-judging plausibility before completing investigation and notification is unsafe practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae becomes the dominant pneumonia pathogen in school-aged children and adolescents and presents with a protracted dry cough, low-grade fever, bilateral interstitial changes on chest x-ray, and characteristically poor response to beta-lactam antibiotics. First-line treatment in Australia is oral azithromycin (10 mg/kg day 1, then 5 mg/kg daily for 4 days). Doxycycline is generally avoided under 8 years; intravenous therapy or admission are reserved for hypoxia, severe respiratory distress, dehydration, complications or failure of oral therapy.
key_points: Mycoplasma pneumoniae predominates in pneumonia from school-age onward
Classic features: prolonged dry cough, low-grade fever, bilateral interstitial infiltrates, classmate clustering
First-line: azithromycin 10 mg/kg day 1 then 5 mg/kg daily for 4 days (5-day total course)
Doxycycline reserved for over-8s; amoxicillin lacks Mycoplasma activity and should not be escalated for atypical pneumonia
explanation.pearls: If a school-aged child fails amoxicillin at 48 to 72 hours with bilateral interstitial changes and ongoing dry cough, switch to azithromycin first rather than escalating beta-lactam dose or jumping to intravenous therapy.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric

options.rationale: The clinical picture (prolonged dry cough, bilateral interstitial infiltrates, lack of response to amoxicillin in a school-aged child) fits Mycoplasma pneumoniae; oral azithromycin is recommended first-line atypical cover in Australian guidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric

options.rationale: Doxycycline is avoided under 8 years in Australia outside specific scenarios (and azithromycin is the standard atypical cover in this age group); dual therapy with amoxicillin is unnecessary when the picture clearly fits atypical pneumonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric

options.rationale: There is a coherent infective explanation with classmate clustering, atypical clinical pattern and a typical chest x-ray; advanced imaging is not indicated as the next investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

Amoxicillin lacks activity against Mycoplasma pneumoniae and dose escalation will not cover the most likely pathogen in this age and clinical pattern; escalating beta-lactam dosing is the wrong axis of change here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric

options.rationale: She is well-perfused, normoxic and tolerating oral fluids; she does not meet admission criteria and intravenous beta-lactam does not cover Mycoplasma pneumoniae. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

explanation.summary: Mild croup is defined by a barking cough with no stridor at rest and no respiratory distress (Westley score 0-2). The Australian standard of care is a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg with discharge home and clear written safety-netting advice. Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate or severe croup with stridor at rest or significant work of breathing. Humidified air is not evidence-based and corticosteroid should still be given even in mild disease.
key_points: Mild croup: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose plus discharge with safety net
Moderate or severe croup: add nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 and observe minimum 4 hours
Bacterial tracheitis: toxic child with high fever and copious purulent secretions, not classic croup
explanation.pearls: RCH uses dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose for mild croup; prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 2 days is an alternative when dexamethasone is unavailable, but dexamethasone has better evidence for reducing return visits.

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate to severe croup with stridor at rest or significant recession; using it in mild croup risks rebound and unnecessary admission for observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Mild croup with no stridor at rest is managed with a single dose of oral dexamethasone and discharge with safety netting, since corticosteroid shortens illness duration and reduces representations. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Inpatient nebulised budesonide every four hours is not standard for mild croup, where a single dose of oral dexamethasone with discharge is preferred and oxygen is not indicated given SpO2 99%. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Humidified air is not effective for croup and corticosteroid should still be given even for mild disease because it shortens duration and reduces representation. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Bacterial tracheitis is suggested by toxic appearance, high fever and copious purulent secretions, none of which are present here; routine antibiotics and IV steroid are not warranted. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a clinical diagnosis based on fever for at least 5 days plus four of five principal clinical criteria (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, oromucosal changes, extremity changes including desquamation, and cervical lymphadenopathy at least 1.5 cm). Treatment with a single IVIG dose 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from ~25% to under 5%. Echocardiography at diagnosis, at 2 weeks and at 6-8 weeks is standard.
key_points: IVIG 2 g/kg + high-dose aspirin within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk
Aspirin is not coronary-protective by itself; IVIG is the key intervention
Echocardiography at diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6-8 weeks
explanation.pearls: If IVIG-resistant fever persists at 36 hours after the first dose, a second dose of IVIG 2 g/kg is given; infliximab and corticosteroid are options in refractory cases per cardiology and rheumatology input.

options.rationale: Kawasaki disease meeting four of five principal clinical criteria with fever beyond 5 days mandates IVIG 2 g/kg single dose plus high-dose aspirin within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Aspirin alone does not reduce coronary aneurysm risk; IVIG plus aspirin must be commenced together within 10 days of fever onset for maximum cardioprotection. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Initial high-dose steroid is reserved for high-risk patients in some protocols (e.g., Kobayashi score) but is not standard first-line in Australia; IVIG plus aspirin remains the standard first dose. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Delay beyond 10 days of fever onset substantially increases the risk of coronary aneurysm; this is unsafe under-treatment of an established Kawasaki diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
The clinical picture is diagnostic for Kawasaki disease rather than bacterial sepsis or scarlet fever; antibiotics are not the answer and delay of IVIG is harmful. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management in Australia follows APEG/ISPAD guidance: assess for shock (rare), give a single 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline if not shocked, then replace assumed 5-7% deficit over 48 hours alongside maintenance. Insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour is started 1 hour after fluids commence; no insulin bolus. Bicarbonate is not used routinely. Dextrose is added once glucose approaches 14-15 mmol/L. Frequent neuro observations are essential to detect cerebral oedema.
key_points: Initial bolus: 10 mL/kg of 0.9% saline (20 mL/kg only if shocked)
Insulin: 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr starting 1 hour after fluids; no bolus
Bicarbonate not routine; monitor for cerebral oedema (headache, GCS drop)
explanation.pearls: Cerebral oedema features include headache, vomiting, GCS deterioration, bradycardia and hypertension; treat with 3% saline or mannitol immediately and reduce fluid rate.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA

options.rationale: Australian paediatric DKA protocols use a single 10 mL/kg bolus (no shock) and 48-hour deficit replacement at 5-7 percent to minimise cerebral oedema risk, with insulin infusion starting after fluid resuscitation. (Source: APEG/RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

Large rapid boluses (20 mL/kg) and an insulin bolus increase cerebral oedema risk in paediatric DKA and should be avoided unless the child is in true hypovolaemic shock. (Source: APEG/RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

Half-normal saline is not the appropriate initial fluid choice in paediatric DKA and skipping an initial bolus delays restoration of perfusion in a tachycardic, dry-mucous-membrane patient. (Source: APEG/RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)
Sodium bicarbonate is not routinely indicated in paediatric DKA and is associated with worsened outcomes including cerebral oedema and hypokalaemia. (Source: APEG/RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

Initial fluid should be 0.9 percent saline without dextrose; dextrose is added once glucose falls to ~14-15 mmol/L to allow continued insulin infusion to clear ketones. (Source: APEG/RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Phototherapy thresholds depend on gestational age, postnatal age in hours and risk factors for neurotoxicity, using nomograms such as those in RCH CPG or AAP. Late preterm infants (35-36 weeks) have lower thresholds than term infants because of greater bilirubin neurotoxicity risk. At 5 days postnatal age and 35 weeks gestation, TSB around 280 micromol/L meets the phototherapy threshold. Feeding optimisation is integral, as inadequate intake worsens jaundice via enterohepatic recirculation.
key_points: Phototherapy threshold = nomogram value at gestational + postnatal age
Late preterm thresholds are lower than term thresholds
Optimise feeding alongside phototherapy; stopping breastfeeding rarely needed
explanation.pearls: Acute bilirubin encephalopathy clinical features (lethargy, hypertonia, opisthotonos, high-pitched cry) mandate immediate exchange transfusion regardless of TSB value.

options.rationale: At 35-week gestation and day 5, a TSB of 280 micromol/L crosses the phototherapy line on the age- and gestation-adjusted nomogram, requiring phototherapy plus feeding optimisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin well above the exchange line or for acute bilirubin encephalopathy; this value sits at the phototherapy line, not exchange. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

TSB at the phototherapy threshold in a late preterm infant warrants active treatment rather than watchful waiting; physiological labelling does not negate the need for phototherapy at threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Cessation of breastfeeding is not first-line; feeding support to optimise breastfeeding is preferred while phototherapy is delivered, since stopping breastfeeding has its own harms. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

IVIG is for confirmed isoimmune haemolytic disease (e.g., DCT positive Rh or ABO incompatibility) where bilirubin rises rapidly despite phototherapy; not indicated here with negative DCT. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline 1:1000 into the mid-anterolateral thigh as first-line therapy; doses are 0.1 mL (10 kg or less), 0.15 mL (10-20 kg, EpiPen Jr), 0.3 mL (20-50 kg, EpiPen) and 0.5 mL (over 50 kg). Repeat every 5 minutes if symptoms persist. Concurrent oxygen, supine positioning with legs elevated, and IV fluid resuscitation are essential. Salbutamol, antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only.
key_points: First-line: IM adrenaline 1:1000 mid-anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 min
Doses by weight: 10 kg = 0.1 mL; 20 kg = 0.15 mL; over 20 kg = 0.3 mL; over 50 kg = 0.5 mL
Adjuncts (steroid, antihistamine, salbutamol) never replace adrenaline
explanation.pearls: Refractory anaphylaxis after 2-3 IM doses warrants IV adrenaline infusion under cardiac monitoring with anaesthetic/ED senior input; biphasic reactions occur in up to 20% and warrant observation.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: At 6 years of age and 24 kg, the appropriate adrenaline dose has moved from the 150 mcg auto-injector to 300 mcg IM (1:1000 0.3 mL); repeating the junior dose underdoses. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: For a school-age child of 24 kg the standard IM adrenaline dose is 300 mcg (0.3 mL of 1:1000) into mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if needed; positioning and oxygen are concurrent. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis under continuous cardiac monitoring after multiple IM doses have failed; it is not the next step here. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Adrenaline is the first-line therapy in anaphylaxis; salbutamol and hydrocortisone are adjuncts but never primary, and delaying adrenaline worsens outcomes. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway compromise or shock in anaphylaxis; adrenaline is the only first-line drug. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: Chronic anterior uveitis is the most important extra-articular complication of JIA. The highest risk is in young (under 7), ANA-positive, oligoarticular JIA - up to 30 percent develop uveitis within the first 4 years. Screening frequency is determined by age at diagnosis, subtype and ANA status. For high-risk children, 3-monthly slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist is recommended for the first 4 years, then 6-monthly, then annually. Uveitis is typically asymptomatic; early detection prevents synechiae, cataract, glaucoma and visual loss.
key_points: Highest uveitis risk: ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA in girls under 7
3-monthly slit-lamp for first 4 years in high-risk category
Symptoms are absent until complications develop; screen don't wait
explanation.pearls: First-line uveitis treatment is topical steroid and mydriatic; refractory cases require methotrexate or adalimumab via paediatric rheumatology coordination with ophthalmology.

options.rationale: Annual screening is insufficient frequency for high-risk patients (ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA in young girls); chronic anterior uveitis is typically asymptomatic until visual loss has occurred. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

HLA-B27 is associated with acute symptomatic uveitis (enthesitis-related arthritis) but the highest absolute risk of chronic asymptomatic uveitis is in ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)
Orthopaedic review may be appropriate for monitoring leg-length discrepancy from chronic knee inflammation but does not address the high uveitis risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA in girls under 7 carries the highest risk of chronic asymptomatic anterior uveitis; 3-monthly slit-lamp screening is standard during the first years after diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

Chronic anterior uveitis in oligoarticular JIA is characteristically asymptomatic; waiting for symptoms allows synechiae, cataract, glaucoma and visual loss to occur. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: Acute paediatric immune thrombocytopenia is a clinical diagnosis after viral illness with isolated thrombocytopenia and otherwise normal blood film. Treatment is guided by bleeding severity, NOT platelet count. Asymptomatic children without major bleeding are managed by observation with safety advice (avoid contact sport, NSAIDs, anticoagulants); most resolve spontaneously within 3 months. IVIG, anti-D, or prednisolone are reserved for major bleeding or planned procedures. Bone marrow examination is needed only when atypical features raise concern for malignancy.
key_points: Treat the bleeding, not the platelet count; observation if asymptomatic
Bone marrow only if atypical features (anaemia, abnormal WCC, lymphadenopathy, organomegaly)
Most acute paediatric ITP resolves within 3 months
explanation.pearls: Intracranial haemorrhage in paediatric ITP is very rare (<1%) even at very low platelet counts; head trauma, NSAIDs and anticoagulants are the main avoidable precipitants.

options.rationale: IVIG is reserved for major bleeding or planned surgery; platelet count alone (even below 20) is not an indication for pharmacological treatment in paediatric ITP. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

Prednisolone is used for major bleeding or where treatment is required; it is not first-line for an asymptomatic well child with no bleeding even at platelet counts below 20. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

Bone marrow examination is required only if atypical features (lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, abnormal blood film, abnormal red or white cell lines), none of which are present. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)
Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for severe bleeding or refractory ITP; it is over-treatment of a well child without bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

Asymptomatic paediatric ITP without major bleeding is managed by observation; platelet count alone is not an indication for pharmacological therapy, and most acute cases resolve spontaneously within 3 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

explanation.summary: Hand foot and mouth disease (HFMD) is caused most commonly by coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71 (EV71 implicated in more severe and rare neurological complications). Clinical features are fever, painful oral ulcers (anywhere in the mouth, often anterior), and a vesicular rash on hands, feet and sometimes buttocks. Management is supportive with adequate analgesia and oral fluid encouragement. Children should be excluded from childcare until vesicles have crusted (usually 7-10 days). Adequate hand hygiene reduces household transmission.
key_points: Triad: fever + oral ulcers + peripheral vesicles (hands and feet)
Coxsackievirus A16 most common; EV71 occasionally causes severe disease
Supportive care only; exclude from childcare until vesicles crust
explanation.pearls: Watch for atypical EV71 disease (myocarditis, brainstem encephalitis, neurogenic pulmonary oedema) - red flags include high persistent fever, hyperhydrosis, myoclonus and listlessness.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

options.rationale: Primary HSV stomatitis typically causes larger painful gingivostomatitis with peri-oral involvement; absence of peripheral hand and foot vesicles makes HSV unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

options.rationale: Varicella has a typical centripetal vesicular truncal rash with lesions at multiple stages and posterior pharynx ulcers; peripheral hand and foot distribution with sparing of the trunk is not consistent with varicella. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

options.rationale: Hand foot and mouth disease is a clinical diagnosis based on oral ulcers plus peripheral hand and foot vesicles in a well child; management is supportive with childcare exclusion until vesicles crust. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

options.rationale: Herpangina is limited to the soft palate, uvula and tonsillar pillars without peripheral vesicles; this patient has peripheral hand and foot vesicles consistent with hand foot and mouth disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

options.rationale: Stevens-Johnson syndrome presents with multiple mucosal involvement plus target lesions and skin denudation in a systemically unwell child, none of which are present here; this child is well. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

explanation.summary: The RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis CPG uses standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen as the first-line respiratory support, titrated to maintain SpO2 at least 90%. HFNC is reserved for low-flow failure (persistent SpO2 below 90% or no improvement after at least 2 hours). Salbutamol, corticosteroids, routine antibiotics, and chest X-ray are not part of routine bronchiolitis care.
key_points: RCH first-line: low-flow nasal prong O2 to SpO2 at least 90%
HFNC after documented low-flow failure
No routine salbutamol, corticosteroids, antibiotics, or chest X-ray
Nasogastric feeds support hydration in moderate disease
explanation.pearls: The 92% SpO2 target is a NICE figure; RCH explicitly uses 90%.

options.rationale: The RCH Bronchiolitis CPG advises against routine salbutamol and corticosteroids in bronchiolitis as neither alters disease course. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

The RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis CPG specifies standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen as the first-line respiratory support, titrated to SpO2 at least 90%, with HFNC reserved for low-flow failure (SpO2 persistently below 90% or no improvement after at least 2 hours). Nasogastric feeds at two-thirds maintenance support hydration. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Empirical antibiotics and routine chest X-rays are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis as bacterial co-infection is uncommon and imaging does not change management. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Intubation is reserved for failure of escalating non-invasive support; the RCH ladder progresses through low-flow oxygen, then HFNC if low-flow fails, with PICU input before intubation. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Reduced feeding, increased work of breathing, and need for respiratory support meet RCH admission criteria; home management is unsafe. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Moderate paediatric asthma exacerbation in a child aged 6 years is treated with salbutamol pMDI plus spacer 6 puffs every 20 minutes for the first hour (three doses) together with oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg. Reassessment after the third dose guides whether to stretch to 1-2 hourly salbutamol or escalate to ipratropium add-on, IV magnesium, or IV salbutamol. Spacer delivery is preferred over nebuliser in conscious cooperative children because it is at least as effective with fewer side effects. Disposition decision occurs after sustained 4 hours on stretched intervals.
key_points: Salbutamol pMDI plus spacer 6 puffs (age 6+) every 20 minutes x 3 plus oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg
Ipratropium 4-8 puffs added if moderate-severe and inadequate response to salbutamol
IV magnesium 50 mg/kg reserved for severe/life-threatening not responding to inhaled therapy
explanation.pearls: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days is standard; a single dose of dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg is an alternative for milder cases or anticipated poor adherence.

options.rationale: Ipratropium is an adjunct, not monotherapy; salbutamol is the first-line bronchodilator in acute paediatric asthma with ipratropium added in moderate to severe disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)

IV magnesium is reserved for severe or life-threatening asthma not responding to inhaled bronchodilators and oral corticosteroid; it is not first-line for moderate exacerbation. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)

Moderate paediatric asthma is treated with salbutamol pMDI plus spacer (4-12 puffs by age) every 20 minutes for the first hour plus oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg, then stretch the salbutamol interval. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)

Up-titrating the preventer and discharging from a moderate exacerbation in ED is inappropriate; acute treatment with salbutamol bursts and supervised reassessment is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)
Speech in short phrases and SpO2 93% does not meet life-threatening asthma criteria; first-line is escalating inhaled bronchodilator and oral corticosteroid. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)

explanation.summary: A simple febrile seizure is defined as a generalised tonic-clonic seizure under 15 minutes duration, single in 24 hours, in a child aged 6 months to 5 years, with no focal features and no postictal neurological deficit. The child requires no investigations beyond clinical assessment if well-appearing and fully immunised. Management is reassurance, antipyretic for comfort, written first-aid advice (lay safely on the side, time the seizure, call ambulance if over 5 minutes), and safety netting for atypical features. Lifetime risk of epilepsy after a simple febrile seizure is only slightly above population baseline.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure: under 15 min, generalised, single in 24 hours, age 6 months to 5 years
No EEG, no neuroimaging, no lumbar puncture routinely required if well
Recurrence approximately 30%; epilepsy risk only marginally above baseline
explanation.pearls: Buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg may be prescribed for parental administration if seizures recur and exceed 5 minutes; routine daily antiepileptic prophylaxis is not recommended.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology: Seizures in children

options.rationale: A simple febrile seizure (under 15 minutes, generalised, single in 24 hours) in a well-appearing child aged 6 months to 5 years requires no investigations and is managed with reassurance, antipyretic for comfort and safety-net advice. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)
Routine lumbar puncture is not indicated for a simple febrile seizure in a well, fully immunised child without meningism; empirical antibiotics are not warranted. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)
EEG and neurology referral are not indicated after a simple febrile seizure as recurrence and epilepsy risk are not affected by EEG findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)
Neuroimaging is not indicated after a simple febrile seizure with normal neurological examination; it carries unjustified radiation and sedation risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)
Continuous antiepileptic prophylaxis is not recommended for simple febrile seizures; risks outweigh modest reduction in recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in children under 2 years carries a higher risk of complications and slower spontaneous resolution. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days as first-line, with watchful waiting reserved for children aged 2 years or older with mild unilateral disease. Analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen is critical for symptom control. Treatment failure at 48-72 hours triggers escalation to amoxicillin-clavulanate to cover beta-lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae.
key_points: Amoxicillin 15 mg/kg TDS for 5 days is first-line under 2 years
Watchful waiting only if 2 years or older and mild unilateral disease
Escalate to amoxicillin-clavulanate at 48-72 hours if failing
explanation.pearls: In Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children with high rates of chronic suppurative otitis media, treatment thresholds and durations differ and ENT outreach review is standard.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is reserved for children 2 years or older with mild unilateral disease; under 2 years, antibiotic treatment is recommended given higher complication risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media

options.rationale: Cefaclor is not first-line for acute otitis media in Australia; amoxicillin has narrower-spectrum cover and is the recommended first-line agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media

options.rationale: Surgical referral is not first-line for a single episode of acute otitis media; antibiotic plus analgesia is the standard initial approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media

options.rationale: Australian guidelines recommend oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days as first-line for acute otitis media in children under 2 years given higher complication risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media

options.rationale: Topical ciprofloxacin is for chronic suppurative otitis media with perforation or grommets; intact tympanic membrane and systemic disease require oral therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Otitis Media

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of mortality in paediatric DKA and is recognised clinically by headache, vomiting, falling GCS, focal neurology, age-inappropriate incontinence, and Cushing's response (bradycardia plus hypertension). Treatment is immediate hypertonic saline 3% at 2.5-5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg over 20 minutes, reduction of maintenance fluid rate by one-third, head-of-bed elevation to 30 degrees, and transfer to the intensive care unit. Imaging is performed only after osmotherapy has been given and the patient is stabilised, never as the first step.
key_points: Cushing's response (bradycardia, hypertension) plus falling GCS is suspected cerebral oedema
Treat first: 3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg, reduce fluids by one-third
Imaging only after osmotic therapy and stabilisation
explanation.pearls: Risk factors for cerebral oedema include younger age, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis at presentation, low corrected sodium, and high urea; bicarbonate use also raises risk and is reserved for cardiovascular instability.

options.rationale: Increasing insulin will worsen rapid osmolar shifts and cerebral oedema; imaging is never the first step when cerebral oedema is clinically suspected. (Source: ISPAD/APEG: Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

Aggressive crystalloid bolus is contraindicated when cerebral oedema is suspected as it worsens cerebral fluid shifts; treatment is osmotic therapy and reducing fluid rate. (Source: ISPAD/APEG: Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

Routine hyperventilation is harmful in DKA cerebral oedema; intubation is reserved for failed osmotherapy and airway compromise, and uses normocapnia not hypocapnia. (Source: ISPAD/APEG: Paediatric DKA Guidelines)
The clinical pattern (headache, falling GCS, bradycardia, hypertension, vomiting) is Cushing's response indicating cerebral oedema; delay is dangerous. (Source: ISPAD/APEG: Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

Suspected cerebral oedema is treated with osmotic therapy (3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg), reduced fluid rate by one-third, head-of-bed elevation, and ICU transfer. (Source: ISPAD/APEG: Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

explanation.summary: A femur fracture in a non-mobile infant (under approximately 9 months) is highly concerning for non-accidental injury, particularly with a changing or implausible history. Mandatory reporting to the statutory child protection service is required on suspicion in every Australian jurisdiction, and notification is not delayed pending investigations. Safety admission allows skeletal survey within 24 hours, ophthalmology review for retinal haemorrhages if intracranial concerns, social work and paediatric forensic input. Imaging including head CT or MRI is added based on clinical features.
key_points: Femur fracture in a non-mobile infant is a non-accidental injury until proven otherwise
Mandatory child protection notification is on suspicion, not on confirmation
Safety admission allows skeletal survey, retinal exam if indicated, social work
explanation.pearls: Other concerning fracture patterns in young infants include posterior rib fractures, metaphyseal corner fractures, and any fracture in a non-mobile child without a clear major-force mechanism.

options.rationale: Outpatient discharge of an infant with a femur fracture and inconsistent history is unsafe; mandatory reporting and safety admission are required while assessment is completed. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

A non-mobile infant with a femur fracture and a changing history meets criteria for mandatory child protection notification and inpatient safety admission with skeletal survey. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)
Child protection notification is not delayed pending imaging; it is mandatory on suspicion and runs in parallel with investigations. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)
Allowing discharge against safety concerns is unsafe and contravenes mandatory reporting obligations once child abuse is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)
A femur fracture in a non-mobile infant is a classic non-accidental injury pattern; accepting the carer's history at face value misses an at-risk presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Septic arthritis of the hip in a child is a surgical emergency. The Kocher criteria (fever above 38.5, refusal to weight-bear, ESR over 40, white cell count over 12) predict over 99% probability when all four are met. Management is blood cultures, urgent operative arthrotomy or arthroscopic washout with synovial fluid sampling, and empirical IV flucloxacillin to cover Staphylococcus aureus. Ceftriaxone or vancomycin add-on is reserved for specific risk factors. Delaying drainage risks femoral head osteonecrosis and irreversible joint damage.
key_points: Kocher criteria 4/4 gives over 99% probability of septic arthritis
Surgical washout plus IV flucloxacillin is standard initial therapy
MRI must not delay drainage of a clinically septic hip
explanation.pearls: In children under 4 years Kingella kingae is an important pathogen; add cefazolin if Kingella suspected (low-grade fever, mildly elevated inflammatory markers, negative gram stain).

options.rationale: The Kocher criteria (fever above 38.5, non-weight-bearing, ESR over 40, WCC over 12) are all met giving over 99% probability of septic arthritis; oral analgesia alone is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

MRI must not delay drainage in suspected septic arthritis; oral antibiotics are inadequate empiric cover for a hip joint with high clinical probability of infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

Septic arthritis of the hip is a surgical emergency requiring operative drainage and empirical IV flucloxacillin after cultures to cover Staphylococcus aureus, the dominant pathogen. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

Antibiotics without joint drainage do not effectively clear septic arthritis; surgical washout is mandatory and routine MRSA cover is not required without local risk factors. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)
Delaying surgical washout of a septic hip risks femoral head necrosis; operative drainage is the time-critical intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis is managed with admission for IV hydration at 1.5 times maintenance, multimodal analgesia (paracetamol, NSAID if no contraindication, parenteral opioid by PCA if severe), warm packs, and active screening for acute chest syndrome (the leading cause of mortality) with serial respiratory observation, oximetry and chest examination. Hydroxycarbamide is continued. Transfusion is reserved for specific complications such as acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic sequestration or aplastic crisis, and exchange transfusion for severe complications. Antibiotics are added if any features of infection or fever above 38.5.
key_points: IV fluids at 1.5x maintenance plus multimodal analgesia including parenteral opioid
Active screening for acute chest syndrome is essential
Transfusion is for ACS, stroke, sequestration or aplastic crisis, not routine VOC
explanation.pearls: Avoid pethidine due to seizure risk from norpethidine accumulation; use morphine or oxycodone for severe pain in paediatric sickle cell disease.

sources.label: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines

options.rationale: Vaso-occlusive crisis is managed with hydration at 1.5x maintenance, multimodal analgesia including parenteral opioid by PCA, and active monitoring for acute chest syndrome which is the leading cause of mortality. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines)
source_refs: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines

options.rationale: Discharge without IV hydration and parenteral analgesia is inappropriate for severe sickle cell crisis with pain score 8 and poor oral intake; hospital admission is required. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines)
source_refs: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines

options.rationale: Transfusion is not routine for uncomplicated vaso-occlusive crisis; it is reserved for acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis or symptomatic severe anaemia. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines)
source_refs: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are reserved for sickle cell disease patients with fever, signs of infection or acute chest syndrome; pain crisis alone without fever does not mandate antibiotics. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines)
source_refs: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines

options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe complications such as acute chest syndrome with hypoxia, stroke, or multi-organ failure; uncomplicated vaso-occlusive crisis does not warrant it. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines)
source_refs: HSANZ Paediatric Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines

explanation.summary: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic SBDS mutations characterised by exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, bone marrow dysfunction (most commonly neutropenia with risk of progression to aplastic anaemia and myelodysplastic syndrome/AML), and skeletal abnormalities (metaphyseal dysostosis). After two normal sweat chlorides this triad strongly points away from cystic fibrosis. Diagnosis is by SBDS gene testing. Management involves pancreatic enzyme replacement, fat-soluble vitamin supplementation, dietitian-led calorie support, regular FBE to monitor cytopenias, and bone marrow surveillance with haematology input.
key_points: Triad: pancreatic insufficiency + cytopenia (often neutropenia) + skeletal dysostosis
Sweat chloride normal rules out CF as cause of pancreatic insufficiency
SBDS gene testing confirms diagnosis; haem surveillance for MDS/AML risk
explanation.pearls: Approximately 20% of Shwachman-Diamond patients develop MDS or AML by adulthood, so lifelong haematology surveillance with annual bone marrow assessment is recommended in symptomatic disease.

options.rationale: Persistent neutropenia 0.4 with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and negative sweat chlorides is not cystic fibrosis; the syndrome to consider is Shwachman-Diamond. (Source: RCH CPG: Failure to Thrive)
Empirical GCSF and transplant workup precede confirmatory genetics; pancreatic enzymes are oral not IV; this plan misorders investigation and management. (Source: RCH CPG: Failure to Thrive)
Normal IgA and negative coeliac serology with profound neutropenia points away from coeliac disease; duodenal biopsy does not explain the bone marrow finding. (Source: RCH CPG: Failure to Thrive)

The triad of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, neutropenia and growth failure with normal sweat chlorides is Shwachman-Diamond syndrome; SBDS gene testing confirms diagnosis and skeletal survey screens for metaphyseal dysostosis. (Source: GHO Australian Paediatric Genetics)
Faecal elastase 78 with neutrophils 0.4 cannot be attributed to functional toddler diarrhoea; a unifying organic diagnosis must be pursued. (Source: RCH CPG: Failure to Thrive)

explanation.summary: The RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis CPG uses standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen as the first-line respiratory support, titrated to maintain SpO2 at least 90%. HFNC is reserved for low-flow failure (persistent SpO2 below 90% or no improvement after at least 2 hours). Salbutamol, adrenaline, and corticosteroids are not routinely used.
key_points: RCH first-line respiratory support: low-flow nasal prong oxygen
Target SpO2 at least 90% (not the NICE 92%)
HFNC reserved for documented low-flow failure
No routine salbutamol, adrenaline or corticosteroids in bronchiolitis
explanation.pearls: Brief desaturations below 90% alone are not an indication to start supplemental oxygen per the RCH CPG.

options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis CPG specifies standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen as the first-line respiratory support, titrated to maintain SpO2 at least 90%, with HFNC reserved for low-flow failure (persistent SpO2 below 90% or no respiratory improvement after at least 2 hours). (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)
