Would be correct only after a documented failure of low-flow oxygen (persistent SpO2 below 90% or no improvement after at least 2 hours); the 92 to 96% target is also a NICE figure rather than the RCH 90% target. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)
The RCH CPG advises against routine salbutamol in bronchiolitis as it does not alter disease course. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Nebulised adrenaline is not part of routine bronchiolitis care per the RCH CPG; it is used for severe croup, not bronchiolitis. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Intubation is reserved for failure of escalating non-invasive support; the RCH ladder is low-flow first, then HFNC if low-flow fails, with PICU input before intubation. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation in preschoolers with a palpable faecal mass requires disimpaction before maintenance therapy will work. Oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes is first-line in Australian pathways. Maintenance follows with a lower macrogol dose plus behavioural toileting and fibre. Red flags for organic disease include delayed meconium beyond 48 hours, ribbon stools, failure to thrive, abnormal lumbosacral examination and abnormal anal tone.
key_points: Disimpaction precedes maintenance in retained faecal mass
Macrogol 3350 with electrolytes oral disimpaction is first-line
Behavioural toileting and fibre are essential maintenance adjuncts, not stand-alone disimpaction
explanation.pearls: Macrogol disimpaction in a 4-year-old typically starts at 4 sachets daily and escalates by 2 sachets per day to a maximum around 8 sachets, continued until a clear watery stool.

options.rationale: Enemas and rectal interventions are distressing in preschoolers and are second-line after oral macrogol failure; they can also cause hyperphosphataemia in small children. (Source: NICE NG99)

Lactulose is an acceptable maintenance osmotic agent if macrogol is not tolerated, but is less effective than macrogol for disimpaction and would not clear a palpable faecal mass. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes is first-line disimpaction in Australian and NICE paediatric constipation pathways; doses are escalated daily until a clear watery stool is produced. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Lifestyle measures are essential adjuncts and form the maintenance backbone, but cannot disimpact a palpable retained faecal mass and will fail without pharmacological clearance first. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Suction rectal biopsy for Hirschsprung disease is indicated when red flags are present such as delayed meconium, failure to thrive or abnormal anal tone, none of which apply here. (Source: NICE NG99)

explanation.summary: Per the RCH croup guideline, dexamethasone dosing is graded to severity: 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild-to-moderate disease (stridor at rest with mild-to-moderate recession, alert and well perfused), and 0.6 mg/kg (maximum 12 mg) for severe or life-threatening disease (marked recession, agitation, exhaustion, hypoxia, or altered consciousness). Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup at a flat dose of 5 mL of 1:1000, with a minimum 3-hour observation afterwards because effects last 30 to 60 minutes. After dexamethasone alone, observation is tied to clinical resolution of stridor at rest rather than a fixed 4-hour clock.
key_points: Mild-to-moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally per RCH
Severe or life-threatening croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000
Nebulised adrenaline observation is 3 hours post-dose per RCH
After dexamethasone alone, observe to clinical resolution (peak effect 1-2 hours)
explanation.pearls: Per-kg adrenaline dosing (0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000) is the older AAP formulation; RCH uses a flat 5 mL of 1:1000 dose regardless of weight for severe or life-threatening croup.

options.rationale: Moderate croup (stridor at rest with moderate recession, alert, drinking, pink) is treated per RCH with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; the 0.6 mg/kg dose and nebulised adrenaline are reserved for severe or life-threatening disease. Observation is tied to clinical resolution rather than a fixed clock; peak dexamethasone effect is 1-2 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Intramuscular dexamethasone is reserved for vomiting or oral intolerance; the 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup, not moderate disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Nebulised budesonide is reserved for children who cannot tolerate oral dexamethasone; oral dexamethasone is preferred for cost, efficacy, and ease of dosing. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

The 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone dose plus nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup (marked recession, agitation, exhaustion, or hypoxia); this child is alert, drinking, and pink after being upset, which is moderate disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Intubation is reserved for impending respiratory failure with exhaustion, cyanosis, or altered consciousness; moderate croup almost always responds to oral dexamethasone alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: HSP is the most common childhood vasculitis with classic palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain and renal involvement. Admission criteria include severe abdominal pain, vomiting, GI bleeding, scrotal involvement, marked joint pain limiting mobility, or renal complications (hypertension, significant proteinuria, AKI). Ileo-ileal intussusception is the feared GI complication, evaluated with ultrasound. Most renal disease is mild and managed with 6 months of urinalysis and BP surveillance.
key_points: Admission triggers in HSP: severe abdominal pain, vomiting, GI bleed, scrotal involvement, renal flags
Ileo-ileal intussusception is the HSP-specific GI complication, evaluated with ultrasound
Renal monitoring: weekly urinalysis and BP for 6 months from onset
explanation.pearls: HSP intussusception is typically ileo-ileal rather than ileo-colic, which is why air enema reduction is less successful and ultrasound is the diagnostic modality of choice.

options.rationale: Crampy abdominal pain with vomiting and positive faecal occult blood in HSP raises concern for intussusception or ischaemic bowel and warrants inpatient observation rather than community follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)

CT exposes a child to substantial ionising radiation and is not first-line for suspected HSP-associated intussusception; ultrasound is the preferred initial imaging modality in paediatric abdominal pain. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)
Steroids can reduce abdominal pain duration but should not be initiated in the community in a child with vomiting and occult blood until intussusception has been excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)

Urine dipstick blood of 1+ without proteinuria, hypertension or renal impairment does not meet criteria for urgent nephrology referral; renal involvement is monitored with weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for 6 months. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)

Significant abdominal pain with vomiting and occult blood is an indication for admission in HSP; ultrasound is the imaging of choice to assess for ileo-ileal intussusception, which is the typical HSP-associated pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)

explanation.summary: Around 10 to 20% of Kawasaki disease is IVIG-resistant, defined as persistent or recrudescent fever at least 36 hours after the IVIG infusion ends. First re-treatment is a second IVIG 2 g/kg in Australian protocols. If still resistant, options are IV methylprednisolone pulse or infliximab, chosen with cardiology guidance and based on coronary risk. Aspirin remains high-dose anti-inflammatory until 48 to 72 hours afebrile, then reduced to antiplatelet dosing. Repeat echocardiogram at 2 weeks and 6 to 8 weeks regardless.
key_points: IVIG resistance: persistent or recrudescent fever 36 hours after first IVIG
Second IVIG 2 g/kg is standard first re-treatment in Australian practice
Pulse methylprednisolone or infliximab follows if second IVIG fails
explanation.pearls: Kobayashi score predicts IVIG resistance in Japanese cohorts; western validation is weaker, so the AHA pathway still uses clinical fever response 36 hours post-IVIG as the primary trigger for re-treatment.

options.rationale: Refractory Kawasaki disease is defined as persistent or recrudescent fever 36 hours after the first IVIG; current Australian and AHA practice is a second IVIG 2 g/kg as the first re-treatment step, with cardiology supervision. (Source: AHA Scientific Statement: Kawasaki 2017)

IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy is reserved for IVIG-resistant disease that has already failed a second IVIG, or for very high-risk patients at initial diagnosis under specialist guidance. (Source: AHA Scientific Statement: Kawasaki 2017)
Infliximab is a third-line option for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki after a second IVIG has failed; using it now would skip the recommended re-treatment sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki)
Aspirin dose is reduced to antiplatelet dosing (3 to 5 mg/kg) after 48 to 72 hours afebrile, not while the child is still febrile and inflamed. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki)

Empirical antibiotics for cervical lymphadenopathy are inappropriate when blood culture is negative, the clinical picture meets Kawasaki criteria and IVIG has already produced a partial CRP fall. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperbilirubinaemia in a term newborn with positive DAT signals ABO or Rh haemolytic disease. Australian neonatal thresholds for exchange transfusion in term babies with haemolysis are around 400 micromol/L at 48 hours, lower than for non-haemolytic jaundice. Adjuncts include IVIG and ensuring adequate hydration, but when the bilirubin exceeds the exchange threshold the double-volume exchange is non-negotiable to prevent kernicterus. Acute neurological signs (lethargy, hypotonia, poor feeding, opisthotonus, retrocollis, high-pitched cry) lower the exchange threshold further.
key_points: DAT-positive haemolytic disease has lower exchange thresholds than non-haemolytic jaundice
Exchange transfusion is indicated when bilirubin exceeds the haemolysis-specific threshold despite intensive phototherapy
Acute bilirubin encephalopathy signs are an immediate exchange indication regardless of level
explanation.pearls: In Australian neonatal jaundice charts the exchange transfusion threshold for haemolytic disease at 48 hours in a term baby is around 400 micromol/L; for non-haemolytic disease it is around 450 micromol/L.

options.rationale: Continuing phototherapy alone is inappropriate when bilirubin has continued to rise on intensive phototherapy and now sits above the exchange transfusion threshold for haemolytic disease; delay risks kernicterus. (Source: RWH Neonatal Jaundice)

IVIG is an adjunct in haemolytic disease when bilirubin rises despite intensive phototherapy, but is given alongside preparation for exchange when bilirubin exceeds the exchange threshold, not as a stand-alone substitute. (Source: RWH Neonatal Jaundice)

A bilirubin of 460 micromol/L at 48 hours in a term infant with DAT-positive ABO haemolytic disease exceeds the Australian exchange threshold of around 400 micromol/L for haemolytic disease and mandates double-volume exchange transfusion. (Source: RWH Neonatal Jaundice)

Breastfeeding cessation is not indicated when ongoing haemolysis is the driver; effective hydration is important but does not substitute for exchange transfusion in severe haemolytic disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Phenobarbital has a slow onset over days and is not used in acute severe hyperbilirubinaemia; it has historical use in some conjugation disorders but no role in DAT-positive haemolytic disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: The RCH Melbourne CPG states most children do not require further imaging after a first UTI once an acute renal tract ultrasound is normal. DMSA at 4 to 6 months is a NICE NG224 recommendation and is not part of the RCH cascade. MCUG is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal ultrasound.
key_points: RCH Melbourne: no routine further imaging after first typical UTI with normal ultrasound
DMSA is a NICE construct not part of the RCH cascade
MCUG reserved for atypical infection or abnormal ultrasound
Counsel parents on prompt presentation for any future fever
explanation.pearls: An atypical UTI per RCH includes non-E. coli organism, septicaemia, raised creatinine, poor urine flow, abdominal mass, or failure to respond within 48 hours.

options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne CPG states most children do not require further imaging after a first UTI once an acute renal tract ultrasound is normal and the child has responded to appropriate antibiotics. DMSA at 4 to 6 months is a NICE NG224 construct that the RCH CPG has not adopted. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

MCUG is invasive and is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal renal tract ultrasound; it is not part of the RCH first-line investigation after a typical first UTI. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

MR urography is reserved for selected complex anomalies and is not part of the RCH post-UTI pathway after a typical first febrile UTI with normal ultrasound. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Would be correct only when following NICE NG224 rather than the local RCH Melbourne pathway; the RCH CPG does not include routine DMSA after a typical first UTI with normal ultrasound. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Long-term prophylaxis is reserved for proven high-grade reflux or recurrent UTI and is not indicated after a single typical UTI with normal ultrasound. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: The 2022 Concussion in Sport Group consensus and AIS guidance for under-19 athletes use a 6-stage graded return-to-sport protocol with at least 24 hours per stage, beginning with symptom-limited activity after 24 to 48 hours of relative rest. A symptom-free interval of at least 14 days off medication is required before full contact in adolescents. Recurrence within 12 months prompts a more conservative pace and specialist follow-up. CT head is reserved for red flags rather than routine return-to-play assessment.
key_points: Under-19s: 6-stage graded return with at least 24 hours per stage
Minimum 14-day symptom-free interval before full contact in adolescents
CT head is reserved for red flags, not for routine return-to-play clearance
explanation.pearls: AIS guidance mandates that an adolescent who sustains a second concussion within 12 months should not return to contact sport for at least 4 weeks symptom-free, longer than the typical 14-day adolescent minimum.

options.rationale: Adolescents require at least a 24- to 48-hour rest period of relative cognitive and physical rest at Stage 1 before initiating graded return-to-play steps. (Source: AIS Concussion in Sport)

A second concussion within 12 months requires careful staged return and longer symptom-free interval, but a single recurrence does not mandate retirement; that decision follows multiple or persistent post-concussion syndrome. (Source: AIS Concussion in Sport)
Prolonged complete rest delays recovery; current evidence supports relative rest for 24 to 48 hours then gradual symptom-limited activity progression. (Source: Concussion in Sport Group 2022)

CT head is indicated in concussion only when red flags such as focal deficit, repeated vomiting, prolonged GCS depression, seizure or skull fracture risk are present; routine CT is not part of return-to-play assessment. (Source: AIS Concussion in Sport)

Current Australian Institute of Sport and Concussion in Sport Group guidance for under-19 athletes is a stepwise return with at least 24 hours per stage and a minimum 14-day symptom-free interval before full contact. (Source: AIS Concussion in Sport)

explanation.summary: Bilateral acute otitis media in a child under 2 years is an indication for antibiotic therapy in Australian guidelines. Amoxicillin 15 mg/kg up to 500 mg twice daily for 5 days is first-line. Watchful waiting suits children over 2 years with unilateral AOM and mild illness. Macrolides and oral cephalosporins are reserved for penicillin allergy.
key_points: Amoxicillin 15 mg/kg BD for 5 days is the AU first-line for AOM requiring antibiotics
Bilateral AOM under 2 years is an indication for antibiotics rather than observation
Macrolides are reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy due to pneumococcal resistance
explanation.pearls: Watchful waiting applies to children over 2 years with unilateral non-severe AOM; bilateral disease, age under 2, otorrhoea, or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander identity shifts the decision to antibiotics.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting suits children over 2 years with unilateral AOM and mild illness; bilateral AOM in a child under 2 has a higher bacterial yield and antibiotics are recommended. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

Macrolides are not first-line in AOM in Australia because of pneumococcal macrolide resistance; they are reserved for confirmed non-severe penicillin allergy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

High-dose three-times-daily amoxicillin for 10 days reflects older North American protocols; Australian guidelines use 15 mg/kg BD for 5 days and reserve longer courses for treatment failure. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend amoxicillin 15 mg/kg up to 500 mg orally twice daily for 5 days for AOM requiring antibiotics, which includes bilateral AOM under 2 years. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

Cefaclor has inferior pharmacokinetics against pneumococcus compared with amoxicillin and is reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy when amoxicillin cannot be used. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

explanation.summary: Pertussis is treated with azithromycin if started within 21 days of cough onset, primarily to reduce onward transmission. Australian guidelines target post-exposure prophylaxis to high-risk contacts: third-trimester pregnant women, infants under 6 months, and household contacts of these vulnerable people. Amoxicillin is ineffective; macrolides are first-line.
key_points: Azithromycin treats pertussis within 21 days of cough onset and reduces transmission
Prophylaxis is targeted to third-trimester pregnant contacts and infants under 6 months
Amoxicillin and beta-lactams have no role in pertussis
explanation.pearls: The pregnant mother is herself eligible for pertussis vaccination in pregnancy (20-32 weeks) and the 6-week-old cousin is the most vulnerable contact; both require attention beyond chemoprophylaxis.

options.rationale: Australian post-exposure prophylaxis is targeted to high-risk contacts (third-trimester pregnancy, infants under 6 months, household contacts of these vulnerable people) rather than the entire household. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)

Pertussis treatment within 21 days of cough onset shortens infectivity and is still warranted at 3 weeks; transmission to vulnerable contacts in the household remains a concern. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Pertussis)

Amoxicillin is not active against Bordetella pertussis; the first-line agent for treatment and prophylaxis is azithromycin (or clarithromycin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole if macrolide intolerant). (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Pertussis)

Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend azithromycin for confirmed pertussis within 21 days of cough onset, and post-exposure prophylaxis with azithromycin for high-risk contacts including pregnant women in the third trimester and infants under 6 months. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Pertussis)
NAAT is the confirmatory test and serology is no longer recommended in this clinical context; treatment and contact tracing should not be delayed. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)

explanation.summary: Microcytic anaemia with very low ferritin and transferrin saturation in a toddler with excess cow's milk intake is iron deficiency anaemia from a dietary cause. Oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day with reduction of cow's milk to under 500 mL/day is first-line. FBC is repeated at 2 to 4 weeks; ongoing iron is continued for 3 months after Hb normalises to replenish stores.
key_points: Elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day orally is first-line in paediatric iron deficiency
Cow's milk above 500 mL/day in toddlers is a major risk factor and must be reduced
Continue oral iron for 3 months after Hb normalises to replenish ferritin stores
explanation.pearls: A reticulocyte rise at day 7 to 10 and a 10 to 20 g/L rise in Hb at 4 weeks confirms response; failure prompts adherence check, dose review, malabsorption work-up, then IV iron.

options.rationale: The microcytic, hypochromic picture with very low ferritin and saturation is diagnostic of iron deficiency; bone marrow biopsy is not warranted before a trial of oral iron with reassessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

Australian paediatric guidance for iron deficiency anaemia is elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day orally, and reducing cow's milk to under 500 mL/day removes the dietary driver. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)
Ferritin 6 microgram/L confirms iron deficiency; electrophoresis is reserved for atypical patterns or persistent microcytosis after iron repletion. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)
IV iron in toddlers is reserved for failure or intolerance of oral therapy or malabsorption; a trial of oral iron with dietary counselling is the first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)
The MCV is low rather than high, making B12 or folate deficiency unlikely; the iron studies confirm iron deficiency as the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Disimpaction precedes maintenance, and the usual Australian first step is an escalating oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes regimen over three to seven days. Persisting soiling with a palpable mass after a full regimen taken correctly means the impaction has not cleared, and the recognised escalation is to add an oral stimulant laxative, typically senna or bisacodyl, while continuing the osmotic agent. Only if that also fails are rectal measures or admission for nasogastric bowel preparation considered, and each of those steps is far less acceptable to a child and family. Two checks come first: confirm the dose was genuinely escalated to the maximum and genuinely taken, since palatability and volume defeat many regimens, and confirm there are no red flags for organic disease. In context, functional constipation accounts for the overwhelming majority of childhood constipation, and the common reason treatment fails is under-dosing rather than a missed diagnosis.
key_points: Escalating oral macrogol is first-line disimpaction in Australian practice.
A stimulant laxative is added to the osmotic agent when disimpaction fails.
Rectal measures and admission come after oral escalation, not before.
Abdominal radiography does not diagnose or monitor functional constipation.
explanation.pearls: Before escalating, ask how many sachets were actually swallowed each day; a regimen that was prescribed to the maximum dose and drunk at half of it is an under-treated child, not a treatment failure.

options.rationale: When a full escalating macrogol regimen has not cleared the impaction, the next step is to add an oral stimulant laxative such as senna or bisacodyl while continuing the osmotic agent, before any rectal or inpatient measure is considered. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Constipation)
Lactulose is a weaker osmotic alternative used when macrogol is not tolerated or is unavailable, not an escalation after macrogol has failed. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

Abdominal imaging is not used to diagnose or monitor functional constipation, which is a clinical diagnosis; it is reserved for suspected obstruction. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Constipation)
Rectal measures are a last resort after oral options have been exhausted, and phosphate enemas carry a risk of electrolyte disturbance in small children. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

A toilet sitting routine is part of every management plan, but reducing the dose while a mass is still palpable guarantees continued overflow soiling. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura with macroscopic haematuria, hypertension and nephrotic-range proteinuria represents severe nephritis. Australian practice is admission for blood pressure control, serial renal function and urinalysis, and early paediatric nephrology consultation. Children with isolated rash and arthralgia, normal BP and bland urine can be managed as outpatients with weekly urinalysis for 6 months.
key_points: BP above the 95th centile with red-cell casts in HSP warrants admission
Steroids treat pain and arthritis but do not prevent or modify HSP nephritis
All HSP children need 6 months of urinalysis and BP monitoring to detect late nephritis
explanation.pearls: Renal biopsy is considered when nephrotic-range proteinuria persists beyond 4 weeks or creatinine rises; ACE inhibitor therapy is started for persistent proteinuria above 100 mg/mmol creatinine ratio.

options.rationale: Hypertension and nephritic-nephrotic urinary findings exceed simple HSP and mandate admission; outpatient management is reserved for isolated rash with normal BP and urinalysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura)

Macroscopic haematuria with hypertension and nephrotic-range proteinuria in HSP signals significant nephritis requiring inpatient monitoring, antihypertensive therapy, and early nephrology input. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura)

Steroids may help abdominal pain or arthritis but do not prevent or treat established nephritis; severe nephritis requires admission, BP control, and nephrology input. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura)
Intussusception screening is reasonable with severe abdominal pain in HSP but does not address the dominant problem of nephritis with hypertension. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura)

The rash, joint involvement, abdominal pain and timing make HSP nephritis the unifying diagnosis; broad-spectrum antibiotics are not indicated in the absence of sepsis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura)

explanation.summary: New onset type 1 diabetes without ketoacidosis is managed with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin, oral hydration and structured inpatient education in Australian paediatric practice. DKA criteria require venous pH under 7.30 or bicarbonate under 18 mmol/L plus ketonaemia. Intravenous insulin and DKA protocols are reserved for those meeting these biochemical criteria or who cannot tolerate oral intake. Cerebral oedema risk increases with aggressive fluid resuscitation in mildly ill children, making the distinction important.
key_points: DKA requires pH under 7.30 OR bicarbonate under 18 mmol/L AND ketones 3 mmol/L or higher
Subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin is first-line for new T1DM without DKA
Metformin has no role in initial type 1 diabetes management
explanation.pearls: Typical starting total daily dose is 0.5 to 0.75 unit/kg/day split as 50% basal, 50% bolus with carbohydrate-counting and correction doses titrated to BSL targets.

options.rationale: Normal venous pH, bicarbonate above 18 mmol/L and beta-hydroxybutyrate under 3 mmol/L exclude DKA; new T1DM without ketoacidosis is managed with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin, oral hydration and structured education. (Source: APEG/ADS New Onset T1DM)
Insulin infusion is reserved for DKA or unable to tolerate oral intake; in mild hyperglycaemia without acidosis it adds risk of hypoglycaemia without benefit. (Source: APEG/ADS New Onset T1DM)
She does not meet DKA criteria; aggressive resuscitation in well-perfused euglycaemic-ketosis risks cerebral oedema and is not warranted. (Source: APEG/ADS DKA)
Metformin is not first-line for type 1 diabetes; insulin is required from diagnosis. New T1DM mandates inpatient education and insulin initiation. (Source: APEG/ADS New Onset T1DM)
Insulin should not be delayed in new T1DM; without insulin ketosis will worsen and DKA may develop overnight. (Source: APEG/ADS New Onset T1DM)

explanation.summary: After a second febrile UTI in a child under 3 years, the RCH Melbourne CPG recommends a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound and paediatric specialist referral. DMSA at 4 to 6 months is a NICE NG224 recommendation and is not part of the RCH algorithm. MCUG is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal renal tract ultrasound.
key_points: RCH Melbourne recurrent-UTI imaging: non-urgent renal tract ultrasound and specialist referral
DMSA is a NICE construct not adopted by RCH
MCUG reserved for atypical infection or abnormal ultrasound
Prophylaxis only for proven high-grade reflux or frequent recurrence
explanation.pearls: The RCH bottom-up strategy of ultrasound plus clinical follow-up reduces invasive imaging without missing significant uropathy.

sources.label: NICE NG: Urinary tract infection in under 16s

options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne pathway reserves prophylaxis for proven high-grade reflux or frequent recurrence and does not defer imaging review in recurrent UTI. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

MCUG is invasive and is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal renal tract ultrasound; it is not the RCH first step after a second uncomplicated febrile UTI. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

The RCH Melbourne CPG recommends a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound for recurrent UTI together with paediatric specialist referral; DMSA is part of the NICE NG224 algorithm and is not part of the RCH cascade. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
CT delivers significant ionising radiation and has no routine role in screening children for scarring or reflux. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Would be correct only when following NICE NG224 rather than the local RCH Melbourne pathway; the RCH CPG does not include routine DMSA in the recurrent UTI cascade. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: A neonate with central cyanosis that fails to rise above 85% in 100% oxygen, single second heart sound and narrow mediastinum on CXR has duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease until proven otherwise. Intravenous prostaglandin E1 at 10 to 50 nanogram/kg/min is started immediately to maintain ductal patency while awaiting paediatric cardiac retrieval. Apnoea, hypotension and fever are recognised side effects requiring monitoring.
key_points: Hyperoxia test failure (SpO2 under 85% in 100% O2) suggests cyanotic congenital heart disease
Prostaglandin E1 10 nanogram/kg/min maintains ductal patency and is started before imaging
Apnoea is a key adverse effect; have intubation ready when starting prostaglandin
explanation.pearls: Pre and post-ductal saturations equal at 78% with the single S2 fits transposition of the great arteries with intact septum; the patient depends on shunting at atrial and ductal level until balloon atrial septostomy or arterial switch surgery.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Failure of SpO2 to rise above 85% in 100% oxygen with single S2 and narrow mediastinum suggests duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease (transposition with intact septum being a key consideration); prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency and is life-saving while awaiting retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Oxygen alone is insufficient in duct-dependent lesions and may further close the ductus; treatment should not await imaging when failure of hyperoxia is documented. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Without ductal patency, dopamine will not raise systemic oxygenation; high FiO2 may accelerate ductal closure and worsen cyanosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Heart rate 168 in a neonate is appropriate for distress and not SVT; adenosine has no role in cyanotic congenital heart disease without arrhythmia. (Source: ANZCOR Neonatal Resuscitation)

Sepsis is in the differential but the hyperoxia test result and cardiac signs point to duct-dependent cardiac lesion; delaying prostaglandin while awaiting cultures risks ductal closure and circulatory collapse. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: Watchful waiting with safety-net analgesia is supported in children over 2 years with unilateral non-severe AOM in Australian guidelines. Immediate antibiotics are reserved for children under 2 with bilateral disease, otorrhoea, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children, or systemic toxicity. Amoxicillin-clavulanate and cephalosporins have specific second-line indications.
key_points: Children over 2 years with unilateral non-severe AOM can be safely observed for 48 hours
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for AOM treatment failure or recurrent disease
Single-dose IM ceftriaxone is reserved for those unable to tolerate oral antibiotics
explanation.pearls: The most reliable AOM antibiotic indications in Australia are bilateral disease under 2 years, otorrhoea at any age, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander identity and systemic toxicity.

options.rationale: Australian guidelines support watchful waiting in children over 2 years with unilateral non-severe acute otitis media; antibiotics are added if not improving at 48 hours or worsening. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

Immediate antibiotics are indicated for bilateral AOM under 2 years, otorrhoea, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children, severe illness or systemic toxicity; this child meets none of those criteria. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure after 48-72 hours of amoxicillin or for recurrent AOM, not for initial therapy of straightforward unilateral disease. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

Oral cephalosporins are reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy and are not first-line in AOM; their pneumococcal pharmacokinetics are inferior to amoxicillin. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

Single-dose IM ceftriaxone is reserved for children vomiting all oral antibiotics or with non-severe penicillin allergy when oral options are inappropriate; it is not first-line in well children. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute otitis media)

explanation.summary: Hand foot and mouth disease is a self-limiting enteroviral illness with oral ulcers and acral vesicles. Management is analgesia, hydration and day care exclusion until all vesicles have dried. Topical lidocaine should be avoided in young children due to seizure and methaemoglobinaemia risk. Antibiotics, antivirals and antifungals are not indicated.
key_points: Hand foot mouth disease is supportive only with analgesia and hydration
Day care exclusion is required until all vesicles have dried per NCIRS
Topical lidocaine is unsafe in young children for oral ulcer pain
explanation.pearls: Watch for dehydration as the main complication; admit if a child cannot maintain oral intake or develops neurological signs suggesting rare enteroviral encephalitis.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease
NCIRS: Enteroviruses and hand, foot and mouth disease

options.rationale: Aciclovir has no role in enteroviral hand foot and mouth disease; it is reserved for herpes simplex stomatitis which typically causes ulcers on the anterior tongue and gingiva without acral vesicles. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease

options.rationale: Hand foot and mouth disease is self-limiting; management is analgesia and hydration, with day care exclusion until all vesicles have dried as per NCIRS recommendations. (Source: NCIRS: Enteroviruses and hand, foot and mouth disease)
source_refs: NCIRS: Enteroviruses and hand, foot and mouth disease

options.rationale: Bacterial pharyngitis would not produce vesicles on the hands and feet; antibiotics are not indicated for the enteroviral exanthem. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease

options.rationale: Topical lidocaine carries a risk of seizures and methaemoglobinaemia in young children and is not recommended in this age group for HFM. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease

options.rationale: Oral candida produces white plaques rather than ulcers and acral vesicles; nystatin is not indicated in the enteroviral exanthem. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease

explanation.summary: Febrile UTI in infants under 6 months is managed with admission for empirical IV gentamicin and a beta-lactam in Australia, given the risk of bacteraemia and pyelonephritis. Oral therapy alone, single-dose IM ceftriaxone, and outpatient discharge are inappropriate at this age. Renal tract imaging is arranged after acute treatment.
key_points: Infants under 6 months with febrile UTI need admission for IV antibiotics
Empirical regimen is IV gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin
Outpatient oral therapy is inappropriate due to bacteraemia risk at this age
explanation.pearls: After first febrile UTI in any child under 6 months, arrange renal tract ultrasound; consider DMSA at 4-6 months and MCUG only if there is high recurrence or imaging abnormality.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: Urinary tract infection in children

options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with febrile UTI require initial parenteral therapy due to the risk of bacteraemia and pyelonephritis; oral therapy alone is inappropriate at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
Outpatient oral therapy is not appropriate for febrile UTI under 6 months; admission for IV antibiotics is required while culture and sensitivities return. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Febrile UTI in infants under 6 months requires admission for empirical IV gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin per Australian paediatric guidance; transition to oral therapy follows clinical improvement and sensitivities. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Urinary tract infection in children)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: Urinary tract infection in children

options.rationale: Single-dose IM ceftriaxone with outpatient follow-up is not the standard Australian approach in young infants and risks under-treatment of bacteraemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Discharge on oral amoxicillin alone is unsafe in a young infant with febrile UTI; renal tract imaging is appropriate after acute treatment but is not the initial step. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Simple febrile seizures are brief generalised tonic-clonic events in well children aged 6 months to 5 years and carry a benign prognosis. Management is reassurance, antipyretics for comfort and written first-aid advice. Lumbar puncture is reserved for suspected meningitis. Daily anti-seizure medication and routine EEG are not indicated.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure is brief, generalised, single in 24 hours, in a well child
Antipyretics improve comfort but do not prevent febrile seizure recurrence
LP, EEG and daily anticonvulsants are not routinely indicated
explanation.pearls: Buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg is reserved for children with previous febrile status epilepticus or known epilepsy, not after a first simple febrile seizure.

sources.label: NSW Health: Febrile convulsions in children

options.rationale: LP is no longer recommended on age alone in a well, alert, fully vaccinated child with a simple febrile seizure; it is reserved for signs of meningitis or atypical features. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

Daily anti-seizure medication is not recommended for simple febrile seizures; the benign natural history and the side effects of valproate outweigh any small reduction in recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

EEG is not routinely indicated for a simple febrile seizure; it does not predict recurrence or epilepsy and is reserved for atypical or complex features. (Source: NSW Health: Febrile convulsions in children)
source_refs: NSW Health: Febrile convulsions in children

options.rationale: Simple febrile seizures are benign with a low risk of epilepsy; management is reassurance, antipyretics for comfort (which do not prevent recurrence) and written seizure first-aid advice. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)
Rescue benzodiazepines are reserved for children with prolonged or recurrent complex febrile seizures, not after a single simple febrile seizure of 2 minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis refractory to 2 doses of IM adrenaline is managed with an IV adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to response, in addition to continued fluid resuscitation and airway support. Corticosteroids, antihistamines and nebulised adrenaline are adjuncts rather than primary therapy. Adult dosing and further IM doses are not recommended in refractory paediatric shock.
key_points: IV adrenaline infusion is indicated when anaphylaxis fails to respond to 2 IM doses
Starting rate is 0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to clinical response in monitored settings
Fluid resuscitation continues alongside vasoactive escalation
explanation.pearls: Always seek airway expertise early in refractory anaphylaxis; angioedema can progress rapidly and a small calibre paediatric airway is at risk during ongoing resuscitation.

sources.label: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: ASCIA recommends that anaphylaxis failing to improve after 2 IM adrenaline doses is escalated to a controlled IV adrenaline infusion rather than further IM doses, due to absorption variability in shock. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Corticosteroids and antihistamines are second-line adjuncts and do not reverse airway compromise or shock; they are not the immediate priority in refractory anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is an adjunct for upper airway oedema but does not address systemic hypotension; an IV adrenaline infusion is preferred when refractory shock coexists. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)

Adult-dose IM adrenaline is not weight-appropriate in a 20 kg child; further IM dosing is not the recommended escalation when 2 doses have failed. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: When anaphylaxis is refractory after 2 IM adrenaline doses, ASCIA recommends a controlled IV adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to response with ongoing fluid resuscitation. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with overflow soiling in a child without red flags is managed with outpatient disimpaction using high-dose macrogol with electrolytes over 3 days, followed by maintenance laxatives and behavioural measures. Inpatient lavage is reserved for outpatient failure. Surgical referral and routine imaging are not indicated when red flags are absent.
key_points: Disimpaction precedes maintenance therapy in functional constipation with overflow
High-dose macrogol with electrolytes over 3 days is the standard outpatient regimen
Red flag features prompt referral but routine imaging is not required
explanation.pearls: Educate that maintenance laxatives are continued for at least 6 months, with toileting routines after meals to use the gastrocolic reflex; weaning is gradual after several months of regular soft stools.

sources.label: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people

options.rationale: Functional constipation with overflow soiling and palpable faecal mass is managed with disimpaction followed by maintenance laxatives; high-dose macrogol with electrolytes outpatient over 3 days is first-line per RCH and NICE. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Hirschsprung disease is unlikely given timely meconium passage, appropriate growth and absence of red flags; surgical referral is not indicated as the initial step. (Source: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people)
source_refs: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people

options.rationale: Inpatient nasogastric PEG lavage is reserved for failure of outpatient disimpaction; an adequate disimpaction regimen has not yet been trialled. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Adding a stimulant without first disimpacting the rectal faecal mass will not relieve overflow soiling and risks ongoing cramping; disimpaction must precede maintenance therapy. (Source: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people)
source_refs: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people

options.rationale: Plain abdominal x-ray is not routinely required when faecal loading is clinically evident and adds radiation without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (West syndrome) presents with clusters of flexor spasms, developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia on EEG. Prompt first-line treatment with hormonal therapy (prednisolone or ACTH) or vigabatrin within days improves developmental outcome. Sodium valproate and phenobarbital are not first-line. Treatment is not delayed for MRI.
key_points: Clustered flexor spasms with developmental regression is the West syndrome triad
First-line therapy is prednisolone or ACTH; vigabatrin if tuberous sclerosis
Delay to treatment worsens neurodevelopmental outcome
explanation.pearls: Look for ash-leaf macules and other neurocutaneous stigmata; tuberous sclerosis with infantile spasms is preferentially treated with vigabatrin.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of Physicians: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome

options.rationale: Loss of developmental skills with clustered flexor spasms is highly suggestive of infantile epileptic spasms syndrome rather than benign myoclonus of infancy and requires urgent assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome requires urgent EEG looking for hypsarrhythmia and prompt first-line therapy with prednisolone or vigabatrin (vigabatrin if tuberous sclerosis); delayed treatment worsens developmental outcome. (Source: Royal Australian College of Physicians: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of Physicians: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome

options.rationale: Phenobarbital is not effective for infantile spasms; first-line therapy is hormonal (prednisolone or ACTH) or vigabatrin, with rapid review for response. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)
Treatment must not be delayed for MRI; commencing first-line therapy promptly while imaging is arranged optimises developmental outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

Sodium valproate is not first-line for infantile spasms; hormonal therapy and vigabatrin have higher response rates and faster resolution of hypsarrhythmia. (Source: Royal Australian College of Physicians: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of Physicians: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome

explanation.summary: Neonatal HSV with CNS or disseminated disease requires IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours for 21 days, with end-of-therapy repeat CSF PCR and ophthalmology review. Oral aciclovir is inadequate as initial therapy. Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates. After completion of IV therapy, suppressive oral aciclovir is given for 6 months.
key_points: Neonatal HSV CNS disease needs IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg q8h for 21 days
Oral aciclovir is inadequate as primary therapy for neonatal HSV
Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates due to bilirubin displacement
explanation.pearls: After IV therapy, neonates receive suppressive oral aciclovir 300 mg/m2 three times daily for 6 months to reduce neurodevelopmental morbidity and recurrent skin disease.

sources.label: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: Empirical bacterial cover does not treat HSV; in any neonate with CSF HSV PCR positive disease, IV aciclovir is mandatory and prolonged. (Source: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: Oral aciclovir has inadequate bioavailability and CNS penetration in neonatal HSV; IV therapy for 21 days is required for disseminated or CNS disease. (Source: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: Neonatal HSV with CNS or disseminated involvement is treated with IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours for 21 days, with ophthalmology assessment and a repeat CSF PCR at the end of therapy to confirm clearance. (Source: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates due to bilirubin displacement and calcium precipitation; HSV CNS disease additionally requires IV aciclovir. (Source: RCH CPG: Herpes simplex virus)
Ganciclovir is reserved for congenital CMV disease; it is not the agent for HSV-2 neonatal CNS infection where aciclovir is the standard. (Source: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in children under 12 months. Admission is indicated for SpO2 under 92 percent on room air, moderate or severe work of breathing, feeding under 50 percent of usual, dehydration, apnoeas or risk factors such as ex-prematurity. Treatment is supportive: oxygen to maintain SpO2 of at least 90 percent, small frequent feeds or NG hydration, and humidified high-flow if escalation is needed. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics and chest X-rays are not routine.
key_points: Admit if SpO2 under 92 percent or moderate-severe work of breathing or feeding under 50 percent of usual
Oxygen target is SpO2 of at least 90 percent, not higher, in stable bronchiolitis
No routine bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics or chest X-rays
explanation.pearls: Oxygen saturation target of at least 90 percent (not 92 percent) is the AU paediatric bronchiolitis admission threshold; aiming higher prolongs admission without outcome benefit.

options.rationale: AU guidance targets SpO2 of at least 90 percent (not 92 percent); the higher threshold prolongs admission without outcome benefit and misstates AU policy. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Bronchodilators and corticosteroids are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; supportive care is the mainstay. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Hypoxia, dehydration and moderate work of breathing meet admission criteria; discharge home is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Antibiotics and chest X-ray are not routinely indicated in straightforward viral bronchiolitis; supportive care is the mainstay. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

AU and RCH guidance for moderate bronchiolitis with hypoxia (SpO2 under 92 percent) and feeding difficulty is admission, oxygen to keep SpO2 of at least 90 percent, and feeding support; no routine antibiotics, bronchodilators or steroids. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Sentinel injuries (bruises in a non-mobile infant, frenal tears, posterior rib fractures) carry high specificity for inflicted injury and trigger inpatient comprehensive evaluation. Workup excludes mimics (coagulopathy, osteogenesis imperfecta, metabolic bone disease) and documents the pattern (skeletal survey under 2 years, neuroimaging, fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhage when intracranial findings or under 2 years). All Australian states mandate reporting suspected child abuse by medical practitioners. Child protection and social work involvement, multidisciplinary case management and safe disposition planning follow.
key_points: Bruising in a non-mobile infant is highly suspicious for inflicted injury until proven otherwise
Posterior rib fractures in infants have high specificity for inflicted injury
Mandatory reporting by medical practitioners applies in all Australian states and territories
explanation.pearls: TEN-4 FACES rule: bruises in non-mobile infants under 4 months, or torso, ear or neck bruises in infants under 4 years, are sentinel injuries warranting safeguarding workup until proven otherwise.

options.rationale: The combination of bruising in a non-mobile infant, frenal tear, sentinel posterior rib fracture and inconsistent history mandates inpatient evaluation, safeguarding referral and mandatory reporting. (Source: RCH CPG: suspected non-accidental injury; AIFS mandatory reporting)
Delayed outpatient review fails the safeguarding threshold; sentinel injuries demand same-day inpatient evaluation. (Source: RCH CPG: suspected non-accidental injury)
Posterior rib fractures in non-mobile infants carry a very high specificity for inflicted injury and require comprehensive workup with safeguarding. (Source: RCH CPG: suspected non-accidental injury)
Reliance on caregiver-reclarification in a sentinel-injury picture risks ongoing harm; mandatory reporting and inpatient workup are required. (Source: AIFS mandatory reporting)

Suspected non-accidental injury in a non-mobile infant requires inpatient comprehensive evaluation (skeletal survey, fundoscopy, neuroimaging, coagulation and bone profile to exclude mimics), child protection consultation and statutory mandatory reporting. (Source: RCH CPG: suspected non-accidental injury; AIFS mandatory reporting)

explanation.summary: Australian practice supports watchful waiting with analgesia for non-severe acute otitis media in children over 24 months who are systemically well. Antibiotics are reserved for children under 6 months, severe systemic illness, perforation with otorrhoea, bilateral disease in under 2-year-olds, or failure to improve at 48 hours. First-line if needed is amoxicillin; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or cefuroxime is used in true penicillin allergy. Recurrent acute otitis media (three episodes in 6 months or four in 12 months) prompts ENT referral for grommet assessment.
key_points: Watch and wait with analgesia suits non-severe acute otitis media in children over 24 months
Amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days is first-line when antibiotics are indicated
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, infants under 6 months, and severe illness skip the wait
explanation.pearls: Adequate paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 4 to 6 hours combined with ibuprofen 10 mg/kg every 6 to 8 hours controls otalgia in the first 48 hours better than antibiotics.

options.rationale: First-line antibiotics are reserved for under 6 months, severe systemic illness, perforation with discharge, bilateral disease in under 2-year-olds, or failure of watchful waiting at 48 hours. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: acute otitis media)
Macrolides are not first-line for acute otitis media in Australia; if antibiotics are indicated, amoxicillin is preferred. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: acute otitis media)
AU practice supports a watch and wait approach with adequate analgesia for non-severe acute otitis media in children over 24 months without high-risk features. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media)
Surgery is reserved for recurrent or chronic otitis media with effusion and hearing impact, not an uncomplicated first presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media)

Topical ear antibiotics treat otitis externa or chronic suppurative otitis media with perforation, not acute otitis media with an intact tympanic membrane. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: acute otitis media)

explanation.summary: The RCH Melbourne Croup CPG uses oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg) is reserved for severe or life-threatening disease where nebulised adrenaline is also given. Post-dexamethasone observation is tied to clinical resolution (stridor at rest settled, oral intake reliable) rather than a fixed time clock; the 3-hour observation rule applies after nebulised adrenaline only.
key_points: RCH dex dose: 0.15 mg/kg for mild/moderate; 0.6 mg/kg for severe/life-threatening only
Post-dex observation tied to clinical resolution, not a fixed 4-hour wait
3-hour rule applies after nebulised adrenaline only
Nebulised adrenaline reserved for severe or life-threatening croup
explanation.pearls: The dexamethasone peak effect is at 1 to 2 hours; reassess airway and feeding before discharge.

options.rationale: Bacterial tracheitis presents with high fever, toxicity and copious tracheal secretions; this child has a typical croup pattern and antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Croup)

Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup with persistent stridor at rest; this child has mild croup that settles when held. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Croup)

The RCH Melbourne Croup CPG uses oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup, reserving 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg) for severe or life-threatening disease. Post-dexamethasone observation is tied to clinical resolution rather than a fixed time clock; the 3-hour rule applies after nebulised adrenaline only. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Croup)
Humidification has not been shown to alter the course of croup; the RCH CPG recommends oral dexamethasone for all severities including mild. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Croup)

Airway instrumentation risks complete obstruction and is not indicated for typical viral croup; the RCH pathway uses oral dexamethasone alone for mild disease. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Acute asthma in school-aged children is graded mild, moderate, severe, or critical based on speech, work of breathing, oxygen saturation, and conscious state. Salbutamol via spacer is the cornerstone of bronchodilator delivery in children. Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days is added in moderate or greater exacerbations and reduces relapse. Severe disease may require ipratropium, intravenous magnesium sulfate, intravenous aminophylline, or intravenous salbutamol with paediatric intensive care input.
key_points: Salbutamol via spacer beats nebuliser for delivery and side effects in mild to moderate disease
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days suits moderate exacerbations from age 1 year
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes is reserved for severe disease
explanation.pearls: Spacer delivered salbutamol gives 6 puffs for a child under 6 years and 12 puffs for older children, repeated every 20 minutes for the first hour in moderate exacerbations.

sources.label: National Asthma Council: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Ipratropium is added to severe exacerbations in the first hour, not as the next single step in a moderate exacerbation with a partial salbutamol response. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)
Intravenous magnesium is reserved for severe asthma not responding to inhaled bronchodilators and oral steroids. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)
Preventer initiation is a planned outpatient decision; it does not treat the acute exacerbation. (Source: National Asthma Council: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Most paediatric asthma exacerbations are viral and antibiotics offer no benefit without focal pneumonia or signs of bacterial infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days is standard AU practice for acute asthma exacerbations of moderate or greater severity in children. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric guidance for a first febrile urinary tract infection in a child under 2 years uses renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks as the screening investigation, looking for hydronephrosis, posterior urethral valves, duplex systems, or other structural abnormality. MCUG and DMSA are second-line and reserved for atypical UTI (non-Escherichia coli organism, septic illness, failure to respond within 48 hours, or abnormal voiding) or an abnormal ultrasound. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis after a single uncomplicated UTI is no longer recommended in the absence of high-grade reflux or other anatomical risk.
key_points: Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks is first-line after a first febrile UTI in a child under 2 years
Atypical illness or abnormal ultrasound triggers MCUG or DMSA
Routine antibiotic prophylaxis after a single uncomplicated UTI is not supported by current evidence
explanation.pearls: An atypical UTI is one with seriously ill child, poor urine flow, abdominal mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, non-Escherichia coli organism, or failure to respond within 48 hours, and prompts additional imaging.

sources.label: NICE NG224: Urinary tract infection in under 16s

options.rationale: Routine MCUG is no longer recommended after a single uncomplicated UTI; it is selected for atypical illness or abnormal ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

AU practice for a first febrile UTI in a child under 2 years is a renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks, with MCUG or DMSA reserved for atypical features or abnormal ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
DMSA is reserved for recurrent or atypical UTI or abnormal ultrasound, not routine for a single uncomplicated infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
CT involves unnecessary radiation in young children and is not part of routine UTI follow up. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
Routine antibiotic prophylaxis without imaging is no longer recommended after a single uncomplicated febrile UTI. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation in preschool children commonly presents with infrequent hard stools, withholding behaviours, and overflow soiling. Australian and UK practice favours oral macrogol (polyethylene glycol) for both disimpaction and maintenance, starting with escalating doses for 3 to 7 days, then a single daily maintenance dose for several months and slow weaning. Toilet training with positive routines, soft stool maintenance, and parental education are central. Red flag features (delayed meconium, ribbon stools, perianal disease, abnormal neurology, failure to thrive) warrant gastroenterology review.
key_points: Oral macrogol disimpaction over 3 to 7 days then maintenance is first-line
Soiling between hard stools usually reflects overflow from impaction, not behaviour
Maintenance laxative is continued for months with slow weaning, not stopped at first improvement
explanation.pearls: Macrogol 3350 with electrolytes is dosed at 1 to 1.5 g/kg daily for disimpaction in divided doses and 0.4 to 0.8 g/kg daily for maintenance in preschool children.

options.rationale: Abdominal radiography correlates poorly with clinical faecal loading and adds radiation without changing management. (Source: NICE CG99: Constipation in children)
Rectal interventions are second-line for non-responders; oral macrogol disimpaction is preferred and acceptable to children. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

AU practice for functional constipation with faecal loading begins with oral macrogol disimpaction then transitions to a maintenance osmotic laxative for several months. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Hirschsprung disease typically presents with delayed meconium, failure to thrive, and an empty rectum; this presentation is functional. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Dietary advice alone is inadequate with established faecal loading and soiling; pharmacological disimpaction is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Eczema herpeticum is herpes simplex virus infection complicating atopic dermatitis, presenting with clustered monomorphic punched-out vesiculo-erosions, often with fever and lymphadenopathy. It is a dermatological emergency in children because of the risk of disseminated viral disease, bacterial superinfection, and keratoconjunctivitis. Intravenous aciclovir is started promptly while viral PCR confirms the diagnosis, with ophthalmology review for periocular disease. Bacterial superinfection is treated with appropriate antibiotics and topical steroids resume only once the viral infection is controlled.
key_points: Monomorphic punched-out erosions with fever in an eczematous child point to eczema herpeticum
Intravenous aciclovir, ophthalmology, and infectious diseases input are warranted for facial or severe disease
Topical steroids alone or wet wraps over active disease can worsen viral spread
explanation.pearls: Periocular eczema herpeticum requires same-day ophthalmology review because herpes simplex keratitis can cause permanent corneal scarring and vision loss.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: Eczema herpeticum is a dermatological emergency requiring intravenous aciclovir, with ophthalmology review if any periocular involvement to prevent corneal disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema herpeticum)
Potent topical steroids alone do not treat herpes simplex infection and may worsen disseminated viral disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Atopic eczema)
Impetigo gives honey crust but lacks the monomorphic punched-out vesicular erosions of eczema herpeticum and would not be treated alone. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: Wet wraps over active herpes simplex virus may spread infection and delay needed antiviral therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Atopic eczema)
Severe eczema herpeticum with systemic features or facial involvement warrants intravenous aciclovir not oral therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema herpeticum)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in early childhood is a common nutritional disorder in Australia, particularly in milk-drinking toddlers and those with restricted diets. Diagnostic criteria are microcytic hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin (below 12 micrograms/L) in the absence of inflammation. Treatment is oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg daily for 3 months with dietary modification to limit cow milk to under 500 mL daily and introduce iron-rich foods. Haemoglobin should rise by 10 g/L within 4 weeks; failure of response prompts evaluation for malabsorption, ongoing losses, or alternative diagnoses.
key_points: Ferritin under 12 micrograms/L without inflammation confirms iron deficiency in children
Oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg daily for 3 months is first-line in stable iron deficiency anaemia
Cow milk over 500 mL daily after 12 months impairs iron status and is a key target for dietary advice
explanation.pearls: Repeat haemoglobin at 4 weeks of oral iron should rise by at least 10 g/L; a flatter response prompts review for adherence, ongoing blood loss, or malabsorption such as coeliac disease.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: paediatric iron deficiency

options.rationale: Intravenous iron is reserved for malabsorption, intolerance of oral iron, or severe symptomatic anaemia not responding to oral therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)
Iron deficiency anaemia in toddlers is treated with oral iron with dietary advice to limit cow milk and increase iron-rich foods. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)
Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia with cardiovascular compromise; this child has stable haemodynamics. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)
Microcytosis with low ferritin in a milk-drinking toddler is iron deficiency until proven otherwise; further workup waits on therapeutic response. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)
Established anaemia with ferritin 8 micrograms/L will not respond to diet alone in clinically meaningful time. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease can be diagnosed when fewer than 4 of the principal clinical features are present alongside fever for at least 5 days, supported by laboratory criteria (elevated CRP/ESR, anaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, raised ALT, sterile pyuria, thrombocytosis after day 7) or coronary changes on echocardiography. Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and aspirin remains indicated even beyond day 10 when fever persists or coronary changes are evident. High-risk features (young age, low albumin, elevated CRP, hyponatraemia, coronary involvement) may prompt addition of corticosteroids or infliximab in tertiary centres. Echocardiography is repeated at 2 and 6 weeks.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed by laboratory criteria or coronary abnormalities supporting prolonged fever with under 4 principal features
IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin is the standard treatment, even after day 10 when inflammation or coronary changes persist
Adjunct steroids or infliximab apply to high-risk or refractory disease
explanation.pearls: A coronary artery z-score of 2.5 or greater on echocardiography is enough to confirm incomplete Kawasaki disease and mandate IVIG, regardless of how many classical criteria are met.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue
American Heart Association Kawasaki disease scientific statement

options.rationale: AU paediatric practice treats Kawasaki disease, including late-presenting and incomplete cases with coronary changes, with IVIG and antiplatelet aspirin to reduce coronary risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Steroids are an adjunct in primary refractory or high-risk disease, not the sole initial treatment in Australian practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome causes flaccid bullae and skin tenderness, not non-purulent conjunctivitis and coronary changes. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: TNF-alpha blockers are reserved for IVIG-refractory disease as second or third line therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Delayed treatment of Kawasaki disease beyond day 10 still benefits from IVIG when coronary or inflammatory markers persist. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is the commonest childhood vasculitis and presents with palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement. Long-term outcome is dominated by renal disease; about 1 in 3 children develop nephritis ranging from microscopic haematuria to nephrotic-nephritic syndrome. AU practice screens with serial urinalysis and urine protein:creatinine ratio for 6 months from onset, with paediatric nephrology referral for persistent proteinuria over 100 to 250 mg/mmol, hypertension, deteriorating function, or nephrotic features. Steroids reduce arthralgia and abdominal pain but their role in altering long-term renal outcome remains debated and they are reserved for selected cases by specialists.
key_points: Significant proteinuria (urine PCR over 250 mg/mmol) in HSP prompts nephrology review
Serial urinalysis and BP measurement are continued for 6 months from onset
Steroids are considered for severe abdominal pain or renal involvement rather than routinely
explanation.pearls: Renal biopsy is considered for HSP children with persistent nephrotic syndrome, deteriorating renal function, or persistent proteinuria over 100 mg/mmol beyond 4 to 6 weeks of conservative management.

options.rationale: Pulsed steroids and mycophenolate apply to crescentic nephritis after biopsy confirmation, not first-line outpatient escalation. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline)
Significant proteinuria is the dominant determinant of long-term renal outcome and requires specialist assessment, not routine general practitioner review. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)
HSP nephritis is immune complex disease, not infection; routine antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

Significant proteinuria with HSP (urine PCR over 250 mg/mmol) warrants nephrology referral and consideration of corticosteroid therapy with biopsy for nephrotic-range disease or persistent abnormality. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)
HSP nephritis is parenchymal glomerular disease; ultrasound has no role in screening for it in this setting. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the leading cause of infant hospital admission in Australia and is managed with supportive care including nasal suction, hydration, and supplemental oxygen. High-flow nasal cannula is used for moderate disease, with thresholds for escalation that include rising CO2, persistent hypoxia despite maximal HFNC, apnoea, or exhaustion. Continuous positive airway pressure or intubation are delivered in paediatric intensive care for failure to respond to HFNC. Bronchodilators, hypertonic saline, antibiotics, and corticosteroids are not recommended for routine bronchiolitis.
key_points: HFNC failure includes rising CO2, exhaustion, apnoea, or persistent hypoxia at maximum settings
CPAP and intubation are the next steps in paediatric intensive care
Bronchodilators and steroids are not effective in viral bronchiolitis under 12 months
explanation.pearls: An infant on maximal HFNC with rising CO2 above 60 mmHg, falling pH below 7.25, exhaustion, or recurrent apnoea needs ICU escalation rather than further HFNC titration.

options.rationale: Rising CO2, respiratory acidosis, exhaustion, and apnoea on maximal HFNC are indications for ICU escalation with CPAP or intubation in infant bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Hypertonic saline is not recommended for routine acute care in bronchiolitis and does not reverse impending respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Salbutamol and corticosteroids are not effective in viral bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Antibiotics are not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis without a focal consolidation or strong evidence of bacterial superinfection. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Continued observation in the face of rising CO2 and exhaustion delays definitive ventilatory support and risks decompensation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice approaching the exchange transfusion threshold in haemolytic disease is a neonatal emergency. Australian guidance recommends intensive phototherapy on multiple sides, intravenous immunoglobulin (1 g/kg) for confirmed haemolytic disease when bilirubin remains within 30 to 50 micromol/L of the exchange threshold or rises rapidly, adequate hydration including possible intravenous fluids, and exchange transfusion preparation. Exchange transfusion replaces the infant blood volume twice, removing bilirubin, antibody, and sensitised red cells. Long-term sequelae of acute bilirubin encephalopathy include athetoid cerebral palsy, hearing loss, and gaze abnormalities.
key_points: Intensive phototherapy, IVIG and exchange preparation are the response to bilirubin near threshold in haemolytic disease
DAT positive ABO or Rh incompatibility increases haemolytic load and the rate of bilirubin rise
Exchange transfusion thresholds depend on gestation, postnatal age, and risk factors
explanation.pearls: Intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg reduces the need for exchange transfusion in haemolytic disease of the newborn when bilirubin is within 30 to 50 micromol/L of the exchange threshold.

sources.label: NICE NG98: Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days

options.rationale: Single phototherapy is inadequate when bilirubin is within 30 micromol/L of the exchange threshold and rising rapidly with positive DAT. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)
Intensive phototherapy with IVIG often averts the need for exchange when bilirubin is within range of the exchange threshold and not yet exceeded. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)
Cessation of breastfeeding is not the management of an acutely rising haemolytic jaundice at threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Rising bilirubin near the exchange threshold with haemolytic disease is managed with intensive phototherapy, IVIG to reduce haemolysis, and exchange transfusion preparation. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)
Phenobarbital is not standard acute therapy for haemolytic neonatal jaundice in current Australian neonatal practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Paediatric parapneumonic effusion progresses through exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organising stages. Empyema (frank pus, positive culture, or pH less than 7.2) and septated effusion failing initial antibiotics are managed by broader spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes plus image-guided chest drainage with intrapleural fibrinolytic. Most children avoid surgical decortication; video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery is reserved for failure of medical and drain-based therapy. Antibiotics typically continue for at least 2 to 4 weeks total with oral step-down once clinically improving.
key_points: Septated effusion failing antibiotics requires drainage and broader spectrum cover
Intrapleural fibrinolytic via chest drain is the AU paediatric step before VATS
Total antibiotic duration is at least 2 to 4 weeks with oral step-down after clinical improvement
explanation.pearls: Intrapleural urokinase via chest drain twice daily for 3 days clears most paediatric septated parapneumonic effusions without recourse to VATS decortication.

sources.label: BTS Guideline: pleural infection in children

options.rationale: Simple diagnostic tap is inadequate to drain a 4 cm septated empyema and leaves the infection undrained. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)
Persistent fever and rising oxygen requirement with a septated effusion are indications for drainage and broader cover, not continued observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)
VATS is reserved for failure of chest drain with intrapleural fibrinolytic in Australian paediatric practice, not first-line for an unoperated septated effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)
Septated paediatric parapneumonic effusion failing antibiotics is treated with broader cover plus image-guided chest drain and intrapleural fibrinolytic per AU practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)
Oral switch is inappropriate in a child with rising oxygen requirement, persistent sepsis features, and an undrained septated effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)
