explanation.summary: Pertussis in an unvaccinated infant under 6 months requires admission for apnoea and cyanosis monitoring and macrolide therapy to reduce transmission. Azithromycin is preferred under 1 month due to the pyloric stenosis signal with erythromycin and remains first-line through 6 months. Antibiotics shorten infectivity but do not abort the paroxysmal phase once established. Household contacts including the index parent should receive post-exposure prophylaxis with the same macrolide course.
key_points: Admit infants under 6 months with confirmed pertussis for cardiorespiratory monitoring
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days is the first-line macrolide for treatment and prophylaxis
Treat up to 6 weeks after cough onset in young infants and start contact prophylaxis simultaneously
explanation.pearls: Pertussis paroxysms peak at week 2-4 and persist for 6-10 weeks; once the cough is established antibiotics will not shorten symptoms but they will cut transmission by about 5 days.

options.rationale: Amoxicillin does not eradicate Bordetella pertussis from the nasopharynx and does not reduce transmission. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: pertussis)

Infants under 6 months warrant admission for monitoring of apnoea and cyanosis; azithromycin reduces transmission and is the preferred macrolide under 1 month and remains first-line up to 6 months. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: pertussis)

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a second-line option only when macrolides are contraindicated; it is also unsafe in infants under 2 months due to kernicterus risk. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)
Bronchodilators and corticosteroids have not demonstrated benefit in pertussis and may delay recognition of deterioration. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)
Under 6 months, treatment is recommended up to 6 weeks after cough onset because of higher complication and transmission risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)

explanation.summary: Measles is suspected in an unvaccinated returned traveller with the prodromal triad of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, plus pathognomonic Koplik spots and a descending rash. Phone notification of the local public health unit and airborne isolation are immediate priorities. Confirmatory testing is measles IgM serology together with throat and urine PCR. Post-exposure prophylaxis with MMR within 72 hours of exposure or NHIG within 6 days is offered to susceptible contacts identified by contact tracing.
key_points: Koplik spots plus fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, and descending rash define a clinical measles case
Negative-pressure isolation and same-day phone notification are mandatory
Confirm with measles IgM plus throat or nasopharyngeal and urine PCR
explanation.pearls: Measles infectivity spans 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset; contacts within that window need urgent susceptibility checks regardless of age.

options.rationale: Measles is a notifiable urgent disease and discharge home without isolation risks community transmission, including to vulnerable contacts. (Source: NSW Health: Measles Control Guideline)
Roseola features defervescence preceding rash in toddlers under 3 and does not include conjunctivitis or buccal enanthem. (Source: RCH CPG: Rash - Viral Exanthems)
Scarlet fever features a sandpaper-rough rash, strawberry tongue, and circumoral pallor; antibiotics are not warranted here. (Source: RCH CPG: Scarlet Fever)

Koplik spots, fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, and travel exposure in an unvaccinated child meet a measles clinical case; airborne isolation and phone-notification within 24 hours are mandated. (Source: CDNA SoNG: Measles)
Varicella presents with pruritic vesicles on an erythematous base in successive crops, not a confluent maculopapular descending rash. (Source: RCH CPG: Chickenpox)

explanation.summary: Persistent unilateral strabismus after 4 months of age is a referral indication to paediatric ophthalmology. The differential includes refractive error, anisometropia, and rarely retinoblastoma if the red reflex is abnormal or leukocoria is present. A symmetric red reflex on examination reduces but does not exclude retinoblastoma and prompt cycloplegic refraction and orthoptic measurements within 4 weeks are essential to start amblyopia therapy. Amblyopia rapidly becomes refractory after 7 years of age, so timely diagnosis matters.
key_points: Any constant strabismus past 4 months of age needs ophthalmology referral
Symmetric red reflex does not exclude retinoblastoma but lowers immediate concern
Cycloplegic refraction and orthoptic assessment within 4 weeks are the diagnostic basis
explanation.pearls: Pseudostrabismus from a wide nasal bridge mimics esotropia but the corneal light reflex remains central in both eyes; if displaced, refer.

options.rationale: Strabismus persisting beyond 4 months of age is abnormal and risks irreversible amblyopia without prompt assessment. (Source: RANZCO: Vision Screening Position Statement)
Patching is a treatment for amblyopia after orthoptic and refractive assessment, not a primary care first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)

Constant unilateral strabismus persisting past 4 months requires paediatric ophthalmology assessment within 4 weeks to prevent amblyopia and exclude organic causes including retinoblastoma. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)
Neuroimaging is not first-line without focal neurology or other red flags; ophthalmology review prioritises refraction and red reflex assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)
Targeted imaging of the globe is determined by the ophthalmologist after clinical examination and is not a primary care ordering pathway. (Source: RANZCO: Vision Screening Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Pediculosis capitis in Australian primary care is managed first with wet combing using copious conditioner every 4 days until no live lice are detected on three consecutive sessions. Pyrethroid-based topicals are next-line given growing pyrethroid resistance. School exclusion is not required once treatment has started. Household members are checked but not treated empirically unless they harbour live lice.
key_points: Wet combing with conditioner is first-line and safe in any age
Treat only contacts with active live lice, not all household members empirically
School attendance is permitted once active treatment has commenced
explanation.pearls: Eggs more than 1 cm from the scalp are usually non-viable; presence alone does not equal active infestation.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: Wet combing with conditioner is the first-line and most cost-effective approach in Australian primary care; it is also safe in pregnancy and infants. (Source: RACGP: Head Lice Management)
Permethrin is an option but Australian resistance rates are substantial and prolonged 6-weekly repetition is excessive. (Source: AMH: Pediculosis)
Oral ivermectin is reserved for treatment-refractory or institutional outbreaks, not as first-line in a routine case. (Source: AMH: Pediculosis)
Antibiotics treat secondary bacterial superinfection only; they have no role in routine pediculosis without impetigo. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: Head-shaving is not recommended and offers no benefit over evidence-based combing or topical therapies. (Source: RACGP: Head Lice Management)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception in a toddler with the classic triad of episodic colicky pain, redcurrant stool, and palpable mass needs rapid resuscitation and pneumatic reduction with theatre standby. Ultrasound demonstrates a target sign with reduced internal colour Doppler when bowel viability is at risk. Image-guided air enema is successful in 70-90% of cases, with surgical reduction reserved for peritonitis, perforation, or failed enema. A pathological lead point should be considered in atypical age groups outside 3 months to 3 years.
key_points: Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg crystalloid before reduction
Air enema is first-line if no peritonitis or perforation
Surgical standby is essential because of perforation risk during pneumatic reduction
explanation.pearls: Recurrence after successful pneumatic reduction is about 10% in the first 24 hours; observe overnight before discharge.

options.rationale: Haemodynamic instability and the classic triad with mass make urgent intervention the priority; delay risks ischaemic perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
There is no clinical indication for vascular imaging; the reduced colour Doppler signal in the loop indicates compromised bowel perfusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Surgery is indicated when pneumatic reduction fails or peritonitis or perforation is suspected; absence of those findings favours image-guided reduction first. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Empiric transfusion is not warranted without haemoglobin documentation and ongoing significant blood loss; volume resuscitation precedes transfusion decisions. (Source: NBA: Paediatric Patient Blood Management)

Stabilise circulation then pneumatic reduction by an experienced radiologist with surgical backup is the standard of care for uncomplicated ileocolic intussusception without peritonitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is associated with hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid and chloride loss. Pre-operative correction with isotonic saline resuscitation followed by 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose and potassium chloride 20 mmol/L is standard. Targets are chloride above 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L, and potassium above 3.5 mmol/L. Surgery is delayed until these targets are met to prevent post-anaesthetic apnoea.
key_points: Pyloric stenosis causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Resuscitate with sodium chloride 0.9% then maintenance saline-dextrose plus potassium
Delay surgery until chloride above 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: Failure to correct alkalosis before anaesthesia is the major preventable cause of post-pyloromyotomy apnoea.

options.rationale: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis predisposes to post-operative apnoea and arrhythmia; correction precedes anaesthesia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)
Hypotonic fluids should not be used; 0.18% saline-dextrose worsens hyponatraemia and is no longer Australian standard maintenance. (Source: RCH CPG: Intravenous Fluids)

Targets bicarbonate under 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L; potassium replacement guards against post-operative apnoea and arrhythmia, and resuscitation precedes pyloromyotomy. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)
Persistent gastric outlet obstruction precludes oral correction; ongoing vomiting will worsen alkalosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)
The metabolic alkalosis is driven by chloride and potassium depletion; bicarbonate worsens the alkalosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acid-Base Disturbances)

explanation.summary: Inhaled foreign body presents with sudden choking, persistent unilateral wheeze, and decreased air entry on the affected side. Expiratory or decubitus chest x-ray shows obstructive hyperinflation with mediastinal shift away from the affected side. Same-day rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is the diagnostic and therapeutic procedure of choice. Salbutamol and steroids do not relieve mechanical obstruction and may delay definitive airway clearance.
key_points: Choking with persistent unilateral signs is rigid bronchoscopy until proven otherwise
Decubitus or expiratory films reveal obstructive emphysema even when inspiratory films appear normal
Bronchodilators and steroids do not relieve mechanical obstruction
explanation.pearls: Peanuts cause acute lipoid pneumonia if retained; do not delay bronchoscopy waiting for normalisation of breath sounds.

options.rationale: Salbutamol does not relieve mechanical airway obstruction and delays definitive airway clearance, with risk of mucus plugging and dislodgement. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)
A witnessed choking event with persistent unilateral signs and obstructive emphysema on imaging is diagnostic and warrants same-day rigid bronchoscopy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

Back blows are reserved for the actively choking child unable to cough; this child has air movement and forced manoeuvres risk dislodging the object into the trachea. (Source: ANZCOR: Paediatric Basic Life Support)
Steroids treat airway inflammation in asthma exacerbations and do not address mechanical obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)
Inspiratory films are commonly normal; the expiratory film here already shows mediastinal shift and the clinical scenario is diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

explanation.summary: A vertical epiphyseal fracture extending to the physis without metaphyseal involvement is a Salter-Harris III pattern. These intra-articular fractures need computed tomography to define displacement and orthopaedic review for possible operative fixation. Initial management is a well-padded backslab with neurovascular checks. Long-term follow-up screens for growth arrest at the affected physis.
key_points: Salter-Harris III involves the epiphysis and physis without crossing the metaphysis
Computed tomography defines articular displacement and informs operative planning
Same-day orthopaedic review is required for intra-articular paediatric fractures
explanation.pearls: Growth arrest risk after Salter-Harris III is around 10-20%; counsel families about possible angular deformity at follow-up.

sources.label: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric Fracture Management

options.rationale: A Salter-Harris III intra-articular fracture risks growth disturbance and articular incongruity if reduction is inadequate; specialist input is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Ankle Fractures)
Outpatient delay over 6 weeks risks malunion and growth arrest; intra-articular incongruity warrants earlier orthopaedic input. (Source: RCH CPG: Ankle Fractures)
This is a confirmed intra-articular fracture, not a soft tissue sprain, and tubular bandaging is inadequate immobilisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Ankle Fractures)

Salter-Harris III patterns require computed tomography to characterise displacement and possible operative fixation; backslab and same-day orthopaedic review are standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Ankle Fractures)
Magnetic resonance imaging is not first-line for an acute Salter-Harris fracture; computed tomography defines bony anatomy more practically. (Source: RCH CPG: Ankle Fractures)

explanation.summary: High-risk paediatric acute lymphoblastic leukaemia carries substantial tumour lysis syndrome risk. Prophylaxis is hyperhydration at twice maintenance with isotonic crystalloid without potassium, plus allopurinol. Rasburicase is reserved for high-risk patients with rising or established hyperuricaemia, but only after glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency has been excluded due to fatal haemolysis risk. Routine alkalinisation is no longer recommended. Renal replacement therapy is reserved for established complications such as refractory hyperkalaemia, severe hyperphosphataemia, or oligo-anuric acute kidney injury.
key_points: Hyperhydration at 3 L/m2/day plus allopurinol is the routine prophylactic platform
Rasburicase is held until glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is excluded
Avoid alkalinisation; it worsens calcium phosphate precipitation
explanation.pearls: Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency and pregnancy; sample for assay before any first dose even if the result will take days to return.

options.rationale: Rasburicase causes severe haemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; until the assay returns, hyperhydration plus allopurinol is appropriate and rasburicase is reserved if the assay is normal or hyperuricaemia escalates. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL Tumour Lysis)
Alkalinisation increases calcium phosphate precipitation and is no longer recommended once allopurinol or rasburicase are available. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL Tumour Lysis)

Rasburicase causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; testing should not be bypassed in elective induction. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL Tumour Lysis)
Fluid restriction worsens tumour lysis nephropathy; hyperhydration with at least 3 L/m2/day is essential. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL Tumour Lysis)

Renal replacement therapy is reserved for established acute kidney injury, refractory hyperkalaemia, or severe hyperphosphataemia, not as routine prophylaxis. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL Tumour Lysis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in infants under 12 months with viral coryzal prodrome progressing to wheeze, crackles and respiratory distress. AU first-line is supportive care with feeding support and minimal-handling oxygen for SpO2 under 92 percent. The PARIS trial established HFNC at 2 L/kg/min as an effective rescue once standard cannulae fail, halving CPAP/intubation rates. Salbutamol, steroids, antibiotics, hypertonic saline and chest physio are NOT recommended; they neither shorten admission nor reduce escalation.
key_points: Diagnose clinically; CXR rarely needed.
Oxygen for SpO2 under 92 percent; minimal handling.
HFNC 2 L/kg/min for failure of standard oxygen (PARIS).
Salbutamol, steroids, antibiotics, hypertonic saline NOT routine.
Watch for apnoea in babies under 6 weeks or ex-preterm.
explanation.pearls: Failure of HFNC at 1 hour (HR not falling, RR not falling, SpO2 not improving) is a strong predictor of CPAP escalation - assess all three trajectories at the 60 minute mark rather than relying on absolute values alone.

options.rationale: Standard low-flow cannulae above 2 L/min in infants is not better tolerated and does not provide positive pressure; HFNC is the next escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Salbutamol does not benefit infants with bronchiolitis (under 12 months) and is not recommended in AU CPGs. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Hypertonic saline has not shown consistent benefit in bronchiolitis and is not part of AU first-line management. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Corticosteroids do not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis and stopping oxygen at SpO2 92 percent risks deterioration. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

PARIS trial criteria are met (SpO2 under 92 percent on standard oxygen or persistent work of breathing); AU practice escalates to HFNC at 2 L/kg/min with reassessment at 1 hour. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; PARIS trial)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for over 90 percent of childhood constipation; behavioural and dietary triggers (toilet training, daycare, low fluid intake) and pain-avoidance withholding are typical. Diagnosis is clinical; investigations are reserved for red flags (delayed meconium, failure to thrive, abnormal lower limb or spine examination, gross perianal pathology). Treatment is structured: disimpaction (oral macrogol over 7 days), then maintenance (macrogol daily for at least 3 to 6 months), behavioural training (timed toileting) and family education.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis; investigations only for red flags.
Macrogol 3350 disimpaction over up to 7 days.
Maintenance macrogol for 3 to 6 months minimum.
Aim 1 soft stool daily with no soiling.
Red flags: delayed meconium, FTT, lumbosacral signs, anal anomaly.
explanation.pearls: Soiling (encopresis) is a sign of overflow incontinence around a faecal mass, NOT diarrhoea or behavioural defiance; ceasing maintenance laxatives too early is the commonest cause of relapse - taper over weeks rather than stopping abruptly.

options.rationale: AU first-line for paediatric faecal impaction is escalating macrogol 3350 disimpaction over up to 7 days followed by maintenance dosing; safe and well tolerated. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Diet alone does not clear established faecal impaction; pharmacological disimpaction is required first. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Phosphate enemas in toddlers carry risks of hyperphosphataemia and rectal trauma; oral macrogol is preferred when feasible. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Manual disimpaction under GA is reserved for failure of medical disimpaction or anatomical concerns; not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Hirschsprung disease usually presents with delayed meconium and failure to thrive; functional constipation does not warrant manometry without red flags. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is a clinical diagnosis in children 6 months to 6 years with a viral prodrome, barking cough and inspiratory stridor (usually parainfluenza). Westley score stratifies mild (0 to 2), moderate (3 to 5), severe (6 to 11) and impending respiratory failure (>= 12). Oral dexamethasone benefits all severities. Nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) provides bridging vasoconstriction in severe disease; rebound at 2 hours mandates observation. Antibiotics, salbutamol and humidifiers do not improve outcomes.
key_points: Westley score 3 to 5 = moderate (stridor at rest, mild recession).
Dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg PO single dose.
Adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL nebulised for severe (Westley >= 6).
Observe at least 4 hours after adrenaline due to rebound.
Antibiotics, salbutamol, humidifiers NOT indicated.
explanation.pearls: Sudden deterioration in an apparently moderate croup with high fever, drooling and inability to lie down should prompt suspicion of bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis - avoid attempts at IV access or oral examination until anaesthetic-led airway support is at hand.

options.rationale: Salbutamol does not treat the upper-airway oedema of croup; it is not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
IV steroids offer no advantage over oral in mild to moderate croup and antibiotics treat bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis, not viral croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Adrenaline is added for SEVERE croup (Westley >= 8 or marked distress); moderate croup with rest stridor responds first to oral dexamethasone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Moderate croup with stridor at rest is treated with a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg plus observation; nebulised adrenaline is added for severe distress. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Stridor at rest indicates moderate croup needing steroid and observation; cool mist has no evidence of benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media is one of the commonest paediatric infections. AU guidance (eTG, RCH) supports watchful waiting with adequate analgesia in non-Indigenous children over 2 with non-severe AOM (no toxicity, no high fever, no severe pain) because most resolve spontaneously and treatment risks (rash, antibiotic resistance, diarrhoea) outweigh small benefits. Antibiotics are indicated for: under 2 years bilateral, Indigenous children, severe symptoms or systemic illness, recurrent or complicated AOM. First-line antibiotic is amoxicillin 15 mg/kg TDS for 5 days (Indigenous: 7 days).
key_points: Watchful waiting with analgesia first-line for non-Indigenous over 2.
Antibiotic: amoxicillin 15 mg/kg TDS 5 days (Indigenous: 7 days).
Indications for immediate antibiotics: under 2 bilateral, Indigenous, severe symptoms, complication.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children: treat all AOM with antibiotics.
Grommet referral for recurrent disease or persistent effusion with hearing impairment.
explanation.pearls: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children have a 4-fold higher rate of chronic suppurative otitis media and warrant antibiotics for every episode of AOM with longer treatment duration; routine watchful waiting does not apply.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting with adequate analgesia is preferred for non-severe AOM in non-Indigenous children over 2 years with no high-risk features. (Source: eTG; RCH CPG: AOM)
Parenteral ceftriaxone is reserved for AOM with severe systemic illness, complications, or oral failure; not appropriate first-line in a well child. (Source: eTG)

AU eTG endorses safety-net or delayed antibiotic prescribing in non-Indigenous children over 2 with non-severe AOM; analgesia first plus filled script only if no improvement in 48 hours. (Source: eTG; RCH CPG: AOM)
Topical antibiotics are for perforated AOM or otitis externa; the intact tympanic membrane here makes them inappropriate. (Source: eTG)
Grommets are considered for recurrent AOM (>= 3 episodes in 6 months or 4 in a year); a single episode does not warrant surgical referral. (Source: RCH CPG: AOM)

explanation.summary: Cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA) is the commonest food allergy in infancy. Non-IgE-mediated CMPA (the proctocolitis form) presents with reflux, crying and small-volume rectal bleeding in well-appearing infants. Diagnosis is by elimination trial: extensively hydrolysed formula for 2 to 4 weeks, with soy avoided under 6 months due to cross-reactivity and phytoestrogen load. Around 10 percent require amino-acid formula; reintroduction at 9 to 12 months using the AU milk ladder confirms tolerance. Most infants outgrow CMPA by age 3 to 5 years.
key_points: Non-IgE CMPA: reflux, crying, rectal bleeding, well-appearing infant.
First-line: extensively hydrolysed formula for 2 to 4 weeks.
Avoid soy formula under 6 months age.
Amino-acid formula for severe or eHF non-responders (around 10 percent).
Reintroduce via milk ladder at 9 to 12 months.
explanation.pearls: Breastfeeding mothers of infants with CMPA can usually continue to breastfeed - the maternal cow's milk protein elimination diet (no dairy, no soy) plus a calcium supplement is preferred over weaning to specialised formula.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cow's milk protein allergy

options.rationale: PPIs do not treat CMPA and rectal bleeding with off-centile weight is not explained by simple reflux; protein elimination is first-line. (Source: ASCIA 2023)
Soy formula is not recommended for infants under 6 months due to cross-reactivity in around 14 percent of CMPA and high phytoestrogen load. (Source: ASCIA 2023)

Non-IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy presents with reflux, irritability and rectal bleeding; AU first-line is eHF trial for 2 to 4 weeks; soy formula avoided in infants under 6 months. (Source: ASCIA cow's milk allergy 2023)
Infant proctocolitis from CMPA is the commonest cause of small-volume rectal bleeding in this age; colonoscopy is reserved for ongoing bleeding despite elimination diet. (Source: ASCIA 2023)
Probiotics may help colic but do not treat allergic proctocolitis; protein elimination is first-line for blood in stools. (Source: ASCIA 2023)

explanation.summary: Fever in infants under 3 months carries a 7 to 12 percent risk of serious bacterial infection (UTI most common, then bacteraemia, then meningitis), with poor predictive value of clinical appearance. AU first-line is full septic screen (FBC, CRP, blood culture, catheter or SPA urine, lumbar puncture in under 6 weeks) plus empirical antibiotics. Under 6 weeks: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin; 6 weeks to 3 months: cefotaxime or benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin. CSF PCR for HSV is added if seizures, hepatitis, or maternal genital herpes.
key_points: All under 3 months with fever >= 38 degrees: septic workup + admission.
Under 6 weeks: full septic screen including LP; benzylpenicillin + gentamicin IV.
6 weeks to 3 months: blood + urine + selective LP per risk; IV antibiotics.
Catheter or SPA urine, NOT bag samples.
Add IV aciclovir if HSV risk factors (seizures, transaminitis, maternal HSV).
explanation.pearls: A 'fever-of-unknown-source' infant under 90 days with a positive urine culture still needs a normal CSF sample before stopping presumptive meningitis cover - around 5 percent of febrile UTIs in this age have concomitant meningitis.

options.rationale: All febrile infants under 3 months require full septic workup; outpatient management of fever in this age group is not safe. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile infant)

AU first-line in fever under 6 weeks is full septic screen (FBC, CRP, blood culture, urine catheter sample, LP) plus empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending cultures. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile infant; eTG)
Empirical antibiotics are required in fever under 6 weeks even when the infant appears well; the consequences of missed bacterial meningitis are catastrophic. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile infant)
Urine bag samples have high contamination rates and oral antibiotics are inadequate; catheter or suprapubic urine plus IV antibiotics are required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile infant)
Single-dose IM ceftriaxone is not adequate empirical therapy in suspected neonatal sepsis under 6 weeks; admission for IV combination therapy is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile infant)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a self-limited medium-vessel vasculitis with a strong predilection for coronary arteries. Classic diagnosis: fever >= 5 days plus 4 of 5 features (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, mucositis, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy). Incomplete KD = fever >= 5 days plus 2 to 3 features plus supportive labs (CRP >= 30, ESR >= 40, plus albumin under 30, anaemia, ALT raised, platelets >= 450 after 7 days, WCC >= 15, sterile pyuria) and/or coronary changes on echo. IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days of fever reduces coronary aneurysm risk five-fold; aspirin is added for anti-inflammatory then antiplatelet effect.
key_points: Classic KD: fever >= 5 days plus 4 of 5 features.
Incomplete KD: 2 to 3 features plus supportive labs or coronary changes.
Treat within 10 days: IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin.
Supportive labs: CRP, ESR, neutrophilia, anaemia, thrombocytosis after day 7.
Echo at diagnosis, 2 weeks and 6 weeks to monitor coronaries.
explanation.pearls: An infant under 6 months with prolonged fever and irritability without classical KD features still warrants echocardiography because around 80 percent of KD-related coronary aneurysms in this age group present as incomplete or 'atypical' disease.

options.rationale: Sustained fever over 5 days with three principal features and supportive labs plus coronary dilation already meets incomplete Kawasaki criteria; delaying IVIG increases aneurysm risk. (Source: AHA Kawasaki 2017; RCH CPG: Kawasaki)

Incomplete KD with fever >= 5 days plus 3 features plus supportive labs (CRP, neutrophilia, anaemia, thrombocytosis, raised ALT, hypoalbuminaemia) and coronary dilation justifies IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin to reduce aneurysm risk. (Source: AHA Kawasaki 2017; RCH CPG)
Corticosteroids are added (KAICA-style) for high-risk KD or IVIG-refractory disease; they are not primary therapy alone in standard initial care. (Source: AHA Kawasaki 2017)

Thrombocytosis and desquamation typically appear in week 2 to 3; waiting risks aneurysm formation - IVIG within 10 days reduces incidence from 25 percent to under 5 percent. (Source: AHA Kawasaki 2017)
Negative streptococcal screen and the clinical phenotype (conjunctivitis, mucositis, hand induration) plus coronary changes make Kawasaki the working diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki)

explanation.summary: Paediatric convulsive status epilepticus follows a tiered approach: 0 to 5 minutes assess airway, oxygen, IV access; 5 to 20 minutes first benzodiazepine (IV midazolam 0.15 mg/kg or buccal 0.3 mg/kg); 20 to 40 minutes second benzodiazepine if still seizing; 30 to 40 minutes second-line anticonvulsant (levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, phenytoin 20 mg/kg, or valproate 40 mg/kg). Refractory status (> 40 minutes) requires intubation and a third-line agent (thiopentone, midazolam infusion or propofol) in PICU. Hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia and pyridoxine deficiency must be excluded.
key_points: Two benzodiazepines then second-line anticonvulsant.
Second-line equivalence: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, phenytoin 20 mg/kg, valproate 40 mg/kg.
Levetiracetam preferred in AU paediatric centres for safety.
Refractory status (> 40 min) = intubate + anaesthetic agent in PICU.
Exclude reversible causes: glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, pyridoxine, drugs.
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy presents under 18 months with apparently medication-refractory status; a single trial of pyridoxine 100 mg IV during ongoing seizures is diagnostic and therapeutic if there is rapid termination of seizure activity within minutes.

options.rationale: Phenytoin remains an acceptable option but carries higher cardiotoxicity and infusion-site risks; AU paediatric practice increasingly prefers levetiracetam. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus)
Further benzodiazepine after two failed doses increases respiratory depression without controlling seizure; second-line anticonvulsant is the correct step. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus)
Valproate is an option but not preferred when the patient is already on regular valproate (risk of overshoot toxicity); levetiracetam or phenytoin is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG)

ConSEPT and EcLiPSE trials showed levetiracetam equivalent to phenytoin for paediatric status epilepticus and it has a more favourable side-effect profile, making it AU first-line second-line in many centres. (Source: ConSEPT/EcLiPSE; ANZICS paediatric)
Refractory status requires anaesthetic agents AFTER a second-line anticonvulsant has been loaded; jumping to thiopentone/propofol is a third-line step. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates 0.5 to 1 percent of paediatric DKA and accounts for the majority of DKA mortality. Risk factors: under 5 years, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis (pH under 7.1), elevated urea, low pCO2, high-volume fluid administration in first 4 hours, bicarbonate use. Warning signs: headache, altered mental state, Cushing triad, focal neurology, falling sodium during treatment. Treatment is immediate hypertonic saline 3 percent (2.5 to 5 mL/kg) OR mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg, halving fluid rate, 30 degree head-up. CT after stabilisation.
key_points: Cerebral oedema in 0.5 to 1 percent of paeds DKA; majority of DKA mortality.
Cushing triad + altered mental state = clinical diagnosis.
Treatment: hypertonic 3 percent NaCl 2.5 to 5 mL/kg OR mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg.
Halve fluid rate, elevate head 30 degrees, secure airway if GCS drops.
Risk factors: under 5, new-onset, pH under 7.1, raised urea, low pCO2.
explanation.pearls: Failure of serum sodium to rise as glucose falls (Hillier corrected sodium not increasing) during DKA treatment is the single best biochemical warning of impending cerebral oedema and warrants slowing fluid rate even before clinical features appear.

options.rationale: Cushing triad (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respiration) plus altered mental status during DKA treatment is presumed cerebral oedema requiring immediate action. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA; ISPAD 2022)
Increasing insulin worsens cerebral oedema by accelerating osmotic shifts; the priority is treating raised ICP. (Source: ISPAD DKA 2022)

Suspected cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA is treated with immediate fluid reduction and hypertonic 3 percent saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg (or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg) plus 30 degree head-up positioning. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA; ISPAD 2022)
Bicarbonate worsens cerebral oedema risk and is not indicated in paediatric DKA except for severe hyperkalaemia with cardiac compromise. (Source: ISPAD DKA 2022)
Cerebral oedema in DKA is a clinical diagnosis and treatment must precede imaging; delays for CT worsen outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (formerly HSP) is the commonest small-vessel vasculitis in children, presenting with palpable purpura, arthritis or arthralgia, abdominal pain, and IgA nephritis. Renal involvement appears in around 40 percent (mostly within 6 weeks, occasionally up to 6 months after diagnosis); 1 to 2 percent progress to CKD. AU monitoring is weekly urinalysis (dipstick) and BP for 4 to 6 weeks, monthly to 6 months. Refer if persistent proteinuria, declining renal function, hypertension, or nephrotic features. Corticosteroids treat severe abdominal pain or scrotal involvement but do not prevent late nephritis.
key_points: Renal involvement in around 40 percent; 1 to 2 percent CKD.
Monitor weekly urinalysis + BP for 4 to 6 weeks, monthly to 6 months.
Refer for persistent proteinuria, declining GFR, hypertension, nephrosis.
Steroids treat severe pain/scrotal, NOT for renal prevention.
Renal biopsy if nephrotic, declining GFR, or persistent abnormalities.
explanation.pearls: Intussusception complicates around 2 percent of paediatric HSP and is typically ileo-ileal (not ileo-colic) - air enema may miss it; consider ultrasound first in any HSP child with severe abdominal pain regardless of stool patterns.

options.rationale: Up to 50 percent of HSP nephritis appears in the first 3 months and a small fraction progresses to CKD; weekly to fortnightly urinalysis and BP monitoring for 6 months is required. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP 2023; RCH CPG)
Corticosteroids do not prevent late nephritis in HSP; they are reserved for severe abdominal pain, scrotal involvement, or biopsy-proven nephritis. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP 2023)

AU and KHA-CARI guidance is weekly urinalysis and BP for 4 to 6 weeks, then monthly to 6 months, referring if persistent proteinuria, declining renal function or hypertension develops. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP 2023; RCH CPG)
Renal biopsy is reserved for nephrotic-range proteinuria, declining GFR, or persistent abnormal urinalysis - none currently present. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP 2023)
Late-presenting nephritis would be missed by such infrequent monitoring; 6 months of structured surveillance is standard. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP 2023)

explanation.summary: Periorbital (pre-septal) cellulitis is anterior to the orbital septum, presenting with eyelid erythema and oedema, normal eye movements, no proptosis, no visual loss. Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis - typically a complication of acute ethmoiditis - presents with the additional findings of proptosis, painful restricted eye movements, diplopia and visual changes. Orbital cellulitis demands urgent CT of orbits and paranasal sinuses, IV ceftriaxone plus flucloxacillin (covering S. pyogenes, S. aureus and sinus organisms), ophthalmology and ENT involvement, and surgical drainage if a subperiosteal abscess is large or visual function declines.
key_points: Pre-septal: eyelid erythema, normal eye movements - oral antibiotics OK.
Post-septal: proptosis, EOM restriction, diplopia, vision change - emergency.
Workup: CT orbits and sinuses with contrast.
AU antibiotics: IV ceftriaxone + flucloxacillin (paeds dosing).
Surgical drainage for medium-large subperiosteal abscess or visual decline.
explanation.pearls: Visual acuity, pupillary reactions and colour vision (red desaturation test) are the most sensitive bedside markers of optic nerve compromise in orbital cellulitis - re-check them every hour during the first 24 hours of treatment to detect occult deterioration.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia and diplopia are post-septal (orbital) cellulitis until proved otherwise; oral monotherapy is inadequate. (Source: eTG; RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Topical antibiotics treat conjunctivitis; established orbital infection requires parenteral antibiotics and imaging. (Source: eTG)

Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis is suggested by proptosis, painful EOM, diplopia or visual loss; AU first-line is urgent CT and IV ceftriaxone plus flucloxacillin plus ENT and ophthalmology review. (Source: eTG; RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Orbital cellulitis can progress to cavernous sinus thrombosis or vision loss within hours; outpatient management is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Canthotomy is for orbital compartment syndrome (retrobulbar haemorrhage), not orbital cellulitis; imaging guides surgical drainage if a subperiosteal abscess is present. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice management in AU uses age-specific phototherapy and exchange transfusion nomograms (eg KEMH/RWH/ANZ consensus 2024). Risk factors raise the action threshold lower: under 38 weeks, haemolysis (positive DAT, ABO/Rh mismatch, G6PD), sepsis, hypoalbuminaemia. Phototherapy is given with eye protection, breastfeeding continued (or expressed milk if too sleepy to feed), with 6-hourly bilirubin once treatment commences. Stop phototherapy when bilirubin falls 50 micromol/L below the line. Direct bilirubin over 20 percent of total prompts conjugated-hyperbilirubinaemia workup (biliary atresia, sepsis, metabolic).
key_points: Use age-specific phototherapy and exchange nomograms.
Lower threshold for risk factors: prematurity, haemolysis, sepsis, hypoalbuminaemia.
Continue breastfeeding during phototherapy; eye protection.
Recheck bilirubin at 6 hours then 6 to 12 hourly to confirm response.
Conjugated fraction > 20 percent of total = workup for cholestasis.
explanation.pearls: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia at any age beyond day 14 in a term infant is biliary atresia until proved otherwise - delay in Kasai portoenterostomy beyond 60 days of life roughly halves the chance of long-term liver-graft-free survival.

options.rationale: Bilirubin above the AU phototherapy line at 96 hours requires admission for phototherapy with continued breastfeeding plus a 6-hour repeat bilirubin to assess response. (Source: ANZ neonatal jaundice consensus 2024)

Total bilirubin 320 micromol/L at 96 hours in a term low-risk infant exceeds the AU phototherapy line; outpatient deferral risks kernicterus. (Source: ANZ neonatal jaundice consensus 2024; RWH paediatric jaundice)
Routine cessation of breastfeeding is not recommended; AU first-line is phototherapy with continued breastfeeding and lactation support. (Source: ANZ consensus 2024)
Exchange transfusion threshold at 96 hours in a low-risk term infant is around 430 to 450 micromol/L; 320 is in the phototherapy not exchange range. (Source: ANZ consensus 2024)
Phenobarbital is not standard for neonatal jaundice; phototherapy is first-line and rapidly effective. (Source: ANZ consensus 2024)

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric practice classifies bronchiolitis severity by oxygenation, respiratory effort, feeding, and hydration. Moderate severity meets admission criteria. Supportive care with oxygen and paced feeds is first-line; bronchodilators, steroids, and nebulised adrenaline are not recommended for typical viral bronchiolitis under 12 months. Feeding under 50% combined with borderline SpO2 mandates admission.
key_points: RCH admission triggers include SpO2 under 92%, RR over 60, feeds under half, or apnoeas
Bronchodilators, steroids, and adrenaline are not routinely indicated under 12 months
Paced NG feeds preserve hydration without increasing aspiration risk
explanation.pearls: RCH bronchiolitis pathway uses SpO2 below 92% as the supplemental oxygen threshold; do not start oxygen at higher saturations as it prolongs admission.

options.rationale: Sustained SpO2 below 92% on room air, RR over 60, and feeding under 50% of normal meet RCH admission criteria for moderate bronchiolitis; supportive oxygen and paced feeds are first-line. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)
Bronchodilators do not improve outcomes in typical viral bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months and are not recommended. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)
Systemic corticosteroids confer no benefit in acute bronchiolitis and are not used routinely. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)
Discharge is unsafe with reduced feeding, reduced wet nappies, and borderline oxygenation, which together indicate moderate severity requiring admission. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)
Nebulised adrenaline is not routinely recommended and does not change admission rates or length of stay. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance from RCH stratifies post-UTI imaging by atypia and recurrence. A first febrile UTI in a child under 24 months who responds promptly and has a normal renal ultrasound needs no further imaging. MCUG and DMSA are reserved for atypical features or recurrence. Routine MCUG or DMSA after a typical first UTI is over-investigation inherited from NICE-derived practice.
key_points: Renal tract ultrasound during admission is standard for febrile UTI under 24 months
Atypical features include non-E coli organism, poor response by 48 hours, abdominal mass, or sepsis
Prophylaxis is not first-line after a single uncomplicated UTI
explanation.pearls: RCH UTI pathway: ultrasound during admission for under-24-months febrile UTI; MCUG only if atypical or recurrent or ultrasound abnormal.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: UTI in children

options.rationale: DMSA is recommended after atypical or recurrent UTIs, not after a first uncomplicated febrile UTI with normal ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)
MCUG is reserved for atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, or abnormal ultrasound findings, not for a first uncomplicated UTI that responded promptly. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)
For a first febrile UTI under 24 months with prompt response to first-line therapy and a normal ultrasound, no further imaging is required. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)
Routine antibiotic prophylaxis after a single uncomplicated UTI is not recommended due to limited benefit and resistance. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)
Test of cure is not required if the child is clinically well at the end of therapy. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA cerebral oedema typically presents 4 to 12 hours into treatment with bradycardia, rising BP, falling GCS, and headache. Recognition is clinical and treatment must precede imaging. Hypertonic 3% saline (2.5 to 5 mL/kg) or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg is first-line, with fluid rate reduction. Mortality remains 20 to 25% even with prompt treatment.
key_points: Cushing triad (bradycardia, hypertension, falling GCS) in DKA equals cerebral oedema until proven otherwise
Hypertonic saline 3% at 2.5 to 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg is first-line osmotherapy
Imaging follows stabilisation, not the other way around
explanation.pearls: Risk factors for paediatric DKA cerebral oedema include younger age, severe acidosis, low pCO2, and rapid sodium correction; ISPAD recommends limiting initial bolus to 10 to 20 mL/kg in 1 to 2 hours.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines DKA

options.rationale: Changing crystalloid type does not treat cerebral oedema; osmotherapy is the time-critical intervention. (Source: RCH CPG DKA)
Glucose is 14 mmol/L, so hypoglycaemia is excluded; stopping insulin would worsen ketosis without addressing cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG DKA)
Aggressive rehydration in established cerebral oedema worsens intracranial pressure and contradicts current PICU guidance. (Source: RCH CPG DKA)
Delaying osmotherapy for imaging worsens outcomes; treatment must precede imaging if cerebral oedema is clinically suspected. (Source: RCH CPG DKA)

Bradycardia with rising blood pressure, falling GCS, and headache in a child being treated for DKA is cerebral oedema; treatment with osmotherapy and fluid reduction must precede imaging. (Source: RCH CPG DKA)

explanation.summary: Infants under 6 months frequently present with incomplete Kawasaki disease, with fewer than 4 of the 5 classic clinical features. The AHA 2017 algorithm allows treatment based on prolonged fever plus 2 clinical features and supplementary labs (CRP over 30, ESR over 40, plus 3 of: platelets over 450, low albumin, low sodium, raised ALT, sterile pyuria, WCC over 15). Early IVIG within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25% to under 5%. Echocardiography is mandatory at diagnosis.
key_points: Under 6 months age group has highest aneurysm risk despite often atypical presentation
AHA supplementary lab criteria allow earlier intervention in incomplete disease
IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within 10 days reduces aneurysm risk substantially
explanation.pearls: BCG site reactivation is highly specific for Kawasaki disease in vaccinated infants; it is not in classical criteria but strongly supports the diagnosis.

options.rationale: Waiting risks coronary aneurysm formation; supplementary laboratory criteria allow earlier diagnosis under 6 months when clinical features are sparse. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki)

Persistent fever beyond 5 days with 2 clinical features plus supportive labs (CRP raised, platelets raised, low albumin, low sodium, raised ALT, sterile pyuria) meets AHA incomplete Kawasaki criteria for treatment and urgent echocardiography. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki)
Sterile pyuria, raised ALT, and low albumin in this pattern point to inflammatory rather than infectious aetiology in the prolonged fever picture. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki)
sJIA requires quotidian fever pattern and evanescent rash, neither of which is present, and outpatient deferral risks aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki)
Delay risks coronary aneurysm; ibuprofen does not address the underlying vasculitis or replace IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki)

explanation.summary: Intussusception classically presents at 3 months to 3 years with paroxysmal crying, drawing up of legs, pallor, lethargy between episodes, and a palpable sausage-shaped mass. Stool changes (redcurrant jelly) are late findings; their absence does not rule out the diagnosis. Ultrasound is highly sensitive and specific. Hydrostatic or pneumatic reduction is first-line management with surgery for failed reduction or perforation.
key_points: Lethargy between episodes is an under-recognised but specific feature in young infants
Ultrasound has sensitivity over 97% and is first-line
Air or contrast enema reduction is therapeutic in most cases without need for surgery
explanation.pearls: Pure lethargy in an infant can be the dominant presentation of intussusception, sometimes mistaken for sepsis or neurological illness; consider ultrasound when no clear cause is found.

options.rationale: Ionising radiation in infants is avoided when ultrasound is diagnostic; CT has no first-line role for intussusception. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)
Plain films may show non-specific signs but cannot reliably confirm or exclude intussusception; ultrasound is preferred first-line. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)
The pattern of inconsolable crying followed by limpness with a palpable mass is classic for intussusception, not seizure activity. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

Pallor, intermittent inconsolable crying, lethargy, and a palpable mass in a 4-month-old strongly suggest intussusception; ultrasound is the first-line investigation with high sensitivity. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)
Without fever, irritability between episodes, or meningism, LP is not the priority and the clinical pattern is surgical. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Paediatric sepsis fluid resuscitation in Australia uses 10 to 20 mL/kg boluses of balanced crystalloid (Plasma-Lyte 148 or Hartmann's preferred over normal saline) with reassessment after each bolus. The FEAST trial showed harm from aggressive fluid boluses in African children with sepsis and informs cautious incremental dosing. Antibiotics within 1 hour and vasoactive support if perfusion does not improve after 40 to 60 mL/kg total are the next steps.
key_points: 10 to 20 mL/kg bolus then reassess, not 40 to 60 mL/kg blindly
Balanced crystalloid preferred over normal saline
Antibiotics within the first hour; vasopressors after 40 to 60 mL/kg if not responding
explanation.pearls: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2020 paediatric update recommends starting vasopressors via peripheral access if not responding after 40 to 60 mL/kg crystalloid rather than delaying for central access.

options.rationale: Current Australian and Surviving Sepsis paediatric guidance favours smaller boluses (10 to 20 mL/kg) with frequent reassessment to avoid fluid overload after the FEAST trial findings. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)
Large rapid boluses without reassessment risk pulmonary oedema and worse mortality in resource-rich settings as well; paediatric guidance is smaller incremental boluses. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)
Vasopressors are second-line after initial crystalloid bolus and reassessment; immediate vasopressor in cold shock is not standard. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)
Blood is not first-line volume; crystalloid is unless there is documented haemorrhage or low haemoglobin requiring transfusion. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)
Albumin is not preferred first-line; balanced crystalloid is recommended and albumin reserved for refractory shock if used at all. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Swimming-triggered syncope is the signature presentation of LQT1, which accounts for around 30 to 35% of LQTS. A QTc above 480 ms in a symptomatic patient plus family sudden death is diagnostic by Schwartz score. Non-selective beta-blockers (nadolol or propranolol) are first-line; selective agents are inferior. ICD is reserved for breakthrough events or aborted cardiac arrest. Genetic testing guides family cascade screening.
key_points: LQT1 triggers: exercise and swimming; LQT2: auditory stimuli, postpartum; LQT3: rest and sleep
Nadolol and propranolol superior to selective beta-blockers in LQTS
ICD for aborted cardiac arrest or recurrent syncope on optimal beta-blockade
explanation.pearls: QTc above 480 ms with unexplained syncope scores 3 on Schwartz criteria; combined with family sudden death under 30, this triggers LQTS workup even without genetic confirmation.

sources.label: CSANZ Genetic Heart Disease Position Statement

options.rationale: Flecainide is not first-line for LQTS and can prolong QT further; sport restriction is part of LQT1 management until confirmed. (Source: HRS Inherited Arrhythmia Statement)

Selective beta1 blockers like metoprolol are inferior to nadolol and propranolol in LQTS and not first-line for paediatric patients with high-risk features. (Source: HRS Inherited Arrhythmia Statement)
Beta-blockers and lifestyle changes are first-line; ICD is reserved for breakthrough events on therapy or aborted cardiac arrest, not initial management. (Source: HRS Inherited Arrhythmia Statement)

Suspected LQT1 with swimming-triggered syncope and prolonged QTc plus family history requires beta-blockade (nadolol or propranolol preferred) and genetic confirmation with family screening. (Source: HRS Inherited Arrhythmia Statement)
Exertion or swimming-triggered syncope with prolonged QTc and family sudden death is not vasovagal; further LQTS evaluation is required. (Source: HRS Inherited Arrhythmia Statement)

explanation.summary: Symptom-free interval followed by lethargy and encephalopathy after milk feeds in a neonate signals an inborn error of metabolism. Urea cycle defects classically cause hyperammonaemia with respiratory alkalosis and absent ketosis; organic acidaemias cause metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap and ketosis. Ammonia above 200 in a neonate is a haemofiltration indication. Stop protein, give 10% dextrose to suppress catabolism, and give ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate, arginine).
key_points: Symptom-free interval after birth then encephalopathy with milk feeds suggests urea cycle defect
Urea cycle defect: respiratory alkalosis, absent ketosis; organic acidaemia: metabolic acidosis with ketosis
Ammonia over 200 micromol/L in a neonate is a haemofiltration trigger
explanation.pearls: Boys with X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency typically present in the first week with this picture; carrier mothers may have a history of protein aversion or postpartum psychiatric symptoms.

options.rationale: Glucose is 4.2 mmol/L, not low; insulin would be inappropriate and dangerous in this context. (Source: ANZSIEM Hyperammonaemia Guideline)

Marked hyperammonaemia (over 200 micromol/L) with respiratory alkalosis and absent ketosis in a previously well neonate after milk feeds points to a urea cycle defect; haemofiltration is the definitive ammonia-lowering treatment alongside protein restriction and ammonia scavengers. (Source: ANZSIEM Hyperammonaemia Guideline)
Anion gap is 14 and pH is alkalotic with absent ketones, which excludes organic acidaemia as the primary problem. (Source: ANZSIEM Hyperammonaemia Guideline)
Lactate is 1.8 mmol/L which is within normal limits and does not support mitochondrial disease as the primary diagnosis. (Source: ANZSIEM Hyperammonaemia Guideline)
Many inborn errors present after milk feeds are established with a symptom-free interval after birth; normal initial examination does not exclude them. (Source: ANZSIEM Hyperammonaemia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Febrile UTI in infants under 3 months is treated as serious bacterial infection until proven otherwise: admission, parenteral antibiotics, blood and urine cultures, and consideration of lumbar puncture if clinically unwell or under 4 weeks. Empirical IV gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) is the standard Australian regimen, with oral switch when stable and afebrile typically after 2 to 4 days. Renal tract ultrasound is recommended after a first febrile UTI under 6 months to identify obstruction or significant abnormality. MCUG is reserved for recurrent UTI, atypical organism, or abnormal ultrasound. DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months assesses cortical scarring when indicated. E. coli accounts for over 80% of paediatric UTIs.
key_points: Under 3 months febrile UTI: admit, IV antibiotics, blood + urine cultures
Empirical IV gentamicin + benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin
Renal tract ultrasound after first febrile UTI under 6 months
MCUG only if recurrent, atypical, or abnormal USS
Catheter or SPA urine specimen preferred under 2 years
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin once-daily at 7.5 mg/kg in neonates and infants is preferred to divided dosing in Australian paediatric practice because of superior peak-to-MIC bactericidal activity and reduced nephrotoxicity.

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics and outpatient management are inappropriate for febrile UTI under 3 months of age; the bacteraemia risk is too high. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Infants under 3 months with febrile UTI require admission and parenteral antibiotics; empirical IV gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) is standard, and renal tract ultrasound is recommended during first febrile UTI in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Ceftriaxone is reserved for late-onset neonatal sepsis or proven resistant organisms; MCUG is not first-line imaging after a first febrile UTI under current Australian practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
Oral antibiotic monotherapy is not acceptable for febrile UTI under 3 months irrespective of agent due to bacteraemia and meningitis risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
Awaiting cultures before treating any febrile infant under 3 months with positive urine dipstick risks progression to urosepsis and meningitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Croup severity is graded as mild (stridor only with agitation, no recession), moderate (stridor at rest with mild-moderate recession), severe (stridor at rest with marked recession or distress, or hypoxia or altered mental state). All grades receive oral dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg (single dose). Moderate to severe croup additionally receives nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (or 0.5 mL/kg, max 5 mL), which acts within 30 minutes. Adrenaline effect lasts 1 to 2 hours; child must be observed for rebound. Disposition depends on response: home if mild and steroid effect achieved, observation for 4 hours post-adrenaline, admission for ongoing stridor at rest. Avoid distressing the child (no IV, no imaging unless essential).
key_points: Severity: mild (stridor with agitation), moderate (stridor at rest), severe (marked recession, hypoxia)
All grades: oral dexamethasone 0.15-0.6 mg/kg single dose
Moderate-severe: add nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000
Adrenaline acts within 30 minutes, effect 1-2 hours
Avoid distressing investigations
explanation.pearls: Nebulised L-adrenaline (1:1000) at 5 mL is equivalent in efficacy to racemic adrenaline 2.25% at 0.5 mL, and is the standard formulation in Australian paediatric ED; rebound stridor at 1 to 2 hours mandates 4-hour observation post-dose.

options.rationale: Stridor at rest with marked sternal recession indicates severe croup not yet responding to dexamethasone; nebulised adrenaline gives rapid (within 30 minutes) symptomatic relief and is indicated for moderate-severe croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Dexamethasone takes 1 to 2 hours for effect; repeating it now does not provide rapid relief and the child needs immediate intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Cochrane evidence shows no benefit of humidified air for croup; oxygen is given only if SpO2 is low, which is not the case here. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Imaging is not indicated in classic croup and risks deterioration if the child is distressed; clinical severity scoring guides management. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Salbutamol does not treat upper airway obstruction; nebulised budesonide is an alternative steroid but oral dexamethasone has already been given. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a urological emergency where time to detorsion determines salvage. Classic features are sudden severe scrotal pain (often waking from sleep), vomiting, high-riding testis with horizontal lie, and absent cremasteric reflex. Salvage rates are around 90% if surgery occurs within 6 hours, falling to under 10% beyond 24 hours. When clinical suspicion is high, the patient goes directly to theatre; ultrasound is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty and must not delay surgery. Surgical exploration includes detorsion, viability assessment, and bilateral orchidopexy because the underlying bell-clapper deformity is bilateral. Differential includes epididymitis (gradual, urinary symptoms), torsion of appendix testis (blue dot sign, less severe), and incarcerated hernia.
key_points: Salvage ~90% if surgery <6 hours, <10% by 24 hours
Classic: sudden pain, vomiting, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex
Do not delay theatre for ultrasound when clinical suspicion is high
Bilateral orchidopexy (bell-clapper is bilateral)
Differential: epididymitis (gradual, urinary symptoms), torsion of appendix testis
explanation.pearls: Absent cremasteric reflex has about 99% sensitivity for testicular torsion in adolescent boys, making it the single most useful bedside finding when paired with sudden severe pain.

options.rationale: Imaging delays definitive treatment and risks loss of the testis; with classic clinical findings, theatre takes priority over imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)
Epididymitis usually has gradual onset, positive cremasteric reflex, and abnormal urinalysis; this presentation is classic torsion. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

Time from onset to detorsion determines testicular salvage (about 90% salvage if under 6 hours, falling to under 10% by 24 hours); classic clinical features mandate theatre without delay for imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

Manual detorsion (open-book, lateral rotation) may be a bridging measure where surgery is delayed, but does not replace urgent theatre; rotation direction is lateral, not medial, in most cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)
Delay beyond 6 hours dramatically reduces testicular salvage; deferring urology assessment is a sentinel error. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

explanation.summary: Classic Kawasaki disease requires fever >=5 days plus 4 of 5 criteria (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, peripheral extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). Incomplete Kawasaki applies when fewer criteria are met, especially in infants under 1 year and children over 8 (highest aneurysm risk groups). The AHA algorithm allows treatment when fever and 2 to 3 criteria coexist with elevated CRP/ESR plus supportive features (anaemia, thrombocytosis after day 7, raised ALT, hypoalbuminaemia, leukocytosis, sterile pyuria) OR coronary abnormalities on echo (Z score >=2.5 or dilation). IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion plus high-dose aspirin within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25% to under 5%. Aspirin is reduced to antiplatelet dose after fever resolution.
key_points: Classic: fever >=5 days + 4 of 5 (CRASH and burn - Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue, Hands/feet)
Incomplete: fewer criteria but suggestive labs or coronary findings
IVIG 2 g/kg + high-dose aspirin within 10 days reduces aneurysm rate 25% to <5%
Infants <1 year highest aneurysm risk - lower threshold to treat
Echo at diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6 to 8 weeks
explanation.pearls: Coronary artery Z score >=2.5 on echocardiogram in a febrile child with under 4 classic criteria is sufficient to diagnose incomplete Kawasaki and commit to IVIG, regardless of inflammatory markers.

options.rationale: Awaiting full criteria delays treatment beyond day 10 and increases coronary aneurysm risk; incomplete Kawasaki with coronary changes is treated as Kawasaki. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Septic workup is reasonable but ceftriaxone alone does not address the most likely diagnosis; coronary changes on echo support incomplete Kawasaki. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for IVIG resistance or as IVIG-adjunct in high-risk; it is not first-line in standard practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Infants under 1 year with prolonged fever, supportive lab features (raised CRP, sterile pyuria, hyponatraemia, low albumin, raised ALT) and coronary changes meet incomplete Kawasaki criteria; IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk from about 25% to under 5%. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease; AHA Kawasaki Statement)
Oral steroid monotherapy is not standard initial therapy; IVIG remains the first-line agent with proven coronary protection. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Infants at risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia (LGA, IDM, SGA, preterm) are screened with bedside BSL from 90 minutes of life and before feeds for 12 to 24 hours. Operational threshold for action is BSL <2.6 mmol/L in the first 48 hours. For asymptomatic at-risk infants, 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) massaged into the buccal mucosa followed by feed is first-line; this Australian Sugar Babies protocol increases breastfeeding success and reduces NICU admissions. Recheck BSL at 30 minutes. IV 10% dextrose at 60 to 80 mL/kg/day is reserved for symptomatic infants, BSL <1.2, or BSL not responsive to gel and feeds. Symptomatic infants (jitteriness, seizures, apnoea, lethargy) require immediate IV dextrose 2 mL/kg of 10% then maintenance infusion. Critical sample (insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ammonia, lactate) is taken before treatment when persistent hypoglycaemia beyond 48 hours raises concern for hyperinsulinism.
key_points: Operational threshold BSL <2.6 in first 48 hours for at-risk infants
Asymptomatic: 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg + feed, recheck 30 min
Symptomatic or BSL <1.2: IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus + infusion
Critical sample if persistent hypoglycaemia beyond 48 hours
IDM: hyperinsulinism, depleted glycogen, vulnerable >48 hours
explanation.pearls: The Sugar Babies trial showed buccal 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg reduced NICU admission for neonatal hypoglycaemia by approximately 50% compared with feeds alone, and is the basis for Australian first-line use.

options.rationale: BSL 1.6 in an at-risk asymptomatic infant requires active intervention; awaiting another feed risks symptomatic hypoglycaemia and neurological injury. (Source: ANZCOR Neonatal Resuscitation; RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)
IV bolus dextrose is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia or BSL persistently <1.2 despite feeds and gel; first-line in asymptomatic at-risk infant is dextrose gel. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

IV dextrose is reserved for symptomatic, severe (<1.2), or refractory hypoglycaemia after dextrose gel and feed; this asymptomatic infant should have buccal gel first. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)
Glucagon is reserved for severe persistent hypoglycaemia where IV access is delayed; infants of diabetic mothers have depleted glycogen stores and respond unreliably. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

For asymptomatic at-risk neonatal hypoglycaemia in the first 48 hours, 40% buccal dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) plus feed is the preferred Australian first-line intervention, with BSL recheck in 30 minutes; this avoids separation and IV access. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia; ANZNN)

explanation.summary: HSP nephritis affects 20 to 50% of children with HSP and is the main determinant of long-term outcome. Most cases (isolated microscopic haematuria or low-grade proteinuria) resolve without specific treatment, but persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hypertension, or impaired GFR carry significant risk of progression to chronic kidney disease (about 5 to 10% develop ESKD over 20 years). Renal biopsy is indicated for nephrotic syndrome, persistent proteinuria after 4 weeks of UPCR >50 mg/mmol, raised creatinine, or hypertension. ISKDC grading by percentage crescents drives therapy: low grade (no crescents) receives ACE inhibitor; moderate (under 50%) receives oral prednisolone; severe (over 50% crescents) requires IV methylprednisolone, cyclophosphamide or MMF, and plasmapheresis in selected cases. All children with HSP need urinalysis surveillance for 6 months minimum.
key_points: HSP nephritis: main determinant of long-term outcome
Biopsy indication: nephrotic, persistent UPCR >50, raised Cr, HTN
ISKDC grade by crescents directs therapy intensity
ACE inhibitor adjunctively for proteinuria reduction
Surveillance urinalysis 6 months minimum after HSP
explanation.pearls: Crescent involvement of >50% of glomeruli on biopsy (ISKDC grade IV to V) in HSP nephritis carries about 25% risk of ESKD by 20 years and triggers aggressive immunosuppression including pulse methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide.

options.rationale: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia carries a high risk of progression and demands biopsy to grade severity, not watchful waiting. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases; KHA-CARI)
Empirical steroids without histology in nephrotic HSP may undertreat crescentic disease and overtreat mild lesions; biopsy guides immunosuppression intensity. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases)

HSP nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, or impaired GFR persisting beyond 4 weeks is an indication for renal biopsy to assess for crescents (ISKDC grading) and direct therapy intensity; isolated microscopic haematuria does not require biopsy. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases; RCH CPG: HSP)
ACE inhibitor is appropriate adjunct for ongoing proteinuria but does not replace biopsy and immunosuppression decision in nephrotic-range disease. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases)

Plasmapheresis and cyclophosphamide are reserved for biopsy-proven crescentic disease (typically >50% crescents) with rapidly progressive renal failure; this stable presentation requires histology first. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases)

explanation.summary: Neuroblastoma and Wilms tumour are the two commonest paediatric solid abdominal malignancies. Neuroblastoma (median age 2 years) arises from neural crest, typically adrenal but can be any sympathetic chain site; it crosses midline, encases vessels, and metastasises to bone marrow, cortical bone, orbits, skin, and liver, with pathognomonic raccoon eyes, opsoclonus-myoclonus, and Horner syndrome. Wilms tumour (median age 3 to 4) arises from kidney, displaces structures, rarely crosses midline, and metastasises to lung and liver; associated with WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann, and Denys-Drash syndromes. Urinary VMA and HVA are elevated in over 90% of neuroblastomas; staging includes MIBG and bilateral bone marrow biopsy; INRG risk stratification (age, MYCN amplification, ploidy, histology, stage) drives therapy intensity from observation through surgery, chemotherapy, autologous SCT, and anti-GD2 immunotherapy.
key_points: Neuroblastoma: neural crest, crosses midline, encases vessels, bone/marrow/orbit metastases
Wilms: renal, displaces, rarely crosses midline, lung/liver metastases
Neuroblastoma paraneoplastic: opsoclonus-myoclonus, racoon eyes, Horner
Urinary VMA/HVA elevated in >90% of neuroblastomas
INRG risk stratification drives treatment intensity
explanation.pearls: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome occurs in 2 to 3% of children with neuroblastoma, often signalling lower-stage tumour with paradoxically worse neurological outcome; immunotherapy with rituximab is increasingly used for the paraneoplastic component.

options.rationale: Abdominal mass is the classical presentation of BOTH Wilms tumour and neuroblastoma; it does not discriminate between them on its own. (Source: COG Neuroblastoma Risk Stratification)
Both Wilms (renin) and neuroblastoma (catecholamines) can cause hypertension; this feature alone does not discriminate. (Source: COG Neuroblastoma Risk Stratification)
Crossing the midline favours neuroblastoma but is not absolutely specific; vascular encasement also occurs in advanced Wilms. (Source: COG Neuroblastoma Risk Stratification)

Periorbital ecchymosis from orbital metastases, opsoclonus-myoclonus paraneoplastic syndrome, and lytic bone metastases are hallmark neuroblastoma features that do not occur with Wilms; metastasis to bone, marrow, orbit, and skin is typical of neuroblastoma stage M. (Source: COG Neuroblastoma Risk Stratification)

Urinary VMA and HVA are highly specific for neuroblastoma but they are a laboratory result rather than a clinical feature; the orbital and bone disease pattern separates the two at the bedside. (Source: COG Neuroblastoma Risk Stratification)

explanation.summary: PFAPA (Periodic Fever, Aphthous stomatitis, Pharyngitis, cervical Adenitis) is the commonest paediatric autoinflammatory syndrome, presenting between ages 2 and 5 with clockwork-regular febrile episodes lasting 3 to 6 days at 3 to 8 week intervals. Diagnosis is clinical after exclusion of monogenic periodic fevers (FMF, TRAPS, HIDS, CAPS) by genetic testing when family history suggests, and after exclusion of cyclic neutropenia by serial neutrophil counts. Pathognomonic feature is dramatic and rapid response to a single oral dose of prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg at fever onset, which aborts the episode within hours but may shorten intervals between episodes. Other options include cimetidine prophylaxis, colchicine, anakinra (refractory cases), or tonsillectomy (70 to 90% remission). Children grow out of PFAPA by adolescence in most cases. PFAPA does not cause amyloidosis or organ damage, unlike untreated FMF.
key_points: PFAPA: commonest paediatric autoinflammatory, ages 2-5
Clockwork fevers, exclude monogenic syndromes (FMF, TRAPS, HIDS, CAPS) genetically
Single oral prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg aborts episode within hours
Tonsillectomy curative in 70-90% if refractory
Resolves by adolescence in most cases without sequelae
explanation.pearls: Steroid response in PFAPA is so brisk and reproducible that resolution of fever within 4 hours of a single oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg dose is considered confirmatory of the diagnosis when other periodic fever syndromes have been excluded.

options.rationale: Colchicine is the treatment for familial Mediterranean fever which has been excluded genetically; PFAPA responds variably to colchicine but it is not first-line. (Source: Eurofever PFAPA Guideline)
Cimetidine has small case-series support for PFAPA prophylaxis but is not first-line; steroids at onset have the most robust evidence and immediate effect. (Source: Eurofever PFAPA Guideline)

Anakinra is reserved for refractory PFAPA or biopsy-proven monogenic syndromes (CAPS, HIDS); it is not first-line and is not appropriate before trial of oral steroids. (Source: Eurofever PFAPA Guideline)

Tonsillectomy is curative in 70 to 90% but is reserved for steroid-responsive PFAPA refractory to medical therapy or significantly affecting quality of life; trial of steroids comes first. (Source: Eurofever PFAPA Guideline)

PFAPA (Periodic Fever, Aphthous stomatitis, Pharyngitis, cervical Adenitis) responds dramatically to a single oral steroid dose at fever onset (response within hours); this is both diagnostic and therapeutic; first-line per Eurofever and Australian paediatric immunology practice. (Source: Eurofever PFAPA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Urea cycle disorders are the most common cause of severe hyperammonaemia in neonates presenting after the first 24 hours. The hallmark is respiratory alkalosis due to direct ammonia stimulation of the brainstem respiratory centre, distinguishing them from organic acidaemias which present with metabolic acidosis. OTC deficiency is the most common UCD and is X-linked. Emergency management requires cessation of protein, high caloric intake via IV dextrose, nitrogen scavenger therapy, and haemodialysis when ammonia exceeds 400 micromol/L.
key_points: Respiratory alkalosis with severe hyperammonaemia in a neonate strongly suggests a urea cycle disorder
Nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, phenylbutyrate) provide alternative pathways for nitrogen excretion bypassing the urea cycle
Haemodialysis is preferred over peritoneal dialysis or exchange transfusion for rapid ammonia clearance above 400 micromol/L
OTC deficiency is X-linked and the most common urea cycle disorder
explanation.pearls: Plasma amino acids showing elevated glutamine with low citrulline localise the defect to OTC or CPS1; urinary orotic acid is elevated in OTC deficiency but normal in CPS1 deficiency, providing definitive biochemical discrimination.

options.rationale: Ammonia >400 micromol/L with respiratory alkalosis (not metabolic acidosis) and normal anion gap is characteristic of a urea cycle disorder. Nitrogen scavenger therapy reduces ammonia via alternative nitrogen excretion pathways, and haemodialysis is the most effective clearance method at this critical level. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

Insulin-dextrose is used in organic acidaemias with ketoacidosis to promote anabolism. This infant has respiratory alkalosis with a normal anion gap, not metabolic acidosis, making organic acidaemia unlikely. (Source: ASIEM: Acute Metabolic Emergencies)

Carnitine supplementation is first-line for fatty acid oxidation disorders and secondary carnitine deficiency in organic acidaemias. It does not address the enzymatic defect in urea cycle disorders and will not lower ammonia at this critical level. (Source: ASIEM: Acute Metabolic Emergencies)

Exchange transfusion is inefficient at removing ammonia compared to haemodialysis. It does not provide the sustained clearance required when ammonia exceeds 400 micromol/L and delays definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

Biotin is specific treatment for biotinidase deficiency and holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency, which present with metabolic acidosis and organic aciduria rather than the respiratory alkalosis pattern seen here. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)
