explanation.summary: PPHN occurs when pulmonary vascular resistance fails to decrease after birth, causing right-to-left shunting and severe hypoxaemia. Meconium aspiration syndrome is a common cause. The oxygenation index (OI = MAP x FiO2 x 100 / PaO2) guides escalation: iNO is initiated when OI exceeds 25, and ECMO referral is considered when OI exceeds 40 despite iNO. A pre-ductal to post-ductal SpO2 gradient greater than 10% is characteristic.
key_points: Oxygenation index >25 is the threshold for initiating iNO in PPHN
ECMO referral is considered when OI exceeds 40 despite optimal medical management
Pre-ductal to post-ductal SpO2 difference >10% is characteristic of right-to-left ductal shunting
iNO provides selective pulmonary vasodilation without systemic hypotension
explanation.pearls: iNO should be weaned gradually once sustained improvement is achieved; abrupt discontinuation can cause rebound pulmonary hypertension with acute deterioration within minutes.

options.rationale: IV milrinone is a useful adjunct in PPHN for its inotropic and pulmonary vasodilatory properties, but it is not the first-line pulmonary vasodilator. Inhaled nitric oxide should be trialled first given the OI >25, as it provides selective pulmonary vasodilation without systemic hypotension. (Source: RCH CPG: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension)

With an OI of 28 and confirmed PPHN on echocardiography, inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) at 20 ppm is the first-line selective pulmonary vasodilator. ECMO referral is generally considered when OI exceeds 40 despite iNO, making iNO the appropriate next escalation step at this OI. (Source: RCH CPG: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension)

ECMO is generally considered when OI exceeds 40 despite optimal medical management including iNO. At an OI of 28, medical optimisation with iNO should be attempted first, as many neonates respond and avoid the significant risks of ECMO. (Source: ANZICS: Neonatal ECMO Guidelines)

IV prostacyclin (epoprostenol) causes non-selective vasodilation including systemic hypotension and is generally reserved as a second-line agent when iNO is unavailable or ineffective. Its systemic effects make it less suitable as first-line therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension)

De-escalating from HFOV to conventional ventilation in worsening PPHN is counterproductive. HFOV optimises lung recruitment and oxygenation. Permissive hypercapnia may worsen pulmonary vasoconstriction as acidosis exacerbates PPHN. (Source: RCH CPG: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Turner syndrome (45,X) affects approximately 1 in 2500 live-born females and presents with short stature, gonadal dysgenesis, and characteristic phenotypic features. Cardiovascular anomalies are the most clinically significant associated condition, with bicuspid aortic valve occurring in up to 30% and coarctation in up to 12%. Screening echocardiography and renal ultrasound are essential at diagnosis. Growth hormone therapy is indicated for short stature without requiring stimulation testing.
key_points: Echocardiography is the highest-priority investigation at Turner syndrome diagnosis due to 25-45% prevalence of cardiac anomalies
Bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta are the most common cardiac associations
Growth hormone therapy is approved for Turner syndrome without stimulation testing
Renal ultrasound, audiometry, thyroid function, and coeliac screening are all part of the standard workup
explanation.pearls: Four-limb blood pressures should be measured at every visit in Turner syndrome; a right arm to leg gradient greater than 20 mmHg suggests coarctation even when echocardiography appears normal, warranting cardiac MRI.

options.rationale: While pelvic ultrasound is part of the Turner syndrome workup, gonadal assessment is not urgent at age 7 as puberty has not yet commenced. Cardiac assessment takes priority given the risk of life-threatening structural anomalies such as bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

Growth hormone therapy in Turner syndrome is approved without the need for stimulation testing. Turner syndrome itself is an indication for GH therapy regardless of GH status. However, cardiac evaluation should precede initiation of any therapy. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

Cardiovascular anomalies occur in 25-45% of Turner syndrome patients. Bicuspid aortic valve (up to 30%) and coarctation of the aorta (up to 12%) are the most significant, carrying risks of aortic dissection and endocarditis. Echocardiography is the highest-priority investigation at diagnosis. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

Renal anomalies (horseshoe kidney, duplicated collecting systems) occur in approximately 30% of Turner syndrome patients. Renal ultrasound is important and should be performed, but cardiac screening takes priority given the potentially life-threatening nature of undetected cardiac anomalies. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

Hearing loss is common in Turner syndrome, affecting up to 60% of patients. While audiometry should be performed as part of the comprehensive workup, it is not the highest priority compared to cardiac screening for potentially life-threatening structural anomalies. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

explanation.summary: Exclusive enteral nutrition is the preferred first-line induction therapy for paediatric Crohn disease in Australian and European guidelines. It achieves remission rates comparable to corticosteroids (80-85%) while promoting mucosal healing, correcting nutritional deficiencies, and preserving linear growth. This is especially important in children with growth faltering and pubertal delay, where corticosteroid-related growth suppression is particularly harmful. EEN involves consuming a polymeric formula as the sole source of nutrition for 6-8 weeks, followed by gradual food reintroduction.
key_points: EEN is first-line induction therapy for paediatric Crohn disease with equivalent remission rates to corticosteroids
Polymeric formulas are as effective as elemental formulas and are better tolerated
EEN promotes mucosal healing and nutritional restoration without corticosteroid growth suppression
Anti-TNF therapy is reserved for refractory, severe, or fistulising disease
explanation.pearls: Faecal calprotectin above 250 microg/g has a sensitivity exceeding 90% for active inflammatory bowel disease in children; levels above 1000 microg/g correlate with endoscopically severe disease and can guide the decision to perform ileocolonoscopy.

options.rationale: While oral corticosteroids are effective for inducing remission in Crohn disease, they are associated with significant growth suppression in children, which is particularly concerning in this patient with growth faltering and pubertal delay. Exclusive enteral nutrition achieves equivalent remission rates with nutritional benefits. (Source: ESPGHAN: Paediatric Crohn Disease)

Azathioprine is an effective maintenance therapy for Crohn disease but has a slow onset of action (8-12 weeks) making it unsuitable as sole induction therapy. It is typically introduced alongside induction therapy with a plan for long-term maintenance. (Source: ESPGHAN: Paediatric Crohn Disease)

Anti-TNF therapy with infliximab is highly effective but is generally reserved for moderate-to-severe disease failing first-line therapy, fistulising disease, or growth failure refractory to nutritional therapy. First-line use in uncomplicated moderate paediatric Crohn disease is not standard practice. (Source: ESPGHAN: Paediatric Crohn Disease)

Exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) is the recommended first-line induction therapy for paediatric Crohn disease, achieving remission rates of 80-85%, equivalent to corticosteroids. EEN has additional benefits of promoting mucosal healing, correcting nutritional deficiencies, and supporting linear growth - critical advantages in this growth-faltering adolescent with pubertal delay. (Source: ESPGHAN: Paediatric Crohn Disease)

Mesalazine (5-ASA) has limited efficacy in Crohn disease, particularly for ileal and transmural inflammation. It is more effective in ulcerative colitis. It would not adequately address this patient's moderate disease activity and nutritional compromise. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by defects in the NADPH oxidase complex, impairing the neutrophil respiratory burst required to kill catalase-positive organisms. The X-linked form (gp91phox/CYBB mutations) accounts for approximately 65% of cases. The classic infection triad involves Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus species, and catalase-positive gram-negative organisms such as Serratia and Burkholderia. The DHR flow cytometry assay is the preferred diagnostic test, demonstrating absent or markedly reduced oxidative burst in affected neutrophils.
key_points: Recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Burkholderia) suggest CGD
Normal neutrophil counts with impaired killing distinguish CGD from neutropenia
DHR flow cytometry has replaced NBT as the standard diagnostic test
Prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and itraconazole significantly reduce infection frequency
explanation.pearls: Catalase-positive organisms are specifically virulent in CGD because they destroy their own hydrogen peroxide, removing the only residual source of reactive oxygen species that CGD neutrophils might otherwise utilise from bacterial metabolism.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Chronic Granulomatous Disease

options.rationale: STAT3 gain-of-function mutations cause early-onset autoimmune disease with lymphoproliferation, not the pattern of catalase-positive bacterial and fungal infections seen here. Hyper-IgE syndrome (STAT3 loss-of-function) causes recurrent staphylococcal infections but characteristically elevates IgE levels. (Source: ASCIA: Primary Immunodeficiency)

MBL deficiency predisposes to recurrent bacterial infections but not the deep-seated abscesses with catalase-positive organisms and invasive fungal disease characteristic of this presentation. Complement studies are already normal. (Source: ASCIA: Primary Immunodeficiency)

Lymphocyte proliferation assays assess T-cell function and are used to investigate combined immunodeficiencies. This child has normal lymphocyte subsets and a pattern of infections pointing to phagocyte dysfunction rather than lymphocyte deficiency. (Source: ASCIA: Primary Immunodeficiency)

Specific antibody deficiency presents with recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated organisms, not the deep-seated abscesses and invasive fungal infections seen here. Immunoglobulin levels are already normal. (Source: ASCIA: Primary Immunodeficiency)

The pattern of recurrent deep-seated infections with catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia) despite normal neutrophil counts is characteristic of chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). The DHR flow cytometry assay measures the neutrophil oxidative burst and has replaced the older nitroblue tetrazolium test as the standard diagnostic test for CGD. (Source: ASCIA: Primary Immunodeficiency)

explanation.summary: Incomplete or atypical Kawasaki disease presents with fewer than 4 of the 5 classic clinical features but is particularly common in infants under 12 months - the age group at highest risk for coronary complications. The AHA algorithm recommends treatment when a child has prolonged fever with 2-3 clinical features and supportive laboratory or echocardiographic findings. Key laboratory supports include CRP 30 mg/L or above, ESR 40 mm/hr or above, hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia, thrombocytosis after day 7, elevated ALT, and sterile pyuria. Any echocardiographic coronary abnormality in this context mandates treatment. IVIG within the first 10 days of illness reduces the incidence of coronary artery aneurysms from 25% to less than 5%.
key_points: Infants under 12 months are at highest risk for incomplete Kawasaki disease and coronary complications
Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed using supportive laboratory and echocardiographic criteria
IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion within 10 days of fever onset is the standard treatment
Sterile pyuria on urine microscopy is a supportive finding often overlooked in the workup
explanation.pearls: A coronary artery Z-score above +2.5 in any segment during a febrile illness in a child should prompt immediate consideration of Kawasaki disease regardless of how many classic clinical features are present - echocardiographic abnormalities mandate treatment.

options.rationale: While a viral illness is a reasonable initial consideration, 6 days of high fever with conjunctival injection, mucositis, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, sterile pyuria, and coronary artery dilation is not consistent with a simple viral illness. The echocardiographic abnormality confirms cardiac involvement consistent with Kawasaki disease. (Source: RCH CPG - Kawasaki Disease)

This infant meets criteria for incomplete Kawasaki disease: fever for 5 or more days with only 2 of 5 classic clinical features (conjunctival injection and lip changes), but with supportive laboratory findings (elevated CRP and ESR, leucocytosis, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, elevated ALT, sterile pyuria) and echocardiographic evidence of coronary involvement. IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days of fever onset significantly reduces coronary aneurysm risk. High-dose aspirin is given until afebrile for 48-72 hours, then low-dose aspirin 3-5 mg/kg/day. (Source: RCH CPG - Kawasaki Disease)

While occult bacteraemia is a consideration in a febrile infant, the combination of specific clinical features (conjunctival injection, mucositis), supportive laboratory findings, and coronary artery changes points to Kawasaki disease rather than bacterial infection. Blood cultures should be taken but empiric antibiotics do not address the vasculitic process. (Source: RCH CPG - Kawasaki Disease)

Waiting for full diagnostic criteria in suspected incomplete Kawasaki disease is inappropriate as it delays treatment and increases coronary aneurysm risk. The AHA algorithm for incomplete Kawasaki disease recommends treatment when supportive laboratory and echocardiographic findings are present. This is particularly important in infants under 12 months. (Source: AHA - Kawasaki Disease Guidelines)

Corticosteroids are not first-line treatment for Kawasaki disease. IVIG is the standard first-line treatment. Corticosteroids may be considered as adjunctive therapy in patients at high risk of IVIG resistance (e.g., Kobayashi score), but they do not replace IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG - Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Non-accidental injury must be considered when the injury pattern is inconsistent with the reported mechanism and the child's developmental stage. Key red flags include fractures in pre-mobile infants, bruising in non-ambulatory children, bruises on protected sites (ears, neck, trunk in non-mobile infants), multiple fractures of different ages, and inconsistent or changing histories. The medical workup includes skeletal survey, ophthalmological examination, and blood tests to exclude medical mimics. All Australian states and territories have mandatory reporting requirements for health professionals.
key_points: Femoral fractures in pre-mobile infants have a very high positive predictive value for NAI
Bruising on ears, neck, and trunk in non-ambulatory infants is highly suspicious for abuse
Skeletal survey is mandatory to identify occult fractures in suspected NAI
Investigations for medical causes must run concurrently with child protection involvement
explanation.pearls: The TEN-4-FACESp clinical decision rule for bruising identifies bruising to the Torso, Ears, Neck in children under 4 years, or any bruising in infants under 4 months, plus Frenulum, Angle of jaw, Cheeks, Eyelids, Subconjunctivae, and patterned bruises as high-risk indicators for abuse.

sources.label: RACP - Health Professionals and Child Protection

options.rationale: Discharging this infant without further investigation is unsafe. A spiral femoral fracture in a pre-mobile 5-month-old with no history of trauma and bruising to the ears raises very high suspicion for non-accidental injury. The child must be admitted for safety and further evaluation. (Source: RCH CPG - Child Abuse)

Spiral femoral fractures are not a normal consequence of rolling in a 5-month-old. Femoral fractures in children under 18 months who are not yet independently mobile carry a very high positive predictive value for non-accidental injury. The ear bruising adds further concern as ears are a protected site. (Source: RCH CPG - Child Abuse)

This presentation has multiple features highly concerning for non-accidental injury: femoral fracture in a pre-mobile infant with no history of trauma, and bruising to the ears (a protected site). Management includes: (1) admit for safety, (2) full skeletal survey to identify occult fractures, (3) blood tests including FBC, coagulation screen, calcium, phosphate, ALP, and vitamin D to exclude medical causes of fractures, (4) notify the hospital child protection unit, and (5) make a mandatory child protection report. (Source: RCH CPG - Child Abuse)

While osteogenesis imperfecta should be considered in the differential, genetic testing takes weeks and must not delay child protection assessment. The combination of fracture pattern, pre-mobile age, no history of trauma, and ear bruising mandates immediate child protection involvement. Investigations for medical causes occur concurrently. (Source: RCH CPG - Child Abuse)

While police involvement may be appropriate, the correct pathway is through the hospital child protection team who coordinate the multidisciplinary response including medical assessment, social work evaluation, police liaison, and mandatory reporting. The medical team's role is to ensure the child's safety, complete investigations, and report. (Source: RCH CPG - Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Congenital hyperinsulinism is the most common cause of persistent hypoglycaemia in neonates and infants. The critical sample during hypoglycaemia is diagnostic: inappropriately detectable insulin (above 2 mIU/L when glucose below 2.6 mmol/L), suppressed ketones and free fatty acids, and an elevated glucose requirement (above 8 mg/kg/min). Diazoxide is first-line treatment, with response predicting diffuse KATP channel disease (responsive) versus focal disease (often unresponsive). Diazoxide-unresponsive disease requires genetic testing and 18F-DOPA PET-CT to distinguish focal from diffuse disease, as focal lesions can be cured by limited pancreatectomy.
key_points: Glucose requirement above 8 mg/kg/min suggests hyperinsulinism as the cause of neonatal hypoglycaemia
The hypoketotic hypoglycaemia pattern is the hallmark of insulin-mediated hypoglycaemia
Diazoxide is first-line medical treatment acting on KATP channels to suppress insulin secretion
18F-DOPA PET-CT localises focal disease amenable to curative limited pancreatectomy
explanation.pearls: During a hypoglycaemic episode, a glucose rise of more than 1.5 mmol/L within 30 minutes of IM glucagon 0.5 mg confirms glycogen-replete hyperinsulinism - this glucagon stimulation test can be diagnostic even before the critical sample results return.

options.rationale: While increasing glucose delivery and glucagon infusion may temporarily manage hypoglycaemia, this does not address the underlying cause. The critical sample confirms hyperinsulinism (inappropriately elevated insulin during hypoglycaemia, suppressed ketones and free fatty acids). Specific medical treatment with diazoxide should be commenced. (Source: RCH CPG - Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

The cortisol level of 420 nmol/L during hypoglycaemia is an appropriate stress response, excluding cortisol deficiency as the cause. The critical sample clearly demonstrates hyperinsulinism - high insulin with suppressed counter-regulatory responses. Hydrocortisone is not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG - Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

Cornstarch supplementation is used in glycogen storage disorders and older children with hypoglycaemia, not as primary treatment for congenital hyperinsulinism in neonates. The severity of this infant's hypoglycaemia (requiring 12 mg/kg/min glucose) necessitates pharmacological treatment. (Source: RCH CPG - Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

The critical sample confirms congenital hyperinsulinism: inappropriately elevated insulin (42 mIU/L) during hypoglycaemia (glucose 1.4 mmol/L), with suppressed ketones and free fatty acids indicating insulin-mediated suppression of lipolysis and ketogenesis. Diazoxide is the first-line medical treatment - it opens KATP channels on beta cells to inhibit insulin secretion. Chlorothiazide is added to counteract fluid retention. Response to diazoxide guides further management including genetic testing. (Source: RCH CPG - Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

Surgery is reserved for congenital hyperinsulinism that is unresponsive to medical therapy (diazoxide-unresponsive disease). Medical management must be trialled first. Standard MRI cannot distinguish focal from diffuse disease - 18F-DOPA PET-CT is the specialised imaging modality used to localise focal lesions. (Source: BMJ Best Practice - Congenital Hyperinsulinism)

explanation.summary: Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (most commonly 21-hydroxylase deficiency) presents in the first 1-3 weeks of life with adrenal crisis in severe cases. The triad of ambiguous genitalia in a 46,XX infant, hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, and cortisol deficiency is diagnostic. The salt-wasting crisis occurs because both cortisol and aldosterone production are impaired. Life-threatening hyperkalaemia with ECG changes requires immediate calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilisation. IV hydrocortisone at stress doses provides both glucocorticoid replacement and, at high doses, sufficient mineralocorticoid activity until fludrocortisone can be started orally.
key_points: Salt-wasting CAH typically presents at days 7-14 of life when maternal steroid influence wanes
Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes requires immediate IV calcium gluconate before other interventions
IV hydrocortisone at stress doses provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid effect
17-hydroxyprogesterone should be drawn before hydrocortisone if possible but must not delay treatment
explanation.pearls: In 21-hydroxylase deficiency, 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels are typically massively elevated (above 300 nmol/L, often above 1000 nmol/L) - the newborn screening test detects this, but results may not be available before the salt-wasting crisis presents at 7-14 days of life.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group - CAH Guidelines
BMJ Best Practice - Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia

options.rationale: While fluid resuscitation, glucose correction, and hydrocortisone are all appropriate, this answer omits the critical emergency treatment of life-threatening hyperkalaemia. With potassium of 8.2 mmol/L and ECG changes (peaked T waves and widened QRS), hyperkalaemia must be addressed immediately to prevent cardiac arrest. Calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilisation is the immediate priority. (Source: RCH CPG - Adrenal Crisis)

While insulin-dextrose is a treatment for hyperkalaemia, it is not the first-line immediate intervention when ECG changes are present. IV calcium gluconate stabilises the cardiac membrane within minutes, providing immediate cardioprotection. This approach fails to address the underlying adrenal crisis with hydrocortisone. (Source: RCH CPG - Hyperkalaemia)

This infant is in acute adrenal crisis with shock, life-threatening hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, severe hyponatraemia, and hypoglycaemia. Oral supplementation is grossly inadequate. Waiting for newborn screening results before treating could be fatal. (Source: RCH CPG - Adrenal Crisis)

While sex determination is important in the longer-term management of ambiguous genitalia and suspected CAH, it has no bearing on the acute emergency management of adrenal crisis. This infant requires immediate resuscitation for shock, hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, and hypoglycaemia. (Source: RCH CPG - Adrenal Crisis)

This infant presents with a salt-wasting adrenal crisis from presumed congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency), evidenced by ambiguous genitalia, severe hyponatraemia, life-threatening hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock. Management priorities in order: (1) IV calcium gluconate for immediate cardiac membrane stabilisation given ECG changes, (2) IV normal saline bolus for volume resuscitation, (3) IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia, (4) IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat. Ideally, a 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is drawn before hydrocortisone but must not delay treatment. (Source: RCH CPG - Adrenal Crisis)

explanation.summary: Recurrent viral-induced wheeze in preschool children is common and poses a management challenge. The modified Asthma Predictive Index helps identify children likely to benefit from preventer therapy. Australian guidelines recommend a low-dose ICS trial when there are 3 or more wheezing episodes in 12 months with risk factors. The trial should last 8 weeks before assessing response, and ICS should be ceased if no clear benefit is demonstrated.
key_points: Modified API: 1 major (parental asthma, personal eczema) or 2 minor (allergic rhinitis, wheeze without colds, eosinophilia >4%)
Low-dose ICS via spacer with mask is first-line preventer for preschool recurrent wheeze
Trial duration of 8 weeks allows adequate assessment before deciding to continue or cease
Montelukast is second-line, reserved for children unable to use or failing ICS
explanation.pearls: A positive modified API in a preschool child with recurrent wheeze predicts a 77% chance of active asthma at school age, making an ICS trial appropriate even without formal spirometry or allergy testing.

options.rationale: Three or more episodes of viral-induced wheeze in 12 months with a positive modified Asthma Predictive Index (maternal asthma) meets the threshold for a low-dose ICS trial per Australian guidelines. An 8-week duration allows adequate response assessment. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

Three episodes in 6 months with a positive API exceeds the threshold for ongoing PRN management alone. Delaying a preventer trial risks further exacerbations and hospital presentations. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

Montelukast is second-line to low-dose ICS in young children with recurrent wheeze. Australian guidelines recommend ICS trial first due to superior efficacy evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Atopic status informs prognosis but does not need confirmation before initiating a preventer trial. The clinical history and positive API are sufficient to begin treatment. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

High-dose ICS is reserved for acute flares or step-up after failed low-dose trial. Starting at high dose in mild recurrent wheeze carries unnecessary adrenal suppression risk without additional benefit. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the most dangerous complication of nutritional rehabilitation in severe anorexia nervosa. It occurs due to a shift from catabolic to anabolic metabolism, driving intracellular movement of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium. Australian hospital protocols recommend starting at approximately 1200 kcal/day with prophylactic phosphate, thiamine, and electrolyte monitoring every 6-12 hours for the first 72 hours. Caloric intake is increased by 200-300 kcal every 2 days as tolerated.
key_points: High refeeding risk: BMI <14, intake <500 kcal/day for >5 days, baseline electrolyte derangement
Start 1200 kcal/day (approximately 20 kcal/kg current weight) with stepwise increases
Prophylactic phosphate (0.5-1 mmol/kg/day), thiamine 200-300 mg daily, and multivitamins
Monitor electrolytes 6-12 hourly for first 72 hours, then daily
explanation.pearls: Refeeding hypophosphataemia typically nadirs at 48-72 hours after nutritional reintroduction; a phosphate drop of >0.16 mmol/L from baseline within 72 hours mandates caloric restriction back to the starting level until phosphate stabilises.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Full caloric loading in a severely malnourished patient risks life-threatening refeeding syndrome with precipitous falls in phosphate, potassium, and magnesium. Gradual reintroduction is essential. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Australian guidelines recommend starting at approximately 1200 kcal/day (or 20 kcal/kg/day of current weight) in high-risk patients, with prophylactic phosphate and thiamine supplementation. This balances nutritional rehabilitation with refeeding risk mitigation. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Eating Disorders)

Starting at 2000 kcal/day is too aggressive in a severely malnourished adolescent with electrolyte derangement. This exceeds safe initial caloric targets and significantly increases refeeding risk. (Source: NICE: Eating Disorders)

TPN is rarely indicated in eating disorders and carries catheter-related risks. Enteral nutrition via oral or nasogastric route is preferred. TPN may paradoxically worsen refeeding risk due to rapid electrolyte shifts. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders)

While cautious, 500 kcal/day is excessively conservative and risks ongoing malnutrition. Australian protocols recommend 1200 kcal/day as the starting point for high-risk patients, with stepwise increases to goal over 5-7 days. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders)

explanation.summary: Paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea affects 1-5% of children, with peak prevalence at 2-8 years. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the most common cause. Australian guidelines recommend adenotonsillectomy as first-line for moderate-severe OSA (AHI >5) in otherwise healthy children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy. Medical therapy is reserved for mild OSA or as an adjunct. Post-operative PSG is recommended for children with severe OSA to confirm resolution.
key_points: Moderate-severe paediatric OSA: AHI >5 events/hour on polysomnography
Adenotonsillectomy cures OSA in approximately 75% of otherwise healthy children
Indications for post-operative monitoring: AHI >10, SpO2 nadir <80%, age <3, obesity, craniofacial anomaly
Behavioural symptoms (hyperactivity, enuresis) often resolve after successful surgery
explanation.pearls: Secondary enuresis in a child with snoring should prompt evaluation for OSA; the mechanism involves increased atrial natriuretic peptide secretion from negative intrathoracic pressure swings, causing nocturnal polyuria.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Medical therapy with intranasal corticosteroids and montelukast is appropriate for mild OSA (AHI 1-5). With moderate-severe OSA (AHI 8.2), significant desaturations, and growth faltering, surgery is first-line. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: CPAP is reserved for children who are not surgical candidates or who have residual OSA after adenotonsillectomy. In an otherwise healthy child with adenotonsillar hypertrophy, surgery is first-line. CPAP adherence in 5-year-olds is poor. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Adenotonsillectomy is first-line treatment for moderate-severe paediatric OSA with adenotonsillar hypertrophy. AHI >5, SpO2 nadir <90%, growth faltering, and behavioural symptoms all support surgical intervention. Post-operative monitoring is required given the severity. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Delaying treatment in a child with moderate-severe OSA, desaturations to 84%, and growth faltering is inappropriate. The PSG already provides clear surgical criteria. Repeat testing would delay necessary intervention. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

In paediatric OSA with grade 3+ tonsils and adenoid facies, both adenoid and tonsillar tissue contribute to obstruction. Adenotonsillectomy is more effective than tonsillectomy alone for resolution of OSA. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: While gastro-oesophageal reflux is common and usually benign in infants, bilious (green) vomiting is a critical red flag that mandates urgent investigation for malrotation with volvulus. Malrotation occurs in approximately 1 in 500 live births and can present with midgut volvulus at any age, most commonly in the first month of life. An upper GI contrast study is the gold standard investigation, and surgical correction (Ladd procedure) should not be delayed if volvulus is confirmed.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise
Upper GI contrast study is the gold standard for diagnosing malrotation
Red flags in infant vomiting: bilious, projectile, haematemesis, weight faltering, abdominal distension
Malrotation with volvulus requires emergency Ladd procedure to prevent bowel necrosis
explanation.pearls: The duodenojejunal flexure (ligament of Treitz) should sit to the left of the left pedicle of L2 on an upper GI contrast study; failure to reach this position has a sensitivity of 95% for malrotation even in the absence of active volvulus.

options.rationale: Empirical acid suppression without investigation is inappropriate when bilious vomiting is present. Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise and requires urgent imaging to exclude malrotation. (Source: RCH CPG: Vomiting in Infants)

pH-impedance testing quantifies reflux burden but does not address the critical concern of bilious vomiting. Malrotation must be excluded first as it is a time-critical surgical diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Vomiting in Infants)

Ultrasound is the investigation of choice for pyloric stenosis (non-bilious projectile vomiting) but is not the appropriate first-line test for suspected malrotation. The position of the SMA and SMV can be assessed but an upper GI contrast study is the gold standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Malrotation)

Bilious vomiting in a neonate or young infant mandates urgent exclusion of malrotation with volvulus. An upper GI contrast study is the gold standard, demonstrating the position of the duodenojejunal flexure. This should not be delayed for other investigations. (Source: RCH CPG: Malrotation)

Reassurance is inappropriate when red flags are present: bilious vomiting, weight faltering, and back-arching. These features mandate investigation rather than watchful waiting. Bilious vomiting alone warrants urgent surgical evaluation. (Source: NICE: GORD in Children)

explanation.summary: Chronic functional constipation with faecal impaction and overflow soiling is common in preschool children, particularly those with stool withholding behaviour. Management follows a two-phase approach: disimpaction first, then long-term maintenance. Australian guidelines recommend oral macrogol (polyethylene glycol 3350) for both phases. The disimpaction phase uses escalating doses over 3-7 days until soft stools are passed. Maintenance continues for at least 6 months with gradual weaning, supported by toileting behaviour programs and dietary modification.
key_points: Disimpaction before maintenance: macrogol escalating dose over 3-7 days
Avoid rectal interventions in children with withholding behaviour to prevent worsening anxiety
Maintenance macrogol for minimum 6 months with slow dose reduction
Soiling in a previously toilet-trained child with constipation is overflow incontinence, not behavioural
explanation.pearls: Macrogol (PEG 3350) disimpaction dosing in children: start at 1 sachet/day and escalate by 1 sachet per day to a maximum of 4 sachets/day for 1-5 year-olds (8 sachets/day for >5 years), continuing the peak dose until soft stools are achieved.

options.rationale: Dietary modification alone is insufficient when faecal impaction is present. Disimpaction must be achieved before maintenance therapy can be effective. Diet changes are important but adjunctive. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Lactulose is an osmotic laxative suitable for maintenance but has insufficient potency for disimpaction of an established faecal mass. Disimpaction requires high-dose macrogol before stepping down to maintenance. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Rectal interventions should be avoided in children with withholding behaviour as they can worsen anxiety and stool refusal. Oral disimpaction with macrogol is preferred. Stimulant laxatives alone are second-line for maintenance. (Source: NICE: Constipation in Children)

Abdominal X-ray is not required when clinical assessment confirms faecal impaction (palpable mass). Routine imaging adds radiation exposure without changing management and delays the start of treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Australian guidelines recommend oral macrogol (PEG 3350) escalating-dose disimpaction over 3-7 days, followed by long-term daily macrogol maintenance for at least 6 months. Oral disimpaction avoids the psychological harm of rectal interventions in a child with withholding behaviour. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Exclusive enteral nutrition is a unique first-line induction therapy in paediatric Crohn disease, distinguishing paediatric from adult management. EEN achieves mucosal healing in 60-80% of children while providing optimal nutrition for linear growth. It is delivered as a polymeric formula for 6-8 weeks with complete dietary exclusion. Following EEN induction, maintenance therapy with an immunomodulator (thiopurine or methotrexate) is typically introduced to sustain remission.
key_points: EEN is first-line induction for active paediatric luminal Crohn disease per international guidelines
EEN achieves equivalent remission rates to corticosteroids without growth-suppressive effects
Duration is 6-8 weeks of exclusive polymeric formula with gradual food reintroduction
Growth deceleration is a key indication to avoid corticosteroids in paediatric Crohn disease
explanation.pearls: Faecal calprotectin >800 mcg/g in a child with known Crohn disease has a >90% positive predictive value for endoscopically active disease and supports the decision to escalate therapy without repeating endoscopy.

options.rationale: Exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) for 6-8 weeks is the preferred first-line induction therapy for active luminal Crohn disease in paediatric patients per ECCO-ESPGHAN guidelines and Australian practice. EEN achieves mucosal healing rates comparable to corticosteroids while supporting growth. (Source: ECCO-ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Guidelines)

While corticosteroids induce remission, they impair linear growth and bone mineralisation - critical concerns in an adolescent with growth deceleration. EEN is preferred in paediatric Crohn disease for its equivalent efficacy and pro-growth effect. (Source: ECCO-ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Guidelines)

Azathioprine is an appropriate maintenance agent after remission induction but takes 8-12 weeks to reach therapeutic effect. It cannot achieve rapid remission induction and should be started concurrently with induction therapy rather than alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Mesalazine has limited efficacy in ileal and severe Crohn disease. Dose escalation is unlikely to achieve remission given the significant inflammatory burden (calprotectin >1800, elevated CRP, hypoalbuminaemia). Escalation of therapy class is needed. (Source: ECCO-ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Guidelines)

Anti-TNF therapy is effective but is typically reserved as second-line induction after EEN failure or for high-risk features (deep ulceration, extensive disease, perianal fistulae). In the absence of these, EEN should be trialled first. (Source: ECCO-ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia management has shifted from emergency surgery to a stabilise-first approach. Initial priorities are endotracheal intubation (avoiding bag-mask ventilation), gastric decompression with a large-bore orogastric tube, and gentle ventilation with permissive hypercapnoea (target pCO2 <65 mmHg). Pre-operative stabilisation over 24-48 hours allows assessment of pulmonary hypertension severity and optimisation before definitive repair.
key_points: Never use bag-mask ventilation in CDH: immediate intubation is required
Large-bore orogastric tube on continuous drainage is the critical first intervention
Gentle ventilation: peak inspiratory pressure <25 cmH2O, permissive hypercapnoea
Surgery is delayed until haemodynamic stability is achieved, typically 24-48 hours
explanation.pearls: Pre-ductal SpO2 target in CDH stabilisation is >85% (not >95%); aggressive ventilation to achieve normal saturations causes ventilator-induced lung injury to the hypoplastic lung and worsens pulmonary hypertension.

options.rationale: Immediate surgery is no longer recommended. Current evidence supports a period of pre-operative stabilisation to optimise gas exchange and haemodynamics before repair. Operating on an unstable neonate increases mortality. (Source: CDH EURO Consortium Guidelines)

A large-bore orogastric or nasogastric tube on continuous low-pressure suction is the critical first step to decompress the herniated bowel in the chest, preventing progressive mediastinal shift and allowing lung expansion. This should occur immediately after intubation. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: CDH)

Inhaled nitric oxide may be considered for refractory pulmonary hypertension but is not the immediate first intervention. Gastric decompression to reduce intrathoracic bowel distension is more urgent and may itself improve oxygenation by reducing mediastinal shift. (Source: CDH EURO Consortium Guidelines)

A chest drain is contraindicated in CDH as it risks injuring herniated abdominal viscera within the thorax. The absent breath sounds and dullness are from bowel, not air. Chest drain insertion before imaging confirmation would be dangerous. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: CDH)

Bag-mask ventilation is contraindicated in CDH as it insufflates the herniated stomach and bowel, worsening mediastinal compression. These infants should be intubated immediately and never receive bag-mask ventilation. (Source: ANZCOR Neonatal Resuscitation Guideline)

explanation.summary: Neonatal abstinence syndrome affects 55-94% of infants exposed to maternal opioids in utero. Australian guidelines use the modified Finnegan Neonatal Abstinence Scoring System to guide pharmacotherapy initiation. Non-pharmacological care is first-line, with pharmacotherapy (oral morphine) commenced when two or more consecutive scores reach 8 or above. Breastfeeding is supported in stable methadone-maintained mothers. The Eat Sleep Console (ESC) model is an alternative assessment tool increasingly used in Australian centres.
key_points: Pharmacotherapy threshold: 2 or more consecutive modified Finnegan scores of 8 or above
Oral morphine is first-line pharmacotherapy for opioid-related NAS in Australia
Breastfeeding is encouraged in stable methadone/buprenorphine-maintained mothers
NAS onset is typically 24-72 hours for heroin, and up to 7 days for methadone
explanation.pearls: Methadone-exposed neonates have a later onset of NAS (48-72 hours, peak at day 4-5) compared to heroin (24-48 hours) due to methadone's longer half-life; early discharge before day 5 risks missing the withdrawal peak.

sources.label: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Non-pharmacological measures (swaddling, reduced stimulation, demand feeding) should already be maximised. Three consecutive Finnegan scores of 9, 11, and 12 (two above the pharmacotherapy threshold of 8) indicate these measures are insufficient. Pharmacotherapy is indicated. (Source: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Phenobarbital is reserved for poly-substance withdrawal (especially benzodiazepines or alcohol) or as second-line adjunctive therapy for opioid NAS refractory to morphine. First-line treatment for opioid NAS is oral morphine. (Source: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Two or more consecutive modified Finnegan scores of 8 or above despite optimised non-pharmacological care meet the threshold for pharmacotherapy. Oral morphine is first-line for opioid NAS per Australian guidelines, using a symptom-based protocol with dose titration guided by ongoing scores. (Source: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Breastfeeding is encouraged in mothers on stable methadone maintenance who are not using illicit substances. Breast milk contains small amounts of methadone which may help ameliorate withdrawal. Cessation would remove this benefit and the bonding opportunity. (Source: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: NICU transfer is not indicated for NAS unless there are complications such as seizures, severe dehydration, or respiratory compromise. This infant can be managed in the special care nursery with pharmacotherapy and monitoring. (Source: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health: NAS Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Meconium ileus is the presenting feature of cystic fibrosis in 10-20% of affected neonates. The inspissated meconium obstructs the distal ileum, presenting with failure to pass meconium, abdominal distension, and bilious vomiting. Abdominal X-ray characteristically shows dilated bowel without air-fluid levels and a ground-glass appearance. A Gastrografin enema is both diagnostic (confirming microcolon) and therapeutic (relieving obstruction in simple cases). All neonates with meconium ileus require sweat chloride testing and CFTR gene analysis regardless of NBS results.
key_points: Meconium ileus: suspect CF in any neonate with failure to pass meconium and echogenic bowel history
Gastrografin enema is first-line: diagnostic and therapeutic in simple meconium ileus
Surgical intervention required for complicated meconium ileus (volvulus, atresia, perforation)
Sweat chloride test after 2 weeks of age and CFTR genotyping for definitive CF diagnosis
explanation.pearls: The absence of air-fluid levels on abdominal X-ray in a neonate with distal bowel obstruction is a hallmark of meconium ileus; the highly viscous meconium prevents layering of air and fluid, producing the characteristic ground-glass appearance instead.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Neonatal Bowel Obstruction

options.rationale: Rectal washouts may help in meconium plug syndrome or Hirschsprung disease but are ineffective for meconium ileus where the obstruction is in the distal ileum. The inspissated meconium requires a different approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Surgical Conditions)

The radiographic pattern of ground-glass opacity without air-fluid levels is characteristic of simple meconium ileus, not atresia. Atresia typically shows distinct air-fluid levels with a transition point. A contrast enema should be attempted before surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Surgical Conditions)

Watchful waiting is inappropriate in a neonate with progressive bilious vomiting and complete distal obstruction. The diagnosis needs confirmation and therapeutic intervention regardless of the NBS result, which takes several days. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Neonatal Bowel Obstruction)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Neonatal Bowel Obstruction

options.rationale: A Gastrografin (water-soluble contrast) enema is both diagnostic and potentially therapeutic in simple meconium ileus. The hyperosmolar contrast draws fluid into the bowel lumen, softening the inspissated meconium. It confirms the microcolon and may relieve the obstruction in up to 50% of cases, avoiding surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Surgical Conditions)

Oral N-acetylcysteine cannot be administered to a vomiting neonate with bowel obstruction. While NAC can thin inspissated meconium, it is used post-operatively or via the enema route, not orally in the setting of obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Surgical Conditions)

explanation.summary: Central precocious puberty is defined as onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls or age 9 in boys, driven by premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Investigation includes bone age, basal gonadotropins, sex steroids, pelvic ultrasound, and MRI brain. GnRH agonist therapy is indicated when there is progressive puberty with significantly advanced bone age, to halt pubertal progression and optimise adult height. Treatment is typically continued until the average age of puberty onset (approximately age 11 in girls).
key_points: Central precocious puberty: puberty before age 8 in girls, age 9 in boys, with central HPG axis activation
MRI brain is mandatory to exclude intracranial pathology (hypothalamic hamartoma, glioma)
GnRH agonist therapy preserves adult height by slowing epiphyseal fusion
Treatment is discontinued at approximately age 11 in girls, allowing normal pubertal progression
explanation.pearls: In girls with central precocious puberty, a bone age advancement of >2 years beyond chronological age predicts significant adult height compromise of 5-12 cm if untreated; GnRH agonist therapy recovers approximately 4-7 cm of predicted adult height when started before age 7.

options.rationale: Observation alone risks significant final height loss. With bone age advanced by 2.7 years and progressive Tanner staging, the growth plates will fuse prematurely. Active intervention is warranted to preserve adult height potential. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

Cyproterone acetate is an anti-androgen used in peripheral precocious puberty (e.g. congenital adrenal hyperplasia). In central precocious puberty, GnRH agonist therapy is the appropriate treatment as it suppresses the central HPG axis. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

A GnRH stimulation test is indicated when the diagnosis is uncertain (e.g. borderline LH, Tanner stage 2 only). This child has clear clinical and biochemical evidence of central precocious puberty: Tanner 3 breasts, advanced bone age, elevated oestradiol, uterine maturation, and normal MRI. Treatment can proceed. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

Aromatase inhibitors like letrozole are used in peripheral precocious puberty (McCune-Albright syndrome) or as adjunctive therapy. In central precocious puberty with a normal MRI, GnRH agonist is first-line as it suppresses the inappropriately activated HPG axis. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline)

GnRH agonist (e.g. leuprorelin depot) is the standard treatment for central precocious puberty in girls under 8 years. This child meets all criteria: progressive pubertal development before age 8, advanced bone age >2 years, and confirmed central activation with normal MRI. Treatment suppresses the HPG axis, halting puberty and preserving final adult height. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

explanation.summary: Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability, detected by newborn screening in approximately 1 in 3000-4000 births in Australia. Levothyroxine is commenced at 10-15 mcg/kg/day and adjusted to normalise TSH (<5 mIU/L) and maintain free T4 in the upper half of the reference range. Rapid normalisation within 2-4 weeks is critical for neurodevelopmental outcomes. Thyroid function tests are monitored at 2 weeks post-initiation, then every 1-2 months in the first year.
key_points: Treatment target: TSH <5 mIU/L and free T4 in upper half of reference range within 2-4 weeks
Starting dose: levothyroxine 10-15 mcg/kg/day, given as crushed tablet with small amount of water
Monitoring: TFTs at 2 weeks post-start, then every 1-2 months in first year, every 2-3 months until age 3
Trial off therapy only at age 3 years in selected uncertain cases
explanation.pearls: In congenital hypothyroidism, the free T4 often normalises before the TSH; dose adjustments should be guided by TSH until it is <5 mIU/L, even if the free T4 appears adequate or slightly elevated.

options.rationale: The TSH remains elevated at 18 mIU/L despite 2 weeks of therapy, indicating insufficient replacement. The target is normalisation of TSH to <5 mIU/L and free T4 in the upper half of the reference range within 2-4 weeks. The dose should be increased and rechecked in 2 weeks. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Congenital Hypothyroidism Guideline)

While free T4 has normalised, the TSH remains elevated, indicating ongoing hypothalamic-pituitary feedback that the peripheral thyroid hormone level is insufficient. Both TSH and free T4 must be optimised to prevent neurodevelopmental harm. (Source: APEG: Congenital Hypothyroidism Guideline)

Reducing the dose would be counterproductive with an elevated TSH. In congenital hypothyroidism, the target free T4 is the upper half of the reference range. A free T4 of 22 pmol/L is appropriate; the TSH needs to fall further. (Source: APEG: Congenital Hypothyroidism Guideline)

Thyroid scintigraphy can define the aetiology (athyreosis, ectopia, dyshormonogenesis) but does not change acute management. The priority is optimising thyroid replacement to protect neurodevelopment. Imaging can be arranged electively. (Source: APEG: Congenital Hypothyroidism Guideline)

Ceasing thyroid replacement in a confirmed case of congenital hypothyroidism risks severe neurodevelopmental harm. Trial off treatment is only considered at age 3 years in selected cases where the diagnosis is uncertain (e.g. ectopic gland with borderline results). (Source: APEG: Congenital Hypothyroidism Guideline)

explanation.summary: Short stature investigation follows a systematic approach: exclude chronic disease, assess growth velocity, check bone age, and measure IGF-1/IGFBP-3. When GH deficiency is suspected (low IGF-1, poor growth velocity, short stature), two pharmacological GH stimulation tests are required for confirmation per Australian PBS criteria. A peak GH response below 10 mIU/L (some centres use 7 mcg/L) on both tests confirms deficiency. MRI pituitary is then performed to identify structural abnormalities.
key_points: GH deficiency diagnosis requires two failed stimulation tests (peak GH <10 mIU/L)
Common stimulation agents: glucagon, arginine, clonidine, insulin (ITT rarely used in children)
Low IGF-1 + poor growth velocity + delayed bone age = strong suspicion for GH deficiency
PBS-funded GH therapy requires confirmed deficiency and height below 3rd centile
explanation.pearls: IGF-1 levels must be interpreted against age-specific and puberty-specific reference ranges; a prepubertal child with a low-normal IGF-1 for age may have GH deficiency masked by the physiologically lower prepubertal range.

options.rationale: MRI pituitary is indicated after confirming GH deficiency with stimulation testing. Imaging before biochemical confirmation would lead to unnecessary investigation in children with constitutional delay or other causes of low IGF-1. (Source: APEG: Growth Hormone Guidelines)

The combination of height below 3rd centile, poor growth velocity (<5 cm/year), low IGF-1, and significantly delayed bone age raises strong suspicion for growth hormone deficiency. Australian guidelines require two separate GH stimulation tests (e.g. glucagon + arginine or clonidine) to confirm the diagnosis before treatment. (Source: APEG: Growth Hormone Guidelines)

Karyotype is essential in short girls to exclude Turner syndrome, but this is a boy with proportionate short stature and no dysmorphic features. Karyotype would not be the priority investigation here; GH axis assessment is more appropriate. (Source: APEG: Growth Hormone Guidelines)

While the delayed bone age is consistent with constitutional delay, the low IGF-1 and poor growth velocity below 3.5 cm/year cannot be dismissed as constitutional delay alone. GH deficiency must be excluded with stimulation testing before attributing the pattern to constitutional delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

GH therapy requires confirmed GH deficiency via stimulation testing for PBS funding in Australia. An empirical trial without biochemical confirmation is not appropriate and would not be subsidised. Two failed stimulation tests are required. (Source: APEG: Growth Hormone Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Paediatric Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in children. Carbimazole (or methimazole) is the first-line antithyroid drug, with propylthiouracil contraindicated as initial therapy due to hepatotoxicity risk. Treatment typically involves 12-24 months of antithyroid drug therapy, with remission rates of 20-30% per treatment course. A beta-blocker is added for symptomatic relief during the initial weeks. Monitoring includes FBC for agranulocytosis and LFTs, with urgent FBC if sore throat or fever develops.
key_points: Carbimazole 0.5-1 mg/kg/day is first-line; PTU contraindicated in children under 16
Beta-blocker (propranolol) for symptomatic control until euthyroid
Agranulocytosis risk: urgent FBC if sore throat or fever on carbimazole
Remission rate 20-30% per 12-24 month treatment course
explanation.pearls: PTU carries a 1 in 2000-4000 risk of fatal hepatic failure in children, leading to an FDA black-box warning; carbimazole-related agranulocytosis (1 in 500) is serious but more predictable and usually reversible with drug cessation.

options.rationale: Propylthiouracil is contraindicated as first-line in children under 16 due to the risk of severe hepatotoxicity (including fatal hepatic failure). Australian and international guidelines mandate carbimazole as first-line in paediatric Graves disease. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

Radioactive iodine is generally avoided in children under 15 years due to radiation exposure concerns and is reserved for relapsed Graves disease after failed antithyroid drug therapy. Initial medical therapy should be trialled first. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

Carbimazole is first-line antithyroid therapy in paediatric Graves disease at 0.5-1 mg/kg/day (max 30 mg/day), combined with a beta-blocker (propranolol) for symptom control during the 4-6 weeks before carbimazole reaches full effect. PTU is contraindicated as first-line due to hepatotoxicity risk. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

Surgery is reserved for children who fail or are intolerant of antithyroid drug therapy, have large goitres with compressive symptoms, or have suspected malignancy. A trial of antithyroid medication for 12-24 months is the standard initial approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Beta-blockers provide symptomatic relief only and do not address the underlying hyperthyroidism. Without antithyroid drug therapy, the free T4 and T3 will remain dangerously elevated, risking thyroid storm. Beta-blockers are adjunctive, not sole therapy. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

explanation.summary: The Australian modification of the Jones criteria was developed by RHDAustralia to improve sensitivity for acute rheumatic fever diagnosis in high-risk populations, where delayed or missed diagnosis leads to worse cardiac outcomes. Key modifications include accepting monoarthritis and polyarthralgia as major criteria, and subclinical carditis (echocardiographic valvulitis without a clinical murmur) as a major criterion. These changes recognise that ARF presentations in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities are often atypical compared to standard teaching descriptions.
key_points: Australian modification elevates polyarthralgia and monoarthritis to major criteria in high-risk populations
High-risk: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, Pacific Islander peoples, and those in high-incidence settings
Subclinical carditis on echocardiography counts as a major criterion in the Australian modification
ASO titre >480 or anti-DNase B >340 confirms preceding streptococcal infection
explanation.pearls: In Australian high-risk populations, aseptic monoarthritis of a large joint with elevated inflammatory markers and streptococcal serology meets one major criterion - under standard Jones criteria this would only be a minor criterion, potentially causing a missed diagnosis.

sources.label: Heart Foundation of Australia: ARF and RHD Guideline

options.rationale: Under the standard Jones criteria, polyarthralgia (without frank arthritis) is a minor criterion. However, the Australian modification for high-risk populations accepts polyarthralgia as a major criterion, giving this child two major criteria. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF Diagnosis Guideline)

This child meets the diagnostic threshold. The Australian modification elevates polyarthralgia and monoarthritis to major criteria in high-risk populations (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, Pacific Islander peoples). Combined with carditis, this gives two major criteria. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF Diagnosis Guideline)

Fever is a minor criterion under all versions of the Jones criteria. He has polyarthralgia (not frank polyarthritis), which is major only under the Australian high-risk modification. Carditis plus polyarthralgia gives two major criteria. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF Diagnosis Guideline)

Under the Australian modification of the Jones criteria for high-risk populations, polyarthralgia (without joint swelling/effusion) is elevated to a major criterion. This child has echocardiographic carditis (major) and polyarthralgia (major under AU modification), meeting the diagnostic threshold of 2 major criteria with evidence of preceding streptococcal infection. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF Diagnosis Guideline)

The child has polyarthralgia (pain without swelling in multiple joints), not polyarthritis (swelling/effusion). Only the left knee and right ankle are swollen, and the description indicates tenderness in others without swelling. The distinction matters because the standard Jones criteria require frank arthritis for a major criterion. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF Diagnosis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin G is the cornerstone of rheumatic heart disease management. Australian guidelines stratify duration by disease severity: ARF without carditis requires minimum 10 years or until age 21; ARF with carditis but no persistent RHD until age 21 or 10 years minimum; ARF with persistent RHD until age 35 or minimum 10 years. Lifelong prophylaxis is considered for severe RHD or after valve surgery. Adherence to the 28-day injection schedule is critical as even brief gaps increase recurrence risk.
key_points: ARF with persistent RHD: benzathine penicillin G until age 35 or minimum 10 years
IM benzathine penicillin G every 28 days (not every 4 weeks, which drifts beyond 28 days)
Oral penicillin V is inferior and only used when injections are refused or contraindicated
Australia has the highest rates of ARF and RHD among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples globally
explanation.pearls: The 28-day injection interval is critical: extending to every 4 weeks (which accumulates a 1-2 day drift per month) has been associated with ARF recurrence in Australian registries - adherence support and recall systems are essential.

sources.label: Heart Foundation of Australia: ARF and RHD Guideline

options.rationale: Five years from the last episode is the minimum duration for ARF without carditis. This child had carditis with persistent valvular disease, which requires a longer duration of prophylaxis. (Source: RHDAustralia: Secondary Prophylaxis Guideline)

Age 18 is insufficient for a child with persistent RHD. Australian guidelines recommend prophylaxis until age 21 for ARF with carditis but no persistent RHD, or longer when RHD persists. (Source: RHDAustralia: Secondary Prophylaxis Guideline)

Two years is insufficient. Recurrence of ARF is highest in the first 5 years and ongoing streptococcal exposure continues to risk further cardiac damage. Minimum duration with any carditis is 10 years or until age 21. (Source: RHDAustralia: Secondary Prophylaxis Guideline)

IM benzathine penicillin G every 28 days is superior to oral penicillin V for secondary prophylaxis due to adherence and bioavailability advantages. Oral prophylaxis is only recommended when IM injections are refused or contraindicated. (Source: RHDAustralia: Secondary Prophylaxis Guideline)

For ARF with persistent rheumatic heart disease (even mild), Australian guidelines recommend secondary prophylaxis until age 35 or for a minimum of 10 years (whichever is longer). This child has persistent mild mitral regurgitation, classifying her as having ongoing RHD. Specialist review may extend this further. (Source: RHDAustralia: Secondary Prophylaxis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Frequent relapsing or steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome affects approximately 50% of children with steroid-sensitive disease. When steroid toxicity develops, steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agents are indicated. The Australian KHA-CARI guidelines recommend mycophenolate mofetil or calcineurin inhibitors (ciclosporin, tacrolimus) as first-line steroid-sparing agents. Cyclophosphamide is effective but reserved for refractory cases due to gonadotoxicity. Rituximab is emerging as a second-line option for difficult cases.
key_points: Frequent relapse: 4 or more relapses in 12 months or 2 or more in 6 months
Steroid-sparing agents: MMF or calcineurin inhibitors are first-line
Cyclophosphamide: cumulative dose limit of 168 mg/kg due to gonadotoxicity risk
Monitor growth, bone density, and metabolic complications of prolonged steroid use
explanation.pearls: Mycophenolate mofetil takes 4-6 weeks to reach therapeutic effect in nephrotic syndrome; overlapping prednisolone cover during this period prevents early relapse before MMF efficacy is established.

options.rationale: Frequent relapsing nephrotic syndrome (>4 relapses/year) or steroid dependence with significant steroid toxicity warrants a steroid-sparing agent. Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is a preferred first-line steroid-sparing agent in Australian paediatric nephrology practice due to a favourable side-effect profile compared to cyclophosphamide. (Source: KHA-CARI: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome)

Escalating steroid exposure in a child already showing significant steroid toxicity (Cushing features, growth failure) would worsen these complications. A steroid-sparing agent is needed rather than more prednisolone. (Source: KHA-CARI: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome)

ACE inhibitors reduce proteinuria but do not prevent relapses in steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome. They are adjunctive in steroid-resistant disease but do not replace immunosuppression in frequent relapsers. (Source: KDIGO: Glomerular Diseases)

Renal biopsy is indicated in steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, not steroid-sensitive frequent relapsing disease. This child responds to steroids with each relapse, and the management decision is about steroid-sparing, not reclassification. (Source: KHA-CARI: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome)

Cyclophosphamide is effective but carries gonadotoxicity risk (cumulative dose-dependent) and is reserved for cases failing first-line steroid-sparing agents. MMF or calcineurin inhibitors are preferred initially due to a better safety profile in children. (Source: KHA-CARI: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Migraine prophylaxis is indicated in children with frequent migraines (>2-4 per month), significant disability, or inadequate response to acute treatment. Australian guidelines recommend propranolol or pizotifen as first-line prophylactic agents. The prophylactic trial should last at least 3 months before efficacy is assessed. Lifestyle measures including sleep hygiene, regular meals, hydration, and identification of triggers are important adjuncts. Neuroimaging is reserved for atypical features or abnormal examination findings.
key_points: Prophylaxis indicated when migraines occur >2-4 per month with functional impairment
First-line prophylaxis in children: propranolol or pizotifen (Australian guidelines)
Trial duration: minimum 3 months before assessing efficacy
Neuroimaging not required for typical migraine with normal neurological examination
explanation.pearls: Propranolol for paediatric migraine prophylaxis should be avoided in children with asthma; pizotifen (a serotonin antagonist with weight gain as the main side effect) is the preferred alternative in asthmatic children.

options.rationale: Topiramate has evidence for migraine prophylaxis but carries cognitive side effects (word-finding difficulty, reduced processing speed) that may impact school performance. Propranolol or pizotifen are preferred first-line prophylactic agents in Australian paediatric practice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Propranolol is a first-line migraine prophylactic agent in children per Australian guidelines. It is well-tolerated with a favourable side-effect profile in this age group. The dose is started low and titrated. A 3-month trial is recommended to assess efficacy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

This child has a typical migraine presentation (unilateral, throbbing, nausea, photophobia, family history, normal examination). Neuroimaging is not required when the clinical picture is consistent with primary headache and the neurological examination is normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

Amitriptyline is used for migraine prophylaxis but is generally second-line in children due to anticholinergic side effects and the need for ECG monitoring. It is more commonly used in adolescents with comorbid tension-type headache or mood symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Sumatriptan is effective for acute migraine but this child needs prophylaxis given the frequency (3-4/month) and functional impact. Triptans address acute attacks but do not reduce attack frequency. Prophylaxis should be the priority here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome in children presents with ascending weakness following an antecedent infection (commonly Campylobacter jejuni or respiratory viruses). IVIG is first-line treatment in children who cannot walk independently. Respiratory monitoring with serial FVC measurements is critical as respiratory failure can develop rapidly. CSF shows albuminocytological dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count). Nerve conduction studies confirm the diagnosis and subtype (AIDP vs AMAN).
key_points: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days is first-line for paediatric GBS when unable to walk
FVC monitoring every 4-6 hours: intubation threshold is FVC <20 mL/kg
CSF: albuminocytological dissociation (protein >0.4 g/L, cells <10)
Autonomic instability (BP fluctuations, arrhythmias) requires cardiac monitoring
explanation.pearls: In paediatric GBS, the FVC decline can be rapid and unpredictable; a falling trend of FVC by >30% from baseline over 24 hours warrants ICU transfer even if the absolute value has not yet reached the intubation threshold of 20 mL/kg.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids have not shown benefit in GBS and are not recommended. Despite their role in other inflammatory neurological conditions, steroids do not improve outcomes in GBS and may worsen them. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Plasma exchange is an effective treatment for GBS but is technically challenging in children and requires central venous access and specialised equipment. IVIG is preferred in paediatric GBS as first-line due to easier administration and equivalent efficacy. (Source: RCH CPG: Guillain-Barre Syndrome)

IVIG at 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (total 2 g/kg) is first-line treatment for paediatric GBS when the child cannot walk independently. Forced vital capacity (FVC) monitoring is essential as respiratory failure occurs in up to 20% of children with GBS. FVC <20 mL/kg indicates need for intubation. (Source: RCH CPG: Guillain-Barre Syndrome)

This child cannot walk independently, which is the threshold for IVIG treatment in GBS. Observation alone risks progression to respiratory failure. Active immunomodulatory treatment should be commenced promptly alongside monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Guillain-Barre Syndrome)

The standard IVIG regimen for GBS is 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (total 2 g/kg), not a single large dose. The 5-day regimen has the best evidence for efficacy and is better tolerated with fewer infusion-related adverse effects. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Infantile spasms (West syndrome) is an epileptic encephalopathy characterised by the triad of flexor or extensor spasms, hypsarrhythmia on EEG, and developmental regression. Treatment is time-critical as delayed therapy worsens neurodevelopmental outcomes. First-line treatment depends on aetiology: vigabatrin for tuberous sclerosis-related spasms, and hormonal therapy (high-dose prednisolone or ACTH) for all other causes. The treatment lag from symptom onset to initiation of effective therapy is the strongest modifiable predictor of developmental outcome.
key_points: Hypsarrhythmia + flexor/extensor spasms + developmental regression = West syndrome
Vigabatrin first-line ONLY for tuberous sclerosis-related infantile spasms
Hormonal therapy (high-dose prednisolone or ACTH) is first-line for non-TSC spasms
Treatment lag of >4 weeks from onset significantly worsens neurodevelopmental outcome
explanation.pearls: The ICISS trial showed that adding vigabatrin to hormonal therapy (combination therapy) achieved higher spasm cessation rates (72%) than hormonal therapy alone (57%) at 2 weeks, supporting combination as an emerging standard of care.

options.rationale: Sodium valproate is not first-line for infantile spasms. It has inferior spasm cessation rates compared to hormonal therapy (ACTH or prednisolone) and vigabatrin. Early effective treatment is critical for neurodevelopmental outcomes. (Source: Epilepsy Foundation: Infantile Spasms Guidelines)

Vigabatrin is first-line specifically for infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis complex. This child has no clinical or MRI features of TSC. For non-TSC infantile spasms, hormonal therapy (ACTH or high-dose prednisolone) is first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Spasms)

Levetiracetam is a broad-spectrum anticonvulsant but has poor evidence for infantile spasms specifically. The hypsarrhythmia pattern and flexor spasms require targeted therapy (hormonal or vigabatrin) rather than a general anticonvulsant approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Spasms)

For infantile spasms without tuberous sclerosis, hormonal therapy is first-line. Australian practice uses high-dose oral prednisolone (or ACTH) as first-line. The ICISS trial demonstrated high-dose prednisolone has equivalent spasm cessation rates to ACTH and is preferred due to oral administration. Treatment is urgent to limit hypsarrhythmia-related developmental regression. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Spasms)

Epilepsy surgery is considered for infantile spasms with a focal structural lesion on MRI that is potentially resectable. This child has a normal MRI, making surgery inappropriate. Medical therapy is indicated first. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Spasms)

explanation.summary: Acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death in sickle cell disease. It is defined as a new pulmonary infiltrate on CXR with at least one of: fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxia. Management includes supplemental oxygen, antibiotics (covering atypical organisms), analgesia (avoiding over-sedation), incentive spirometry, and transfusion. Simple transfusion is indicated when Hb is below baseline; exchange transfusion is reserved for severe ACS with Hb near baseline or rapidly deteriorating gas exchange despite simple transfusion.
key_points: ACS diagnosis: new CXR infiltrate + fever or respiratory symptoms or hypoxia in sickle cell disease
Simple transfusion when Hb is below baseline; target Hb 90-100 g/L (never >100 g/L to avoid hyperviscosity)
Exchange transfusion for severe/deteriorating ACS or when Hb is near baseline (>90 g/L)
Antibiotics must cover atypical organisms (macrolide + beta-lactam)
explanation.pearls: In ACS, a low reticulocyte count (<2%) in the context of a falling Hb suggests aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19 co-infection) superimposed on ACS, which mandates urgent transfusion as the bone marrow is unable to compensate for the acute haemolysis.

sources.label: British Society for Haematology: Sickle Cell

options.rationale: Broad-spectrum antibiotics are important but do not address the rapidly falling Hb and hypoxia. The primary intervention needed is to reduce HbS percentage and improve oxygen delivery. Antibiotics should be given alongside the definitive treatment. (Source: HSANZ: Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines)

Supplemental oxygen is important but does not address the underlying pathology of HbS polymerisation and progressive sickling. With dropping Hb, bilateral infiltrates, and hypoxia on 6 L, the child needs transfusion to reduce HbS concentration. (Source: HSANZ: Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines)

Corticosteroids in acute chest syndrome are controversial. While some studies show reduced length of stay, rebound vaso-occlusive crises occur frequently after cessation. They are not recommended as primary therapy and do not substitute for transfusion. (Source: British Society for Haematology: Sickle Cell)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology: Sickle Cell

options.rationale: Automated red cell exchange (erythrocytapheresis) is indicated for severe or rapidly deteriorating ACS, but simple top-up transfusion should be attempted first when Hb is significantly below baseline. Exchange transfusion is reserved for Hb >90 g/L where simple transfusion would cause hyperviscosity. (Source: HSANZ: Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines)

With Hb dropped to 62 g/L (below baseline of 80), worsening hypoxia, and bilateral infiltrates, urgent simple transfusion is indicated. The target is Hb 90-100 g/L (not >100 to avoid hyperviscosity). Simple transfusion is appropriate as the Hb is well below baseline. Phenotyped, sickle-negative, crossmatched blood should be used. (Source: HSANZ: Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Distinguishing beta-thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency anaemia is a common paediatric challenge.
